Whenever Muhammad had a personal wish, a verse making it lawful for him came down at once. The list: The limit on wives: While Muslim men were limited to at most four wives (Qur’an 4:3), Muhammad was exempt from this limit. Women who offered themselves to him freely were also made lawful to him, with the words “for you alone” (Qur’an 33:50). His wives’ future: After Muhammad’s death, his wives were not allowed to marry any other man (Qur’an 33:53). A share of the wealth: A fifth of the spoils of war was set aside directly for God and the Prophet (Qur’an 8:41). Total authority: In Medina all political, military and religious power was gathered in his hands; those who criticized or mocked him were eliminated. Women, wealth, power and protection from criticism: Islam’s own sources describe the opposite of “he gained nothing”.
Muhammad as an Example: The adopted son’s wife

Muhammad’s adopted son Zayd was married to Zaynab bint Jahsh. When Zayd divorced his wife, Muhammad married Zaynab. Since Arab society at the time regarded an adopted son’s wife as a true daughter-in-law, this caused a great outcry. The Qur’an answered with this verse: “So when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you, so that there be no difficulty for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons” (Qur’an 33:37). The same verse also says that in this matter Muhammad hid certain things within himself, fearing what people would say. After this, the Qur’an abolished adoption altogether: adopted sons would not count as true sons and would be called by the names of their biological fathers (Qur’an 33:4-5). And a verse that follows says, “Muhammad is not the father of any of your men” (Qur’an 33:40). In the end, a divine rule was introduced on the grounds that believers must be free to marry the former wives of their adopted sons. But right afterwards adoption was abolished, so that no other believer could ever make use of this rule. And the only person who benefited from the arrangement was, once again, Muhammad himself.
Muhammad as an Example: Permission to break an oath

According to the report in Nasa’i, after a reaction from Aisha and Hafsa, Muhammad declared his slave woman forbidden to himself. Then Qur’an 66:1-2 came down, allowing him to break his oath (Nasa’i 3959). Bukhari 4912, however, ties the event to an oath about a honey drink. Whatever the background, God provided a way to expiate the oath. And in Qur’an 66:5 the wives were threatened with divorce and with being replaced by better ones. Muhammad really was persecuted in Mecca and really did flee to Medina. But sincerity doesn’t make someone right. The apostles, by contrast, bore witness to Christ’s resurrection without gaining political power, spoils or slave women, and gave their lives for it.

Bukhari tells of Muhammad’s first experience in the cave of Hira as Aisha reported it. The being says to him, “Read!” Muhammad replies, “I cannot read.” The being seizes him and squeezes him until he has no strength left to bear it, then lets him go. This happens three times. Muhammad returns home trembling with fear and says, “Cover me.” As he tells his wife Khadija what he went through, he says, “I feared for myself” (Bukhari 3). According to Ibn Ishaq’s biography of the prophet, Muhammad’s first reaction to this event was this: of all God’s creatures, the ones he hated most were poets and the possessed, and he feared he had become one of them. So he thought of climbing to the top of the mountain and throwing himself down. Bukhari, too, reports that during the period when revelation stopped, Muhammad set out again and again to throw himself from the mountains (Bukhari 6982). The first person to suspect a dark power was not some outside critic. It was Muhammad. And those who convinced him that what came to him was an angel were his wife Khadija and her Christian relative Waraqa ibn Nawfal. Some Muslim apologists compare this event to the prophet Daniel being shaken before Gabriel. Put them side by side: when Gabriel approaches, Daniel falls on his face, and Gabriel touches him and raises him to his feet (Daniel 8:17-18). In another vision, when Daniel loses his strength, he is again touched, given strength and told: “O man greatly beloved, fear not, peace be with you; be strong” (Daniel 10:10-19). Gabriel spoke to both Zechariah and Mary with the same reassurance: “Do not be afraid” (Luke 1:13; 1:30). Likewise, when the risen Jesus appeared to John, and John fell at His feet as though dead, Jesus laid His right hand on him and said, “Fear not, I am the first and the last” (Revelation 1:17). The angel in the Bible lifts up the frightened man, gives him strength and wishes him peace. The being at Hira, however, squeezes a terrified man three times until he is breathless, and brings him to the brink of suicide. These are not the same Gabriel. The way revelation came followed a similar pattern in later years. Muhammad said revelation sometimes came “like the ringing of a bell”, and that this was the hardest. Aisha reports that even in freezing cold, sweat poured from his forehead when revelation came (Bukhari 2). Because those around him thought he had lost his mind, the Qur’an had to declare again and again, “You are not mad”, “Your companion is not insane” (Qur’an 68:2; 52:29; 81:22).
What Happened at Hira?: The Satanic verses

The first generation of Muslim historians (Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari and Ibn Sa’d) report that Muhammad once spoke words praising al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat, the idols of Mecca. Muhammad later said these words had been put into his mind by Satan. The Qur’an itself accepts that Satan can interfere with a prophet’s wishes and recitation (Qur’an 22:52; see Qur’an 53:19-23). The first Muslim generations reported this event openly, but scholars of later centuries, uncomfortable with it, chose to reject it. Once you accept that Satan spoke through the prophet’s mouth even once, there is no way to be sure how often it happened. The Bible is clear on this. The best-known verse Muslims claim points to Muhammad is Deuteronomy 18:18: “I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brethren.” But two verses later the same text gives this warning: “But the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name which I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that same prophet shall die” (Deuteronomy 18:20). By the Torah of Moses, anyone who speaks in praise of idols like al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat is a false prophet.
What Happened at Hira?: The bewitched prophet

According to a report in Bukhari, a man named Labid ibn al-A’sam cast a spell on Muhammad. While under its effect, Muhammad for a time imagined he had done things he had not actually done (Bukhari 5763). If a man couldn’t trust his own memory for a time, how far can we trust the messages he said came from God?
What Happened at Hira?: The aorta

The Qur’an itself says what will happen to one who invents words in God’s name: “And if he had invented against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut his aorta.” Qur’an 69:44-46 At Khaybar, Muhammad had eaten from the lamb that a Jewish woman had poisoned and served to him (Bukhari 3169). According to Bukhari, on his deathbed he said to Aisha: “O Aisha! I still feel the pain of the food I ate at Khaybar. At this moment I feel as if my aorta is being cut by that poison.” Bukhari 4428 The Qur’an’s “al-watin” (Qur’an 69:46) and the hadith’s “al-abhar” (Bukhari 4428) are two different words that Arab linguists use for the main artery leaving the heart (the aorta). The Qur’an clearly stated that a false prophet who spoke invented words would have his aorta cut; and on his deathbed Muhammad described his own end as the severing of that same artery. We did not set this standard; the Qur’an itself did.
What Happened at Hira?: The Lamb of God

John the Baptist pointed to Jesus and said: “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29). According to the Bible, the father of lies is Satan (John 8:44), and false prophecy is his work too. The Son of God came into the world to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8). And in the Book of Revelation, the Lamb defeats all the powers that make war on Him together with the false prophet (Revelation 17:14; 19:20). The book says that whoever invents words in God’s name will have his aorta cut; its prophet died poisoned by the meat of a lamb. Just as the Lamb takes away the sin of the world, He also destroys false prophecy and the Satan behind it. Part III
Who Is the Lord of the Kaaba?: Father or master?

Islam claims to have restored the pure monotheism (tawhid) of Abraham. Yet Christianity is fully monotheistic too: God is one, and He reveals Himself as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The real, fundamental difference lies not in monotheism but in who God is. According to the Bible, the God of Abraham is a Father; the god of the Qur’an is no one’s father. “There is no one in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a slave.” Qur’an 19:93 The Qur’an rejects the claim of Jews and Christians, “We are the children of Allah”, and asks, “Then why does He punish you for your sins?” (Qur’an 5:18). The Bible says exactly the opposite: “The Lord disciplines him whom he loves”; being disciplined is the proof that you are His child (Hebrews 12:6-8). God told Moses, “Israel is my first-born son” (Exodus 4:22). Jesus teaches us to pray “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matthew 6:9). And Paul says, “You are no longer a slave but a son” (Galatians 4:7). This isn’t the same God seen from another angle. It’s a different idea of God altogether. The word “Islam” means “submission”. The Qur’an asks for this submission to be shown to Muhammad: “He who obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah” (Qur’an 4:80). In the Gospel, however, there is someone else who wants people to bow down to him: Satan (Matthew 4:8-9). Christ, by contrast, gives this assurance: “If the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36).
Who Is the Lord of the Kaaba?: Hubal, the idol of the Kaaba

Islam’s own classical sources tell the story. According to Ibn Hisham and Ibn Kathir, the Meccan leader Amr ibn Luhayy made a journey to the old land of Moab. There he saw a people worshipping idols and asked what they were doing; he was told, “We ask them for rain, and they send us rain.” Amr asked for an idol of his own, and they gave him Hubal. Amr brought this idol back and set it up at the Kaaba. The Muslim scholar Martin Lings also confirms that Hubal was the chief idol of Mecca. Even Karen Armstrong, known for her sympathy toward Islam, grants that in Muhammad’s time the Kaaba was officially dedicated to Hubal. Moab, where Hubal came from, was one of the main centers of Baal worship in the Bible (Numbers 25:1-3), and like Baal, Hubal was begged for rain. According to the Qur’an, the Meccans before Muhammad also acknowledged Allah as the creator (Qur’an 29:61). So “Allah” was not a new name brought by Muhammad: the pagan Meccans already used it while Hubal stood in the Kaaba. Yet there is not a single pre-Islamic historical record confirming that Abraham or Ishmael ever went to Mecca. The Bible states plainly that Ishmael lived in the wilderness of Paran, hundreds of miles from Mecca (Genesis 21:21).
Hubal, the idol of the Kaaba
Who Is the Lord of the Kaaba?: Traces that remain today

The Black Stone: Kissing the Black Stone, Umar said: “I know that you are a stone; you can neither harm nor benefit anyone. Had I not seen the Messenger of Allah kissing you, I would never have kissed you” (Bukhari 1597). Human sacrifice: Muhammad’s grandfather Abd al-Muttalib had vowed to sacrifice one of his sons at the Kaaba. The divining arrow, cast before Hubal, fell on Abdullah, Muhammad’s father. Abdullah was saved only by advice that a female soothsayer received from her jinn. In the Bible’s account, by contrast, the God of Abraham firmly stopped a human sacrifice (Genesis 22:12). In saying all this we keep one thing in mind: Muslims are not our enemies. They are people we long to see find the truth. Our fight is with the error, not with them. Part IV
Objections Against Christianity: “But the Old Testament is full of violence too”

It comes up in almost every debate. Read the texts and the difference is obvious: A land with fixed borders: God did not send Israel to war against all the nations of the world; He gave it a piece of land with clearly drawn borders (Numbers 34:1-12). He even strictly forbade touching the lands of the neighboring peoples of Edom, Moab and Ammon: “do not contend with them; for I will not give you any of their land, no, not so much as for the sole of the foot to tread on” (Deuteronomy 2:4-5, 9, 19). A historical verdict: God did not give that land to Abraham’s descendants at once; He waited four hundred years, saying, “the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete” (Genesis 15:16). The wars in Canaan carried out a divine judgment that had been held back for centuries. They came not from Israel’s righteousness, but from the moral collapse of those nations (Deuteronomy 9:4-5). A finished process: These wars took place at a particular moment in history, in a particular place, and they ended. Today no Christian is commanded to fight on the basis of these texts. The command the Gospel gives to Christ’s community is to go and make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19). The Qur’an, by contrast, commands fighting Jews and Christians, not in response to an attack but simply because they do not believe, until they submit and pay the jizya (Qur’an 9:29). It sets the goal of the fighting as “until there is no more oppression and discord, and religion is wholly for Allah” (Qur’an 8:39). Muhammad, too, says he was commanded to fight people until they believe (Bukhari 25). These commands have no limit in time or place. So while the Old Testament records a judgment carried out in the past, the Qur’an lays out an ongoing program. Compare family law too. The Torah forbids a woman who divorced and married another man to return to her first husband, and calls this “an abomination before the LORD” (Deuteronomy 24:4). The Qur’an, however, requires a woman divorced three times to marry another man first before she can return to her first husband (Qur’an 2:230). Muhammad also requires that this second marriage be actually consummated (Bukhari 5260). So what the Torah rejects, the Qur’an presents as a precondition. This is yet another contradiction in a text that claims to confirm the earlier revelations.
“But the Old Testament is full of violence too”
Objections Against Christianity: “The Bible is full of contradictions”

One of the methods Muslim apologists use most often is to present a list of supposed “contradictions” in the Bible. David Wood and Avery Austin answer these lists as a whole. Muhammad confirmed these texts, with all their nuances and differences, as the word of God valid in his own day. Every alleged “contradiction” was also present in the copies available in the seventh century. This leaves two possibilities: either Muhammad did not know about these differences and confirmed texts whose content he did not know, or he knew and gave his approval anyway. Either way, anyone who thinks he has refuted the Bible has really refuted Muhammad’s testimony as a prophet. Such an argument might pull someone away from the Bible, but it can never pull them toward Islam, because Muhammad himself vouched for these texts. Besides, most of the claims on these lists are either statements torn from their context or historical copying errors by scribes. For example: in the Hebrew text, Ahaziah’s age when he came to the throne is given as twenty-two in 2 Kings 8:26 and as forty-two in 2 Chronicles 22:2. Since in ancient Hebrew numbers were written with letters, confusing two similar letters produced this kind of copying difference. Some ancient translations, such as the Syriac, even give twenty-two in the second passage. All ancient texts copied by hand have technical differences of this kind; the same is true of the earliest copies of the Qur’an. What really matters is that, thanks to the wealth of manuscripts, such scribal errors can be easily identified. None of them can change who Jesus Christ is, what He taught, or His death on the cross and His resurrection.

The apostle Paul, who wrote a large part of the New Testament, is one of the names Muslim apologists target most often. The claim is that Jesus’s real followers were monotheistic Muslims, and that Paul later appeared and distorted the faith. The Qur’an rules this out too. According to the Qur’an, Jesus’s disciples said, “We are the helpers of Allah; we have believed in Allah, so bear witness that we are Muslims” (Qur’an 3:52). And God made this promise to Jesus: “I will make those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection” (Qur’an 3:55). The Qur’an also confirms that this promise was fulfilled in history: “A faction of the Children of Israel believed and a faction disbelieved. So We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant” (Qur’an 61:14). So which followers of Jesus actually prevailed in history? They are the Church community that read Paul’s letters, proclaimed Jesus as the Son of God, and preached His death on the cross and His resurrection. A separate, “Muslim” community of Jesus awaiting Muhammad’s coming never held sway in history; not even a historical trace of such a group has been found. If Paul really defeated Jesus’s own disciples and corrupted their teaching, two unavoidable conclusions follow: either God failed to keep His promise in the Qur’an, or Paul proved stronger than God’s will. The only consistent answer: Paul was himself part of the very community that God supported and made to prevail. In one of his letters Paul records that the apostle James the Less, Peter and John gave him “the right hand of fellowship” (Galatians 2:9). And the Church has always held that Paul was martyred in Rome, together with the apostle Peter, for his witness to Christ. In the end

This page wasn’t written against Muslims. It was written for them. We speak plainly not to belittle anyone, but because Christ loves Muslims as much as anyone else. Vague, careful words don’t carry the truth to a Muslim; they just leave him more sure of his own faith. The most respectful thing we can do is take his sources seriously and say what they say. The Bible teaches us both to be “wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16) and to destroy every thought raised up against the knowledge of God (2 Corinthians 10:5). Experience says the same: while the walls Islam builds in the mind are standing, the Trinity, the Son of God and the cross make no sense to a Muslim. Once they come down, it starts to make sense. Many Muslims are already questioning them. The hadith and the commentaries are a search away. Imams hold conferences about young Muslims doubting and leaving. And across the Muslim world, people tell of seeing Jesus Christ in a dream, calling them out of darkness into light. One of these people was Nabeel Qureshi. He grew up a devout Muslim and for years debated faith with his friend David Wood. But when he examined his own sources for himself, he saw that the stories he had been taught were not in them. In a time of deep doubt he asked God for guidance. In a dream he saw himself standing outside a narrow door, with a banquet being prepared inside. Later he read the same scene in the Gospel: “Strive to enter by the narrow door” (Luke 13:24). In the end he came to faith in Christ and told this journey in his book Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus. If you are a Muslim and you’ve read this far, check the sources yourself. Read Bukhari, Muslim and the Qur’an; then read the Gospel. Jesus says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). If you have questions, write to us, or walk into the nearest Catholic church and ask for the priest. And know this: every day, at every Mass, Catholics pray for you, for every one of you. God bless you.

The whole page in plain words. The Qur’an calls the Torah and the Gospel God’s word, but it disagrees with them. If they are true, the Qur’an is wrong. If they were changed, the Qur’an is wrong to call them God’s word. Islam says the Qur’an was kept perfect, letter for letter. Islam’s own early sources say parts were lost or added later. The Qur’an contains mistakes, and it doesn’t seem to know what the Gospel it praises actually says. Muhammad is called the perfect example, but Islam’s own sources record things about his life that are hard to follow as an example. Muhammad’s first meeting with the spirit in the cave of Hira was violent and frightening. Islam’s own sources raise hard questions about where his message came from. The main rituals of the pilgrimage to Mecca were already practiced by pagan Arabs before Islam. The usual objections to Christianity don’t hold up. The wars in the Old Testament were limited to one place and time; the Qur’an’s command to fight (9:29) has no such limit. Muslims already honor Jesus as a great prophet. The Gospel invites you to meet Him as He really is: God with us.

Patron of Lost Things, Doctor of the Church · 1195-1231 Anthony was born in Lisbon and christened Fernando. He first joined the Augustinian canons, but in 1220 he saw the bodies of five Franciscan missionaries who had been martyred in Morocco being brought back to Portugal. It moved him so deeply that he asked to join the Franciscans, and when they accepted him he took the name Anthony. He hoped to go to Morocco as a missionary himself, but he fell seriously ill on the way, and his ship was blown off course to Italy.

In Italy he lived as an ordinary friar nobody had heard of, until one day, at an ordination, it turned out that nobody had prepared a sermon, and at the last minute Anthony was asked to speak. No one there had any idea how learned and powerful a preacher he was, and his unprepared sermon amazed them all. Soon afterwards Francis of Assisi himself put him in charge of teaching theology to the friars, an unusual step at the time, since Francis was wary of learning and academic titles.

Anthony went on to preach all over Italy and France, and the crowds that came to hear him are said to have been too big for any church, so he preached in the squares. One story says that when some heretics refused to listen to him, he went down to the shore and preached to the fish instead, and the fish lifted their heads out of the water to listen, a picture of how powerful his words were. After his death, a friar who had lost a precious book of psalms got it back after praying to him, and people began to call on Anthony whenever they lost something. To this day, Catholics all over the world searching for something they’ve lost pray, "Saint Anthony, Saint Anthony, please come around." Anthony died at thirty-five, worn out by work. He was canonized in 1232, only a year after his death, one of the fastest canonizations in the Church’s history, and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1946. His feast day is June 13.

Latin text: Magnificat Magníficat ánima mea Dóminum, et exsultávit spíritus meus in Deo salvatóre meo, quia respéxit humilitátem ancíllæ suæ. Ecce enim ex hoc beátam me dicent omnes generatiónes, quia fecit mihi magna, qui potens est, et sanctum nomen eius, et misericórdia eius in progénies et progénies timéntibus eum. Fecit poténtiam in bráchio suo, dispérsit supérbos mente cordis sui; depósuit poténtes de sede et exaltávit húmiles. Esuriéntes implévit bonis et dívites dimísit inánes. Suscépit Ísrael púerum suum, recordátus misericórdiæ, sicut locútus est ad patres nostros, Ábraham et sémini eius in sæcula. Glória Patri et Fílio et Spirítui Sancto. Sicut erat in princípio, et nunc et semper, et in sæcula sæculórum. Amen.

We fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God. Despise not our petitions in our necessities, but deliver us always from all dangers O glorious and blessed Virgin. Latin text: Sub tuum præsidium Sub tuum præsídium confúgimus, sancta Dei Génetrix; nostras deprecatiónes ne despícias in necessitátibus; sed a perículis cunctis líbera nos semper, Virgo gloriósa et benedícta.

Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel; he has come to his people and set them free. He has raised up for us a mighty savior, born of the house of his servant David. Through his holy prophets he promised of old that he would save us from our enemies, from the hands of all who hate us. He promised to show mercy to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant. This was the oath he swore to our father Abraham: to set us free from the hands of our enemies, free to worship him without fear, holy and righteous in his sight all the days of our life. You, my child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his way, to give his people knowledge of salvation by the forgiveness of their sins. In the tender compassion of our God the dawn from on high shall break upon us, to shine on those who dwell in darkness and the shadow of death, and to guide our feet into the way of peace. Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning, is now, and will be forever. Amen. Latin text: Benedictus Benedíctus Dóminus, Deus Ísrael, quia visitávit et fecit redemptiónem plebi suæ, et eréxit cornu salútis nobis in domo David púeri sui, sicut locútus est per os sanctórum, qui a sæculo sunt, prophetárum eius, salútem ex inimícis nostris et de manu ómnium, qui odérunt nos; ad faciéndam misericórdiam cum pátribus nostris et memorári testaménti sui sancti, iusiurándum, quod iurávit ad Ábraham patrem nostrum, datúrum se nobis, ut sine timóre, de manu inimicórum liberáti, serviámus illi in sanctitáte et iustítia coram ipso ómnibus diébus nostris. Et tu, puer, prophéta Altíssimi vocáberis: præíbis enim ante fáciem Dómini paráre vias eius, ad dandam sciéntiam salútis plebi eius in remissiónem peccatórum eórum, per víscera misericórdiæ Dei nostri, in quibus visitábit nos óriens ex alto, illumináre his, qui in ténebris et in umbra mortis sedent, ad dirigéndos pedes nostros in viam pacis. Glória Patri et Fílio et Spirítui Sancto. Sicut erat in princípio, et nunc et semper, et in sæcula sæculórum. Amen.

You are God: we praise you; You are God: we acclaim you; You are the eternal Father: All creation worships you. To you all angels, all the powers of heaven, Cherubim and Seraphim, sing in endless praise: Holy, holy, holy, Lord, God of power and might, Heaven and earth are full of your glory. The glorious company of apostles praise you. The noble fellowship of prophets praise you. The white-robed army of martyrs praise you. Throughout the world the holy Church acclaims you: Father, of majesty unbounded, Your true and only Son, worthy of all worship, And the Holy Spirit, advocate and guide. You, Christ, are the king of glory, The eternal Son of the Father. When you became man to set us free You did not spurn the Virgin’s womb. You overcame the sting of death, And opened the kingdom of heaven to all believers. You are seated at God’s right hand in glory. We believe that you will come, and be our judge. Come then, Lord, and help your people, Bought with the price of your own blood, And bring us with your saints To glory everlasting. Save your people, Lord, and bless your inheritance. Govern and uphold them now and always. Day by day we bless you. We praise your name forever. Keep us today, Lord, from all sin. Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy. Lord, show us your love and mercy; For we put our trust in you. In you, Lord, is our hope: And we shall never hope in vain. Latin text: Te Deum Te Deum laudámus: te Dóminum confitémur. Te ætérnum Patrem, omnis terra venerátur. Tibi omnes ángeli, tibi cæli et univérsæ potestátes: tibi chérubim et séraphim incessábili voce proclámant: Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus, Dóminus Deus Sábaoth. Pleni sunt cæli et terra maiestátis glóriæ tuæ. Te gloriósus apostolórum chorus, te prophetárum laudábilis númerus, te mártyrum candidátus laudat exércitus. Te per orbem terrárum sancta confitétur Ecclésia, Patrem imménsæ maiestátis; venerándum tuum verum et únicum Fílium; Sanctum quoque Paráclitum Spíritum. Tu rex glóriæ, Christe. Tu Patris sempitérnus es Fílius. Tu, ad liberándum susceptúrus hóminem, non horruísti Vírginis úterum. Tu, devícto mortis acúleo, aperuísti credéntibus regna cælórum. Tu ad déxteram Dei sedes, in glória Patris. Iudex créderis esse ventúrus. Te ergo quæsumus, tuis fámulis súbveni, quos pretióso sánguine redemísti. Ætérna fac cum sanctis tuis in glória numerári. Salvum fac pópulum tuum, Dómine, et bénedic hereditáti tuæ. Et rege eos, et extólle illos usque in ætérnum. Per síngulos dies benedícimus te; et laudámus nomen tuum in sæculum, et in sæculum sæculi. Dignáre, Dómine, die isto sine peccáto nos custodíre. Miserére nostri, Dómine, miserére nostri. Fiat misericórdia tua, Dómine, super nos, quemádmodum sperávimus in te. In te, Dómine, sperávi: non confúndar in ætérnum.

Come, Holy Spirit, Creator come, From your bright heavenly throne! Come, take possession of our souls, And make them all your own. You who are called the Paraclete, Best gift of God above, The living spring, the living fire, Sweet unction, and true love! You who are sevenfold in your grace, Finger of God’s right hand, His promise, teaching little ones To speak and understand! O guide our minds with your blessed light, With love our hearts inflame, And with your strength which never decays Confirm our mortal frame. Far from us drive our hellish foe True peace unto us bring, And through all perils guide us safe Beneath your sacred wing. Through you may we the Father know, Through you the eternal Son And you the Spirit of them both Thrice-blessed three in one. All glory to the Father be, And to the risen Son; The same to you, O Paraclete, While endless ages run. Amen. Latin text: Veni, Creator Spiritus Veni, creátor Spíritus, mentes tuórum vísita, imple supérna grátia, quæ tu creásti péctora. Qui díceris Paráclitus, altíssimi donum Dei, fons vivus, ignis, cáritas, et spiritális únctio. Tu septifórmis múnere, dígitus patérnæ déxteræ, tu rite promíssum Patris, sermóne ditans gúttura. Accénde lumen sénsibus, infúnde amórem córdibus, infírma nostri córporis virtúte firmans pérpeti. Hostem repéllas lóngius pacémque dones prótinus; ductóre sic te prævio vitémus omne nóxium. Per Te sciámus da Patrem noscámus atque Fílium, teque utriúsque Spíritum credámus omni témpore. Deo Patri sit glória, et Fílio, qui a mórtuis surréxit, ac Paráclito, in sæculórum sæcula. Amen.

Come, Holy Spirit, come! And from your celestial home Shed a ray of light divine! Come, Father of the poor! Come, source of all our store! Come, within our bosoms shine. You, of comforters the best; You, the soul’s most welcome guest; Sweet refreshment here below; In our labor, rest most sweet; Grateful coolness in the heat; Solace in the midst of woe. O most blessed Light divine, Shine within these hearts of yours, And our inmost being fill! Where you are not, we have naught, Nothing good in deed or thought, Nothing free from taint of ill. Heal our wounds, our strength renew; On our dryness pour your dew; Wash the stains of guilt away: Bend the stubborn heart and will; Melt the frozen, warm the chill; Guide the steps that go astray. On the faithful, who adore And confess you, evermore In your sevenfold gift descend: Give them virtue’s sure reward; Give them your salvation, Lord; Give them joys that never end. Latin text: Veni, Sancte Spiritus Veni, Sancte Spíritus, et emítte cælitus lucis tuæ rádium. Veni, pater páuperum, veni, dator múnerum, veni, lumen córdium. Consolátor óptime, dulcis hospes ánimæ, dulce refrigérium. In labóre réquies, in æstu tempéries, in fletu solácium. O lux beatíssima, reple cordis íntima tuórum fidélium. Sine tuo númine, nihil est in hómine nihil est innóxium. Lava quod est sórdidum, riga quod est áridum, sana quod est sáucium. Flecte quod est rígidum, fove quod est frígidum, rege quod est dévium. Da tuis fidélibus, in te confidéntibus, sacrum septenárium. Da virtútis méritum, da salútis éxitum, da perénne gáudium. Amen.

Soul of Christ, be my sanctification. Body of Christ, be my salvation. Blood of Christ, fill all my veins. Water of Christ’s side, wash out my stains. Passion of Christ, my comfort be. O good Jesus, listen to me. In Thy wounds I fain would hide, N’er to be parted from Thy side, Guard me, should the foe assail me. Call me when my life shall fail me. Bid me come to Thee above, With Thy saints to sing Thy love, World without end. Amen. Latin text: Anima Christi Ánima Christi, sanctífica me. Corpus Christi, salva me. Sanguis Christi, inébria me. Aqua láteris Christi, lava me. Pássio Christi, confórta me. O bone Iesu, exáudi me. Intra tua vúlnera abscónde me. Ne permíttas me separári a te. Ab hoste malígno defénde me. In hora mortis meæ voca me. Et iube me veníre ad te, ut cum Sanctis tuis laudem te in sæcula sæculórum. Amen.

Remember, O most gracious Virgin Mary, that never was it known that anyone who fled to thy protection, implored thy help, or sought thy intercession, was left unaided. Inspired by this confidence I fly unto thee, O Virgin of virgins, my Mother. To thee do I come, before thee I stand, sinful and sorrowful. O Mother of the Word Incarnate, despise not my petitions, but in thy mercy hear and answer me. Amen. Latin text: Memorare Memoráre, o piíssima Virgo María, non esse audítum a sæculo, quemquam ad tua curréntem præsídia, tua implorántem auxília, tua peténtem suffrágia, esse derelíctum. Ego tali animátus confidéntia, ad te, Virgo Vírginum, Mater, curro, ad te vénio, coram te gemens peccátor assísto. Noli, Mater Verbi, verba mea despícere; sed áudi propítia et exáudi. Amen.

THE JOYFUL MYSTERIES (recited Monday and Saturday) The Annunciation The Visitation The Nativity The Presentation The Finding in the Temple THE MYSTERIES OF LIGHT (recited Thursday) The Baptism of Jesus The Wedding Feast of Cana The Proclamation of the Kingdom, with the call to Conversion The Transfiguration The Institution of the Eucharist THE SORROWFUL MYSTERIES (recited Tuesday and Friday) The Agony in the Garden The Scourging at the Pillar The Crowning with Thorns The Carrying of the Cross The Crucifixion THE GLORIOUS MYSTERIES (recited Wednesday and Sunday) The Resurrection The Ascension The Descent of the Holy Spirit The Assumption The Coronation of Mary Queen of Heaven and Earth PRAYER CONCLUDING THE ROSARY Hail, Holy Queen, etc. as above V. Pray for us, O holy Mother of God. R. That we may be made worthy of the promises of Christ. Let us pray. O God, whose only-begotten Son, by his life, death and resurrection, has purchased for us the rewards of eternal life, grant, we beseech thee, that meditating on these mysteries of the most holy Rosary of the Blessed Virgin Mary, we may imitate what they contain and obtain what they promise, through the same Christ our Lord. Amen. Latin text: Rosarium MYSTÉRIA GAUDIÓSA (in feria secunda et sabbato) Annuntiátio. Visitátio. Natívitas. Præsentátio. Invéntio in Templo. MYSTÉRIA LUMINÓSA (in feria quinta) Baptísma apud Iordánem. Autorevelátio apud Cananénse matrimónium. Regni Dei proclamátio coniúncta cum invitaménto ad conversiónem. Transfigurátio. Eucharístiæ Institútio. MYSTÉRIA DOLORÓSA (in feria tertia et feria sexta) Agonía in Hortu. Flagellátio. Coronátio Spinis. Baiulátio Crucis. Crucifíxio et Mors. MYSTÉRIA GLORIÓSA (in feria quarta et Dominica) Resurréctio. Ascénsio. Descénsus Spíritus Sancti. Assúmptio. Coronátio in Cælo. ORATIO AD FINEM ROSARII DICENDA V. Ora pro nobis, sancta Dei génetrix. R. Ut digni efficiámur promissiónibus Christi. Orémus. Deus, cuius Unigénitus per vitam, mortem et resurrectiónem suam nobis salútis ætérnæ præmia comparávit, concéde, quæsumus: ut hæc mystéria sacratíssimo beátæ Maríæ Vírginis Rosário recoléntes, et imitémur quod cóntinent, et quod promíttunt assequámur. Per Christum Dóminum nostrum. Amen.

O King of peace, give us your peace and pardon our sins. Dismiss the enemies of the Church and protect her so that she never fail. Emmanuel our God is in our midst in the glory of the Father and of the Holy Spirit. May he bless us and purify our hearts and cure the sicknesses of our soul and body. We adore you, O Christ, with your good Father and the Holy Spirit because you have come and you have saved us.

Remain in peace, O Altar of God. May the offering that I have taken from you be for the remission of my debts and the pardon of my sins and may it obtain for me that I may stand before the tribunal of Christ without condemnation and without confusion. I do not know if I will have the opportunity to return and offer another sacrifice upon you. Protect me, O Lord, and preserve your holy Church as the way to truth and salvation. Amen.

God of the spirits and of all flesh, who have trampled death and annihilated the devil and given life to your world, may you yourself, O Lord, grant to the soul of your deceased servant N. rest in a place of light, a verdant place, a place of freshness, from where suffering, pain and cries are far removed. Do You, O good and compassionate God forgive every fault committed by him in word, work or thought because there is no man who lives and does not sin. You alone are without sin and your justice is justice throughout the ages and your word is truth. Since you, O Christ our God, are the resurrection, the life and the repose of your deceased servant N., we give you glory together with your un-begotten Father and your most holy, good and life-creating Spirit, now and always and forever and ever.

O my God, I firmly believe that you are one God in three divine Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I believe that your divine Son became man and died for our sins and that he will come to judge the living and the dead. I believe these and all the truths which the Holy Catholic Church teaches because you have revealed them who are eternal truth and wisdom, who can neither deceive nor be deceived. In this faith I intend to live and die. Amen. Latin text: Actus fidei Dómine Deus, firma fide credo et confíteor ómnia et síngula quæ sancta Ecclésia Cathólica propónit, quia tu, Deus, ea ómnia revelásti, qui es ætérna véritas et sapiéntia quæ nec fállere nec falli potest. In hac fide vívere et mori státuo. Amen.

O Lord God, I hope by your grace for the pardon of all my sins and after life here to gain eternal happiness because you have promised it who are infinitely powerful, faithful, kind, and merciful. In this hope I intend to live and die. Amen. Latin text: Actus spei Dómine Deus, spero per grátiam tuam remissiónem ómnium peccatórum, et post hanc vitam ætérnam felicitátem me esse consecutúrum: quia tu promisísti, qui es infiníte potens, fidélis, benígnus, et miséricors. In hac spe vívere et mori státuo. Amen.

O Lord God, I love you above all things and I love my neighbor for your sake because you are the highest, infinite and perfect good, worthy of all my love. In this love I intend to live and die. Amen. Latin text: Actus caritatis Dómine Deus, amo te super ómnia et próximum meum propter te, quia tu es summum, infinítum, et perfectíssimum bonum, omni dilectióne dignum. In hac caritáte vívere et mori státuo. Amen.

O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended Thee, and I detest all my sins because of thy just punishments, but most of all because they offend Thee, my God, who art all good and deserving of all my love. I firmly resolve with the help of Thy grace to sin no more and to avoid the near occasion of sin. Amen. Latin text: Actus contritionis Deus meus, ex toto corde pænitet me ómnium meórum peccatórum, éaque detéstor, quia peccándo, non solum pœnas a te iuste statútas proméritus sum, sed præsértim quia offéndi te, summum bonum, ac dignum qui super ómnia diligáris. Ídeo fírmiter propóno, adiuvánte grátia tua, de cétero me non peccatúrum peccandíque occasiónes próximas fugitúrum. Amen.
You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. You shall love your neighbor as yourself.
Do to others as you would have them do to you.

Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are they who mourn, for they will be comforted. Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth. Blessed are they who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied. Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy. Blessed are the pure of heart, for they will see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God. Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when people revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward will be great in heaven.

Wisdom Understanding Counsel Fortitude Knowledge Piety Fear of the Lord
The twelve fruits of the Holy Spirit
Charity Joy Peace Patience Kindness Goodness Generosity Gentleness Faithfulness Modesty Self-control Chastity
The five precepts of the Church

You shall attend Mass on Sundays and on holy days of obligation and remain free from work or activity that could impede the sanctification of such days. You shall confess your sins at least once a year. You shall receive the sacrament of the Eucharist at least during the Easter season. You shall observe the days of fasting and abstinence established by the Church. You shall help to provide for the needs of the Church.
The seven corporal works of mercy
Feed the hungry. Give drink to the thirsty. Clothe the naked. Shelter the homeless. Visit the sick. Visit the imprisoned. Bury the dead.
The seven spiritual works of mercy
Counsel the doubtful. Instruct the ignorant. Admonish sinners. Comfort the afflicted. Forgive offenses. Bear wrongs patiently. Pray for the living and the dead.

To become Catholic, you contact a parish, meet the priest and prepare for a few months. How you prepare depends on one question: have you been baptized? Contact a parish before September. Most parishes start their OCIA group in September or October. If you come after it has started, you may have to wait a full year for the next one. Call or email the parish office in spring or summer, so the pries
If you have never been baptized

The preparation of adults is called OCIA, the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults (it used to be called RCIA). In many parishes a group starts in September or October and is baptized at the Easter Vigil, about seven months later. The Church sets no fixed length, though. If you need more time, you take more time. 1 Inquiry You come to meetings, ask questions and get to know the faith. You promi

The dates move every year, because Easter moves. These are the next four: Year Rite of Election Easter Vigil Pentecost 2027 14 February 27 March 16 May 2028 5 March 15 April 4 June 2029 18 February 31 March 20 May 2030 10 March 20 April 9 June If you talk to a priest by late summer, you can usually join that autumn’s group and be baptized at the next Easter Vigil. If you were baptized in another church

If you were baptized with water in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, you are already a Christian. You are not baptized again. You are received into full communion with the Catholic Church. 1 Talk to a priest Tell him which church baptized you and when. He will ask for proof of your baptism, so ask that church for a certificate. 2 A preparation that fits you If you alr
“Late have I loved you, beauty so ancient and so new, late have I loved you.” “From the time that I became a Catholic … I have been in perfect peace and contentment. I never have had one doubt.”
Do I have to believe everything already?

No. Nobody starts with every answer. The preparation exists for your questions and doubts, so bring them. What the Church asks is that by the day you are received, you can honestly say you believe what she teaches.
Can I go to Mass before I am received?

Yes, and you should. Anyone may come to Mass. Until you are received, you do not go up for Communion. In many parishes you can go up with your arms crossed over your chest and the priest will give you a blessing. If you are not sure what happens when, the guide to the Mass walks through it.
Do I need a sponsor or godparent?

Yes. A sponsor walks with you through the preparation and stands beside you at the rites. For baptism this person is your godparent. They must be a Catholic who is at least 16, confirmed, has received Communion and lives the faith, and they cannot be your parent or spouse (canon 874). If you do not know anyone, tell the priest. The parish will find someone.
The sacraments are free. Some parishes ask a small amount for books, and nobody is turned away for lack of money.
I am divorced and remarried, or married outside the Church

Tell the priest at your first meeting. Your marriage may need to be sorted out before you can be received. If you or your spouse were married before, that may mean asking a Church tribunal whether the first marriage was valid. This can take months, which is one more reason to start early. It does not stop you from beginning the preparation now.
What if my family is against it?

This is hard, and you are not the first. Tell the priest, so he knows what you are carrying. Be patient with your family and kind to them: they will learn more from how you live than from arguments. If you are still a minor, the parish will talk with your parents.
What if I am not sure my baptism was valid?

Every baptism is presumed valid unless shown otherwise. If there is serious doubt whether it was done with water and “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” the priest gives a conditional baptism: “If you are not already baptized, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Adults who were baptized Catholic but never received any t

No. Becoming Catholic changes your whole life, and that takes time. You are not outside the Church while you wait. If you are baptized, your baptism already binds you to the Church (CCC 1271). If you are not, your wish to be baptized already joins you to her, and the Church treats you as her own (CCC 1249).
Do I need to go to confession?
If you are already baptized, yes: you go to confession before you are received. If you have never been baptized, no: baptism washes away every earlier sin. See the step-by-step confession guide.

1 Find your parish. Search for “Catholic church” and your town, or ask any Catholic you know. Call the office or send an email and say you want to become Catholic. 2 Go to a Sunday Mass. Sit anywhere and follow along. Take the printable Order of the Mass with you so you know the words. 3 Read one Gospel. Start with Mark. It is the shortest, and you can read it in two evenings.
