Why do Catholics call priests “Father,” pray the Rosary and use a crucifix?

Each one points to Christ. A priest is a spiritual father, as Paul was. The Rosary prays Bible words while thinking about Jesus’ life. The crucifix shows what our salvation cost. Calling a priest Father. “Call no man father” (Matthew 23:9). Here Jesus warns against pride and against putting anyone in God’s place. He does not ban the word: He speaks of honoring “your father and mother” (Matthew 15:4), and Paul writes, “I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15). A priest is called Father because He gives spiritual life through the sacraments. The Rosary. Jesus warned against “empty phrases,” praying as if many words could force God to listen (Matthew 6:7). He did not forbid repeating a prayer: He prayed the same words three times in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:44), and in heaven the angels say “Holy, holy, holy” without end (Revelation 4:8). The Hail Mary comes from the Bible (Luke 1:28, 42), and while saying it we think about the life of Christ. The crucifix. Many Protestants prefer an empty cross because Christ is risen. Catholics believe that too, but with Paul “we proclaim Christ crucified” (1 Corinthians 1:23). The crucifix shows the price of our salvation and how much God loves us. Learn more: The Rosary → CCC 971, 1548, 2678, 2708 Read the full answer
Why do Catholics confess to a priest instead of going directly to God?

God forgives, through the priest. Christ gave the apostles power to forgive sins, and the priest acts in His person. Hearing “I absolve you” makes forgiveness certain, and the priest may never reveal what he hears. Christ’s own plan. The question is not whether God forgives, but how He chose to give that forgiveness. After the Resurrection, Christ breathed on the apostles and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:22–23). They could not decide to forgive or retain without hearing the sins. The priest acts in persona Christi, “in the person of Christ”: Christ forgives through him. The priest may never reveal what he hears (the seal of confession, canon 983). We are bodies, not just souls, so we need to hear with our own ears that we are forgiven. “I suppose I’m forgiven” is not the same as hearing “I absolve you from your sins.” Catholics also confess to God directly, and for venial sins that is enough. Mortal sin needs the sacrament (canon 960). Learn more: Confession → CCC 1441–1445, 1461–1467, 1484 · CIC can. 959–960, 983, 988 Read the full answer
Are the bread and wine at Mass just a symbol of Jesus?

No. It is truly Christ. After the consecration the bread and wine still look the same, but they are now the Body and Blood of Christ. Transubstantiation. The bread and wine still look, taste and test the same, but their substance, what they are, has changed. The Church calls this transubstantiation, a change of substance. Christ is truly, really and substantially present: Body and Blood, Soul and Divinity (canon 899). Not part of Him, all of Him; not a symbol, Himself. Jesus said, “This is my body” (Matthew 26:26). In John 6 He said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you,” and many followers left Him. He didn’t call them back to say He meant it symbolically. Christians have died for this belief. In 304, forty-nine Christians in Abitina, North Africa, were arrested for holding Sunday Mass against the emperor’s order. They told the judge, “Without Sunday we cannot live,” and were put to death. Saint Tarcisius, a young man in Rome, was killed rather than give up the Eucharist he was carrying to prisoners. People do not die for a symbol. Learn more: The Holy Mass → CCC 1374–1377, 1413 · CIC can. 897–899 Read the full answer
Do I have to go to Mass every Sunday and keep the fasts?

Yes, both are Church precepts. Sunday Mass is required unless you have a serious reason. Fasting binds on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and Fridays are days of penance. Sunday Mass. Catholics must attend Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation (canon 1247); a Saturday evening Mass also counts (canon 1248). Missing it on purpose, without a serious reason, is a mortal sin. Serious reasons include illness, caring for small children or the sick, having no church nearby, or work you truly can’t avoid. If unsure, ask your pastor. This is how we keep the Third Commandment: “Remember the sabbath day, and keep it holy” (Exodus 20:8). If you love God, you can give Him one hour a week. Fasting. In the Latin Church, Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of fasting and no meat (canon 1251). Fasting binds ages 18 to 59 and means one full meal plus two small ones. No meat binds from age 14 (canon 1252), and every Friday in Lent is meatless. Every Friday of the year is a day of penance, and in many countries the bishops let you replace the meat rule with another act of penance or charity (canon 1253). Illness, pregnancy, hard physical work and similar reasons excuse you from fasting. With prayer and almsgiving, fasting keeps our appetites in order and makes room for God. Learn more: The Holy Mass → CCC 1438, 2042–2043, 2180–2183 · CIC can. 1246–1253 Read the full answer

Catholics in a state of grace. You must be a baptized Catholic, believe Christ is truly present, have no unconfessed mortal sin, and fast for one hour beforehand. The details. “Full communion” means a baptized Catholic, not every baptized Christian. After a mortal sin, go to confession first (canon 916). In the one-hour fast, water and medicine don’t count (canon 919). Asking non-Catholics not to receive is not a snub (canon 844). Communion expresses a unity that already exists; it doesn’t create one. Acting out a shared faith that isn’t shared yet wouldn’t be honest. If you can’t receive, in many parishes, especially in North America, you can come forward with your arms crossed over your chest for a blessing. Where that isn’t the custom, stay in your pew and pray a spiritual communion. Learn more: The Holy Mass → CCC 1385, 1387, 1400, 1415, 1650 · CIC can. 844, 912, 915–916, 919 Read the full answer
Is the Pope sinless? What about claims that he is the Antichrist, or that Catholic customs are pagan?

No, and no. Popes sin and go to confession; infallibility covers only rare, final teachings. The Antichrist denies that Christ came in the flesh, which every Pope has taught. Customs that look pagan were given a Christian meaning. Sinless? Infallibility and sinlessness are two very different things. Popes sin, popes go to confession, and some popes in history sinned badly. Infallibility is very narrow. The Pope is infallible only when, as shepherd of the whole Church, he defines a teaching on faith or morals as final (ex cathedra, canon 749 §1). His politics, management, views on science and casual remarks are not covered. It has been used very rarely, and it does not let him invent new teaching; it only guarantees that he faithfully guards the faith handed down to him. The Antichrist claim. The Bible defines the antichrist as one who denies that “Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” (2 John 7; 1 John 2:22). Every Pope has taught exactly that Jesus is God made man. The “great whore” of Babylon (Revelation 17) is best read as pagan Rome, “drunk with the blood of the saints,” which killed the first martyrs, Peter and Paul among them. Calling the Pope the Antichrist began in the bitter arguments of the 1500s. The pagan claim. Christians did not copy pagan religion; they took ordinary human things, such as candles, incense, robes and feast days, and gave them to Christ. Paul did the same in Athens, using an altar “to an unknown god” to preach the true God (Acts 17:23). Easter comes from the Jewish Passover and the Gospel, not from pagan feasts. A custom that is older than Christianity no more makes you pagan than a wedding ring does, though rings were a Roman custom too. Learn more: Saint Peter → CCC 675–677, 890–892, 1149 · CIC can. 331, 749 §1 Read the full answer
How are the Orthodox different from Catholics?

Very close, but not yet united. The Orthodox have apostolic bishops and real sacraments. The split of 1054 is mainly about the Pope’s authority. Apostolic roots. The Orthodox Churches also trace their bishops back to the apostles in an unbroken line (apostolic succession). The Church of Constantinople, for example, traces itself to St. Andrew, Peter’s brother. In Orthodox tradition he is called the “First-Called,” because he was the first of the disciples to follow Jesus (John 1:40–41). Because of this, the Orthodox have valid sacraments, a real priesthood, the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, and a deep devotion to Mary and the saints. We share a great deal. The split, which became final in 1054, is mainly about the authority of the Bishop of Rome, Peter’s successor, plus a few points of doctrine (such as the Filioque: whether the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son). The Church sees this split as a wound and prays for full unity. Learn more: History of the Church → CCC 816–819, 838 Read the full answer
Does the Catholic Church think Protestants are of the devil?

No. The Church never taught that Protestants are of the devil. The harsh documents of the 1500s condemned ideas and the break, not people. Why they broke away. Protestants broke away in the 1500s over four points: whether Scripture alone is the rule or Tradition and the Church’s teaching office also have authority; the number and nature of the sacraments; Christ’s real presence in the Eucharist; and how we are justified. The harsh documents of the 1500s. The language of that age was fierce on both sides. Pope Leo X’s 1520 bull Exsurge Domine (“Arise, O Lord”) compared the new teaching to “the wild boar from the forest” destroying the Lord’s vineyard, and spoke of people “blinded in mind by the father of lies.” It condemned 41 of Luther’s propositions as “heretical, scandalous, false, offensive to pious ears or seductive of simple minds.” The Council of Trent (1545–1563) then issued more than a hundred canons with anathemas, formal condemnations of teachings such as justification by faith alone. Older catechisms and manuals classified Protestantism as heresy and schism. Ideas, not people. These texts condemned teachings and the act of breaking away, not every Protestant. Canon law defines heresy as the obstinate denial of a truth of faith after baptism (canon 751), which requires knowing what one rejects. Someone raised in a Protestant family is in a very different place: “one cannot charge with the sin of the separation those who at present are born into these communities,” and the Church “accepts them with respect and affection as brothers” (CCC 818). The Second Vatican Council calls them “brothers in the Lord.” In 1999 Catholics and Lutherans even agreed that the 16th-century condemnations on justification do not apply to the Lutheran teaching as presented in their joint statement. Every validly baptized Christian is in a real, if incomplete, communion with the Catholic Church (canon 205). Division is a scandal, and we are bound to pray for unity. Learn more: History of the Church → CCC 817–819, 838 · CIC can. 205, 751 Read the full answer

Final cleansing before heaven. Everyone in Purgatory is saved; they are being made ready to see God. An indulgence is the Church’s help with that healing. Selling them was an abuse, long since banned. Purgatory. It is not a “second chance” or a mild hell. Everyone in Purgatory is saved for good. It is the cleansing of people who die in God’s friendship but are not yet fully purified, so they can enter heaven. Being forgiven and being healed are two different things: a forgiven liar doesn’t lose the habit of lying overnight, and nothing unholy can see God. The Church has prayed for the dead from the beginning, which only makes sense if our prayers can still help them. Indulgences. An indulgence is the Church’s help with that healing. God removes part or all of the remaining punishment for sins that are already forgiven (canon 992), usually in return for prayer, confession, Communion and acts of charity. It can be offered for the dead (canon 994). Luther was right that in his time some clergy sold indulgences; that was a real abuse. The Council of Trent (1562) abolished the preachers who collected money for indulgences, and in 1567 Pope Pius V banned tying an indulgence to any payment. Luther was wrong to throw out the teaching itself. Learn more: The Profession of Faith → CCC 1030–1032, 1471–1479 · CIC can. 992–994 Read the full answer
Does the Catholic Church reject science and the theory of evolution?

No. Faith and science don’t conflict. Catholics are free to study how life developed. Genesis teaches who made the world and why, not how. One source of truth. All truth comes from the same God, so honest science can never truly contradict faith. Genesis isn’t a science book; it teaches that a good God made everything good and for a purpose. The Church holds two things firmly: God created everything, and God creates each human soul directly. Science asks “how”; faith asks “why” and “by whom.” History shows this. The universities grew out of the Church, and many founders of modern science were devout Catholics, some of them priests: Nicolaus Copernicus, a church canon, showed that the earth goes around the sun. Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar, founded genetics. Fr. Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest, first proposed the Big Bang theory. Louis Pasteur proved that germs cause disease and made the first rabies and anthrax vaccines. Blaise Pascal, André-Marie Ampère and Alessandro Volta laid foundations in mathematics, physics and electricity. Nicolas Steno, a father of geology, became a bishop. In our time, Jérôme Lejeune discovered the cause of Down syndrome. The Church still runs the Vatican Observatory, one of the oldest in the world. Learn more: Why We're Catholic → CCC 159, 283–284, 366 Read the full answer
Can the Church’s core teachings of faith change over time?

No. Understanding grows; truth doesn’t. Revelation was complete in Christ. Teaching can deepen like a seed becoming a tree, but never contradict itself. Growth, not change. Nothing new will be added to what God revealed in Christ. A seed growing into a tree looks different, but it is the same plant. A new teaching that made an old one false would be a break, and the Church has no power to do that. Church rules can change, such as fasting rules, the language of the Mass or celibacy for Latin priests. Defined teaching on faith and morals cannot (canon 750). Learn more: The Catechism → CCC 66–67, 94 · CIC can. 747, 750 Read the full answer
Why does God allow suffering and evil in the world?

There is no short answer. God does not want evil; most of it comes from misused freedom. And God did not stay distant: in Jesus He suffered with us and rose again. The Catechism says no single sentence can answer it: the whole Christian faith together is the answer. Here are three parts of it. God does not want evil. He does not cause it, and He did not make it. Evil is something good that is missing, the way blindness is missing sight. Most evil comes from free choices. God made us free so that we can truly love, but people can misuse their freedom. If God stopped every bad choice, we would not really be free. God came to suffer with us. The deepest Christian answer is not an idea but a person: Jesus. God did not watch our pain from far away. He became a man and suffered: He was hungry, betrayed, tortured, and He died on the cross. Then He rose from the dead, showing that suffering and death do not have the last word. This does not make suffering good or explain all of it. But God can bring good even out of evil, and we will understand this fully only at the end of time. Learn more: Answering Atheism → CCC 309–314, 324, 385, 1500–1505 Read the full answer
How can a loving God allow hell to exist?

God wants no one lost. Hell is the free choice to reject God to the end. God respects it, because forced love isn’t love. No one is made for hell. God “desires everyone to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4), and the Church prays for the salvation of every person. God doesn’t send anyone to hell. People choose it by rejecting Him freely, to the very end. The root of that choice is pride, the first of the deadly sins. Pride puts self in God’s place and refuses His love, breaking the first commandment: “You shall have no other gods before me” (Exodus 20:3). Whoever rejects God to the end is saying, “I will not have you as my God,” and follows Satan, who fell through pride. God respects that choice, because forced love isn’t love. As the saying goes, the doors of hell are locked from the inside. Learn more: The Profession of Faith → CCC 1033–1037, 1058, 1866, 2084, 2094 Read the full answer
With so many religions, why Christianity? Can people who never heard of Christ be saved?

Because God came looking for us. In Christ God became man and rose from the dead. Those who never knew the Gospel through no fault of their own can still be saved by His grace. Why Christianity. The Church respects what is true and holy in other religions. But Christianity makes a different claim. In other religions people search for God; in Christianity God comes looking for us and becomes a man. Jesus did not say He shows a way; He said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). And the faith rests on a public event that can be examined, the Resurrection: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Salvation comes only through Christ, but people who don’t know the Gospel through no fault of their own, and who sincerely seek God and follow their conscience, can be saved. The grace that reaches them is Christ’s, even if they don’t know it. Baptism of desire. Jesus commanded baptism (John 3:5), and it is necessary “by actual reception or at least by desire” (canon 849): “God has bound salvation to the sacrament of Baptism, but he himself is not bound by his sacraments.” A catechumen who dies before baptism, wanting it and sorry for sin, is saved by that desire. Someone who never heard the Gospel but does God’s will as they understand it would have wanted baptism had they known of it; this is an implicit desire. Those who die for Christ before baptism (baptism of blood) are saved as well. The thief on the cross was never baptized. Dying, he admitted his guilt, defended Jesus as innocent and asked, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” Jesus answered: “Today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:39–43). It is never too late to turn to Christ, and God can save outside the sacraments. But this is no excuse to skip baptism: the thief had no chance to be baptized, and we do. Jesus gave the command to baptize all nations only after his Resurrection (Matthew 28:19). None of this makes preaching pointless: the Church owes everyone the truth and the sure road of the sacraments. Children who die without baptism are entrusted to God’s mercy, and may have a Church funeral if their parents meant to baptize them (canon 1183 §2). Learn more: Why We're Catholic → CCC 843–848, 1257–1261 · CIC can. 849, 1183 Read the full answer
Don’t the Church’s sins, the Crusades and the Inquisition disprove its claim to be holy?

No. The Church is holy through Christ. Its members sin, and those sins betray its own standard. Crusade crimes and Inquisition executions were real, fewer than legend says, and the Church has asked forgiveness. Holy, with sinful members. The Church is holy because of Christ, its Head, and the Holy Spirit, not because of its members. Its members, from laypeople to popes, can sin and have sinned. The Catechism calls the Church “at once holy and always in need of purification.” A teaching isn’t false because its followers fail to live it; a bad doctor doesn’t disprove medicine. These sins are scandals precisely because they betray the Church’s own standard, and Christ’s harshest words were for those who lead the little ones astray. Wars, Crusades and the Inquisition. Religion is not the main cause of war: the bloodiest century, the 20th, was driven by nationalism and by atheist regimes like those of Stalin and Mao. The Crusades began in 1095, when the Christian East asked for help after Muslim armies had conquered Christian lands and attacked pilgrims. But crusaders also committed real crimes, such as the sack of Constantinople in 1204. The Inquisition was a system of Church courts for heresy cases. Historians now count its executions in the thousands over several centuries, far fewer than legend says, but each one was wrong. In 2000 John Paul II publicly asked forgiveness for these sins, including violence used “in the service of truth.” Learn more: History of the Church → CCC 827, 1428, 2104–2109 Read the full answer
If God really exists, why doesn’t He show Himself plainly?

He shows Himself, but forces no one. God speaks through creation, conscience and Christ. Love must be free, so He gives light to those who seek without overwhelming those who don’t. Not hiding. God shows Himself in creation, in conscience, in the history of Israel and most clearly in Christ. A sign in the sky would compel belief, but that would be submission, not love, and love must be free. So He gives enough light for anyone who seeks Him, but not so much that it blinds those who don’t want to see. Faith isn’t a blind leap: it goes beyond reason, not against it. And Christians believe not only that seekers find God, but that God came looking for us first. Learn more: Answering Atheism → CCC 35–38, 143–150, 156–159 Read the full answer
If Jesus is God, why did He cry out on the cross, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

He was praying a psalm, not losing His faith. These are the first words of Psalm 22, a prayer that begins in anguish and ends in victory. The Father never abandoned His Son. The first line of a psalm. Jesus is quoting Psalm 22:1 ( Matthew 27:46 , Mark 15:34 ). In Jewish teaching and oral tradition, a psalm was called to mind by its first line. Reciting that line pointed the listeners to the whole psalm and its context, much as naming the first words of a hymn brings the whole hymn to mind. A psalm about the cross. Read the rest of Psalm 22 and it sounds like an account of Calvary: the mocking crowd shaking their heads, the pierced hands and feet, the soldiers casting lots for His garments ( Matthew 27:39–43 , John 19:23–24 ). Jesus is showing that the Scripture is being fulfilled in Him. It does not end in despair. The psalm moves from anguish to praise, ending with God delivering the sufferer and all the ends of the earth turning to the Lord ( Psalm 22:27 ). From the depth of His agony, Jesus points to the victory beyond it. Did the Father turn away from Him? No. The Father and the Son are one God and can never be separated. Jesus was truly man and truly suffered, and He took our place: He carried the weight of our sin and our distance from God, and prayed in our name. He never stopped trusting the Father. His last words, in Luke, are a prayer of trust: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” ( Luke 23:46 ). CCC 603 , 2605 Read the full answer
Did Christ really found the Catholic Church, or did Constantine?

Christ founded it, on Peter. Jesus called Peter the rock, and Peter led the Church and died in Rome. Constantine only made Christianity legal, nearly 300 years later. Founded on Peter. Christ built His Church on Peter and the apostles: “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). He gave them His authority and sent them out (Matthew 28:18–20; John 20:21). The early Church had bishops who succeeded the apostles, and it looked to the Bishop of Rome as Peter’s successor (canons 330–331). A merely human institution would have collapsed long ago; the Church has lasted because Christ promised to stay with it. Peter the rock. Jesus spoke Aramaic, in which “Peter” and “rock” are the same word, Kepha (John 1:42). The Greek Petros is simply the male form of petra, “rock,” used for a man’s name. Peter in Rome. 1 Peter 5:13 sends greetings from “Babylon,” an early Christian code name for Rome. Christian writers of the first and second centuries say Peter taught and died there, and excavations found his tomb under St. Peter’s Basilica. Constantine made Christianity legal in 313, almost 300 years after Pentecost, when Rome had already had more than thirty bishops in a row. The Council of Nicaea (325) did not invent doctrine; it defended what Christians already believed. Learn more: History of the Church → CCC 156, 552–553, 880–882 · CIC can. 330–331 Read the full answer

A valid marriage can’t be dissolved. A Church court may find a marriage was never valid (an annulment). Divorced Catholics who have not remarried can still receive the sacraments. Marriage is for life. A valid, consummated marriage between two baptized people cannot be dissolved by any human power (canon 1141). “What God has joined together, let no one separate” (Matthew 19:6). A civil divorce ends the marriage only in the eyes of the law. A Church court can examine whether something essential was missing at the wedding (canon 1671). If so, it issues a declaration of nullity (an annulment): a finding that the marriage was never valid, not a Catholic divorce. A divorced person who remarries without an annulment cannot receive Communion while that situation lasts. Divorced Catholics who have not remarried can receive the sacraments, and a spouse who separates to protect themselves or their children commits no sin (canons 1151–1155). Learn more: The Celebration of the Mystery → CCC 1625–1629, 1650, 2382–2386 · CIC can. 1056, 1141, 1151–1155, 1671 Read the full answer
Why does the Church reject sex before marriage, living together and contraception?

Sex belongs in marriage. It unites spouses and is open to life. Sex outside marriage and contraception split these apart. Couples may space births with natural family planning. Two purposes. Sex belongs in marriage and has two purposes that belong together: it unites husband and wife, and it is open to new life. With the body it says, “I give you my whole life.” Outside marriage the body says what the couple has not yet promised, so the Church calls sex before marriage a grave sin. Couples living together who want to marry in the Church are welcome: talk to your priest. Many such couples choose to live chastely until the wedding. Contraception separates the two purposes by making a sexual act unable to give life. This doesn’t mean having as many children as possible. For serious reasons, a couple may space births or avoid pregnancy with natural family planning (NFP): they learn the wife’s fertile days and don’t have sex on those days. Contraception changes the act itself; NFP leaves each act whole and only chooses when. Ask your parish about an NFP class. Learn more: Life in Christ → CCC 2353, 2366–2372, 2390–2391, 2399 Read the full answer
Why does the Church reject IVF and surrogacy?

A child is a gift, not a product. IVF conceives apart from the parents’ act of love and usually destroys embryos. Surrogacy uses the mother and treats the baby as goods. Every child born this way is still fully loved. IVF. It makes a child in a laboratory, apart from the parents’ act of love. A child is a gift, never something owed, and has the right “to be the fruit of the specific act of the conjugal love of his parents” (CCC 2378). IVF also usually creates extra embryos that are frozen or destroyed, and each one is a human life. A child born through IVF is fully loved by God and has the same dignity as any other child. But that does not make the method right. Surrogacy goes further: a woman carries a child for others and hands the baby over after birth, usually for money. The child is treated as a product and the mother’s body as a service. In January 2024 Pope Francis called surrogacy “deplorable” and “a grave violation of the dignity of the woman and the child, based on the exploitation of situations of the mother’s material needs,” and asked for a worldwide ban. The Church’s 2024 document Dignitas Infinita repeats this. The Church supports fertility treatment that helps a couple conceive through their own act of love, such as NaProTechnology. Learn more: Life in Christ → CCC 2373–2379 Read the full answer
Why does the Church say masturbation is wrong?

It is gravely wrong, but guilt can be lessened. Sex is meant as a gift to a spouse. If you struggle, don’t lose heart: confess, pray and ask for help. Why it is wrong. Masturbation seeks sexual pleasure alone, apart from the gift of oneself to a spouse. The Church calls it “gravely disordered” (CCC 2352), but also says habit, anxiety, immaturity and other factors can lessen a person’s guilt. If you struggle with it, don’t lose heart: go to confession often, pray, and talk to a priest. Many people find freedom over time. Follow-up: What if a doctor asks me for a sperm sample for fertility tests? Fertility testing is good, but giving the sample by masturbation is not morally acceptable. There is a moral way: a special collection sheath, perforated and without spermicide, used during normal intercourse between husband and wife. Ask your doctor for one. Doctors trained in NaProTechnology or other Catholic-friendly fertility care know it well, and your priest can help with questions. Learn more: Life in Christ → CCC 2352 Read the full answer
How should we treat people who struggle with same-sex attraction or their sexual identity?

With love first. Every person is made in God’s image and deserves respect. Having these feelings is not a sin. Respect and closeness. Every person is made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27). The Church asks that people with same-sex attraction be treated with “respect, compassion, and sensitivity,” without unjust discrimination. Having these feelings or struggles is not a sin; most people don’t choose them, and many carry deep pain. Our first job is to stay close, listen and pray. The Church also teaches that body and soul belong together, and being a man or a woman is a gift from God. Dignitas Infinita (2024) warns that sex-change treatments risk harming that God-given dignity. Everyone outside marriage between a man and a woman is called to chastity. The Church calls homosexual acts gravely wrong, never the person. You can welcome someone and be kind to them without agreeing with everything they believe. For hard family situations, talk with your priest. Learn more: Life in Christ → CCC 357, 364–365, 2332–2333, 2357–2359 Read the full answer
Which baptisms does the Church accept, and are Mormons Christian?

Trinitarian baptisms with water. Orthodox and most Protestant baptisms are valid. Mormon baptisms are not, because they deny that Jesus is eternal God. What makes a baptism valid. A baptism is valid with real water, the words “I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” and the intention to do what the Church does (canon 849). So the Church accepts Orthodox baptisms and those of most Protestant churches (Anglican, Lutheran, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist). These Christians are not baptized again (canon 845); they are received into full communion. A baptism is invalid without water (Quakers, the Salvation Army, Christian Science) or when the words deny the Trinity (Jehovah’s Witnesses, Unitarians, “Jesus only” Pentecostals, Mormons). In 2001 the Church declared Mormon baptisms invalid: Mormons use the right words but believe Jesus is a created spirit child of the Father, not God from all eternity. So they are not Christians in the Church’s sense, though they are often devout people we treat with respect. If you are unsure about your own baptism, your priest or catechist will check your record and, if needed, arrange a conditional or full baptism (canon 869). Learn more: Becoming Catholic → CCC 232–234, 1239–1240, 1256 · CIC can. 845, 849, 869 Read the full answer
We married before either of us was baptized. What happens to our marriage?

Your marriage is already valid. A marriage of two unbaptized people is a valid natural marriage. Once you are both baptized, it becomes a sacrament with no extra ceremony. No convalidation needed. The Church sees a marriage between two unbaptized people as a valid natural marriage, even if it was only a civil wedding. It does not need convalidation and is no obstacle to receiving the sacraments through OCIA. Convalidation is only for marriages the Church considers invalid, for example when a Catholic married outside the Church, or married an unbaptized person without a dispensation (canon 1086). Once you are both baptized, your marriage becomes a sacrament automatically (canon 1055 §2). If one spouse is baptized at Easter and the other later, it becomes a sacrament at the second baptism. No extra ceremony is needed. Learn more: Becoming Catholic → CCC 1601, 1617, 1631 · CIC can. 1055 §2, 1086 Read the full answer
Why does the Church oppose abortion?

Every human life is sacred. Life has full worth from conception. Directly ending an innocent life is always gravely wrong. Life from conception. Every human life is a gift from God and has full worth from conception to natural death. Directly ending an innocent life is always gravely wrong, whatever the motive. Christians have taught this about abortion since the first century. From conception there is a new human being with its own DNA, growing as each of us once grew. The hard cases are real: rape, poverty, fear, a frightening diagnosis. But how a child was conceived or how sick the child is does not change who the child is. Two lives are involved, and the Church asks us to care for both, with real help for mothers in need. Treating a serious illness in the mother is allowed even if the baby may die as a side effect, as long as the baby’s death is not the aim. Procuring an abortion brings automatic excommunication (canon 1397 §2), yet anyone who has had or taken part in one can be forgiven in confession, and priests will receive you with mercy. Learn more: Life in Christ → CCC 2270–2275 · CIC can. 1397 §2 Read the full answer
Why does the Church oppose euthanasia and assisted suicide?

It is killing, whatever the motive. A patient’s request or the law does not change that. Each life keeps its worth to its natural end. Mercy or killing? Ending a sick person’s life to end their suffering, or helping them end it (in Canada, MAID), is killing. The patient’s request or the law’s permission does not change that. Each life belongs to God and keeps its worth to its natural end. You don’t have to keep someone alive at any cost. A patient may refuse treatment that is too burdensome or out of proportion, and strong painkillers are allowed even if they may shorten life, as long as the aim is to relieve pain. Basic care such as food, water and comfort is still owed. The Church’s answer to suffering is good palliative care and never leaving the sick alone. The Church does not give up hope for people who take their own lives. Fear, depression or great pain can lessen their responsibility, and we pray for them. Learn more: Life in Christ → CCC 2276–2283 Read the full answer
Why did the Church change its teaching on the death penalty?

It is now “inadmissible.” In 2018 the Catechism was revised: the death penalty attacks human dignity, and the Church works to end it. The 2018 change. Pope Francis revised the Catechism. It now says that, in the light of the Gospel, the death penalty is “inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” and that the Church works to end it worldwide. In the past, the Church accepted the death penalty in very serious cases, when it was the only way to protect people from a dangerous criminal. In 1995 John Paul II wrote that such cases were “very rare, if not practically non-existent,” because modern prisons can keep society safe. The principles stay the same: every human life has dignity, and society may protect itself. What changed is the judgment that killing is still needed for that, along with a clearer sense that even a guilty person keeps his dignity. Learn more: Life in Christ → CCC 2266–2267 Read the full answer
Why can’t women be ordained priests?

The Church has no authority to. Jesus chose only men as apostles, though He broke many customs about women. This teaching is final. Christ’s choice. The Church teaches that it has no authority to ordain women (canon 1024). Jesus chose only men as His twelve apostles, and the apostles also chose men to succeed them. Jesus broke many customs of His day about women: He spoke with them in public, taught them and had women among His closest followers. So His choice of men was not just following the culture. In 1994 John Paul II declared that all the faithful must hold this teaching as final. This says nothing against the worth of women. Men and women are equal in dignity before God. Mary, the greatest of all saints, was never a priest. Women serve the Church as teachers, catechists, sisters, missionaries and leaders, and Catherine of Siena and Teresa of Avila are Doctors of the Church, a title given to its greatest teachers. The priesthood is not a higher rank, a prize or an honor, and no one has a right to it. Jesus told His apostles: “Whoever wishes to become great among you must be your servant… for the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:43–45). He washed their feet and told them to do the same (John 13:14–15). The Catechism says the priest’s office “is in the strict sense of the term a service.” Learn more: The Celebration of the Mystery → CCC 876, 1551, 1577–1578 · CIC can. 1024 Read the full answer

Celibacy is a rule, not a doctrine. Latin-rite priests don’t marry, but Eastern Catholic Churches ordain married men. Who may be ordained. Celibacy is a Church rule (canon 277 §1), not a doctrine, and it could change. In the Latin Church a married man is normally barred from becoming a priest (canon 1042), but the Eastern Catholic Churches ordain married men, and some married Protestant ministers who became Catholic have been ordained with a dispensation. A man who is already a priest cannot marry (canon 1087). The Latin Church keeps the rule because Jesus never married and praised those who give up marriage “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:12). An unmarried man can give his full attention to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:32–33) and his whole life to his people. His life also points to heaven, where people “neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30). Learn more: The Celebration of the Mystery → CCC 1579–1580 · CIC can. 277, 1042, 1087 Read the full answer
Why baptize babies who can’t choose for themselves?

Grace is a gift, not a choice we earn. Children need God’s grace too, so parents give it early, as they give food and medicine. A gift, not a reward. Baptism is a free gift from God that nobody earns, adults included. Children are born with original sin and need God’s grace like everyone else. Parents don’t wait for a child to choose food or medicine, and the Church asks them to have the child baptized in the first few weeks (canon 867 §1). The practice is very old: the New Testament tells of whole households being baptized (Acts 16:15, 33; 1 Corinthians 1:16). The child still says yes later, growing into the faith that parents and godparents promise to teach (canon 872), especially at Confirmation. Learn more: The Celebration of the Mystery → CCC 1250–1252 · CIC can. 867, 872–874 Read the full answer
What does the Church teach about Mary: was she sinless, ever-virgin, taken into heaven?

Yes, all three. Mary was kept free from sin from conception, stayed a virgin all her life, and was taken body and soul into heaven. Sinless. From the first moment of her life, God kept Mary free from original sin (the Immaculate Conception, defined in 1854). She was saved by Jesus like us, but in advance. The angel greets her as “full of grace” (Luke 1:28). “All have sinned” (Romans 3:23) speaks of people in general; it does not include Jesus either, or a baby who has done nothing. Taken into heaven. At the end of her life Mary was taken body and soul into heaven (the Assumption, defined in 1950), the first to share fully in her Son’s Resurrection. The Bible does not describe it, but Christians believed it from early on, and no city ever claimed to have her body. Ever-virgin. Mary remained a virgin all her life, and Jesus is her only son. The Gospels name “brothers” of Jesus (Mark 6:3), but Hebrew and Aramaic had no word for “cousin,” so “brother” was used for close relatives; Lot, Abraham’s nephew, is called his “brother” (Genesis 14:14). James and Joses were sons of another Mary (Matthew 27:56). At the cross Jesus gave His mother to John’s care (John 19:26–27), which makes little sense if she had other sons. Learn more: The Blessed Virgin Mary → CCC 490–493, 499–501, 966 Read the full answer
Are we saved by faith alone, or by works?

By grace, through a living faith. Salvation is God’s free gift. True faith shows itself in works, but even those works are His grace in us. Grace first. We are saved by God’s grace, a free gift we cannot earn. The first grace, being made right with God, comes through faith and baptism, and no one can merit it. Catholics and many Protestants agree on this; in 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint statement on it. Saving faith is a living faith. “Faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead” (James 2:17). The only time the Bible says “faith alone” is: “a person is justified by works and not by faith alone” (James 2:24). Paul speaks of “faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). Good works do not earn heaven. God’s grace comes first and works in us, and we respond by doing good. So even our good works are His gift. Learn more: Life in Christ → CCC 1987–1996, 2006–2011 Read the full answer
Why is the God of the Old Testament so violent?

God revealed Himself step by step. He met a violent people where they were. The Bible is read as a whole with Christ as its key, and ancient war stories often exaggerate. Read as one whole. The Old Testament has hard passages, and the Church doesn’t hide them. It reads the Bible as one whole, with Christ as the key. God revealed Himself step by step to a people in a violent age, starting where they were. The Catechism says these books “contain matters imperfect and provisional.” The writers also used the styles of their time, and ancient war stories often exaggerated: Joshua says whole peoples were wiped out, and a few chapters later they are still there (Joshua 10; Judges 1). Jesus shows us fully who God is: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). He taught us to love our enemies and died for His. We read the hard passages in His light. Learn more: The Bible → CCC 110, 121–123, 128–130 Read the full answer
Can Catholics believe in reincarnation, or be cremated?

Reincarnation: no. Cremation: yes. We live once and rise in our own bodies. Cremation is allowed, but the ashes belong in a sacred place, not scattered or kept at home. Reincarnation: no. We each live one life on earth. “It is appointed for mortals to die once, and after that the judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). The Catechism says plainly: “There is no ‘reincarnation’ after death.” At the end of time we will rise in our own bodies. Cremation: yes, unless it is chosen to deny faith in the resurrection, although the Church prefers burial of the body (canon 1176 §3). The ashes are to be kept in a sacred place such as a cemetery. They should not be scattered or kept at home (Ad resurgendum cum Christo, 2016). Learn more: The Profession of Faith → CCC 1013, 2300–2301 · CIC can. 1176 §3 Read the full answer
Do Catholics believe in angels, demons and exorcism? What about horoscopes and tarot?

Angels and demons are real; the occult is off limits. Christ has already defeated Satan, and exorcism is done only with the bishop’s permission. Horoscopes, tarot and mediums turn us away from God. Angels and demons. Both are real. God created angels as spiritual beings, and each of us has a guardian angel (Matthew 18:10). Some angels freely rejected God and became demons, led by Satan. Jesus drove out demons many times. Satan is real but only a creature, not God’s equal, and Christ has already defeated him. Exorcism. Every baptism includes a simple prayer of exorcism. A full exorcism may be done only by a priest with the bishop’s permission (canon 1172), after doctors have ruled out mental or physical illness. True possession is rare. Horoscopes, tarot, fortune-telling, mediums and Ouija boards must all be rejected. They try to know or control the future without God, or turn to powers other than God. Even “just for fun,” they teach us to look for guidance in the wrong place and can do real spiritual harm. Trust God, who holds the future. If you have used these things, mention it in confession and get rid of tarot cards, charms and the like. Learn more: Life in Christ → CCC 328–336, 391–395, 1673, 2115–2117 · CIC can. 1172 Read the full answer

Authority and Teachings The Pope, other Christians, Purgatory and science. Faith and Reason Suffering, hell, other religions and the Church’s past. Hard Questions Marriage, life and death, the priesthood, Mary and salvation.

The Little Poor Man · 1181-1226 Francis was the son of a rich cloth merchant in Assisi, in Italy. As a young man he lived for parties, poetry and dreams of becoming a knight. He was taken prisoner in a local war and spent a year in captivity, then fell seriously ill, and both experiences shook him badly. One day, praying in a ruined church outside Assisi, he heard Christ speak to him from the crucifix: "Francis, go, repair my house, which you see is falling into ruin." At first he took it literally and started hauling stones to rebuild that church. Only later did he understand that the call was about the whole Church.

His conversion came to a head in a dramatic break with his family. His father, furious that Francis had sold some of the family’s cloth to pay for repairing the church, dragged him before the bishop. There, in front of everyone, Francis took off all his clothes, handed them back to his father and said, "From now on I call no man father, but only my Father in heaven." He embraced poverty not as a burden but as a bride, whom he called "Lady Poverty." He lived by working and begging, looked after lepers and preached. Others soon joined him, wanting to live the same radical poverty, and Pope Innocent III, after some hesitation, approved the new order: the Franciscans.

What people remember most about Francis is the way he felt related to the whole of creation. In his "Canticle of Brother Sun" he calls the sun, the moon, the wind, water and even death his "brother" and "sister," because he saw God reflected in everything God made. The stories of him preaching to the birds and making peace between a wolf and a town say more about his spirit than about history. In 1223, in the Italian town of Greccio, he is said to have set up the first living Nativity scene, with real animals, and today’s Christmas cribs go back to him. Two years before he died, during a long time of fasting and prayer, marks like Christ’s wounds from the cross (the stigmata) are said to have appeared on his body, the first case on record. He died in 1226, at forty-four, welcoming "Sister Death." Pope Francis took his name from him. His feast day is October 4.
Free e-books, free Catholic books to read online. Great Catholic books, free to read online in updated English: The Confessions of St. Augustine, with more to come.

An Aramaic word for "Father," expressing a child's intimate trust, used by Jesus in addressing God. Through the Holy Spirit, the baptized share His filial relationship and may also cry out, "Abba! Father!" (Mark 14:36, Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6). CCC 683, 742, 2605, 2766

The superior of an autonomous community of nuns (an abbey), usually elected by the community according to its rule and constitutions. She receives a liturgical blessing from the bishop, which is not ordination, and governs her community in spiritual and temporal matters. CCC 1672
A priest who exercises ecclesiastical jurisdiction over a monastery or religious community of monks, similar in leadership to a bishop over a diocese.

Deliberate termination of pregnancy by killing the unborn child. Direct abortion, willed either as an end or a means, is gravely contrary to the moral law, and the Church attaches the canonical penalty of excommunication to this crime against human life. CCC 2271-2272

The Old Testament patriarch with whom God established a covenant, promising land and countless descendants. Abraham served as the father in faith for Israel and for all Christians, preparing the way for Christ, in whom all nations are blessed. CCC 59, 72, 145, 2570

The act by which an ordained priest, acting in the person of Christ (in persona Christi) and by authority granted to the Church, grants divine forgiveness of sins to a repentant penitent in the Sacrament of Reconciliation. CCC 1424, 1442, 1449
Refraining from eating meat or specified foods on designated penitential days (such as Ash Wednesday and Fridays during Lent) as a spiritual discipline and act of interior penance. CCC 1438, 2043
A state of spiritual sloth, apathy, or listlessness regarding divine love and heavenly goods; one of the seven capital sins. CCC 1866, 2094, 2733

A liturgical minister instituted to assist the priest and deacon at the altar during Mass and other liturgical rites. While formally instituted acolytes are traditionally candidates for Holy Orders or installed laymen, altar servers also fulfill this role. CCC 903, 1672

A prayer in which the penitent expresses sorrow for sin, above all for having offended God who is all good, and firmly resolves with His grace to sin no more and to avoid the occasions of sin. It is said in the Sacrament of Penance before absolution and is fitting in daily prayer. CCC 1451-1453
A temporary, supernatural help from God that enlightens the mind and strengthens the human will to perform a good action, resist temptation, or avoid sin. CCC 1996, 2000
Any willful thought, word, deed, desire, or omission forbidden by the law of God, committed by a person with the use of reason (contrasted with Original Sin). CCC 1849-1850, 1853

From the Latin ad limina Apostolorum, "to the thresholds of the Apostles"; the visit that diocesan bishops are obliged to make to Rome, ordinarily every five years, to venerate the tombs of Saints Peter and Paul, meet the Pope, and report on the state of their dioceses.

According to Genesis, the first human being, created in original holiness and justice. Through Adam's disobedience ("original sin"), humanity lost this original grace. Christ is called the "New Adam" because He restores humanity through His perfect obedience. CCC 359, 375, 402-404, 504

The highest worship and praise due to God alone (latria), acknowledging Him as Creator, Savior, and Lord. Eucharistic Adoration specifically refers to the practice of praying directly before Jesus Christ, truly present in the Holy Eucharist. CCC 2096, 2628
Marital infidelity, or sexual relations between two individuals where at least one is married to someone else; forbidden absolutely by the Sixth Commandment. CCC 2380, 2381

The four-week liturgical season of prayerful preparation preceding Christmas, beginning after the Feast of Christ the King. It possesses a twofold character: preparing for the Second Coming of Christ in glory and celebrating His first coming at the Incarnation. CCC 524
One who pleads or intercedes on behalf of another; a title applied to Jesus Christ, our heavenly Intercessor, and to the Holy Spirit (Paraclete). CCC 692, 2634
The self-giving, unconditional divine love that seeks the supreme good of others, reflecting God's own nature and inner life (1 John 4:8). CCC 218-221
One of the four traditional qualities of a glorified body following the final resurrection, enabling it to move effortlessly according to the soul's desire. CCC 645, 999

(pronounced AH-nyoos DEH-ee) Latin for " Lamb of God "; a title applied to Jesus Christ (John 1:29). Refers both to the liturgical invocation sung before Holy Communion during Mass and to a blessed wax emblem bearing the image of a lamb. CCC 608
A long, white linen garment worn by priests, deacons, and liturgical ministers, recalling the white robe received at Baptism and symbolizing purity of soul. CCC 1269
A Holy Day of Obligation celebrated on November 1st to honor all the saints in Heaven, both known and unknown. CCC 954-959
Commemorated on November 2nd as a day of solemn prayer and Mass offerings for all the faithful departed undergoing purification in Purgatory. CCC 1032
A joyful Hebrew acclamation meaning " Praise the Lord," sung or proclaimed before the Reading of the Gospel during Mass (omitted during Lent).
Possessing infinite power, wisdom, and authority; an essential attribute belonging to God alone. CCC 268-274
Money, food, or resources given to the poor as an act of fraternal charity, justice, and interior penance. CCC 1434, 2447
The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, applied to Jesus Christ to signify that He is the beginning, center, and ultimate fulfillment of all creation (Revelation 1:8). CCC 668

The sacred table in the sanctuary upon which the Sacrifice of the Mass is offered. It represents both the altar of Christ's sacrifice on the cross and the table of the Eucharistic banquet. CCC 1182, 1383
An elevated lectern, podium, or pulpit in the sanctuary from which Sacred Scripture is proclaimed, the homily is delivered, and announcements or intercessions are made during Mass. CCC 1184
A secure niche or cabinet in a church where the three holy oils blessed by the bishop at the Chrism Mass (Oil of the Sick, Oil of Catechumens, and Sacred Chrism) are kept.
A Hebrew word meaning "truly," "so be it," or "it is true." Used at the end of prayers, creeds, and Eucharistic acclamations to signify personal assent and faith. CCC 1061-1065, 2856
A square white linen cloth worn around the neck and shoulders by clergy beneath the alb, historically symbolizing the "helmet of salvation."
The spiritual sense of Sacred Scripture that interprets biblical events in light of their eternal significance, leading believers toward Heaven. CCC 117
The inner harmony and coherence that exists among all the truths of divine revelation defined by the Church. CCC 114
The liturgical commemoration and "remembrance" of God's saving acts in salvation history, particularly Christ's Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension made present in the Mass. CCC 1103, 1354, 1362
The Eucharistic Prayer, the central prayer of thanksgiving and consecration during the Mass. CCC 1352
A formal condemnation or excommunication issued by the Church regarding opinions or teachings directly opposed to Catholic dogma.
A purely spiritual, personal, and immortal creature endowed with intelligence and free will, serving as a messenger and servant of God. CCC 328-336
A traditional Catholic prayer commemorating the Incarnation of Christ, recited three times daily (6 a.m., 12 p.m., 6 p.m.) accompanied by the ringing of church bells.
An uncontrolled passion or desire for revenge; when unchecked by reason, it becomes one of the seven capital sins. CCC 1765, 1866, 2262
An official declaration by a Catholic ecclesiastical tribunal that a marriage was invalid from its inception due to a lack of essential conditions, freedom, or canonical form. CCC 1629

The visit of the Archangel Gabriel to the Virgin Mary on March 25th (nine months before Christmas) to obtain her consent to God's plan that she become the Mother of the Savior Jesus Christ through the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:26-38). CCC 484, 494

To anoint is to pour or rub oil on a person as a sign of consecration, healing, or strength. In Israel kings, priests, and sometimes prophets were anointed; Jesus is the Anointed One (Messiah, Christ) of the Holy Spirit, and Christians share His anointing in Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders. CCC 436, 695, 1294
The liturgical application of consecrated oil on a person or sacred object, symbolizing the gift of the Holy Spirit, healing, or dedication to sacred service. CCC 695, 1289

One of the Seven Sacraments of Healing, administered by a priest to a baptized Christian facing serious illness, major surgery, or old age, conferring spiritual comfort, peace, physical healing, and the forgiveness of sins. CCC 1499-1532
An ultimate false messianic movement or figure mentioned in Sacred Scripture that exalts human achievement over God, preceding Christ's Second Coming. CCC 675-677
A short sentence, verse, or refrain chanted or sung before and after a psalm or canticle during liturgical worship.
A genre of biblical literature revealing hidden divine truths through vivid imagery; specifically refers to the Book of Revelation. CCC 677

Books or writings of uncertain authorship or lacking canonical authority. In Protestant usage, refers to books Catholics call Deuterocanonical; in Catholic usage, refers to non-inspired ancient writings omitted from the biblical canon.
The branch of Christian theology dedicated to explaining, defending, and giving a reasoned justification (apologia) for the Catholic faith. CCC 156
A way of approaching God by articulating what He is not, acknowledging that the divine essence infinitely transcends human language and concepts. CCC 230
The total rejection and repudiation of the Christian faith by a baptized person. CCC 2089
One of the twelve men chosen directly by Jesus Christ to be His primary witnesses, sent forth to preach the Gospel and lay the foundation of the Church. CCC 857-860
An ancient summary of Christian belief developed from the early baptismal liturgy of the Church in Rome. CCC 194
The activity and organization of the Christian directed toward serving, spreading the Gospel, and extending Christ's kingdom across the world. CCC 863
Pertaining to the Apostles, their authority, teachings, or succession maintained by the Church. CCC 857

A prelate, usually a bishop, appointed by the Holy See to govern a particular church in the Pope 's name, either temporarily (when a diocese is vacant or its bishop is impeded) or stably, in a territory called an apostolic administration that has not yet been erected as a diocese.
A special blessing imparted by the Pope, or by a bishop or priest with papal delegation, often granted at the hour of death accompanied by a plenary indulgence.
A pastoral message issued by a Pope or Bishop offering encouragement and clear direction on a specific issue or aspect of Christian living.

The Christian writers of the late first and early second centuries who knew the Apostles or their immediate disciples, such as Saint Clement of Rome, Saint Ignatius of Antioch, and Saint Polycarp of Smyrna. Their writings, together with works like the Didache, are precious witnesses to the faith, worship, and order of the early Church.
A formal papal document issued by the Pope addressing specific doctrinal, administrative, or pastoral matters.
The official diplomatic embassy of the Holy See in a specific nation.

A diplomat, usually with the rank of archbishop, who represents the Pope both to the government of a country and to the Catholic Church there. He strengthens the bonds between the Holy See and the local bishops and assists in the process of selecting candidates for the episcopate.

A portion of the People of God, usually in mission territory, not yet established as a diocese, and entrusted to a prefect apostolic, often a priest rather than a bishop, who governs it in the name of the Pope. It is ordinarily an early stage toward a vicariate or diocese.
The unbroken line of sacred preaching and authority handed down from the Apostles to Catholic bishops through the laying on of hands in Holy Orders. CCC 77, 861

The living transmission of the Gospel that the Apostles received from Christ and the Holy Spirit and handed on by their preaching, example, and institutions; the bishops, their successors, preserve it. Together with Sacred Scripture it forms the one deposit of faith, and it is distinct from local customs and lesser traditions. CCC 76-78, 83

A portion of the People of God, usually in mission territory, not yet established as a diocese and entrusted to a vicar apostolic, ordinarily a titular bishop, who governs it in the name of the Pope. Many vicariates later become dioceses as the local Church matures.
A supernatural manifestation of Christ, the Virgin Mary, an angel, or a saint to individuals on earth. CCC 67

The semicircular or polygonal recess, often vaulted, at the end of a church behind or around the altar, traditionally at the east end. In ancient basilicas the bishop's chair stood in the apse with a bench for the presbyters, and the apse is often adorned with mosaics or paintings of Christ.
A high-ranking angel entrusted with solemn, pivotal messages in salvation history (e.g., Saints Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael). CCC 335
A bishop who governs an archdiocese, often serving as the Metropolitan of an ecclesiastical province overseeing neighboring dioceses.

A diocese given the rank of archdiocese and governed by an archbishop. Most archdioceses are metropolitan sees, heading an ecclesiastical province of neighboring dioceses, though some are not; the title gives honor and certain duties but no authority over the internal government of other dioceses.

In the Eastern Catholic Churches, an eparchy whose bishop holds the title of archbishop (archeparch). It is often the metropolitan see of an ecclesiastical province, corresponding to an archdiocese in the Latin Church.
A private repository maintained by a diocese or religious community to preserve church history, administrative documents, and sacramental registers.

A title of precedence among priests. In the Latin Church it may designate a dean (vicar forane) who coordinates a group of parishes, and the cardinals who head the major papal basilicas bear the title; in Eastern Churches it is an honorary rank conferred on senior priests.

The gold-covered chest of acacia wood made at God's command in the desert, holding the tablets of the Law and topped by the mercy seat with two cherubim; it was the sign of God's presence among Israel. Christian tradition sees in Mary the Ark of the New Covenant, in whom the Lord dwelt (Exodus 25:10-22). CCC 2130, 2578, 2676
The entry of Jesus' humanity into divine glory in Heaven forty days (six weeks) after His Resurrection. CCC 659-667
The practice of self-denial, spiritual discipline, mortification, and fasting undertaken to grow in holiness and overcome sinful inclinations. CCC 2015
The divine attribute of God existing in and of Himself, dependent on no other cause or creator. CCC 213
The first day of the penitential season of Lent, marked by fasting, abstinence, and the imposition of ashes on the forehead as a public sign of repentance and human mortality. CCC 1438
The rite of sprinkling holy water upon the congregation or sacred objects, using a perforated vessel or brush called an aspergillium.
A brief, fervent prayer uttered mentally or aloud throughout the day to elevate the heart to God. CCC 2688
The gathered congregation of the faithful participating in a liturgical service. CCC 1140
A priest assigned to assist the pastor in the care and administration of a parish.
The Catholic dogma declared in 1950 recognizing Mary 's singular participation in her Son's Resurrection, by which she was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory on August 15th. CCC 966
The denial or rejection of the existence of God; a violation of the First Commandment. CCC 2124-2126
The reconciliation of God and humanity accomplished through the sacrificial death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. CCC 613-618
An essential quality or perfection belonging to God's infinite nature, such as eternal existence, omnipotence, omniscience, and unchangeability. CCC 212-213, 268
Sorrow for sin motivated primarily by fear of God's punishment or the ugliness of sin, rather than pure love for God. CCC 1453
One or more additional bishops assigned to a diocese by the Pope to assist the diocesan bishop in governing and pastoring the local Church.

The principal Marian prayer, joining the greetings of the angel Gabriel and of Elizabeth to a petition for Mary 's intercession: "Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death." It forms the heart of the Rosary and the Angelus (Luke 1:28, 42). CCC 2676-2677
A sweet-smelling resin derived from aromatic plants, mixed with olive oil by the bishop to create Sacred Chrism.
Public announcements made in a parish church prior to a wedding to ensure there are no canonical impediments to the union.
The foundational Sacrament of Initiation that cleanses original and personal sin, incorporates a person into the Body of Christ, and welcomes them into the Church. CCC 1213-1274
The grace of Baptism received by an unbaptized person who suffers martyrdom for the Christian faith. CCC 1258

The grace of Baptism conferred on an unbaptized person who possesses explicit or implicit sorrow for sin, perfect charity, and the desire to fulfill God's will when sacramental Baptism is impossible. CCC 1259

The feast commemorating Jesus' baptism by John in the Jordan, when the Holy Spirit descended upon Him like a dove and the Father proclaimed Him His beloved Son. In the Roman Rite it closes the Christmas season; in the Eastern Churches it is celebrated as the Theophany on January 6 (Matthew 3:13-17). CCC 535-536, 1224
A permanent vessel or basin in a church containing the water used for celebrating the Sacrament of Baptism. CCC 1185

The renunciation of sin and Satan and the profession of faith made at Baptism, by the candidate or, for an infant, by parents and godparents. The faithful renew them each year at Easter, and confirmands renew them in the celebration of Confirmation. CCC 1237, 1254, 1298

Small communities of Catholics, especially widespread in Latin America, Africa, and Asia, who gather regularly for prayer, the reading of Scripture, mutual support, and service of their neighbors. The Church commends them as a hope for evangelization when they remain united with their parish, their bishop, and the universal Church.
A designation of honor granted by the Pope to specific church buildings due to exceptional historical, architectural, or liturgical significance.
The direct, face-to-face contemplation and ultimate enjoyment of God in Heaven experienced by the saints and angels. CCC 1023, 1028
A formal papal declaration permitting local veneration of a deceased faithful person, bestowing the title " Blessed," the final step before canonization.
The teachings of Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:3-12) outlining the spiritual conditions and moral attitudes that bring true eternal happiness in God's kingdom. CCC 1716-1724
A biblical title given to Satan, the prince of demons. CCC 391

In the Byzantine tradition, the raised sanctuary behind the iconostasis where the altar stands. In the Syriac tradition, the word designates a raised platform in the middle of the nave from which the Liturgy of the Word is celebrated; the term also names the reading platform of a synagogue.
A liturgical devotional service in which the priest blesses the assembled congregation with the exposed Eucharist displayed in a monstrance. CCC 1378
A long vestment draped over the shoulders and hands of a priest or deacon when holding the monstrance during Eucharistic Benediction.
The historic town in Judea where Jesus Christ was born in a stable, fulfilling messianic prophecy. CCC 525
The inspired collection of 73 canonical books (46 Old Testament, 27 New Testament) that record God's salvation history and divine revelation for humanity. CCC 101-133

Renderings of Sacred Scripture from the original Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek into other languages, such as the Greek Septuagint and Saint Jerome's Latin Vulgate. Catholic editions contain all seventy-three books and require approval by Church authority; translations for liturgical use are approved by the bishops and confirmed by the Holy See.

(From Greek episkopos, "overseer") A successor to the Apostles appointed by the Pope who possesses the fullness of Holy Orders and serves as the chief shepherd, teacher, and governor of a diocese. CCC 1560, 1594

The title of a diocesan or auxiliary bishop whose resignation from office has been accepted by the Pope. Diocesan bishops are asked to submit their resignation at age seventy-five, or earlier for illness or another grave reason; a bishop emeritus remains a bishop and a member of the College of Bishops.

The permanent assembly of the bishops of a nation or territory, who jointly exercise certain pastoral functions for the faithful there, such as approving liturgical translations. Its general decrees bind only in cases set by law or by mandate of the Holy See, and after review by it. CCC 887
Uttering words of hatred, reproach, defiance, or disrespect against God, the Church, or sacred things. CCC 2148
A title given to the Holy Eucharist reserved in the tabernacle for adoration or distribution to the sick, containing the true Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity of Jesus Christ. CCC 1330, 1378
The official title bestowed upon a deceased member of the faithful who has been beatified by the Pope, permitting public veneration on the pathway to canonization.

A divine and life-giving action whose source is the Father; in response, man blesses God in adoration and thanksgiving. As a sacramental, a blessing praises God and asks His gifts for persons, meals, objects, or places, usually with the Sign of the Cross; some are reserved to the ordained. CCC 1078, 1669, 1671-1672
The liturgical book containing the Gospel readings proclaimed by a deacon or priest during Mass.
A metallic vessel used to hold burning charcoal for burning incense during liturgical services.
The physical elements of unleavened wheat bread and pure grape wine transformed during Mass into the Body and Blood of Christ. CCC 1333-1336
The liturgical action performed by the priest before Communion, recalling Christ's actions at the Last Supper and symbolizing unity among believers. CCC 1329, 1383

From the Latin breviarium, "summary"; the book containing the texts of the Liturgy of the Hours, including psalms, canticles, hymns, readings, and prayers for each day and hour. It is used by clergy and religious obliged to pray the Office and by many lay faithful.
One of the four qualities of a glorified body following the resurrection, causing it to shine with heavenly splendor and light. CCC 999

A man who belongs to a religious institute and has professed the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity, and obedience, but is not ordained and is not preparing for the priesthood. Brothers serve through prayer, community life, and works such as teaching, nursing, and care of the poor; some institutes consist entirely of brothers.
An official, formal decree or document issued by the Pope, traditionally sealed with a lead stamp (bulla).
The sin of harming another person's reputation by spreading false statements or lies. CCC 2477, 2479
The hill outside the walls of Jerusalem where Jesus Christ was crucified for the salvation of the world. CCC 616

In Christian initiation, a person who is already validly baptized in another Christian denomination (or an uncatechized Catholic) who is preparing for full reception into communion with the Catholic Church through a profession of faith, Confirmation, and Holy Eucharist.

The feast on February 2, forty days after Christmas, commemorating Mary and Joseph's presentation of the infant Jesus in the Temple, where Simeon hailed Him as "a light for revelation to the Gentiles." Candles are blessed and carried in procession; the Byzantine tradition calls the feast the Meeting (Luke 2:22-38). CCC 529

Lights used in the liturgy and in devotion as signs of Christ, the Light of the world, and of faith, prayer, and joy. Candles are placed on or near the altar at Mass, carried in processions, and given at Baptism, lit from the Paschal candle to signify that Christ has enlightened the newly baptized. CCC 1154, 1189, 1243

A rule, standard, or official list. Refers to the official collection of inspired books of the Bible (Canon of Scripture), the body of Church law, or the principal Eucharistic prayer of the Mass. CCC 120
The body of ecclesiastical laws and norms governing good order and discipline in the visible society of the Catholic Church.

The complete list of the books that the Church, guided by apostolic Tradition, recognizes as divinely inspired Sacred Scripture: forty-six books of the Old Testament and twenty-seven of the New. It was taught by early councils and solemnly defined by the Council of Trent. CCC 120, 138

The ancient Eucharistic Prayer of the Roman Rite, for centuries its only Eucharistic Prayer and now Eucharistic Prayer I of the Roman Missal. "Canon" means "rule," referring to its fixed text, which commemorates the Virgin Mary, the Apostles, and many early martyrs. CCC 1352-1354

The solemn declaration by the Pope that a deceased member of the faithful lived a life of heroic virtue or suffered martyrdom, is in Heaven, and is proposed as an intercessor and model of holiness for universal veneration. CCC 828

A song of praise found in Sacred Scripture outside the Book of Psalms, such as the Canticle of Moses, the Canticle of Daniel, or the Magnificat. In the Liturgy of the Hours, the Benedictus is sung at Morning Prayer, the Magnificat at Evening Prayer, and the Nunc Dimittis at Night Prayer. CCC 1196, 2619
A lay or ordained minister who leads the congregation in singing scripture, hymns, and responses during the liturgy.
The seven primary moral vices that engender other sins: pride, covetousness (greed), lust, anger (wrath), gluttony, envy, and sloth (acedia). CCC 1866
A high-ranking prelate appointed by the Pope to serve in the College of Cardinals, advising the Holy See and electing new Popes during a Conclave.

The cardinal who, in the name of the Pope as Bishop of Rome, exercises the ordinary pastoral governance of the Diocese of Rome, assisted by auxiliary bishops. Vatican City has its own vicar general, distinct from the Cardinal Vicar.
The four principal moral virtues upon which all other human virtues hinge: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. CCC 1805-1809

The days of festivity before Lent, culminating on Shrove Tuesday, called Mardi Gras ("Fat Tuesday"), the day before Ash Wednesday. Rooted in the custom of using up rich foods before the Lenten fast, it is a popular tradition rather than a liturgical observance.
A full-length ankle-level robe worn as ecclesiastical dress by clergy and altar servers (black for priests, violet for bishops, red for cardinals, white for the Pope).

In moral theology, the method of resolving particular cases of conscience by applying general moral principles to concrete circumstances. Rightly used, it helps confessors and the faithful form prudent judgments; when it loses sight of the virtues and the call to holiness, it can become legalistic or lax.

Underground burial galleries, chiefly outside the walls of ancient Rome, where early Christians buried their dead and honored the martyrs, especially on the anniversaries of their deaths. Their inscriptions and paintings are among the earliest witnesses to Christian faith and art.

Systematic religious instruction and spiritual formation (from the Greek for "teaching") oriented toward introducing believers into the fullness of Christian life and making them disciples of Jesus Christ. CCC 4-10
Relating to the methods, theories, and practice of religious teaching and instruction. CCC 4-6
The age of reason (traditionally around seven years old) at which a child is considered capable of moral responsibility, personal faith discernment, and receiving the Sacraments of Initiation.
A compendium or comprehensive summary of Catholic doctrine regarding faith, morals, sacraments, and prayer intended for popular use and catechesis. CCC 11-12
The official compendium of Catholic doctrine promulgated by Pope John Paul II in 1992 as an authoritative reference for faith and morals.

A member of the faithful, most often a layperson, who teaches the faith in the name of the Church, preparing children, youth, and adults for the sacraments and accompanying their growth in Christian life. In 2021 Pope Francis instituted the lay ministry of catechist for the universal Church.
An unbaptized person preparing for entry into the Catholic Church through the Sacraments of Initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist). CCC 1247-1249
The second extended period in the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults (OCIA) involving intense formation through God's Word, worship, community life, and apostolic service. CCC 1230, 1247
The official chair of the bishop located in his cathedral, symbolizing his pastoral authority and teaching office within the diocese. CCC 1558
The principal church of a diocese, housing the bishop's official cathedra.

Derived from Greek katholikos, meaning "universal" or "comprehensive." One of the four marks of the Church in the Nicene Creed, used since at least the early 2nd century (St. Ignatius of Antioch) to designate the universal Church founded by Christ. CCC 830-835
The active participation and apostolic work of lay Catholics under the guidance and leadership of their bishops.

The one Church founded by Christ, which subsists in the Church governed by the successor of Peter and the bishops in communion with him. She is "catholic," meaning universal, because Christ is fully present in her and she is sent to all peoples; she comprises the Latin Church and the Eastern Catholic Churches. CCC 816, 830-831

The seven New Testament letters of James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2, and 3 John, and Jude. They are called "catholic," meaning universal, because most of them are addressed to the Church at large rather than to one local community or person.
The national assembly of Catholic bishops in Canada responsible for publishing ritual texts, liturgical translations, and pastoral directives.
The bishop or priest who presides over a liturgical assembly and consecrates the Eucharist. CCC 1348
The seat in the sanctuary occupied by the presiding priest, representing his role of leading prayer and presiding over the worshiping assembly. CCC 1184
The voluntary state of remaining unmarried for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven, embraced by bishops, priests in the Latin Rite, and religious to dedicate themselves entirely to God. CCC 1579, 1599
The sacred cup made of durable, precious material used to hold the wine that becomes the Precious Blood of Christ during Mass.

The diocesan official or curia employee responsible for gathering, safeguarding, and maintaining official archdiocesan archives, records, and sacramental registers, serving as the official notary on diocesan documents.
The administrative offices and executive headquarters of a diocese where the bishop and his curia oversee church administration.

A papal honor granted to a priest at the request of his bishop, carrying the title " Monsignor." Since 2014 it is the only such honor granted to diocesan priests, ordinarily to those who have reached sixty-five years of age.
