A traditional title for the Church, who gives birth to her children to new life through Baptism, nourishes them with the Word and the sacraments, and teaches them the faith. The term also designates a cathedral or the original church from which other churches were founded. CCC 169, 507, 2040

The mountain in the wilderness where God revealed Himself to Moses, established His covenant with Israel, and gave the Ten Commandments. It is also called Horeb, especially in Deuteronomy; there the prophet Elijah also encountered God in a still small voice (Exodus 19:16-20, 1 Kings 19:8-12). CCC 62, 2060
The post-baptismal period in Christian initiation (from Easter to Pentecost) dedicated to reflecting on the sacraments received and integrating into full parish life. CCC 1075
"The Mystery of Faith ": the acclamation proclaimed by the priest and faithful immediately following the consecration during Mass.
A truth revealed by God that transcends human reason's full comprehension, though not contrary to reason. CCC 50, 774

Mysticism is the intimate union of the soul with God, called "mystical" because it shares in the mystery of Christ through the sacraments and, in Him, in the mystery of the Trinity. All are called to this union; a mystic is one who receives it to a high degree, sometimes with extraordinary graces. CCC 2014
The spiritual reality of the Church, in which Christ is the Head and all baptized believers are united as members. CCC 787-795
The vestibule or enclosed entryway located directly inside the main entrance of a church building leading into the nave.

A personal parish established not for a territory but for Catholics of a particular nationality or language, so that they may receive pastoral care, the liturgy, and preaching in their own tongue and culture. Canon law provides for such personal parishes alongside territorial ones.
The universal moral principles inscribed by God upon the human heart and accessible through human reason. CCC 1954-1960

The knowledge of God that human beings can attain with certainty by the natural light of reason from the created world and the human person. Because of sin this knowledge is difficult, so humanity needs God’s supernatural Revelation, which completes and surpasses it (Romans 1:19-20). CCC 32, 36-38

The main body of a church building, between the narthex and the sanctuary, where the faithful assemble for the liturgy. Its name comes from the Latin navis, "ship," recalling the image of the Church as the ark of salvation.

The town in Galilee where the Annunciation took place and where Jesus lived the greater part of His life with Mary and Joseph, obedient to them and working with His hands. The hidden life at Nazareth sanctifies ordinary daily life and work (Luke 1:26-27, 2:51). CCC 531-534
(From Greek for "new plant/sprout") A newly baptized person during their first year of full communion in the Catholic Church. CCC 1248
The definitive covenant established by Jesus Christ through His blood on the Cross, fulfilling and perfecting the Old Covenant. CCC 73, 580

The perfection on earth of the divine law, natural and revealed, given by Christ and expressed especially in the Sermon on the Mount. It is above all the grace of the Holy Spirit, an interior law of charity, which uses the sacraments to give us the strength to live it. CCC 1965-1966

The twenty-seven inspired books of Sacred Scripture written after Christ: the four Gospels, Acts, the apostolic Letters, and Revelation. Their central object is Jesus Christ, and the Gospels form the heart of all the Scriptures. CCC 120, 124-127
The solemn profession of faith formulated at the Councils of Nicaea (A.D. 325) and Constantinople (A.D. 381), recited at Mass on Sundays and Solemnities. CCC 195
A formal declaration by an official Church censor stating that a book or publication contains nothing contrary to Catholic faith or morals.
Nine consecutive days of prayer offered for a specific intention or spiritual grace, modeled after the nine days the Apostles prayed before Pentecost. CCC 2688

A person admitted to the novitiate of a religious institute, who begins the life of the institute under a director of novices in order to discern the vocation and be formed in its spirit. A novice is not yet bound by religious vows and may freely leave.
A formal period of spiritual discernment, study, and training undertaken before a candidate takes vows in a religious order.

An informal name (Latin, "new order") for the Order of Mass of the Roman Missal promulgated by Pope St. Paul VI in 1969 after the Second Vatican Council. It is the ordinary form of celebrating Mass in the Roman Rite today.
A woman who has taken solemn, perpetual vows in a cloistered religious order, dedicating her life to contemplative prayer. CCC 918

A Ritual Mass within which the Sacrament of Matrimony is celebrated, normally the case for a marriage between two Catholics in the Latin Church. Its Nuptial Blessing, given after the Lord’s Prayer, invokes God’s grace and the Holy Spirit upon the new couple, especially the bride. CCC 1621, 1624
The moral virtue and evangelical counsel that disposes a person to submit their will to legitimate authority and ultimately to God's directives. CCC 144, 915

An oblation is an offering to God. An oblate is a person who offers himself to God in association with a religious community, such as a lay or secular oblate attached to a Benedictine monastery. The term also forms the name of several congregations, such as the Oblates of Mary Immaculate.
OCIA / RCIA (Order / Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults)

The official process through which unbaptized adults (catechumens) and baptized non-Catholics (candidates) are formed and received into full communion with the Catholic Church. CCC 1232-1233, 1247-1249
The portion of the Mass in which the bread, wine, and gifts of the faithful are presented at the altar. CCC 1350-1351

The chant or hymn sung during the Preparation of the Gifts at Mass, while the bread and wine (and gifts for the poor) are brought in procession to the altar and placed upon it. It continues at least until the gifts are placed on the altar.
Holy olive oil blessed by the bishop, used to anoint candidates before Baptism to strengthen them against temptation. CCC 1237
Holy olive oil blessed by the bishop, used in the Sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick. CCC 1513
The covenant made by God with the people of Israel through Abraham, Moses, and the prophets, preparing for the Coming of Christ. CCC 54-64

The Law given by God to Israel through Moses, the first stage of revealed law, whose moral precepts are summed up in the Ten Commandments. Holy and good yet imperfect, it prepared for the Gospel and is fulfilled in Christ. CCC 1961-1964

The forty-six inspired books of Sacred Scripture written before the coming of Christ, from Genesis to Malachi. Christians venerate them as the true Word of God, for they prepare for and announce Christ, and the Old Covenant has never been revoked. CCC 120-123

The divine attribute by which God is present everywhere, not as one thing among others, but as Creator sustaining all things in being and present to His creatures’ inmost being, while remaining infinitely greater than all His works (Psalm 139:7-10, Acts 17:28). CCC 300

The prayer said by the priest at the end of the Introductory Rites of Mass. After the invitation "Let us pray" and a moment of silence, he gathers (collects) the prayers of the people into one, expressing the character of the day’s celebration; the people respond " Amen." It ends by naming the Trinity: “… who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever.” Since 2021 the English no longer says “one God” here, which could suggest that Christ is one God among others; the Latin is simply Deus , “God”.

The fixed structure and texts of the Mass as given in the Roman Missal (Ordo Missae): the Introductory Rites, the Liturgy of the Word, the Liturgy of the Eucharist, and the Concluding Rites. Its two principal parts form one single act of worship. CCC 1346-1347
A bishop or religious superior exercising territorial or jurisdictional authority within the Church.
The weeks of the liturgical year outside the major seasons of Advent, Christmas, Lent, and Easter, providing opportunity to reflect on Christ's public ministry and daily Christian living. CCC 1163
The liturgical rite of Holy Orders by which a man is consecrated as a deacon, priest, or bishop. CCC 1538
The initial state of harmony, grace, and innocence enjoyed by Adam and Eve prior to Original Sin. CCC 374-379
The fallen state of human nature inherited by all descendants of Adam and Eve, depriving humanity of original holiness and cleansed through Baptism. CCC 396-409

The Eastern Churches not in full communion with the See of Rome, chiefly those separated since the eleventh century, together with the ancient Oriental Orthodox Churches. They possess true sacraments, above all the priesthood and the Eucharist by apostolic succession, and are joined to the Catholic Church in a profound, though imperfect, communion. CCC 838, 1399
Sound, correct belief adhering to the defined doctrines and sacred tradition of the Church (contrasted with heterodoxy/heresy).

Historically, a person who worships many gods or follows a religion other than Judaism, Christianity, or Islam; from the Latin paganus, "country dweller." The Church calls all people to the knowledge of the one true God while respecting whatever is true and holy in their traditions.
A stiffened white linen square used to cover the chalice during Mass; also the large white cloth draped over a casket during a Catholic funeral.

A narrow band of white lamb’s wool marked with black crosses, worn over the chasuble around the shoulders by the Pope and by metropolitan archbishops. It signifies the metropolitan’s authority and communion with the Successor of Peter, and is given by the Pope, usually on the Solemnity of Sts. Peter and Paul.
The Sunday before Easter celebrating Jesus' triumphant entrance into Jerusalem, marking the beginning of Holy Week. CCC 559
The supreme office, jurisdiction, and ministry of the Pope as the Successor of St. Peter and earthly head of the Catholic Church. CCC 880-882
A short story or allegory drawn from everyday life used by Jesus to illustrate spiritual truths and the mysteries of the Kingdom of God. CCC 546
A title for the Holy Spirit derived from Greek, meaning " Advocate," "Helper," "Comforter," or "Counselor" (John 14:16). CCC 692
A biblical name for Heaven and the original state of innocence in the Garden of Eden. CCC 374, 1023
A distinct community of Catholic faithful established within a diocese under the pastoral care of a pastor appointed by the bishop. CCC 2179

A consultative body of clergy, religious, and lay faithful in a parish who, under the presidency of the pastor, help promote pastoral activity. The diocesan bishop decides whether to establish such councils; they are distinct from the parish finance council, which every parish must have. CCC 911

A period of several days of special preaching, prayer, and opportunities for Confession, often given by a visiting priest or religious, to renew the faith and Christian life of a parish and call back those who have drifted from the practice of the faith.

The priest to whom a parish is entrusted as its proper shepherd under the authority of the diocesan bishop (in Latin, parochus; usually called the pastor in the United States). The term is also used broadly of any priest serving in a parish. CCC 2179
The glorious Second Coming of Jesus Christ at the end of time to judge the living and the dead. CCC 668-674, 1040

A diocese (or eparchy in the Eastern Churches), or a community equivalent to it, of the Christian faithful in communion of faith and sacraments with their bishop ordained in apostolic succession. In it the one, holy, catholic, and apostolic Church is truly present. CCC 833-835

The unblemished lamb sacrificed and eaten by Israel at the Passover, whose blood marked the doors and spared the people. It prefigured Jesus Christ, the true Lamb of God, sacrificed for the sins of the world and given as food in the Eucharist (Exodus 12:1-13, 1 Corinthians 5:7). CCC 608, 1340
The passion, death, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus Christ, by which He redeemed humanity. CCC 571, 1067
The suffering underwent by Jesus during His agony in the garden, trial, flagellation, and crucifixion. CCC 599-618

The Sunday before Easter, now officially called Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord, which opens Holy Week with the commemoration of Christ’s entry into Jerusalem and the reading of the Passion. Before the liturgical reform of 1969, the name designated the Fifth Sunday of Lent. CCC 560

Emotions or movements of the sensitive appetite, such as love, desire, joy, fear, and anger, which incline us to act or not to act toward something perceived as good or evil. In themselves neither good nor evil, they become morally good or evil as they engage reason and will. CCC 1763-1767
The annual Jewish feast commemorating Israel 's liberation from Egyptian slavery, serving as the prefiguration of Christ's Paschal sacrifice. CCC 1334, 1363
A priest (from Latin pastor, "shepherd") delegated by the bishop to exercise direct pastoral, spiritual, and administrative care over a parish community. CCC 2179

The care of souls (cura animarum) by which pastors, in the name of Christ the Good Shepherd, teach, sanctify, and guide the faithful entrusted to them. The term also covers the works of service by which priests, deacons, religious, and lay faithful accompany people, especially the sick, the poor, and the grieving.

A letter addressed by a bishop to the faithful of his diocese, or by a conference of bishops to the faithful of its territory, to teach, exhort, or give guidance on matters of faith, morals, and Christian life.
A small plate, usually of precious metal, used at Mass to hold the bread that becomes the Body of Christ. With the chalice, it is a sacred vessel reserved for the celebration of the Eucharist.
An Old Testament father of faith (e.g., Abraham, Isaac, Jacob); also a high-ranking bishop presiding over an Eastern Catholic Patriarchate. CCC 59-61
A saint chosen as a special intercessor and advocate for a person, profession, parish, or nation. CCC 2156
A cross worn on a chain or cord over the breast by the Pope, cardinals, bishops, and abbots as a sign of their office. In some Eastern Churches, priests also wear a pectoral cross.
A 5th-century heresy denying Original Sin and asserting that human beings can achieve salvation through free will without divine grace. CCC 406
Interior repentance expressed through prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and physical or spiritual works assigned by a priest in Confession to make amends for sin. CCC 1434, 1459

The part of the Introductory Rites of Mass in which the community, after a brief silence, acknowledges its sinfulness, using the Confiteor or another form with the Kyrie, and the priest prays for God’s mercy. It does not have the effect of sacramental absolution.

The first five books of the Old Testament: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. Called the Torah ("Law") in Jewish tradition and traditionally attributed to Moses, they recount creation, the patriarchs, the Exodus, and the giving of the Law.
The solemn feast celebrated fifty days after Easter, commemorating the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon Mary and the Apostles. CCC 731-741
A scriptural title for the Church, emphasizing that all baptized believers constitute a chosen, priestly people (1 Peter 2:9). CCC 781-786

A passage or section of Sacred Scripture taken as a unit, especially one appointed to be read in the liturgy. From the Greek for "a cutting around," the term is used for the readings arranged in the Lectionary.

The sin of making a promise under oath with no intention of keeping it, or of failing to keep a promise made on oath, and also of stating a falsehood under oath. It gravely dishonors God, the Lord of all speech, and compromises justice. CCC 2152, 2476

A man ordained to the diaconate as a lasting rank of the hierarchy, not as a step toward the priesthood. Restored in the Latin Church by the Second Vatican Council and always kept in the Eastern Churches, the permanent diaconate can be conferred on married men. CCC 1571
The continuous, uninterrupted exposition and adoration of the Blessed Sacrament 24 hours a day in a dedicated chapel or church. CCC 1378-1379

The doctrine that Mary remained a virgin before, during, and after the birth of Jesus throughout her life. The "brothers and sisters of Jesus" mentioned in Scripture are understood as close relatives, not other children of Mary. CCC 499-500, 510

Each human being, created in the image of God, a unity of body and spiritual soul, who is not just something but someone. The person is capable of self-knowledge, self-possession, and free self-giving, and is called by grace to a covenant with God. CCC 357, 362-365

A jurisdiction, juridically comparable to a diocese, established under Pope Benedict XVI’s apostolic constitution Anglicanorum Coetibus (2009) for groups of former Anglicans entering full communion with the Catholic Church. It allows them to preserve elements of their Anglican liturgical and spiritual patrimony.

A canonical structure erected by the Apostolic See, composed of secular priests and deacons under a prelate, to carry out particular pastoral or missionary works; lay people may cooperate in its works by agreement. Opus Dei is the only personal prelature established to date.

The form of prayer in which we ask God for what we need, expressing our awareness that we are creatures dependent on Him. It begins with asking forgiveness and seeks first the Kingdom, then whatever is necessary to welcome it (Matthew 6:33). CCC 2629-2633
A fixed bench, usually with a back and often a kneeler, on which the faithful sit and kneel in the nave of a church.

A Jewish religious movement of Jesus’ time, devoted to the faithful observance of the Law of Moses in letter and spirit and to the oral traditions of the elders. Jesus rebuked hypocrisy among some of them, yet shared their belief in the resurrection; St. Paul was a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). CCC 575, 579

One of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which disposes us to honor God as our Father with filial love and to respect others as His children. The word also describes devotional practices, such as popular piety, that extend the liturgy without replacing it. CCC 1831, 1674-1676

A journey made for religious motives to a holy place, such as a shrine, the Holy Land, or the tombs of the Apostles and saints. Pilgrimages evoke our earthly journey toward heaven and are special occasions for prayer and conversion. CCC 1674, 2691

The practice of having more than one spouse at the same time. It is contrary to the moral law and to conjugal love, which is undivided and exclusive, and denies the equal personal dignity of husband and wife. CCC 1645, 2387
The belief in or worship of multiple gods; forbidden by the First Commandment. CCC 2112
A title derived from Latin (pontifex), referring to a bishop, and specifically to the Supreme Pontiff (the Pope). CCC 882
The Bishop of Rome, Vicar of Christ, Successor of Saint Peter, and chief Pastor of the universal Catholic Church elected by the College of Cardinals. CCC 880-882
A candidate in the first stage of formation for religious life (the postulancy), living with the community to test the vocation and prepare for admission to the novitiate.

The person appointed to promote a cause of beatification or canonization, who gathers documents and witnesses on the life, virtues or martyrdom, and miracles of a Servant of God and guides the cause through the diocesan inquiry and the Holy See.

Detachment from riches for the sake of Christ and the Kingdom, to which all the faithful are called as poverty of spirit, and which consecrated persons embrace by vow as an evangelical counsel. The term also denotes material want, which calls forth the Church’s love for the poor (Matthew 5:3). CCC 915, 2544-2546

The form of prayer which most directly recognizes that God is God, glorifying Him for His own sake, beyond what He does, simply because He is. It reaches its fullness in the Eucharist, the "sacrifice of praise". CCC 2639-2643

The raising of one’s mind and heart to God, or the requesting of good things from God. It is a gift of grace, a covenant relationship, and a living communion with the Holy Trinity, expressed in blessing, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, and praise. CCC 2559-2565, 2626-2643

The prayer said by the priest after the period of silence or song following Holy Communion, in which he asks that the mystery celebrated may bear fruit in the lives of the faithful. It concludes the Communion Rite; the people respond " Amen."

The prayer said by the priest at the end of the Preparation of the Gifts, after the invitation "Pray, brethren," asking God to accept the gifts placed on the altar. It leads into the Eucharistic Prayer; the people respond " Amen."

The proclamation of the Word of God, especially by bishops, priests, and deacons, to call people to faith and conversion and to build up the faithful. In the liturgy it takes the form of the homily, which explains the Scriptures and exhorts the faithful to put them into practice. CCC 875, 888, 1349
The initial period of Christian initiation (Period of Inquiry) characterized by initial evangelization, faith sharing, and welcoming.

Positive laws of the Church that guarantee the faithful the indispensable minimum of prayer and moral effort, such as attending Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation, confessing one’s sins at least once a year, receiving Holy Communion at least during the Easter season, fasting and abstaining on prescribed days, and supporting the Church. CCC 2041-2043

God’s eternal plan of salvation, in which He calls and destines the elect to share the image of His Son, while including in it each person’s free response to His grace. God predestines no one to hell, which requires a willful turning away from Him until the end (Romans 8:29-30). CCC 600, 1037

The opening part of the Eucharistic Prayer, in which the priest, after the dialogue with the people ("The Lord be with you... Lift up your hearts... Let us give thanks to the Lord our God"), gives thanks to the Father for His works of creation, redemption, and sanctification. It concludes with the Sanctus. CCC 1352

The Church’s special love and concern for the poor, the oppressed, and the suffering, which she has never ceased to work to relieve, defend, and liberate. Drawn from Christ’s own compassion, it shapes Christian social teaching and the choices of every disciple. CCC 2443-2448

A cleric, usually a bishop, who exercises ordinary power of governance over a portion of the faithful, such as a diocese, territorial prelature, or personal prelature. An honorary prelate (Prelate of Honor of His Holiness) is a priest given this title by the Pope, with the style of Monsignor.

The rite beginning the Liturgy of the Eucharist, in which the bread and wine, sometimes brought in procession together with gifts for the poor, are placed on the altar. The priest offers them in Christ’s name, for they will become His Body and Blood. CCC 1350-1351
A priest; "presbyterium" refers collectively to the body of priests serving within a diocese under their bishop. CCC 1554, 1562

A body of priests representing the presbyterate of a diocese, which canon law requires in every diocese, to act as the bishop’s senate and to aid him in governing the diocese for the pastoral good of the faithful. Its role is ordinarily consultative.

The area of the sanctuary surrounding the altar, reserved for the clergy and ministers. In some English-speaking countries, the term also denotes the residence of the parish priests (a rectory), and it is sometimes used for the body of priests of a diocese (the presbyterium).
Ritual actions during the Period of Purification in OCIA wherein the Elect are presented with the Creed and the Lord's Prayer.
A sin against Hope wherein a person expects salvation without personal conversion or assumes God will forgive sin without repentance. CCC 2092
An inordinate self-esteem or self-exaltation that rejects dependence on God; the root of all capital sins. CCC 1866
A man ordained through Holy Orders who is granted care of souls, empowered to celebrate the Sacraments, and offer the Sacrifice of the Mass in persona Christi under his bishop. CCC 1562-1568

The unique, eternal priesthood of Jesus Christ, the one Mediator and high priest of the New Covenant after the order of Melchizedek, who offered Himself once for all on the Cross. All other Christian priesthood shares in it and makes it present without diminishing it (Hebrews 7:24-27). CCC 662, 1544-1545

The share in the priesthood of Christ that all the baptized receive, by which they offer their lives, prayers, and work as spiritual sacrifices. It differs in essence, not only in degree, from the ministerial priesthood, which serves it (1 Peter 2:5, 9). CCC 901, 1268, 1546-1547

The full, supreme, and universal power of the Pope over the whole Church, received from Christ, who made Peter the rock and shepherd of the Church. As Bishop of Rome and Successor of Peter, the Pope is the perpetual and visible source and foundation of unity (Matthew 16:18-19). CCC 881-882

The superior of certain religious communities. In monastic orders a prior is either the deputy of an abbot or the head of a priory; in orders such as the Dominicans, Carmelites, and Augustinians, he is the superior of a local house or, as prior provincial or general, of a larger body.

A revelation given to an individual after the close of public Revelation, such as an approved apparition. Private revelations do not belong to the deposit of faith and cannot improve or complete Christ’s definitive Revelation, but may help the faithful live it more fully in a given age. CCC 67
The cross carried at the head of a liturgical procession.

The orderly movement of the faithful or ministers from one place to another as an act of worship, such as the entrance, Gospel, and Communion processions at Mass, or those of Palm Sunday and Corpus Christi. They express the pilgrim Church journeying toward God. CCC 1674
The public proclamation or recitation of Christian beliefs (such as the Creed). CCC 185-197

The public act by which a member of a religious institute takes vows of chastity, poverty, and obedience, consecrating himself or herself to God. Temporary profession follows the novitiate and precedes perpetual (or solemn) profession. CCC 915-916, 925, 2103
The official publication and legal enactment of a decree, law, or document by Church authority.
One called by God to speak in His name, proclaim His truth, and call people to repentance and fidelity. CCC 64, 2581

The atoning sacrifice of Christ, by which He offered Himself for our sins and reconciled us with God. Scripture calls Him the expiation (or propitiation) for our sins, whose blood fulfills the sprinkling of the mercy seat; the Mass, which makes this sacrifice present, is truly propitiatory (1 John 2:2). CCC 433, 604, 1367

Lying face down on the ground as a sign of deep humility, supplication, and adoration. In the Roman Rite it is done by candidates for ordination during the Litany of the Saints and by the priest and deacon at the beginning of the Good Friday liturgy; many Eastern Christians make frequent prostrations in prayer.

A member of one of the Christian ecclesial communities that arose from the sixteenth-century Reformation, such as Lutherans, Reformed, and Anglicans, and of the communities descended from them. Those baptized and justified by faith are incorporated into Christ and rightly called brothers and sisters in the Lord. CCC 817-819, 838
Genesis 3:15 ("the First Gospel "), the first biblical prophecy announcing the eventual victory over Satan through the offspring of the Woman. CCC 410
God's loving guidance, care, and governance by which He directs all creation toward its ultimate perfection. CCC 302-305
A grouping of neighboring dioceses, headed by a metropolitan archbishop, whose own archdiocese is joined by the suffragan dioceses. The bishops of a province may meet in provincial councils. CCC 887
The cardinal virtue that disposes practical reason to discern our true good in every circumstance and choose the right means of achieving it. CCC 1806

One of the 150 inspired songs and prayers of the Book of Psalms, used in the worship of Israel and by Jesus Himself. Hymns, laments, and thanksgivings, the psalms are a mirror of God’s marvelous deeds and form the core of the Liturgy of the Hours. CCC 2585-2589, 1177

The Book of Psalms, called the masterwork of prayer in the Old Testament, in which the Word of God becomes man’s prayer. The term also designates the arrangement of the psalms for liturgical prayer, as in the four-week psalter of the Liturgy of the Hours. CCC 2585, 2587

The everlasting punishment of hell, whose chief pain is eternal separation from God, incurred by those who die in a state of mortal sin. Grave sin deprives us of communion with God and so of eternal life; its privation is called the eternal punishment of sin (Matthew 25:46). CCC 1035, 1472
The state of final purification after death for those who die in God's grace but still require cleansing from the temporal effects of sin before entering Heaven. CCC 1030-1032
The Lenten period of spiritual preparation preceding Easter in OCIA, marked by prayerful reflection and the Scrutinies.

A small rectangular white linen cloth used at Mass to wipe the chalice after the distribution of the Precious Blood and at the purification of the sacred vessels, and to dry the priest’s fingers and lips.
A small, sacred metal container used to carry the Blessed Sacrament to the sick, elderly, or homebound.

A title of the Blessed Virgin Mary, who, assumed body and soul into heavenly glory, was exalted by the Lord as Queen over all things, sharing in the kingship of her Son. The Church celebrates her Queenship on August 22 and sings the Regina Caeli in Eastertide. CCC 966
A 17th-century spiritual error asserting that spiritual perfection consists in total passivity and annihilation of human effort, neglecting active virtue.

Any belief, attitude, or practice that holds some races superior to others or that discriminates against persons because of race, color, or ethnic origin. It is a sin against the equal dignity of every human being created in God’s image and is incompatible with God’s design. CCC 1934-1935

Latin for "ratified but not consummated," a valid marriage between baptized persons that has not been consummated by the conjugal act. Unlike a consummated sacramental marriage, which no human power can dissolve, it may be dissolved by the Roman Pontiff for a just cause. CCC 1640
The unique, true, and substantial presence of Jesus Christ (Body, Blood, Soul, and Divinity) under the Eucharistic species of bread and wine. CCC 1373-1381

The natural power of the human mind, by which a person, made in the image of God, knows truth, understands the order of creation, and can come to know God with certainty. Faith is above reason but never contrary to it, since both come from God. CCC 36, 159, 1704
The Sacrament of Healing through which sins committed after Baptism are confessed to a priest and forgiven by God. CCC 1422-1484

A priest entrusted with the direction of a church that is not a parish church, such as a shrine, or of an institution such as a seminary, Catholic college, or university. In some places the title is also used for the pastor of a cathedral or parish.
The salvation and liberation of humanity from sin and death accomplished through the ransom paid by Christ's sacrificial death. CCC 517, 606-618

Suffering accepted in faith and united to the Passion of Christ, which by grace shares in His saving work for oneself and for others. St. Paul could rejoice that in his flesh he completed "what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church" (Colossians 1:24). CCC 618, 1505, 1521

The sixteenth-century movement, begun by Martin Luther in 1517 and carried on by others such as Zwingli and Calvin, that sought to reform the Church and led to the separation of the Protestant communities from full communion with Rome. Catholics regard Christians of these communities with respect and affection as brothers and sisters in the Lord. CCC 817-819

The Marian antiphon " Queen of Heaven, rejoice, alleluia," which rejoices with Mary in the Resurrection of her Son. During the Easter season it replaces the Angelus at morning, noon, and evening, and it is sung as the final Marian antiphon of Night Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours.

Physical remains or personal belongings of a saint (First-Class: body/remains; Second-Class: clothing/belongings; Third-Class: object touched to a first-class relic) venerated by the faithful. CCC 1674

The bond between the human person and God, and in particular the moral virtue by which one gives God the worship and service owed to Him in justice, above all through adoration, prayer, and sacrifice. The duty of offering God genuine worship binds both individuals and societies. CCC 2095-2096, 2105

The natural right of every person to immunity from coercion by individuals, groups, or civil authority in religious matters, so that no one is forced to act against conscience or prevented, within due limits, from acting according to it. Founded on human dignity, it is not a license to adhere to error. CCC 2104-2109

The form of consecrated life lived in institutes canonically erected by the Church, distinguished by its liturgical character, the public profession of the evangelical counsels, fraternal life in common, and witness to the union of Christ and the Church. It arose in the East in the first Christian centuries. CCC 925-927

Ecclesial movements and new communities, often born of a founder's charism and including laity, clergy, and consecrated persons, that foster a particular way of living the Gospel through prayer, formation, and mission. The Church recognizes them, often as associations of the faithful, and they remain subject to the discernment of the bishops and the Holy See.

A member of a religious institute who has professed the evangelical counsels of poverty, chastity, and obedience by public vows and lives a fraternal life in common, such as a monk, nun, friar, religious sister, or religious brother. Religious may be lay persons or clerics. CCC 916, 925-927

An institute of religious life whose members profess public vows and live in common under an approved rule, such as the Benedictines, Franciscans, Dominicans, or Jesuits. Canon law now calls all such bodies religious institutes; "order" refers especially to the older institutes whose members take solemn vows. CCC 925

The public vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience by which a religious, received by a legitimate superior in the name of the Church, is consecrated to God within a religious institute. They are first made for a time and later perpetually, may be simple or solemn, and are fulfilled by the virtue of religion. CCC 915, 925, 2102-2103

The forgiveness of sins by God through Christ, a power the risen Lord entrusted to His Church and which the Creed professes. Baptism is the first and chief sacrament of the remission of sins; those who sin gravely after Baptism are reconciled with God and the Church through the Sacrament of Penance. CCC 976-980
Making amends for an offense or injury done to God or neighbor through prayer, penance, or justice. CCC 1459, 2487

Interior sorrow for sin and a turning of the whole heart back to God, with the resolve to change one's life and trust in His mercy. Jesus began His preaching with the call, "Repent, and believe in the gospel" (Mark 1:15). CCC 1430-1431, 1451

The psalm or biblical canticle sung or recited after the first reading at Mass, in which the people answer with a refrain the verses proclaimed by a psalmist or cantor. It is an integral part of the Liturgy of the Word and helps the assembly meditate on the Word of God just heard.

The return of stolen or unjustly held goods, or fair compensation for them, to their rightful owner, as commutative justice requires of anyone who has wronged another in his property. Zacchaeus pledged, "If I have defrauded any one of anything, I restore it fourfold" (Luke 19:8). CCC 1459, 2412, 2487
The bodily rising of Jesus Christ from the dead on the third day after His death, the foundational truth of the Christian faith. CCC 638-658
The Catholic belief that at Christ's Second Coming, the bodies of all the dead will be resurrected and reunited with their souls. CCC 988-1004

A period of withdrawal from ordinary activities, from a day to several weeks, devoted to prayer, silence, reflection, and spiritual renewal, often with conferences or guidance from a director. The Spiritual Exercises of St. Ignatius of Loyola are a classic model, following the example of Christ, who withdrew to lonely places to pray (Mark 1:35).
God's communication of Himself and His divine plan of salvation to humanity through historical deeds, words, and supremely through Jesus Christ. CCC 50-67
Rite of Acceptance into the Order of Catechumens
The liturgical rite marking the transition from the pre-catechumenate (inquiry) into the formal catechumenate for unbaptized persons.
Rite of Calling to Lenten Renewal
A liturgical rite celebrated alongside Election for candidates who are already validly baptized.
The liturgical rite presided over by the bishop on the First Sunday of Lent marking the entry of catechumens into the final period of preparation (Purification and Enlightenment).
The liturgical rite marking the transition from inquiry into the catechumenate phase for already baptized candidates.

A liturgical celebration with its prescribed words and actions, such as the rite of Baptism. The term also names a liturgical, spiritual, and disciplinary tradition of the Church, such as the Roman, Ambrosian, Byzantine, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Maronite, or Chaldean rite; the Church holds all lawfully recognized rites to be of equal right and dignity. CCC 1200-1203

The official liturgical book of the Roman Rite that lists, for each day of the year, the saints and blessed commemorated by the Church, with brief notices of their lives and deaths. It may be read in choir or in community, and it is revised periodically as new saints are canonized.

The liturgical tradition of the Church of Rome, the principal rite of the Latin Church and the most widely celebrated in the world. Its ordinary form is the liturgy as revised after the Second Vatican Council, celebrated in Latin or in approved vernacular translations. CCC 1203

The liturgical book, or collection of books, of the Roman Rite (Rituale Romanum) containing the rites of sacraments and sacramentals not found in the Missal or the Pontifical, such as Baptism, Penance, Anointing of the Sick, Marriage, funerals, and blessings. Since the Second Vatican Council its parts have been issued as separate books.
A scriptural Catholic prayer devotion focusing on the mysteries of the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus and Mary, counted on a string of beads. CCC 971, 2678
The Hebrew word for "wind," "breath," or "spirit," used in Sacred Scripture to describe the life-giving presence and action of the Holy Spirit. CCC 691, 703

The seventh day of the week, which God blessed and made holy, kept by Israel as a day of rest and worship in memory of creation and of the liberation from Egypt, and as a sign of the covenant. For Christians, Sunday, the day of the Resurrection, fulfills the spiritual truth of the Sabbath (Exodus 20:8-11). CCC 2168-2172, 2175
An outward sign instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church to dispense divine grace to the soul. CCC 1113-1131
Sacred signs, objects, or actions (such as holy water, rosaries, crucifixes, or ashes) instituted by the Church to prepare believers to receive grace. CCC 1667-1673
An indelible spiritual mark imprinted on the soul by Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders that can never be removed. CCC 1121

A liturgical book containing the prayers said by the priest at Mass and other rites, such as the ancient Gelasian and Gregorian Sacramentaries. In some English-speaking countries, the name was also given to the English translation of the Roman Missal used from the 1970s until the new translation of 2011.
Sacraments at the Service of Communion

Holy Orders and Matrimony, the two sacraments directed toward the salvation of others. They contribute to personal salvation through service to others, confer a particular mission in the Church, and serve to build up the People of God. CCC 1533-1535

Penance (Reconciliation) and the Anointing of the Sick, by which Christ, physician of our souls and bodies, continues through His Church His work of healing and salvation for those whose new life in Him has been weakened by sin or burdened by illness. CCC 1420-1421
The three foundational sacraments (Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Eucharist) that fully initiate a person into the Catholic Church. CCC 1212, 1275, 1285
A devotion centered on the physical heart of Jesus Christ as the symbol of His divine and human love for humanity. CCC 478
The written Word of God, inspired by the Holy Spirit and contained in the canonical books of the Bible. CCC 101-133
The living transmission of the Word of God handed down through the practice, preaching, and teaching authority of the Church across generations. CCC 75-83
An offering made to God as an act of adoration, thanksgiving, petition, or atonement. The Sacrifice of the Mass is the same sacrifice as that of Calvary made present. CCC 1362-1372

Love that gives itself freely for the good of another at personal cost, perfectly revealed in Christ, who died for us while we were still sinners. The Lord asks us to love as He loves: "Greater love has no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends" (John 15:13). CCC 616, 1825
Profaning, mistreating, or treating disrespectfully the Sacraments, liturgical actions, persons, or objects consecrated to God. CCC 2120

The person, lay or religious, responsible for the care of the sacristy and for preparing the books, vessels, vestments, and other items needed for liturgical celebrations, as well as for the good order and cleanliness of the church.

The room in or beside a church where vestments, sacred vessels, liturgical books, and other furnishings are kept, and where ministers vest and prepare for celebrations. It often contains a sacrarium, a basin draining directly into the earth for the reverent disposal of water used for sacred purposes.
A holy person who lived a life of heroic virtue on earth and is now in Heaven with God in eternal glory. CCC 828, 956

Deliverance from sin and its consequences, above all eternal death, and the gift of eternal life in communion with God. Salvation comes from God alone through Jesus Christ, whose name means "God saves," and is received through faith and Baptism in the Church. CCC 161, 169, 430, 620
The story of God's saving actions across human history to redeem humanity from sin and death. CCC 54-67

The work of God, especially of the Holy Spirit, by which persons and things are made holy and set apart for Him. Begun in Baptism together with justification, it grows through grace, the sacraments, prayer, and charity; the Church, sanctified by Christ, in turn becomes sanctifying. CCC 824, 1989, 2813
The divine, permanent grace received in Baptism that heals human nature, makes us children of God, and grants a share in the divine life. CCC 1999-2000
The elevated, sacred area of a church where the altar, ambo, and celebrant's chair are located.
A red candle kept burning near the tabernacle to signify and honor the Real Presence of Christ in the reserved Eucharist.

The acclamation sung by the people with the priest at the end of the Preface of the Eucharistic Prayer, joining the praise of the angels and saints to the thrice-holy God. It unites the song of the seraphim with the cry of the crowds who welcomed Jesus into Jerusalem (Isaiah 6:3, Matthew 21:9). CCC 335, 1352
A fallen angel who freely rejected God, the leader of demons and enemy of human salvation. CCC 391-395

The penitent's act of making amends for sin through prayer, works of mercy, self-denial, or other penances, especially those given by the confessor, and by repairing harm done to others. Its value comes from Christ, whose loving sacrifice is the perfect satisfaction for the sins of all. CCC 615-616, 1459-1460

A title of Jesus Christ, whose name means "God saves," for He saves His people from their sins and accomplishes the universal and definitive redemption that only God can bring about. In the Old Testament God Himself is the Savior of Israel (Matthew 1:21). CCC 430-432
An attitude or behavior that leads another person to commit sin or moral harm. CCC 2284-2287

Originally a long piece of cloth worn over the shoulders as part of the habit of many religious orders. The small scapular, two pieces of cloth joined by cords and worn by the faithful as a sacramental, signifies association with an order and its spirituality; the best known is the brown scapular of Our Lady of Mount Carmel.
The refusal of submission to the Supreme Pontiff or of communion with the members of the Church subject to him. CCC 2089

In the time of Jesus, Jewish scholars and teachers who copied, interpreted, and applied the Law of Moses, many of them associated with the Pharisees. Jesus taught "as one who had authority, and not as their scribes," and called for a righteousness exceeding theirs (Matthew 5:20, Matthew 7:29). CCC 581, 2054
A psychological and spiritual condition characterized by persistent, unfounded anxiety that one's thoughts or actions are sinful when they are not.
Three solemn rites of exorcism and spiritual healing celebrated for the Elect on the 3rd, 4th, and 5th Sundays of Lent during Mass.
The absolute, unbreakable obligation of a priest never to reveal any sin disclosed to him in Sacramental Confession. CCC 1467

An institute of consecrated life whose members, living in the world rather than in community, profess the evangelical counsels and strive for the perfection of charity, working for the sanctification of the world from within, like leaven. Members may be lay persons or clerics. CCC 928-929

The period during which an episcopal see has no bishop, through death, resignation, transfer, or removal. The term is used especially of the Holy See after a Pope dies or resigns, when the College of Cardinals sees to ordinary business, makes no innovations, and prepares the conclave to elect a new Pope.

The seat of a bishop's authority, from the Latin sedes, "seat," and hence the diocese or particular Church he governs. The Holy See is the see of the Bishop of Rome; an archdiocese heading a province is a metropolitan see, and a titular see survives only in name.

An institution for the human, spiritual, intellectual, and pastoral formation of men preparing for ordination to the priesthood, directed by a rector and formators appointed by the Church. Minor seminaries serve younger students, while major seminaries provide the philosophical and theological program required by canon law.

The levels of meaning in Sacred Scripture: the literal sense, conveyed by the words themselves, on which all the others rest, and the spiritual sense, by which the realities and events described are themselves signs. The spiritual sense is subdivided into the allegorical, moral, and anagogical senses. CCC 115-119

The supernatural appreciation of the faith, aroused and sustained by the Holy Spirit, by which the whole People of God, guided by the Magisterium, adheres unfailingly to the faith, penetrates it more deeply, and applies it more fully in daily life. The whole body of the faithful cannot err in matters of belief. CCC 91-93, 889
The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament produced in the 3rd to 2nd centuries B.C.. CCC 120

A tomb or burial place, above all the tomb in Jerusalem where the body of Jesus was laid and which was found empty on Easter morning. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, built over the traditional sites of Calvary and the tomb, is among the holiest shrines of Christianity. CCC 640, 657

A church or other sacred place to which, with the approval of the local bishop, the faithful make pilgrimage for a particular reason of piety, such as the tomb of a saint or a place of Marian devotion. Shrines are special places for renewal in prayer and for receiving the sacraments. CCC 2691

The gesture exchanged at Mass by which the faithful express peace, communion, and mutual charity before receiving the Body of Christ. In the Roman Rite it comes before Communion, its form set by local custom; in the Eastern liturgies and the Ambrosian Rite it precedes the offering of the gifts (Matthew 5:23-24).

A prayer and gesture tracing the cross on oneself while invoking the Holy Trinity: "In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." It recalls Baptism and the redemption won on the cross; Latin Catholics usually touch the left shoulder first, Eastern Christians the right. CCC 1235, 1668, 2157

A term from popular devotion, not from the Church's official teaching, for a sign or prompting a person believes God has given in answer to prayer, often in connection with a particular saint. Such signs may be received with gratitude, but the Church urges discernment and warns against demanding signs or treating them superstitiously.
The buying or selling of spiritual things, graces, sacraments, or ecclesiastical offices; a grave sin against the First Commandment. CCC 2121
An offense against reason, truth, and right conscience, consisting of a transgression against God's moral law. CCC 1849-1869

A woman religious who belongs to an institute of consecrated life. Strictly, "nun" denotes a woman of a contemplative order with solemn vows and papal enclosure, while "sister" denotes one of an active institute with simple vows, though the two words are often used interchangeably.
Spiritual apathy or listlessness regarding divine love and holiness; one of the seven capital sins. CCC 1866, 2094
The body of Catholic teachings regarding economic, political, and social order, upholding human dignity and the common good. CCC 2419-2425

An encyclical letter of a Pope applying the Gospel and the Church's moral teaching to social, economic, and political life, beginning with Leo XIII's Rerum Novarum (1891) on the condition of workers. Later examples include Quadragesimo Anno, Pacem in Terris, Centesimus Annus, and Laudato Si’. CCC 2421-2422

An analogous term for social situations, institutions, and "structures of sin" that are contrary to God's goodness and arise as the expression and effect of personal sins. Such structures lead their victims to do evil in turn, yet responsibility always rests ultimately with the persons who commit sin. CCC 1869

Communities, alongside the institutes of consecrated life, whose members, without religious vows, pursue the apostolic purpose of their society and live a fraternal life in common under its constitutions; some also embrace the evangelical counsels by other bonds. Examples include the Oratorians and the Daughters of Charity. CCC 930

The highest rank of liturgical celebration in the Roman Rite, kept for the principal mysteries of the Lord, of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and of certain saints, such as Easter, Christmas, the Assumption, and Sts. Peter and Paul. A solemnity begins with Evening Prayer I on the previous day and includes the Gloria and Creed at Mass.

The principle and virtue, also called "friendship" or "social charity," by which people recognize their common origin and dignity and commit themselves to the good of all and of each. It is shown in the just distribution of goods and pay for work, and among individuals, workers, and nations. CCC 1939-1942

The title of Jesus that expresses His unique and eternal relationship to the Father as the only-begotten Son, true God from true God. In the Old Testament the title signified adoptive sonship, but Peter's confession, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," affirms Jesus' divine sonship (Matthew 16:16). CCC 441-445

The title Jesus most often used of Himself, recalling Daniel's vision of one "like a son of man" coming with the clouds of heaven. It joins His transcendent origin and future glory to His mission to suffer, give His life as a ransom for many, and rise (Daniel 7:13-14, Mark 10:45). CCC 440
The branch of theology dedicated to the study of salvation and the redeeming work of Jesus Christ.

The spiritual principle in the human person, by which a person is most especially in God's image. Created immediately by God and immortal, the soul is the "form" of the body, so that body and soul make one human nature; at death it separates from the body, to be reunited with it at the resurrection. CCC 363-366

A priest, religious, or lay person gifted with wisdom, faith, and discernment, who helps another grow in prayer and the Christian life through regular conversation, counsel, and the discernment of God's will. St. John of the Cross urged that a director be learned, discreet, and experienced. CCC 2690, 2695

A particular way of living the Christian life and prayer, often drawn from the charism of a saint or founder or from liturgical and theological currents, such as Benedictine, Franciscan, Carmelite, or Ignatian spirituality. The different schools share in the one living tradition of prayer and are precious guides for the spiritual life. CCC 2684, 2693
Stations of the Cross (Way of the Cross)

A devotion in which the faithful follow Jesus' path from His condemnation to His burial, pausing at fourteen stations, usually images on the church walls, to meditate on His Passion. It grew from pilgrims' practice of retracing His steps in Jerusalem and is prayed especially during Lent. CCC 1674, 2669

Taking or unjustly keeping another's property against the reasonable will of the owner, forbidden by the seventh commandment, "You shall not steal." There is no theft when, in obvious and urgent necessity, using another's goods is the only way to meet essential needs; one who steals is bound to restitution (Exodus 20:15). CCC 2408-2409, 2412

The responsible care of the gifts God has entrusted to human beings: life, talents, time, possessions, and creation itself. Since the goods of creation are destined for all, owners are stewards of Providence, bound to make their goods fruitful and to share the benefits with others, first of all their families (Matthew 25:14-30). CCC 2280, 2402-2404

Wounds or marks corresponding to the wounds of Christ's Passion that appear on the body of certain persons, such as St. Francis of Assisi and St. Pio of Pietrelcina. The Church examines such phenomena with great caution; holiness is judged by heroic virtue, not by extraordinary signs, and no one is bound to believe in a particular case.

A long, narrow band of fabric, the vestment proper to the ordained. A bishop or priest wears it around the neck, hanging down in front, while a deacon wears it over the left shoulder, fastened at the right side. In the Eastern Churches the corresponding vestments are the priest's epitrachelion and the deacon's orarion.
A key principle of Catholic Social Teaching stating that higher social authorities should not usurp the function of lower, local bodies unless necessary for the common good. CCC 1883, 2209
One of the four traditional qualities of a glorified body following the resurrection, allowing it to transcend physical barriers (as Christ passed through locked doors). CCC 645, 999

The deliberate taking of one's own life, gravely contrary to the just love of self, to love of neighbor, and to the love of the living God, the sovereign Master of life. Grave psychological disturbance or fear can diminish responsibility, and the Church prays for those who have taken their own lives, not despairing of their salvation. CCC 2280-2283
The first day of the Christian week, commemorating Christ's Resurrection; the foundational feast day and center of the liturgical calendar. CCC 1166-1167, 2174-2178

A member of a religious institute who, by election or appointment according to its constitutions, exercises authority over a community, a province, or the whole institute, such as an abbot, prior, provincial, or superior general. Superiors govern in a spirit of service, and members owe them obedience according to their vows.

Whatever surpasses the powers and capacities of created nature and comes as a free gift of God, above all grace, the theological virtues, and the vocation to eternal life in the vision of God. The supernatural does not destroy nature but heals and elevates it. CCC 1722, 1998
An irrational or improper religious practice attributing magical efficacy to actions, objects, or recitations. CCC 2111

A loose white liturgical garment with wide sleeves, reaching about to the knees and derived from the alb, worn over the cassock by clergy and other ministers, including servers. It is used for the Liturgy of the Hours, for sacraments celebrated outside Mass, in processions, and in other rites.

A canonical penalty (censure) that affects only clerics, forbidding some or all acts of the power of orders, of the power of governance, or of the rights and functions attached to an office. Like other censures, it aims at the offender's repentance and is to be lifted once he withdraws from his contumacy.

A sign that points beyond itself to a spiritual reality. In the liturgy, words, gestures, and created things such as water, oil, light, bread, and wine become symbols of God's saving action. A summary of the faith is also called a "symbol" (Greek symbolon), as in the Apostles' Creed. CCC 188, 1145-1146

An assembly of bishops, or of clergy and faithful with their bishop, gathered to deliberate on the life of the Church, such as the Synod of Bishops, which advises the Pope, a diocesan synod, or a provincial synod. In many Eastern Catholic Churches the synod of bishops also holds legislative and electoral authority. CCC 887, 911

The Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, so called (from the Greek for "seeing together") because they share much of the same material, order, and wording and can be read side by side. The Gospel of John follows its own plan and style, though all four proclaim the one Gospel of Jesus Christ.
A sacred, secure furnishing (meaning "dwelling place") used to house and reserve the Holy Eucharist outside of Mass for adoration or distribution to the sick. CCC 1379

The cardinal virtue that moderates the attraction of pleasures and provides balance in the use of created goods, ensuring the will's mastery over instincts and keeping desires within honorable limits. Chastity, sobriety, and moderation in food and drink belong to it. CCC 1809, 2341

The sanctuary in Jerusalem, built by Solomon and later rebuilt, where God dwelt among His people and sacrifice was offered. Jesus loved and honored the Temple, foretold its destruction, and identified it with His own Body; by grace, Christians become temples of the Holy Spirit (John 2:19-21, 1 Corinthians 3:16). CCC 583-586, 593, 1197
The temporary consequence or purification remaining due to forgiven sins, satisfied on earth or in Purgatory. CCC 1471-1473

An attraction or incitement to sin, coming from the world, the flesh, or the devil. Being tempted is not itself a sin; sin lies in consenting. Jesus overcame Satan 's temptations in the desert, and in the Lord's Prayer we ask not to be led into temptation, trusting in God's faithful help (1 Corinthians 10:13). CCC 538, 2847-2849
The moral directives given by God to Moses on Mount Sinai (Decalogue), providing the essential framework for human morality. CCC 2052-2074

A portion of the People of God within a defined territory which, for special circumstances, is not erected as a diocese but is entrusted to a prelate who governs it as its own pastor, in the manner of a diocesan bishop. Most are found in mission or remote regions.

Prayer that expresses gratitude to God for His gifts, characteristic of the Church's prayer and above all of the Eucharist, whose name means "thanksgiving." Every joy and suffering, every event and need can become matter for thanksgiving: "Give thanks in all circumstances" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). CCC 1360, 2637-2638, 2648

A major seminary or house of formation, or the stage of priestly formation within it, devoted to the study of theology, usually for four years after the study of philosophy and before ordination to the priesthood. The term is also used of houses of study where members of religious institutes complete their theology.
The three supernatural virtues infused into the soul at Baptism: Faith, Hope, and Charity. CCC 1812-1829
The systematic study of God and divine revelation ("faith seeking understanding"). CCC 73, 158
A visible manifestation or appearance of God to human beings (e.g., God appearing to Moses in the burning bush or on Mount Sinai). CCC 2058
A Greek title for the Blessed Virgin Mary meaning "God-bearer" or "Mother of God," solemnly defined at the Council of Ephesus (A.D. 431). CCC 495

A diocese that no longer exists as a residential see, often in lands of the ancient Church, whose title is given to a bishop who has no diocese of his own, such as an auxiliary bishop, an apostolic nuncio, or an official of the Roman Curia.

The Hebrew word for "instruction" or "law," naming the first five books of the Bible (the Pentateuch) and, more broadly, the teaching God revealed to Israel through Moses. The Old Law is the first stage of revealed law, which Christ came not to abolish but to fulfill (Matthew 5:17). CCC 1961-1962
(see Extraordinary Form) The celebration of the Liturgy according to the Roman Missal promulgated prior to the Second Vatican Council.

The attribute by which God infinitely surpasses all creatures, the world, and history, so that no human concept can contain or fully express Him. Transcendent, God is yet present to His creatures' inmost being, "higher than my highest and more inward than my innermost self". CCC 42, 212, 300

The event on a high mountain when Jesus, before Peter, James, and John, shone with divine glory while Moses and Elijah spoke with Him of His coming death, and the Father's voice declared, "This is my beloved Son." It anticipates the Resurrection and is celebrated on August 6 (Matthew 17:1-8). CCC 554-556

The theological term describing the complete change of the whole substance of bread and wine into the substance of the Body and Blood of Christ during Mass, while the physical appearances remain. CCC 1376

A court of the Church that judges cases under canon law, especially petitions for the declaration of nullity of a marriage. Each diocese has a tribunal of first instance under the judicial vicar; appeals go to a higher tribunal, and the Roman Rota and the Apostolic Signatura are tribunals of the Holy See.
The three holy days spanning Holy Thursday evening, Good Friday, Holy Saturday, and Easter Sunday. CCC 1168
The central mystery of Christian faith: one God existing in three distinct divine Persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. CCC 232-260

The Solemnity of the Most Holy Trinity, celebrated in the Roman Rite on the Sunday after Pentecost, honoring the central mystery of the faith: one God in three divine Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In the Byzantine tradition, Pentecost itself is celebrated as the feast of the Holy Trinity.

The method of biblical interpretation where persons, events, or objects in the Old Testament ("types") prefigure realities fulfilled in the New Testament ("antitypes"), such as Isaac prefiguring Christ. CCC 128-130
The teaching of the Church that all baptized Christians, regardless of their state of life, are called to the fullness of Christian life and perfection of charity. CCC 2012-2016
USCCB (United States Conference of Catholic Bishops)
The official episcopal conference of Catholic bishops in the United States who assemble to promote the Church's pastoral mission, policy guidelines, and public advocacy.

Whether a sacrament or juridical act truly takes effect. A sacrament is valid when the proper minister, matter, and form are present with the intention of doing what the Church does; an invalid act lacks an essential element and has no effect, while an illicit act is valid but unlawful. CCC 1128, 1256
The independent sovereign city-state in Rome that serves as the administrative center and Holy See of the Catholic Church.

The twentieth ecumenical council, held in Rome from 1869 to 1870 under Pope Pius IX. In Dei Filius it taught on God, revelation, and faith and reason, and in Pastor Aeternus it defined the primacy and infallibility of the Roman Pontiff; it was suspended when Rome was occupied.
The 21st ecumenical council of the Catholic Church (1962–1965), convened by Pope St. John XXIII to address the modern presentation of Church doctrine, pastoral renewal, and liturgical reform.
The title given to a deceased candidate for sainthood whose heroic virtue or martyrdom has been officially recognized by the Pope.
Honoring and revering saints (dulia) or Mary (hyperdulia), distinguished from worship due to God alone (latria). CCC 971, 2132

The marks of reverence shown to the altar, which is a symbol of Christ Himself: the priest and deacon kiss it at the beginning and end of Mass, ministers bow to it, and it may be incensed. The altar is honored as the place of the sacrifice and the table of the Lord. CCC 1182, 1383
A lesser sin that weakens charity and offends God but does not deprive the soul of sanctifying grace or cause spiritual death. CCC 1862-1863

The evening hour of the Liturgy of the Hours, one of its two principal hours with Lauds (Morning Prayer), comprising a hymn, psalms and a New Testament canticle, a reading, the Magnificat, intercessions, the Lord's Prayer, and a concluding prayer. Pastors are urged to celebrate it in common on Sundays and feasts. CCC 1174-1175

The special garments worn by ministers in liturgical celebrations, which signify their office and add dignity and beauty to worship, such as the alb, stole, chasuble, dalmatic, and cope in the Latin Church, with corresponding vestments in the Eastern Churches. Their colors usually follow the liturgical season or feast.
Holy Communion administered to a dying Christian as spiritual food for their passage from this earthly life to eternity. CCC 1524-1525
A priest delegated by the bishop to oversee the formation, assignment, support, and administrative care of diocesan priests.
A priest appointed by the bishop to lead a regional grouping of parishes (deanery) and foster fraternal support among local clergy.
The principal deputy or delegate of a diocesan bishop empowered with executive administrative authority over the diocese.
A traditional title for the Pope, highlighting his role as Christ's earthly representative and visible head of the Church. CCC 882

A habit of sin, a perverse inclination formed by repeating the same evil acts, which clouds conscience and corrupts the judgment of good and evil. Vices are opposed to the virtues and are linked to the capital sins: pride, avarice, envy, wrath, lust, gluttony, and sloth. CCC 1865-1866

The prayer service in the Order of Christian Funerals held between death and the funeral liturgy, often in the presence of the body, in the home, a funeral home, or the church. The community gathers to pray for the deceased, console the family, and keep watch in hope of the resurrection.

The doctrine that Jesus was conceived in the womb of the Virgin Mary solely by the power of the Holy Spirit, without a human father, and born of her without loss of her virginity. It manifests God's absolute initiative in the Incarnation: Jesus has only God as Father (Luke 1:34-35). CCC 496-499, 503

A habitual and firm disposition to do good, which allows a person not only to perform good acts but to give the best of himself. The human virtues, acquired by effort and grace, order the passions; the theological virtues of faith, hope, and charity are infused by God. CCC 1803-1804, 1812-1813

Prayer expressed in words, spoken or sung, alone or with others, such as the Our Father, which Jesus taught His disciples. It is an essential element of the Christian life, suited to our nature as body and spirit, and becomes true prayer when the heart is present to God. CCC 2700-2704
A divine call from God to a specific state of life: priesthood, consecrated religious life, holy matrimony, or committed single life. CCC 873, 1601, 1877

A Mass celebrated, on days when the liturgical norms permit, in honor of a mystery of the Lord, the Blessed Virgin Mary, the angels, or a saint, or for a particular devotion, in place of the Mass of the day; examples include Masses of the Sacred Heart and of the Holy Spirit.
A deliberate and free promise made to God concerning a possible and better good (e.g., the vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience). CCC 2101-2103
The official Latin translation of the Bible produced primarily by St. Jerome in the late 4th century. CCC 120

The rite in which the priest, after the gifts have been prepared at the altar, washes his hands at its side, praying quietly, "Wash me, O Lord, from my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin," as a sign of the desire for interior purification. The name is the first word, in Latin, of the verse "I will wash my hands among the innocent" (Psalm 26:6, Psalm 51:2).
The living testimony given by Christians through their daily words, actions, fidelity, and good works in accordance with the Gospel. CCC 2471-2472

God's self-communication in human words, above all in Jesus Christ, the eternal Word made flesh, and in Sacred Scripture and Tradition, which form one sacred deposit. Through all the words of Scripture God speaks one single Word, and the Church venerates the Scriptures as she venerates the Lord's Body (John 1:14). CCC 97, 101-104

Acts done in grace and charity that fulfill God's will, such as the works of mercy, prayer, and faithfulness to one's duties. No one can merit the first grace of justification, a free gift, but living faith bears fruit in works, which by grace merit eternal life (Ephesians 2:8-10, James 2:17). CCC 1815, 2008-2010
Charitable actions by which we come to the aid of our neighbor in their spiritual and bodily necessities (Corporal and Spiritual Works of Mercy). CCC 2447
The adoration and supreme homage paid to God alone as Creator and Lord of all. CCC 2096
The sacred Hebrew name of God revealed to Moses at the burning bush, meaning "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14). CCC 203-213
Burning love and devotion for God, His truth, and the salvation of souls.

The small, round silk skullcap worn by clergy, colored according to rank: white for the Pope, scarlet for cardinals, and violet for bishops, while priests may wear black. It is removed from the Preface until after Communion and in the presence of the Blessed Sacrament exposed.
877 words of the faith, from Abba to Zucchetto, with the Catechism paragraphs that teach them

The Holy Spirit comes down and the Church is born. The Holy Spirit comes down on the apostles gathered in Jerusalem. Peter preaches that day, and three thousand people are baptized. The Church counts this day as its birthday.

After Peter: Linus, Anacletus, Clement. After Peter and Paul are martyred in Rome, the Church of Rome is led in turn by Linus, Anacletus and Clement. Linus is named in one of Paul’s letters (2 Tim 4:21). Irenaeus writes the list down around 180.

Rome steps into a quarrel in Corinth. Clement, bishop of Rome, intervenes in a dispute in the Church of Corinth and asks that the priests who were removed be restored. The apostle John is most likely still alive at the time.

The first Christians’ little handbook. This short handbook, also called the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, describes the life of the first Christians. It plainly forbids abortion and infanticide, says that if there is no running water one may baptize by pouring water on the head three times, and asks for fasting on Wednesdays and Fridays.

The name “Catholic Church” is written for the first time. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, writes letters on his way to martyrdom in Rome. In them he becomes the first person known to use the phrase “Catholic Church”, and he describes the order of bishops, priests and deacons. Tradition holds that he was a disciple of the apostle John.
About 107 · Those who reject the Eucharist

The Eucharist is the body of Christ. Ignatius writes to the Church of Smyrna: the heretics stay away from the Eucharist and from prayer, because they do not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ.

The first Christians through pagan eyes. In a letter to the Emperor Trajan, the pagan governor Pliny the Younger reports that Christians meet before dawn on a fixed day, sing hymns to Christ as to a god, and bind themselves by an oath (sacramentum).
About 155 · The oldest description of Sunday Mass

A Sunday Mass in the second century. In his defense of the faith addressed to the emperor, the philosopher Justin describes the Sunday gathering: the writings of the apostles and prophets are read, a homily is given, prayers are said, and bread and wine are offered. This food is not ordinary bread, he says; it is the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus.

Different calendars, the same communion. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and a disciple of the apostle John, goes to Rome to discuss the date of Easter with Pope Anicetus. They do not agree, but their communion is not broken: Anicetus lets Polycarp celebrate the Eucharist in his own church.
About 156 · Bones more precious than gold

Veneration of the martyrs’ relics begins. The account of Polycarp’s martyrdom says that the Christians of Smyrna gathered his bones as “more precious than precious stones and finer than gold,” and kept the day of his martyrdom every year.

The first monument on Peter’s tomb. On the Vatican hill in Rome, a small monument (tropaion) is built right over Peter’s tomb. The altar of Constantine’s basilica and today’s high altar stand exactly above this spot. The custom of building altars over martyrs’ tombs and placing relics in the altar stone goes back to this tradition.
2nd and 3rd centuries · The witness of the catacombs

Prayers to the martyrs, the first image of Mary. Inscriptions in the Roman catacombs ask the martyrs to pray for the living, and pray for loved ones who have died. In a fresco in the Catacomb of Priscilla, Mary appears with the Child Jesus in her lap, long before Christianity became the state religion.

Every church must agree with Rome. In a work written while he was bishop of Lyon, Irenaeus of Smyrna says that every church must agree with the Church of Rome, founded by Peter and Paul, because of its pre-eminent authority, and he lists the bishops of Rome one by one from Peter to his own day.
About 204 · The sign of the cross
Everything starts with the sign of the cross. Tertullian writes that Christians trace the sign of the cross on their foreheads whenever they begin anything: setting out, bathing, sitting down to eat.
About 215 · A prayer still said at Mass

An ancient prayer still said today. The Apostolic Tradition, written in Rome and attributed to Hippolytus, gives the Eucharistic prayer of consecration word for word. Eucharistic Prayer II, said at Mass today, is largely based on this text.
Baptizing infants comes from the apostles. Origen of Alexandria writes that the Church received the tradition of baptizing infants directly from the apostles.
3rd century · The oldest prayer to Mary
“We fly to your protection.” A papyrus fragment found in Egypt preserves the oldest known prayer to Mary: “We fly to your protection, O Mother of God.” The prayer is still said today.
The Church is mother, God is father. In his work on the unity of the Church, Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, writes: no one can have God as father who does not have the Church as mother.

The Creed is born. The bishops gathered at Nicaea proclaim, against Arius, that the Son is “of one substance” (homoousios) with the Father. This Greek word, which is not found in the Bible, shows that the Church can speak in its own words to protect the faith. The first form of the Creed is written at this council.
About 325 · Eusebius’ History of the Church

Unbroken lists of bishops. In the first history of the Church, Eusebius of Caesarea lists the bishops of Rome, Jerusalem, Antioch and Alexandria without a break from the apostles to his own day. He also records how the books of the New Testament were discussed and discerned.

The Bible with its deuterocanonical books. The Sinai and Vatican manuscripts are the oldest great copies of the Bible we have. Their Old Testament includes Tobit, Judith, Wisdom and the other books that Protestants later removed, alongside the rest.

Ask, “Where is the Catholic Church?” Cyril of Jerusalem advises those preparing for baptism: when you go to a city, do not just ask “Where is the house of the Lord?”, because the heretics call their places that too; ask “Where is the Catholic Church?”
393 and 397 · The 27 books of the New Testament

The New Testament list is approved. The councils held at Hippo and Carthage approve the 27 books of today’s New Testament and the Old Testament list, including the deuterocanonical books. The same list is proclaimed again at the councils of Florence (1442) and Trent (1546).
No Gospel without the Church’s authority. Augustine of Hippo writes: I would not believe the Gospel either, if the authority of the Catholic Church did not move me to it.

Written and unwritten tradition together. John Chrysostom says that the apostles did not hand everything down by letter, that they passed on much without writing, and that both are equally worthy of belief. “It is a tradition; seek no further.”

Perseverance is a grace to be prayed for. Augustine writes that even someone baptized and born again can lose salvation through grave sin, and that persevering to the end is a further grace that must be asked for.
Mary is the Mother of God. The council gathered at Ephesus proclaims that Mary is the “Mother of God” (Theotokos), because the child she bore is Jesus, one single person who is both God and man.

“Peter has spoken through Leo!” At Chalcedon, today’s Kadıköy in Istanbul, more than 500 bishops hear Pope Leo’s letter on the two natures of Christ in one person, and cry out: “Peter has spoken through Leo!”

“Pray and work.” Benedict of Nursia founds his monastery at Monte Cassino and writes his Rule, built on the principle “pray and work.” After the fall of Rome, monasteries living by this Rule keep books and learning alive in the West for centuries.

The pope who held Rome together. As pope, Gregory holds Rome together through plague and war, has the chants of the liturgy put in order, and in 597 sends missionaries to the English. He calls himself “the servant of the servants of God,” a title the popes still use.
The veneration of icons is defended. Meeting again at Nicaea, the council defends the veneration of icons: the honor goes not to the image but to the person it shows. Worship belongs to God alone.
