The Great Schism. Tensions between Rome and Constantinople end in a break, with each side excommunicating the other. The excommunications were lifted in 1965 by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras, and prayer for unity continues today.

Transubstantiation, and confession once a year. The council uses the word “transubstantiation” to describe how the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the body and blood of Christ, and asks every Catholic to confess at least once a year and receive Communion at Easter.

Faith and reason do not conflict. Thomas Aquinas writes his great work showing that faith and reason do not conflict. Six hundred years later, Pope Leo XIII will make his thought the foundation of Catholic education.

The list of 73 books is proclaimed again. The council lists the books of the Bible one by one: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and Maccabees are on the list. So the 73-book Bible was the Church’s official list a century before the Reformation.
The first great printed book. The first great book printed on a press is the Latin Vulgate Bible, the Bible of the Catholic Church. The deuterocanonical books are in it too.
The Reformation begins. The Augustinian priest Martin Luther publishes his 95 theses on indulgences in Wittenberg. What starts as a call to debate ends up dividing Western Christianity.

Letters moved to the end, “alone” added. In his German New Testament, Luther calls the Letter of James “an epistle of straw”; he puts Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation unnumbered at the end of the book. In Romans 3:28 he also adds the word “alone” (allein), which is not in the Greek: “justified by faith alone.”

“This is my body.” At the meeting in Marburg, Zwingli argues that the Lord’s Supper is only a symbol. Luther insists that Christ is truly present in the bread, and chalks on the table: “Hoc est corpus meum,” this is my body.

The Reformers also believed Mary was ever-virgin. All his life Luther believed that Mary remained a virgin before, during and after giving birth. Zwingli too held that Mary was ever-virgin and called her the “Mother of God.”

The deuterocanonical books between the Testaments. Luther’s complete German Bible does not throw out the deuterocanonical books; he places them between the two Testaments under the heading “books not held equal to Holy Scripture, but useful and good to read.”

The translator of the English Bible dies. William Tyndale, who translated the Bible into English, is executed for heresy by imperial authorities at Vilvoorde, in today’s Belgium. Two years earlier England had broken with Rome over Henry VIII’s divorce; Henry too had banned Tyndale’s translation.

A city run by strict rules. Calvin writes that the “brothers” of Jesus were his relatives and that Mary remained a virgin. In Calvin’s Geneva, missing services, dancing or opposing his teaching was punished with fines, prison or exile; Servetus was burned for heresy in 1553.

The Church renews itself from within. In answer to the Reformation, the Church undertakes a great renewal from within: the 73-book Bible, the seven sacraments and the unity of faith and works are proclaimed again, and seminaries are founded to train priests.
A victory won with the Rosary. At the naval battle of Lepanto, Pope Pius V calls on all Christians to pray the Rosary. After the victory he declares 7 October the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary.
1826 · The books taken out of the Bible

The 66-book Protestant Bible. After a long debate, the largest Bible society in the Protestant world decides to stop supporting editions that include the deuterocanonical books. From then on, Protestant Bibles are printed with 66 books instead of 73.

To know history is to cease to be Protestant. John Henry Newman, one of Anglicanism’s most brilliant defenders, becomes a Catholic while studying the early Church, and writes: “To be deep in history is to cease to be a Protestant.”

Mary was preserved from original sin. Pope Pius IX proclaims as a dogma that Mary was preserved from every stain of original sin from the first moment of her conception. Four years later at Lourdes, Mary introduces herself to Bernadette: “I am the Immaculate Conception.”

Papal infallibility is defined. The council defines papal infallibility: the pope is protected from error only when, from the chair of Peter, he proclaims a teaching on faith or morals that binds the whole Church. His personal opinions and everyday decisions are not covered.
Thomas Aquinas back at the center. Pope Leo XIII makes the philosophy of Thomas Aquinas the foundation of seminary training and of the defense of the faith once again.

Catholic social teaching begins. This encyclical of Leo XIII begins Catholic social teaching: it defends workers’ right to a just wage and to organize, and rejects both unbridled capitalism and state socialism.

Scripture is inspired and without error. Leo XIII calls Catholic Bible scholars to engage with the historical and linguistic studies of the age, while restating that Scripture is inspired and without error.

Anglican orders are declared invalid. Leo XIII declares Anglican orders “absolutely null and utterly void” because of the changes made to the form and intention of the rite of ordination during the English Reformation.

Against watering down the faith. Pope Pius X asks priests, pastors and teachers of theology to swear an oath of loyalty to the faith against Modernism, which treated doctrine as something that changes with the times.
The Church’s first single book of law. Replacing centuries of scattered rulings, the Church’s first single book of law (Codex Iuris Canonici) is published.

Vatican City becomes a state. The treaty signed between the Holy See and Italy establishes Vatican City as an independent state and settles the “Roman Question” that began with the fall of the Papal States in 1870.
The pope’s voice around the world. Vatican Radio, founded by Guglielmo Marconi, carries the voice of Pope Pius XI to the whole world with no government in between.

An open condemnation of Nazi racism. Pius XI has the encyclical, written in German rather than Latin, smuggled into Germany and read in every Catholic church on the same Sunday. It openly condemns Nazi racism and the totalitarian state.

Peter’s tomb beneath the high altar. Excavations under St Peter’s Basilica uncover, right beneath the high altar, the 2nd-century monument and the inscriptions written in his honor. In 1950 Pope Pius XII announces that Peter’s tomb has been found.
The Bible is studied in its original languages. Pope Pius XII encourages Catholic scholars to study the Bible in its original languages, using the methods of archaeology, linguistics and history.
Mary is taken up body and soul into heaven. Pius XII proclaims as a dogma that at the end of her earthly life Mary was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory.
Everyone is called to holiness. Bishops from all over the world allow local languages in the liturgy, strengthen dialogue with other Christians and stress that everyone is called to holiness.
From Pentecost to the Second Vatican Council, 62 events. 33-100
The apostles set out from Jerusalem. Peter and Paul are martyred in Rome. The writings that survive from these years show how the first Christians lived. 100-451

The Church grows despite persecution. Bishops defend the faith. The councils of Nicaea and Ephesus proclaim the Creed and that Mary is the Mother of God. The list of the books of the Bible is settled. 451-1500
Rome falls, and the monasteries preserve learning. East and West split in 1054. Thomas Aquinas shows that faith and reason do not conflict. 1517-1600
Luther’s 95 Theses divide Western Christianity. The Church renews itself at the Council of Trent. 1800-1965

Two dogmas about Mary are proclaimed, the rights of workers are defended, and totalitarian regimes are condemned. The Second Vatican Council calls everyone to holiness. The story goes on in the lives of the saints.

The Second Vatican Council met in Rome from 1962 to 1965. This page covers what happened there, what its sixteen documents say, how the Mass developed from the Last Supper to today, and how the Church asks Catholics to read the Council.

How it started On January 25, 1959, three months after his election, Pope John XXIII told a small group of cardinals at the Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls that he meant to call an ecumenical council. He later wrote that they answered with a “devout silence”. He was 77, and most people expected a short, quiet pontificate. An ecumenical council is a gathering of the world’s bishops in union with the Pope. The Church counts twenty-one of them, from Nicaea in 325 to Vatican II. The one before, the First Vatican Council (1869-1870), defined papal infallibility and was then cut short when Italian troops took Rome. The Council opened on October 11, 1962. In his opening speech, John XXIII said he disagreed with the “prophets of gloom, who are always forecasting disaster”, and described the Council’s purpose: The substance of the ancient doctrine of the deposit of faith is one thing, and the way in which it is presented is another. Pope St. John XXIII, opening address, 1962 He did not plan to define new dogmas or issue condemnations. The aim was to teach the same faith in a way people of the time could understand. John died on June 3, 1963, after the first session. Pope Paul VI, elected on June 21, carried the Council through three more autumn sessions and closed it on December 8, 1965.

Who took part Nearly 2,500 bishops voted, more than at any earlier council; the First Vatican Council had about 700. They sat on tiered benches built along the nave of St. Peter’s, and the debates were held in Latin. For the first time, Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant churches sent official observers. From 1964 lay auditors were admitted too, women among them. Theologians served as advisers to the bishops; one of them, a young German priest named Joseph Ratzinger, would become Pope Benedict XVI. Five popes took part in the Council. John XXIII called it, Paul VI attended as a cardinal and then led it, and three future popes attended as bishops or advisers: Albino Luciani (John Paul I), Karol Wojtyła (John Paul II), who helped draft Gaudium et Spes , and Ratzinger. Among the bishops was also Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre, who would later found the Society of St. Pius X.

Some facts The Moonlight Speech. On the evening the Council opened, a crowd with torches filled St. Peter’s Square. John XXIII came to his window and spoke without notes: “When you go home, you will find your children. Give your children a caress and tell them: this is the Pope’s caress.” Bar Jonah and Bar Abbas. Two coffee bars were set up inside St. Peter’s for the bishops. The bishops nicknamed them after Simon Peter, “son of Jonah” ( Matthew 16:17 ), and after Barabbas. Paul VI’s tiara. On November 13, 1964, during the Council, Paul VI laid his papal tiara on the altar of St. Peter’s as a gift for the poor. It was bought by American Catholics and is kept today at the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception in Washington. The votes. The Constitution on the Liturgy passed by 2,147 votes to 4, and the Constitution on the Church by 2,151 to 5. Rome and Constantinople. On December 7, 1965, the day before the Council closed, Paul VI in Rome and Patriarch Athenagoras in Istanbul lifted the excommunications of 1054 at the same hour. No new dogma. The Council defined no new dogma. In January 1966 Paul VI explained that its teaching still carries the authority of the Church’s supreme ordinary magisterium, which all the faithful are to accept “docilely and sincerely”.

The first Christians (about 30-100) On the night before He died, Jesus took bread and said, “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me” ( Luke 22:19-20 ). After Pentecost the first believers “devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” ( Acts 2:42 ), and met “on the first day of the week” to break bread ( Acts 20:7 ). Around the year 55, St. Paul wrote down what he had “received from the Lord” about the Last Supper ( 1 Corinthians 11:23-29 ), the oldest written account we have. The Didache , a church manual from the late first century, already says: “Every Lord’s day gather yourselves together, and break bread, and give thanksgiving after having confessed your transgressions, that your sacrifice may be pure.”

A Sunday in Rome, about 155 St. Justin Martyr, writing to the Roman emperor to explain what Christians do, left us the first full description of the Mass: On the day called Sunday, all who live in cities or in the country gather together to one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits; then, when the reader has ceased, the president verbally instructs, and exhorts to the imitation of these good things. Then we all rise together and pray, and, as we before said, when our prayer is ended, bread and wine and water are brought, and the president in like manner offers prayers and thanksgivings, according to his ability, and the people assent, saying Amen. St. Justin Martyr, First Apology 67 Readings, a homily, the prayer of the faithful, the offering of bread and wine, the Eucharistic Prayer, the people’s Amen, Communion: both forms of the Mass today follow this same order.

Fixed prayers (200-400) El Greco · Pentecost A Roman church order from the early third century, traditionally credited to St. Hippolytus, gives a full Eucharistic Prayer with the dialogue still heard today: “Lift up your hearts.” “We lift them up to the Lord.” Today’s Eucharistic Prayer II is modeled on it. Bishops still prayed in their own words, but within a set shape. After Emperor Constantine ended the persecutions in 313, the Mass moved from homes into great basilicas. Processions, candles, incense and vestments (at first simply the formal clothes of a Roman gentleman) became part of worship.
When Latin was the people’s language

When Latin was the people’s language Rome’s first Christians worshiped in Greek, the common language of the empire. In the second half of the fourth century, as fewer Romans spoke Greek, the Church of Rome switched to Latin, the language of the street. Around 390, St. Ambrose of Milan quoted the heart of the Roman Canon, the Eucharistic Prayer still in the Missal today, in words that are almost the same as ours. The Latin Mass itself began as a change to the language people spoke, as the reform of the 1960s was. In the East, meanwhile, the Church prayed in Greek, Syriac, Coptic, Armenian and later Slavonic, and the Eastern Catholic Churches still keep their own ancient liturgies.
Gregory the Great and the Middle Ages

Gregory the Great and the Middle Ages Pope St. Gregory the Great (590-604) set the Our Father right after the Eucharistic Prayer, where it still is, and added a line to the Canon: “order our days in your peace.” Gregorian chant is named after him. Charlemagne spread the Roman Mass across his empire, where it absorbed northern customs and more private prayers for the priest. The Creed was added to the Mass in Rome only in 1014, at the request of Emperor Henry II. Around 1200, priests in Paris began lifting the Host high after the consecration so the people could see it, and bells were rung. The Eucharistic miracle of Bolsena (1263) is linked by tradition to the feast of Corpus Christi, which Pope Urban IV extended to the whole Church in 1264. In the same period the people took less part. The quiet “Low Mass” became common, most people received Communion rarely (the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 had to require it at least once a year), and many prayed the Rosary or other devotions while the priest prayed at the altar. Raphael · The Mass at Bolsena

Trent and one Missal (1570) The Protestant Reformers rejected the Mass as a sacrifice. The Council of Trent answered by restating the Church’s faith, and in 1570 Pope St. Pius V issued one Roman Missal for the whole Latin Church. The printing press made such uniformity possible for the first time. Rites at least 200 years old, such as those of Milan, Toledo and the Dominicans, were allowed to continue. This Missal, revised several times (1604, 1634, 1884, 1920, 1962), was used for four centuries. It is what people mean by “the Tridentine Mass”, and its 1962 edition is the one used for the traditional Latin Mass today.

Renewal before the Council (1903-1962) Liturgical reform started before Vatican II. In 1903 Pope St. Pius X wrote that the faithful should find the true Christian spirit in their “active participation” in the liturgy, the first time a pope used the phrase. He also urged frequent Communion and, in 1910, opened it to young children. Monasteries such as Solesmes led a revival of Gregorian chant. Pius XII’s encyclical Mediator Dei (1947) endorsed the liturgical movement while warning against its excesses. He restored the Easter Vigil to the night (1951-1955), shortened the Communion fast, and allowed evening Masses. In 1962 John XXIII added St. Joseph to the list of saints in the Roman Canon, the first change to that list in many centuries.

The reform (1963-1970) Sacrosanctum Concilium asked for a revision of the rites so that they would be clearer and the people could take part more fully. It also warned: “there must be no innovations unless the good of the Church genuinely and certainly requires them; and care must be taken that any new forms adopted should in some way grow organically from forms already existing” (23). The changes came within a few years. In 1964 and 1965 parts of the Mass were allowed in the vernacular; by 1967 the whole Mass could be. In 1968 three new Eucharistic Prayers were approved. On April 3, 1969, Paul VI promulgated the new Roman Missal, and the new Order of Mass came into use on the First Sunday of Advent that year. Two cardinals, Ottaviani and Bacci, sent the Pope a critical study of it. Paul VI defended the reform. He said the Church was giving up something valuable, the language of the Christian centuries, because the people’s understanding of their prayer was worth more.

Since then 1971: English writers and artists, Agatha Christie among them, petitioned Paul VI to keep the old Mass. He allowed its occasional use in England and Wales, a permission still known as the “Agatha Christie indult”. 1984 and 1988: John Paul II allowed the 1962 Missal more widely with the bishop’s permission, and after Archbishop Lefebvre ordained bishops without papal approval in 1988, he asked bishops to be generous to Catholics attached to it. 2002 and 2011: A third edition of the Roman Missal, and a new English translation closer to the Latin (“And with your spirit”). 2007: Benedict XVI’s Summorum Pontificum let every priest celebrate the 1962 Missal, describing the two Missals as “a twofold use of one and the same rite”. 2021 and 2022: Pope Francis’s Traditionis Custodes made the Missal of Paul VI and John Paul II the one expression of the Roman Rite’s law of prayer and placed the older Missal under each bishop’s regulation. In Desiderio Desideravi he called the whole Church to rediscover the beauty of the liturgy and to be formed by it.

Everything the Council taught is in sixteen documents, about 103,000 words in all. The four constitutions are the main texts; the decrees and declarations apply them to particular parts of the Church’s life. All are free to read at vatican.va . Document Kind, year In one line Sacrosanctum Concilium Constitution, 1963 The liturgy is “the summit” of the Church’s life; the faithful should take a full, conscious and active part in it. Lumen Gentium Dogmatic constitution, 1964 What the Church is: the People of God, built on the apostles under Peter, with every member called to holiness. Dei Verbum Dogmatic constitution, 1965 God speaks through Scripture and Tradition, faithfully taught by the Church; the Bible should be open to every believer. Gaudium et Spes Pastoral constitution, 1965 The Church in the modern world: human dignity, marriage and family, work, culture, war and peace. Inter Mirifica Decree, 1963 The press, radio, film and television, and the duty to use them well. Orientalium Ecclesiarum Decree, 1964 The Eastern Catholic Churches keep their own rites, laws and heritage. Unitatis Redintegratio Decree, 1964 Working and praying for the unity of all Christians. Christus Dominus Decree, 1965 The bishop’s work in his diocese; national bishops’ conferences. Perfectae Caritatis Decree, 1965 Renewing religious life by returning to each order’s founding spirit. Optatam Totius Decree, 1965 How priests are to be trained. Apostolicam Actuositatem Decree, 1965 The mission of lay people in the Church and the world. Ad Gentes Decree, 1965 The Church is missionary by her nature. Presbyterorum Ordinis Decree, 1965 The life and ministry of priests, including celibacy. Gravissimum Educationis Declaration, 1965 Christian education and the rights of parents. Nostra Aetate Declaration, 1965 How the Church looks at other religions, with special words for Jews and Muslims. Dignitatis Humanae Declaration, 1965 No state may force anyone to believe, or stop anyone from worshiping.

Many claims about Vatican II describe what was done after it, not what it wrote. Here are the most common ones, checked against the documents. Did the Council abolish Latin? No. “The use of the Latin language is to be preserved in the Latin rites” ( Sacrosanctum Concilium 36). It allowed the mother tongue a wider place, especially in the readings and some prayers, and asked that the faithful still be able to “say or sing together in Latin” their parts of the Mass (54). Gregorian chant, it said, should be given “pride of place” (116), and the pipe organ “held in high esteem” (120). The Council did not ask for Latin and chant to disappear from parishes, as they did within a few years. Did it turn the altars around? No Council document mentions the direction the priest faces. A 1964 instruction recommended building new altars free of the wall so that Mass could be said facing the people, and the current Missal calls that desirable wherever possible. Celebrating toward the east, with priest and people facing the same way, is still permitted, and the Missal’s own rubrics still tell the priest to turn toward the people at certain moments. Did it make the Pope one bishop among many? No. The Council taught that the bishops form a college with the Pope, but the college “has no authority unless it is understood together with the Roman Pontiff” and acts “never without this head”, while the Pope has “full, supreme and universal power over the Church. And he is always free to exercise this power” ( Lumen Gentium 22). It restated the First Vatican Council’s teaching on papal infallibility in full (25). In 1964 Paul VI had a note of explanation added to make this clear. Did it say my conscience can overrule the Church? No. The Council calls conscience man’s “most secret core and sanctuary” ( Gaudium et Spes 16), but says that in forming their consciences, Christians “ought carefully to attend to the sacred and certain doctrine of the Church” ( Dignitatis Humanae 14). Its teaching on religious freedom is about the state, not about Catholics and the Church, and it “leaves untouched traditional Catholic doctrine on the moral duty of men and societies toward the true religion and toward the one Church of Christ” (1). As the Catechism puts it, “conscience must be informed”, and its education “is indispensable” (CCC 1783). Did it say all religions are equally true? No. Nostra Aetate says the Church “rejects nothing that is true and holy” in other religions, and speaks with esteem of Muslims, who “adore the one God”, and of the Jewish people, from whom Christ came (3-4). It also says the Church “ever must proclaim Christ ‘the way, the truth, and the life’” (2). Lumen Gentium teaches that the one Church of Christ “subsists in” the Catholic Church (8), and Ad Gentes that the Church is missionary by her very nature (2). See also Answering Islam and A Call to Our Jewish Friends . Did it end celibacy or change the teaching on marriage? No. The Council praised priestly celibacy and “again approves and confirms” the law of the Latin Church ( Presbyterorum Ordinis 16). It called married love a gift to be lived in fidelity and openness to life ( Gaudium et Spes 48-51) and left the question of birth regulation to the Pope, who answered in Humanae Vitae (1968). Did it change doctrine? No. The Council itself says the Church’s teaching office “is not above the word of God, but serves it, teaching only what has been handed on” ( Dei Verbum 10). What changed was the way the faith was presented, as John XXIII had said in his opening speech, and much of the Church’s discipline and worship.

This table compares the two Missals as their rubrics describe them. Some differences people notice, like altar rails or music, come from local custom, not from either Missal. 1962 Missal Missal of Paul VI (1970) Language Latin throughout; the readings are often repeated in the vernacular before the homily. Usually the people’s language; Latin remains the Missal’s official language and may always be used. Direction Priest and people face the same way, usually toward the apse ( ad orientem ). Usually facing the people; facing east is still permitted. Beginning Prayers at the foot of the altar, with Psalm 43: “I will go in to the altar of God”, said by priest and server. A greeting, then the Penitential Act said by everyone. Readings A one-year cycle, usually an Epistle and a Gospel. A three-year Sunday cycle: usually an Old Testament reading, a Psalm, a New Testament reading and the Gospel; a two-year weekday cycle. Prayer of the Faithful Not part of the Roman Mass for many centuries. Restored, as in Justin’s day. Offertory Prayers of offering: “Receive, O holy Father, this spotless host”. Shorter prayers modeled on Jewish table blessings: “Blessed are you, Lord God of all creation”. Eucharistic Prayer The Roman Canon only, said quietly. The Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I) or one of several others, said aloud. Sign of peace Passed among the clergy at a solemn Mass. May be offered among the people. Communion Kneeling, on the tongue, under the form of bread. Kneeling or standing; on the tongue, or in the hand where bishops allow it; sometimes under both kinds. Who answers The server answers for the people; at a sung Mass, the choir sings. The whole congregation answers and sings. Lay roles Servers; lay readers are rare. Lay readers, and extraordinary ministers of Holy Communion when needed. Ending The blessing, then the Last Gospel ( John 1:1-14 ). The blessing and the dismissal. What stayed the same In both Missals the Mass is the one sacrifice of Calvary made present; Christ is truly present, body, blood, soul and divinity; the ordained priest acts in the person of Christ; the Word comes first and the Eucharist follows; and the Roman Canon is still in the Missal, word for word. To follow the newer Mass step by step, see The Holy Mass and Celebrating the Mass .

In 1971 the English Catholic writer John Eppstein, a convert who had worked in international affairs, published Has the Catholic Church Gone Mad? Eppstein accepted the Council, and he wrote while the changes were happening. He did not blame the documents. He found in them “a deep spirituality, great scholarship, an abounding charity”. His concern was what happened next: a stream of priests and nuns leaving their vows, seminaries thrown into turmoil, open defiance of Humanae Vitae , a Dutch catechism that a commission of cardinals ordered amended, translations of the Mass settled by majority vote, and a press campaign for a new “Conciliar Church” cut loose from the Pope. He argued that much of the crisis came from what commentators and the press claimed in the Council’s name, not from its documents. He showed, for example, how one sentence about freedom from state coercion was being used to justify Catholics rejecting the Church’s own teaching, a reading the Council itself rejects ( Dignitatis Humanae 14). Paul VI himself said in 1972 that “from some fissure the smoke of Satan has entered the temple of God”. He also pointed out that the confusion was mostly in the rich West. In Africa, he wrote, the young Church was solid and sane, and its bishops wanted seminary discipline kept. His book ends with this line: The first and most important mark of the Church of Christ is holiness. John Eppstein, Has the Catholic Church Gone Mad? (1971) Some of Eppstein’s political views, such as his defense of colonial rule in Africa, are not ours, and his book quotes Archbishop Lefebvre, who later broke communion with Rome. We draw on him as a witness to those years, not as a guide on every question.

In 2005 Pope Benedict XVI, who had attended the Council as a theologian, described two ways of reading it. One, a “hermeneutic of discontinuity and rupture”, treated the Council as a break with the Church before it, so that its “spirit” mattered more than its words. The other, the “hermeneutic of reform”, reads the Council as “renewal in the continuity of the one subject-Church”. He said the second is the right one, and the one that has borne fruit (Address to the Roman Curia, December 22, 2005). St. John Paul II called the Council “a sure compass by which to take our bearings in the century now beginning”. In 1985 the world’s bishops met to look back on the Council, and asked for a catechism for the whole Church. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992) draws on the Council on almost every page, and reads it alongside Scripture, the Fathers and every earlier council. In practice this means: Read the texts Read the documents, not summaries of them. Most are short, and all are online. Read them with the whole Tradition The Council quotes Scripture, the Fathers, Trent and the First Vatican Council constantly. It is meant to be read with them. Tell the texts from what followed The documents, the “spirit” claimed for them and the way they were carried out are three different things. Do what it actually asked Read the Bible. Pray the liturgy with understanding. Keep Latin and chant alive. Seek holiness in ordinary life. Bring the Gospel to everyone.

Hubert and Jan van Eyck · The Adoration of the Lamb Can a faithful Catholic accept the Second Vatican Council? Yes, and Catholics are required to. It was a lawful ecumenical council, called and confirmed by two popes and received by every pope since. Its teaching belongs to the Church’s magisterium. A Catholic may not set it aside, any more than Trent or Nicaea. Things also went wrong. The years after the Council brought real losses: empty seminaries and convents, catechesis that taught little, beauty stripped from churches, and changes that many Catholics felt were done to them rather than with them. Catholics who were hurt by these changes are not opponents of the Council. Many of them want what it actually asked for. Much also went well. Catholics read the Bible far more than before. Lay people know they are called to holiness, not only priests and nuns. Friendship has grown with the Orthodox and with the Jewish people. The Council’s defense of religious freedom gave the Church a voice against communist states, and a Polish bishop who helped write its texts later, as Pope John Paul II, helped bring communism down in his own country. Catholics still disagree about altars, music and Latin. But in every Mass, in either Missal, Christ offers the same sacrifice to the Father. Catholics who prefer the older form and those who prefer the newer one are not two parties: they share one faith and one Pope, and owe the same obedience to their bishops. A parish that celebrates Mass the way the Council asked, with reverence and silence, Scripture and chant, a homily that teaches and people who understand what is happening, gives both groups most of what they want. That work is not finished, and it depends on holiness more than on arguments: reverence, humility and prayer. Before the Council, John XXIII prayed that God would renew His wonders “in this our day, as by a new Pentecost”. After the first Pentecost, the believers were “of one heart and soul” ( Acts 4:32 ). That is still the goal.

Eight centuries of one simple prayer: how a bag of pebbles became a string of beads, how St. Dominic, a sea battle, Lourdes and Fatima shaped it, and why Catholics still pray it every day. The beginning
Where does the name come from?

Where does the name come from? The name “Rosary” comes from the Latin rosarium, meaning “rose garden” or “garland of roses”. Each Hail Mary is like a rose offered to the Virgin Mary; fifty of them make a garland. Even the English word “bead” comes from the Old English “bede”, which meant “prayer”. A rosary isn’t a lucky charm or a piece of jewelry; the beads just help you keep count.

Rooted in the Gospel The Rosary is also called “the Bible on beads”, because every prayer in it either comes straight from Scripture or sums up what Scripture teaches. Jesus Himself taught us the Our Father. The first half of the Hail Mary is simply what Gabriel and Elizabeth said to Mary. Where each prayer comes from in the Bible The Apostles’ Creed: a short summary of what the Apostles taught. It grew out of the creed recited by those being baptized in Rome in the 2nd century. The Our Father: the prayer Jesus taught (Matthew 6:9-13). The Hail Mary (first half): the words “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee” are Gabriel’s (Luke 1:28). The words “Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb” are Elizabeth’s (Luke 1:42). The names “Mary” and “Jesus” were added only to make clear who is meant. “Holy Mary”: Scripture calls all believers “saints”, that is, holy ones (Ephesians 1:1). Mary, the first to welcome Jesus, has every right to the title. “Mother of God”: a mother does not give birth to a “nature”; she gives birth to a “person”. The person Mary gave birth to is the Son of God, who took on a human nature. Elizabeth, too, calls her “the mother of my Lord” (Luke 1:43). The Church formally proclaimed this at the Council of Ephesus in 431. “Pray for us sinners”: Paul asks Christians to pray for one another (1 Timothy 2:1-4). Those in heaven also offer the prayers of the faithful to God (Revelation 5:8). The Glory Be: a short hymn of praise to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). The Hail Holy Queen: in David’s kingdom the queen was not the king’s wife but his mother; Solomon seated his mother at his right hand (1 Kings 2:19). Since Jesus is the King of David’s line, His mother is the Queen. One more thing: “pray” doesn’t automatically mean “worship”. Its old meaning is simply “ask”, as in “pray tell”. When we pray to the Virgin Mary, we are not worshipping her. Just as we might ask a friend, “Will you pray for me?”, we are asking her to pray to God for us.

Isn’t this vain repetition? Jesus says, “When you are praying, speak not much, as the heathens” (Matthew 6:7). But what He forbids is not repetition as such; it is empty repetition, words that do not come from the heart and try to win over the gods by sheer quantity. Scripture itself is full of repetition: in the garden of Gethsemane Jesus prayed the same words three times (Matthew 26:44). In Psalm 136 the words “for his steadfast love endures for ever” are repeated twenty-six times. Day and night, the angels never stop saying, “Holy, holy, holy” (Revelation 4:8). What really matters is not the number of Hail Marys but the mysteries: taking time over the life of Jesus. Fr. Chris Alar compares this to a film score: the music does not replace the film, but it lets you feel the scene more deeply. The Hail Marys of the Rosary are the music playing in the background; the film itself is the life of Jesus. Twenty mysteries, twenty Gospel scenes
Isn’t this vain repetition?: The Joyful Mysteries
The Annunciation (Luke 1:26-38) The Visitation (Luke 1:39-56) The Nativity (Luke 2:1-20) The Presentation (Luke 2:22-38) The Finding in the Temple (Luke 2:41-52)
Isn’t this vain repetition?: The Luminous Mysteries

The Baptism of Jesus (Matthew 3:13-17) The Wedding Feast of Cana (John 2:1-11) The Proclamation of the Kingdom (Mark 1:14-15) The Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-8) The Institution of the Eucharist (Luke 22:19-20)
Isn’t this vain repetition?: The Sorrowful Mysteries
The Agony in the Garden (Matthew 26:36-46) The Scourging at the Pillar (John 19:1) The Crowning with Thorns (Matthew 27:27-31) The Carrying of the Cross (John 19:17) The Crucifixion (Luke 23:33-46)
Isn’t this vain repetition?: The Glorious Mysteries

The Resurrection (Luke 24:1-12) The Ascension (Acts 1:9-11) The Descent of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:1-4) The Assumption The Coronation of Mary The last two mysteries are not described in the Gospels; they rest on the Church’s tradition and are read in the light of the “woman clothed with the sun, and on her head a crown of twelve stars” in the Book of Revelation (Revelation 12:1). So in the space of a few minutes, the Rosary takes you through the whole Gospel, from the birth of Jesus to His resurrection. In the words of Pope Pius XII, the Rosary is “a compendium of the entire Gospel”. The Middle Ages

From pebbles to beads Monks prayed all 150 psalms every day. But there was no printing press yet, a handwritten book cost a fortune, and most people couldn’t read anyway. So lay people who wanted to join in prayed 150 Our Fathers instead. To keep count, they carried a bag of pebbles and moved one aside with each prayer. Over time the pebbles gave way to knotted cords and beads. Later, people did the same with 150 Hail Marys, and this came to be called “Mary’s Psalter”. To this day the Joyful, Sorrowful and Glorious Mysteries each have 50 Hail Marys. Together they make exactly 150, the number of the Psalms.

St. Dominic At the beginning of the 13th century St. Dominic was preaching in southern France to people caught up in the Albigensian heresy. He was a gifted preacher, but his sermons weren’t getting through. According to tradition, in 1214 he withdrew to a forest near Toulouse and fasted and prayed for three days and three nights. When at last he collapsed from exhaustion, the Virgin Mary appeared to him and said: In this kind of warfare, the battering ram has always been the Angelic Salutation. Preach my Psalter. Our Lady to St. Dominic, according to tradition Tradition also credits Dominic with linking each decade to a scene from the life of Jesus. His order’s name gave rise to a well-known Latin pun: the Dominicans are the “Domini canes”, “the hounds of the Lord”, watchdogs guarding the flock from wolves. Some historians think the story only took its present form in the 15th century, and it’s true that no written record survives from Dominic’s lifetime. Even so, the Church has honored the tradition for centuries. One more detail: in Dominic’s day the Hail Mary was only the first half, ending with the words “...and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus.” Matt Fradd suggests that Protestant friends who are drawn to the Rosary could pray it as people did in St. Dominic’s day, using only this first half, which comes entirely from Scripture.

Forgotten and reborn After the Black Death swept through Europe in the 14th century, the Rosary fell out of use. In the 15th century the Dominican Blessed Alan de la Roche had every gift he needed to bring it back, yet he did nothing. The story goes that one day at Mass, as he raised the Host, he heard a voice rebuking him, and from then on he got to work. Alan spread the Rosary throughout Europe and in 1470 founded the first Rosary Confraternity. He was so successful that people thought he had invented the Rosary. He answered, “No, this is Dominic’s prayer.” The well-known “15 Promises of the Rosary” also come from the private revelations Alan passed on. One of these promises reads: “The Rosary shall be a powerful armor against hell; it will destroy vice and decrease sin.” 1571 and after
Lepanto and the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary (1571)

Lepanto and the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary (1571) Under Pope Pius V, himself a Dominican friar, the Ottoman fleet was pushing west across the Mediterranean. Spain, Venice and the Papal States joined forces in the “Holy League”. The Pope called all Christians to pray the Rosary. Churches were kept open day and night, and the Pope himself walked barefoot in processions through the streets of Rome. On 7 October 1571 the Christian fleet defeated the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto. The Pope credited the victory to the intercession of the Virgin Mary and set up a feast on that date. The Church still keeps it every year on 7 October as the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary. In 1569 Pius V fixed the form of the Rosary with its 15 mysteries. A year earlier, in 1568, he had placed the second half of the Hail Mary, ending “Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death”, in the Church’s official prayer book, the Breviary. So it was a pope who doubled the length of the Hail Mary.
The Rosary goes to the world

The Rosary goes to the world In the same century, missionaries set out for the Americas, Asia and Africa. They couldn’t carry heavy books everywhere, but a rosary in the pocket was enough to tell the whole life of Jesus. That is how “the Bible on beads” reached every corner of the world. Many saints prayed it every day: Teresa of Ávila, Francis de Sales, John Bosco and Mother Teresa of Calcutta, to name only a few. Padre Pio called the Rosary “my weapon” and gave his spiritual children this advice: “Pray as many as you can.” Blessed Miguel Pro, shot by a firing squad in Mexico in 1927 for his faith, died with his arms stretched out like a cross, a crucifix in one hand and a rosary in the other, shouting “Long live Christ the King!” A photograph of that moment survives. The 19th and 20th centuries
From the occult to sainthood: Bartolo Longo

From the occult to sainthood: Bartolo Longo Few stories show the power of the Rosary better than Bartolo Longo’s. As a law student in 19th-century Naples, Longo lost his faith; he went to séances and was even made a “priest” of an occult sect. He was left with terrible nightmares, deep depression and thoughts of suicide. A Dominican priest told him about the Rosary. Longo broke with the occult and even walked into a séance to call those present to repentance. He spent the rest of his life spreading the Rosary in the town of Pompeii. He built orphanages, schools and the Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary of Pompeii, today one of the best-known Rosary shrines in the world. St. John Paul II called him “a true apostle of the Rosary”. Longo was canonized in 2025.

Lourdes and Fatima In the 19th century Pope Leo XIII wrote eleven encyclicals on the Rosary and declared October the month of the Rosary. In 1858 at Lourdes, fourteen-year-old Bernadette was praying the Rosary alone in front of the grotto when the Virgin Mary appeared to her. Mary had a rosary on her arm. As Bernadette prayed, Mary passed the beads through her fingers, but she did not say the Hail Mary; she joined in only at the Glory Be. Mary appeared eighteen times in all, and every apparition began with the Rosary. In 1917 at Fatima she appeared to three shepherd children. The youngest of them, Jacinta, was only seven. Mary told them, “I am the Lady of the Rosary,” and asked that the Rosary be prayed every day for peace in the world. The “Fatima Prayer” said at the end of each decade (“O my Jesus, forgive us our sins...”) also comes from these apparitions. Today
St. John Paul II and the Luminous Mysteries

St. John Paul II and the Luminous Mysteries Karol Wojtyła lost his mother when he was eight. The story goes that he went into a church, looked at an image of the Virgin Mary and said, “Now you are my mother.” When he became pope he took the motto “Totus Tuus” (Entirely Yours). Two weeks after his election he said, “The Rosary is my favorite prayer.” On 13 May 1981, the feast of Our Lady of Fatima, he was shot in St. Peter’s Square by Mehmet Ali Ağca. The bullets missed his vital organs by millimeters. The Pope later said: “One hand fired, and another guided the bullet.” Two years later he visited Ağca in prison and forgave him. That bullet is now set in the crown of the statue of Our Lady at Fatima. In 2002 he added a fourth set of five mysteries to the Rosary: the Luminous Mysteries. Fr. Chris Alar explains why: the Joyful Mysteries tell of Jesus’ birth, the Sorrowful Mysteries of His death, and the Glorious Mysteries of His resurrection. So what is missing? His life. The Luminous Mysteries fill that gap: Jesus’ baptism, the wedding at Cana, His proclamation of the Kingdom of God, His Transfiguration on the mountain and His institution of the Eucharist. Nor was this an entirely new idea. In the 20th century the Maltese priest St. George Preca had written a similar set called the “Mysteries of Light”. Still, the Luminous Mysteries are optional: the Pope proposed them, he didn’t require them.

The heart of the Rosary The form of the Rosary has changed over the centuries, but its heart never has: looking at Jesus through the eyes of the Virgin Mary. Who better to show us Jesus than Mary, who was there from the manger to the cross? And at the very center of every Hail Mary stands the same name: Jesus. Gabriel Castillo suggests three simple steps: Pause Before you begin to pray, stop for a few seconds and remember that God is present. Picture it Imagine the scene of the mystery as if you were there. If you cannot picture it, look at an image or tell yourself what happened. Talk In that scene, speak to Jesus and Mary in your own words. You do not have to finish the Rosary in one sitting. You can pray one decade in the morning, another on the way to work and another after a meal. If you told someone during the day, “I’ll pray for you,” remember them in your evening Rosary; you can offer each bead for a different person. Spiritual warfare
Why does the devil fear the Hail Mary?

The Rosary is not only a prayer that brings peace; it is a weapon in a spiritual battle that begins on the first pages of the Bible. After the disobedience of Adam and Eve, God says to the serpent: “I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed: she shall crush thy head, and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel” (Genesis 3:15). This verse is known as the Protoevangelium, the “first Gospel”. Read plainly, the woman is Eve; but the Church Fathers also saw in her Mary, the “new Eve”, and in her offspring, Jesus Christ. The decades of the Rosary are like a machine-gun belt: every bead is a bullet, every affection of the soul is an explosion of faith that frightens off Satan, and Mary once more crushes his head. Fr. Dolindo Ruotolo In the Hebrew text, the pronoun refers to the woman’s offspring, that is, to Christ. Older Latin translations such as the Vulgate, however, use a feminine pronoun (ipsa conteret caput tuum, “she shall crush thy head”), and this inspired the traditional images of Mary crushing the serpent. In Catholic teaching, Mary takes an indirect but active part in this victory: she shares in the work of salvation through her “yes” at the Incarnation and her suffering at the foot of the cross. The wound to the heel stands for Jesus’ death on the cross: the devil thought he had defeated Christ, but it was by that very death that Jesus crushed the serpent’s head. In the Bible’s last book, Revelation, the story ends with the dragon waging war against the woman (Revelation 12). Gabriel greeted Mary with the words “Hail, full of grace.” In these words the Church sees the Immaculate Conception: the teaching that God kept Mary free from all sin from the first moment of her conception in her mother’s womb. With the same greeting the angel also announced that the Son of God would become man. That moment is the devil’s greatest defeat. This is why saints and exorcists say that the devil trembles when he hears the Hail Mary. The proud angel cannot bear to be reminded that he was defeated by the “yes” of a humble young girl. Prayed faithfully every day, the Rosary opens the soul to God’s grace; someone whose mind is filled with the life of Christ grows stronger against sin and evil. But be warned: at first, things may feel like they’re getting worse, not better. Restlessness, reluctance, an inner voice saying “Give it up, what’s the point?”... That is because the devil does not give up easily; he fights back. Don’t stop. Keep going, more stubbornly than before. By God’s grace, those who persevere in prayer see darkness turn into light, and in that light they find Christ, the New Adam, and Mary, the New Eve, who bring new life to humanity. In the end, this is a struggle between good and evil. Evil wants us to give up; we must never stop praying. And we do not have to face this struggle alone. The words Fr. Patrick Peyton spread around the world still hold true: “The family that prays together stays together.” Ready to try? Start now with Pray the Rosary, Bead by Bead.
