Mother of God · 1st century AD Mary was a young Jewish girl, probably no more than fifteen, from Nazareth, a small town in Galilee. Luke’s Gospel tells how the angel Gabriel came to her and announced that she would bear the Son of God by the power of the Holy Spirit, with no human father. Her answer became one of the turning points of the whole Christian story: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."
Fiat: The Woman Who Said Yes

The Church calls this short sentence Mary’s fiat (Latin for "let it be done") and sees it as one of the decisive moments in the history of salvation. Eve said no to God in the garden of Eden; Mary said yes, and so the early Church Fathers called her the "new Eve." While she was expecting, Mary went to visit her relative Elizabeth, who greeted her with the words "Blessed art thou among women." Mary answered with the Magnificat, the hymn the Church still prays every evening in the Liturgy of the Hours: "My soul doth magnify the Lord."
From Bethlehem to the Foot of the Cross

The Gospels show Mary in only a handful of scenes, but each one stays with you: giving birth in a stable in Bethlehem; searching for three days for the twelve-year-old Jesus and finding Him in the Temple; at the wedding at Cana, when the wine ran out, telling the servants, "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye," and so prompting His first miracle. The hardest scene of all is at the foot of the cross. John’s Gospel tells us she stayed with her son through His last hours, and from the cross Jesus gave her into the care of His beloved disciple, John. The Church remembers her grief in the devotion to Our Lady of Sorrows.

Over the centuries the Church has defined four dogmas about Mary: that she is the Mother of God (Council of Ephesus, 431); that she remained a virgin all her life; the Immaculate Conception, meaning she was kept free from original sin from the first moment of her existence (1854); and the Assumption, meaning that at the end of her earthly life she was taken up body and soul into heaven (1950). Catholics do not worship Mary. They ask her to pray to God for them, the way you would ask a friend, except that this friend is the most reliable of all. The Rosary, the apparitions at places like Lourdes and Fatima, and the shrines all over the world are different ways of showing that love. For Catholics, Mary is the most complete "yes" any human being has ever given to God, and a mother whose faith every believer can learn from.

At Mass, the sacrifice Christ offered once on the cross is made present on the altar. Below are the six parts of the Mass in order, with what the Priest says and how the people answer. Fr. Mike Schmitz explains each part of the Mass in this video. Download the Order of the Mass (PDF, 8 pages) The full text, with when to sit, stand and kneel. You can print it and take it with you. Part 1

Everyone stands as the Priest and the servers come in, usually during the entrance hymn. The Priest may announce the intention for which the Mass is offered, for example: “This Mass is offered for the repose of the soul of N.” If it is a weekday Mass with no choir or organ, he may then say the Entrance Antiphon himself. The Priest then makes the Sign of the Cross with everyone. Before anything else, we ask God’s forgiveness. Priest In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. People Amen. Priest The Lord be with you. People And with your spirit. The Priest invites everyone to call to mind their sins: Priest Brothers and sisters, let us acknowledge our sins, and so prepare ourselves to celebrate the sacred mysteries. On Sundays and feast days: Priest and People I confess to almighty God, and to you, my brothers and sisters, that I have greatly sinned, in my thoughts and in my words, in what I have done and in what I have failed to do, (striking the breast) through my fault, through my fault, through my most grievous fault. Therefore I ask blessed Mary ever-Virgin, all the Angels and Saints, and you, my brothers and sisters, to pray for me to the Lord our God. On weekdays: Priest You were sent to heal the contrite of heart: Lord, have mercy. People Lord, have mercy. Priest You came to call sinners: Christ, have mercy. People Christ, have mercy. Priest You are seated at the right hand of the Father to intercede for us: Lord, have mercy. People Lord, have mercy. Priest May almighty God have mercy on us, forgive us our sins, and bring us to everlasting life. People Amen. At a weekday Mass the Priest now says the Opening Prayer, which ends: “… through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever.” The people answer: “Amen.” On Sundays and feast days we say the Kyrie and sing the Gloria: Priest Lord, have mercy. People Lord, have mercy. Priest Christ, have mercy. People Christ, have mercy. Priest Lord, have mercy. People Lord, have mercy. Priest and People Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will. We praise you, we bless you, we adore you, we glorify you. We give you thanks for your great glory, Lord God, heavenly King, O God, almighty Father. Lord Jesus Christ, Only Begotten Son, Lord God, Lamb of God, Son of the Father, you take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us; you take away the sins of the world, receive our prayer; you are seated at the right hand of the Father, have mercy on us. For you alone are the Holy One, you alone are the Lord, you alone are the Most High, Jesus Christ, with the Holy Spirit, in the glory of God the Father. Amen. The Priest says the Collect, the opening prayer of the day. Priest Let us pray. At the end, the people answer: People Amen. Everyone sits for the First Reading. Part 2

The readings of the day: The First Reading is usually from the Old Testament, such as Genesis, Exodus, Isaiah or Jeremiah, chosen to connect with the Gospel. In Easter Time it is from the Acts of the Apostles, the story of the early Church. The Responsorial Psalm follows, from the Book of Psalms, and answers the First Reading. The Second Reading, on Sundays and solemnities, is from the letters of the New Testament: Saint Paul’s, or those of Peter, James and John. It follows a plan of its own rather than the Gospel’s theme. The Gospel is from Matthew, Mark, Luke or John, and is the high point of the Liturgy of the Word. On Sundays, Matthew, Mark and Luke take turns over a three-year cycle (Years A, B and C); John is read especially in Lent and Easter Time. On weekdays there is only one reading before the Gospel, from the Old Testament or the Acts of the Apostles, then the Psalm and the Gospel. Everyone stays seated for the readings and the Psalm, and stands for the Gospel. A reader proclaims the readings; only a priest or deacon reads the Gospel. Each reading ends: Priest The word of the Lord. People Thanks be to God. Everyone stands for the Alleluia, the acclamation before the Gospel (in Lent, another acclamation is sung instead). Before the Gospel, the Priest prays quietly: Priest Cleanse my heart and my lips, almighty God, that I may worthily proclaim your holy Gospel. Then he says: Priest The Lord be with you. People And with your spirit. Priest A reading from the holy Gospel according to Saint N. With the Priest, everyone traces a small cross with the thumb on the forehead, the lips and the heart. People Glory to you, O Lord. At the end of the Gospel: Priest The Gospel of the Lord. People Praise to you, Lord Jesus Christ. The Priest kisses the book and says quietly: Priest May the words of the Gospel wipe away our sins. Everyone sits for the homily. After the homily, on Sundays and solemnities, everyone stands for the Creed: either the Apostles’ Creed or the Nicene Creed is said together. The Apostles’ Creed: Priest and People I believe in God, the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried; he descended into hell; on the third day he rose again from the dead; he ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting. Amen. Or the Nicene Creed (at the words “and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man,” everyone bows): Priest and People I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible. I believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Only Begotten Son of God, born of the Father before all ages. God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father; through him all things were made. For us men and for our salvation he came down from heaven, and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man. For our sake he was crucified under Pontius Pilate, he suffered death and was buried, and rose again on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures. He ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father. He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end. I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, who with the Father and the Son is adored and glorified, who has spoken through the prophets. I believe in one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church. I confess one Baptism for the forgiveness of sins, and I look forward to the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. Amen. Everyone remains standing for the Prayers of the Faithful. After each petition: Priest We pray to the Lord. People Lord, hear our prayer. After the last petition, everyone sits while the gifts are brought to the altar. Part 3

The Priest lifts the bread a little and says: Priest Blessed are you, Lord God of all creation, for through your goodness we have received the bread we offer you: fruit of the earth and work of human hands, it will become for us the bread of life. People Blessed be God for ever. He pours wine and a drop of water into the chalice, saying quietly: Priest By the mystery of this water and wine may we come to share in the divinity of Christ, who humbled himself to share in our humanity. He lifts the chalice: Priest Blessed are you, Lord God of all creation, for through your goodness we have received the wine we offer you: fruit of the vine and work of human hands, it will become our spiritual drink. People Blessed be God for ever. Bowing, he says quietly: Priest With humble spirit and contrite heart may we be accepted by you, O Lord, and may our sacrifice in your sight this day be pleasing to you, Lord God. He washes his hands, saying quietly: Priest Wash me, O Lord, from my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin. Then he turns to the people: Priest Pray, brothers and sisters, that my sacrifice and yours may be acceptable to God, the almighty Father. Everyone stands. People May the Lord accept the sacrifice at your hands for the praise and glory of his name, for our good and the good of all his holy Church. The Priest says the Prayer over the Offerings. The people answer: People Amen. Part 4

Priest The Lord be with you. People And with your spirit. Priest Lift up your hearts. People We lift them up to the Lord. Priest Let us give thanks to the Lord our God. People It is right and just. The Priest says the Preface of the day, and everyone joins in the Holy, Holy: Priest and People Holy, Holy, Holy Lord God of hosts. Heaven and earth are full of your glory. Hosanna in the highest. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest. The Eucharistic Prayer continues. Everyone kneels at this point. Priest You are indeed Holy, O Lord, the fount of all holiness. Make holy, therefore, these gifts, we pray, by sending down your Spirit upon them like the dewfall, so that they may become for us the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. The words of consecration: Priest At the time he was betrayed and entered willingly into his Passion, he took bread and, giving thanks, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: TAKE THIS, ALL OF YOU, AND EAT OF IT, FOR THIS IS MY BODY, WHICH WILL BE GIVEN UP FOR YOU. In a similar way, when supper was ended, he took the chalice and, once more giving thanks, he gave it to his disciples, saying: TAKE THIS, ALL OF YOU, AND DRINK FROM IT, FOR THIS IS THE CHALICE OF MY BLOOD, THE BLOOD OF THE NEW AND ETERNAL COVENANT, WHICH WILL BE POURED OUT FOR YOU AND FOR MANY FOR THE FORGIVENESS OF SINS. DO THIS IN MEMORY OF ME. Priest The mystery of faith. People We proclaim your Death, O Lord, and profess your Resurrection until you come again. Priest Therefore, as we celebrate the memorial of his Death and Resurrection, we offer you, Lord, the Bread of life and the Chalice of salvation, giving thanks that you have held us worthy to be in your presence and minister to you. Humbly we pray that, partaking of the Body and Blood of Christ, we may be gathered into one by the Holy Spirit. Priest Remember, Lord, your Church, spread throughout the world, and bring her to the fullness of charity, together with N. our Pope and N. our Bishop and all the clergy. Priest Remember also our brothers and sisters who have fallen asleep in the hope of the resurrection, and all who have died in your mercy: welcome them into the light of your face. Have mercy on us all, we pray, that with the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, with blessed Joseph, her Spouse, with the blessed Apostles, and all the Saints who have pleased you throughout the ages, we may merit to be coheirs to eternal life, and may praise and glorify you through your Son, Jesus Christ. Priest Through him, and with him, and in him, O God, almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, all glory and honor is yours, for ever and ever. People Amen. Everyone stands. Part 5

Priest At the Savior’s command and formed by divine teaching, we dare to say: Priest and People Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Priest Deliver us, Lord, we pray, from every evil, graciously grant peace in our days, that, by the help of your mercy, we may be always free from sin and safe from all distress, as we await the blessed hope and the coming of our Savior, Jesus Christ. People For the kingdom, the power and the glory are yours, now and for ever. Priest Lord Jesus Christ, who said to your Apostles: Peace I leave you, my peace I give you; look not on our sins, but on the faith of your Church, and graciously grant her peace and unity in accordance with your will, who live and reign for ever and ever. People Amen. Priest The peace of the Lord be with you always. People And with your spirit. Priest Let us offer each other the sign of peace. The Priest continues quietly: Priest May this mingling of the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ bring eternal life to us who receive it. Everyone offers a sign of peace to those nearby. Priest and People Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. Lamb of God, you take away the sins of the world, grant us peace. After the Lamb of God, everyone kneels. The Priest raises the Host for all to see. Priest Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world. Blessed are those called to the supper of the Lamb. People Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed. Receiving the Body of Christ, the Priest says quietly: Priest May the Body of Christ keep me safe for eternal life. Receiving from the chalice: Priest May the Blood of Christ keep me safe for eternal life. Row by row, everyone comes forward for Communion, then returns to their pew to kneel or sit in prayer. To each person the Priest or minister says, “The Body of Christ,” and they answer, “Amen.” If you are not Catholic, or not ready to receive, you are still welcome: come forward with your arms crossed over your chest for a blessing, or stay in your pew and pray. Not every parish offers this blessing: it is mainly a North American custom and is not part of the Communion rite itself. If you are unsure, stay in your pew and pray. The Priest then places the Hosts in the tabernacle and kneels. The people may kneel or sit. The Priest cleans the chalice and the altar; when he has finished, everyone stands for the Prayer after Communion. Priest Let us pray… People Amen. Part 6

Before the blessing, the parish announcements are read. Everyone may sit. Everyone stands for the blessing. Priest The Lord be with you. People And with your spirit. Priest May almighty God bless you, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Everyone makes the Sign of the Cross: People Amen. Priest The Mass is ended, go in peace to love and serve the Lord. People Thanks be to God. Depending on the parish, the Hail Mary and the Prayer to Saint Michael may be said. Everyone remains standing until the Priest has left, usually during the closing hymn.

Tens of thousands saw the sun “dance” on the very day three children had named months before. Fatima, Portugal · 1917 “The Miracle of Fatima”, the crowd looking at the sun · Ilustração Portuguesa, 29 October 1917 What happened On 13 May 1917, three shepherd children in Portugal, Lucia (10), Francisco (9) and Jacinta (7), saw a woman of light above a small holm oak. She asked them to come back to the same place on the thirteenth of each month for six months. In July she said that in October she would work a miracle “so that everyone will believe.” At noon on 13 October, between 30,000 and 100,000 people gathered in pouring rain. The rain stopped, the clouds parted, and a pale, silvery disc like the sun spun in the sky, threw off colors in every direction and plunged three times toward the crowd. Avelino de Almeida, a reporter for the anticlerical newspaper O Século, wrote the next day that the sun had “danced.” The Church approved the apparitions in 1930. At a glance Where the Cova da Iria, a pasture outside Fatima, Portugal When six apparitions, 13 May to 13 October 1917 Who saw her Lucia, Francisco and Jacinta, aged 10, 9 and 7 The sign the miracle of the sun, seen by 30,000 to 100,000 people Why it can’t be explained away The children were not lying. They were questioned again and again, separately, by priests, lawyers, doctors and hostile officials. The local administrator arrested them and threatened them with death; they cried, but they didn’t change their story. It wasn’t hallucination. Hallucinations are private and don’t keep a schedule announced in advance. All three children saw the same figure in the same place, on the days they had named months before. Lucia kept looking away because the light dazzled her; an imagined light doesn’t dazzle. It wasn’t the sun. No one can look at the noon sun for more than a few seconds. The crowd looked at the disc comfortably for ten minutes, and not a single case of eye damage was reported. It was seen from far away. People in villages miles away, some of them facing away from the sun, described the same event. Fr. Philippe Dalleur, a priest and scientist, used the shadows in photographs taken that day to calculate that the light source stood lower in the sky than the sun. Soaked clothes dried in minutes. On a cool, damp day, that would have taken hours. Everything had been foretold. Lucia’s words were written down in a priest’s interview notes weeks before, and the event came at exactly the place and day announced. The skeptics’ objections “It was a mass illusion.” There were unbelievers in the crowd, and people miles away who expected no miracle saw the same thing. No illusion shows tens of thousands of people the same thing, in the same order, from different angles. Even the skeptical writer Scott Alexander, who studied the case at length, wrote that at times during his research he was “genuinely scared and confused.” “Some said they saw nothing.” Among tens of thousands of witnesses there are one or two known exceptions, and they too say they could look at the disc without pain. If the event was real, a few exceptions are no surprise; if it was imagined, it is surprising there were so few. What it means Fatima’s message is simple and old: pray, do penance, stop offending God. What is new is the sign that came with it, announced in advance so that no one could say it was chance. Heaven chose three children who could barely read, and a crowd that included the people most eager to laugh at them. What the Church teaches The bishop of Leiria approved the apparitions in 1930. Francisco and Jacinta were canonized in 2017. Like every private revelation, Fatima adds nothing to the faith; it calls us back to live the Gospel more fully in our own time. CCC 67 For your life Mary asked the children to pray the Rosary every day. Could I pray one decade today? What would it take for me to believe a sign, and what do I do with the signs I have already been given? Go further Revelation 12:1 ↗ Watch a video ↗ The History of the Rosary →

For three years, crowds of Christians and Muslims saw a figure of light above a Cairo church. Cairo, Egypt · 1968-1971 The 1968 photograph of the apparition at Zeitoun · Anonymous photograph What happened On the night of 2 April 1968, a figure of light appeared on the dome of a Coptic church in the Zeitoun district of Cairo. The first to see it were two Muslim bus mechanics, who thought a woman was about to jump and shouted for help. The apparitions went on for three years. Close to a million people, including Christians, Muslims and foreign journalists, saw a glowing figure and dove-shaped lights above the dome. She never spoke and gave no message. At a glance Where the Coptic church of St. Mary in Zeitoun, Cairo When April 1968 to 1971 Who saw her close to a million people: Christians, Muslims and journalists The first witnesses two Muslim bus mechanics What it means Zeitoun is the apparition without words. There was no message and no single visionary to doubt; only a silent figure seen night after night by whole crowds, many of them not Christian at all. It speaks the language of the Gospel without speaking: Mary pointing beyond herself, over a church where her Son is worshipped. What the Church teaches The Coptic Orthodox Church formally approved the apparitions. They never went through the Catholic Church’s process, but both Churches honor them. The Church teaches that devotion to Mary is part of Christian worship and always leads to her Son. CCC 971 For your life The first witnesses were not looking for a miracle. Where might God be trying to catch my attention without my expecting it? How can I honor Mary in a way that brings me closer to Jesus? Go further Luke 1:46–48 ↗ The Blessed Virgin Mary →

Mary came to a poor Aztec convert, spoke his language, and left her image on his cloak. Mexico City, Mexico · 1531 The image of Our Lady of Guadalupe · The image on the tilma, 1531 What happened In December 1531, Juan Diego, a newly baptized Aztec, saw a woman on Tepeyac hill near Mexico City. Speaking in Nahuatl, she asked for a church to be built there. When the bishop wanted a sign, she sent Juan Diego to gather roses that were blooming on the hill in midwinter. He carried them to the bishop in his cloak (tilma); when he opened it, the roses fell out and the image of Mary, still visible today, appeared on the cloth. The image played a major part in the conversion of millions of native people in the years that followed. The basilica in Mexico City is the most visited Marian shrine in the world. At a glance Where Tepeyac hill, near Mexico City When December 1531 Who saw her St. Juan Diego, a newly baptized Aztec The sign roses in midwinter, and the image on his cloak What it means Mary did not appear to the bishop or the conquerors, but to a poor native man, in his own language, looking like one of his own people. The message of Guadalupe is that the Gospel belongs to every nation. Within a few years millions of native people asked for baptism. What the Church teaches St. Juan Diego was canonized in 2002. Our Lady of Guadalupe is honored as Patroness of the Americas, and her feast falls on 12 December. The Church teaches that Mary, given to us as our mother at the foot of the Cross, cares for all her children. CCC 971 For your life Juan Diego felt too small for the task he was given. Where do I feel too small for what God asks of me? Do I bring God my requests with the trust of a child speaking to his mother? Go further Luke 1:46–48 ↗ The Blessed Virgin Mary →

“I am the Immaculate Conception”: words a peasant girl could not have invented. Lourdes, France · 1858 The grotto at Lourdes, 1890s · Detroit Publishing Co. What happened On 11 February 1858, in Lourdes in southern France, Bernadette Soubirous, a poor, sickly fourteen-year-old, saw a young woman dressed in white at the entrance to a grotto. Over eighteen apparitions the woman called her to prayer and penance. Asked her name, she answered: "I am the Immaculate Conception." A peasant girl with no theological training could hardly have known the phrase, and it weighed heavily in the Church’s decision to take the apparitions seriously. Millions of pilgrims now visit the spring that appeared where Bernadette pointed. Out of thousands of reported cures, only about seventy have been recognized as miracles, after independent doctors found them medically inexplicable. At a glance Where the grotto of Massabielle, Lourdes, France When eighteen apparitions, February to July 1858 Who saw her St. Bernadette Soubirous, aged fourteen The fruit a spring, and about seventy cures recognized as miracles What it means Four years before Lourdes, Pope Pius IX had defined the Immaculate Conception: Mary was kept free from sin from the first moment of her life. At Lourdes, Mary used the phrase as her name, to a girl who did not understand it. Lourdes is also a place of the sick, and the greatest healing there is often not of the body. What the Church teaches The local bishop recognized the apparitions in 1862, after a four-year inquiry. Each reported cure is examined by an international medical committee before the Church calls it a miracle. CCC 491, 67 For your life Mary called Bernadette to prayer and penance. What is one concrete act of penance I could offer this week? Who do I know who is sick and needs my prayer or my visit? Go further Luke 1:28 ↗ The History of the Rosary → St. Bernadette, incorrupt →

A burial cloth bearing an image that science still cannot explain. Turin, Italy The Shroud of Turin: the cloth and its negative · Photo: Dianelos Georgoudis · CC BY-SA 3.0 What happened The Shroud of Turin is a 4.4-meter linen cloth bearing the front and back image of a crucified man. Tradition holds it to be Jesus' burial cloth. It is documented from the 1350s and has been kept in Turin since 1578. When it was first photographed in 1898, the negative showed a strikingly clear human face: the image on the cloth behaves like a photographic negative. In 1978 the STURP team of about thirty scientists showed that the image isn't made with paint, pigment or brushstrokes. The color sits only on the outermost surface of the linen fibers, in a layer thinner than a wavelength of light. When it was analyzed in 1976 with the VP-8, a device built for space photographs, the image produced a consistent three-dimensional relief, which ordinary paintings and photos don't. The bloodstains are real human blood, and there is no image beneath them: the blood reached the cloth before the image formed. The 1988 radiocarbon test dated the cloth to 1260-1390, but the sample came from a corner repaired after a fire in 1532; in 2005 chemist Raymond Rogers found cotton fibers and dye in the sample that are absent from the rest of the shroud. Researchers at Italy's ENEA could reproduce similar coloring only with extremely powerful ultraviolet laser pulses. At a glance What it is a linen cloth 4.4 meters long with the image of a crucified man Where Turin Cathedral, Italy (in Turin since 1578) First recorded the 1350s Studied by the STURP team of about thirty scientists, 1978 What it means The Shroud shows in detail what the Gospels tell in a few words: the scourging, the crown of thorns, the nails, the wound in the side. Whatever science one day concludes, it puts the Passion before our eyes, and many who have stood before it say it changed the way they read the Gospel. What the Church teaches The Church hasn’t declared the shroud “authentic,” because that is a scientific question, not a matter of faith; but popes visit it with deep reverence. St. John Paul II called it a “mirror of the Gospel.” The honor given to a sacred image passes to the one it shows. CCC 2132 For your life Spend a few minutes with an image of Christ’s Passion. What does it ask of me? Which of my sufferings could I unite to His? Go further John 19:38–42 ↗ John 20:5–7 ↗ Who is Jesus? →

A cloak of cactus fiber that should have rotted centuries ago still carries Mary’s image. Mexico City, Mexico The face on the tilma, close up · Photo: Lyricmac What happened Juan Diego's cloak is a coarse cloth woven from maguey fiber, which normally rots within a few decades. Yet despite being displayed for centuries without glass, the image is still clear today. In 1979, biophysicist Philip Callahan's infrared study found no underdrawing or layers of paint in the main part of the image, while showing that some details, such as the moon, the angel and the rays, were added later. Engineer José Aste Tonsmann reported seeing tiny reflected figures of people standing before her in Mary's pupils, as a living eye would reflect them. The tilma is Mexico's most sacred object, visited by more than twenty million pilgrims a year. At a glance What it is Juan Diego’s cloak, woven from maguey fiber Where the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, Mexico City Since 1531 Studied by Philip Callahan, infrared study, 1979 What it means The tilma is the sign Mary gave to a doubting bishop, and it is still giving it. A poor man’s working cloak became the most visited image of Mary in the world: God likes to use humble things to carry His greatest gifts. What the Church teaches The Church does not rest the faith on scientific studies of the image. It honors the tilma as a sacred image, and the honor given to it passes to the one it shows. CCC 2132, 971 For your life What “ordinary cloth” in my life could God use to show His love to others? Have I ever asked God for a sign? How did I respond when one came? Go further Revelation 12:1 ↗ Our Lady of Guadalupe →

The host became human heart muscle; the wine became blood of type AB. Lanciano, Italy · 8th century The flesh and blood relics at Lanciano · Photo: AFC photo · CC BY-SA 3.0 What happened According to tradition, in the 8th century in Lanciano, Italy, a priest who doubted the Eucharist saw the bread turn into flesh and the wine into blood as he spoke the words of consecration. The flesh and the blood, in five clots, are still on display. In 1970, with the archbishop’s permission, the seals were broken and the pathologist Odoardo Linoli took samples. The flesh proved to be human heart muscle and the blood human blood of type AB. Ruggero Bertelli, an anatomy professor who was not a believer, examined the slides separately and reached the same conclusion. Linoli published his findings in a scientific journal, and the AB result was reproduced at the University of Siena in 1991. At a glance Where the Church of St. Francis, Lanciano, Italy When the 8th century, by tradition What remains flesh, and blood in five clots Studied by Odoardo Linoli, 1970; confirmed at Siena in 1991 Why it can’t be explained away A forger wouldn’t have used a human heart. Back then there was no way to tell human flesh from animal flesh. Cutting a heart from a fresh corpse was hard and risky; animal flesh was cheap and easy. The flesh looks like a cross-section of a heart, yet the tradition never says so. It is a round slice, hollow in the middle: the view a cardiologist sees on an ultrasound today. A forger who had done this on purpose would have made a point of it in the story. There is no preservative. Linoli found no trace of salt, resin or alcohol. A forger would certainly have salted or treated the flesh, or it would have rotted within days. Blood clots normally break down and putrefy within a day or two. Those at Lanciano sat for centuries in vessels open to the air, yet their proteins kept proportions like those of fresh blood. The records are old. In the 11th century Guitmund, Archbishop of Aversa, tells of a miracle in Italy in which bread became flesh and wine became blood, and the relics were sealed in the altar. The bishop’s inspection of 1574 is recorded on a marble inscription in the church. The skeptics’ objections “The test can’t tell human from animal.” Linoli used a forensic test that courts relied on to determine species. The reaction was strong and came within minutes; the cattle and rabbit controls were completely negative. “Bacteria produced the AB result.” Linoli found no bacterial colonies where the sample was taken. And studies show that bacteria very rarely produce a false AB result. “The flesh might simply have dried out and kept.” Heart muscle is watery and spoils fast; flesh left to dry in the open rots before its inside dries. And clotted blood can’t be preserved by drying. What it means Every Mass, the bread and wine truly become the Body and Blood of Christ, while still looking like bread and wine. At Lanciano, tradition holds, God let a doubting priest see with his eyes what faith sees every day. The miracle does not change what happens at Mass; it shows it. What the Church teaches The Church teaches that in the Eucharist Christ is present “truly, really and substantially”: His Body and Blood, soul and divinity. This change is called transubstantiation. CCC 1374, 1376 For your life Do I come to Communion as if Christ were truly there? Like the priest of Lanciano, where do I doubt? Could I bring that doubt to Jesus in prayer? Go further John 6:53–56 ↗ Watch a video ↗ The Holy Mass →

Blood on an altar cloth gave the whole Church the feast of Corpus Christi. Bolsena / Orvieto, Italy · 1263 The Mass at Bolsena · Raphael, Apostolic Palace, Vatican What happened In 1263 a Bohemian priest who doubted the Eucharist was saying Mass in Bolsena when blood seeped from the host he broke onto the altar cloth. Pope Urban IV had the event investigated and the cloth brought to Orvieto. The next year he established the feast of Corpus Christi for the whole Church and asked St. Thomas Aquinas to write its prayers. The cloth is kept in Orvieto Cathedral and carried in procession every year on the feast. At a glance Where Bolsena; the cloth is kept in Orvieto Cathedral When 1263 What remains the bloodstained altar cloth What came of it the feast of Corpus Christi, from 1264 What it means A single priest’s doubt became the occasion for a feast the whole Church still keeps. Every Corpus Christi procession through the streets goes back to Bolsena: the Lord who is hidden in the host is carried out to meet His people. What the Church teaches The Church honors Christ in the Eucharist with worship due to God alone, inside Mass and outside it, in adoration and processions. CCC 1378, 1376 For your life When did I last spend time in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament? How can I take part in the Corpus Christi procession or a holy hour this year? Go further Luke 22:19–20 ↗ The Holy Mass → Saint Thomas Aquinas →

A discarded host turned into human heart tissue, examined by a scientist who never knew its source. Buenos Aires, Argentina · 1996 Buenos Aires Metropolitan Cathedral · Photo: Alexis González Molina · CC BY-SA 3.0 What happened In 1996, in a Buenos Aires church, a consecrated host that had been found discarded was placed in water to dissolve. A few days later red, blood-like spots appeared on it and kept growing. The archbishop at the time, Jorge Mario Bergoglio, the future Pope Francis, had it studied scientifically. In 1999 in New York, cardiologist Frederick Zugibe, who wasn't told where the sample came from, reported that it was human heart muscle from the left ventricle of an inflamed heart; the blood type was AB, as at Lanciano. At a glance Where a parish church in Buenos Aires, Argentina When 1996 Studied by cardiologist Frederick Zugibe, New York, 1999 Finding heart muscle from the left ventricle; blood type AB What it means The host had been thrown away, and the tissue it became was from a heart under great strain. It is hard not to see in it the heart of Christ, wounded by indifference and still offering Himself. What the Church teaches The Church teaches that Christ is present whole and entire in each consecrated host, and remains present as long as the appearances of bread last; that is why a host is never thrown away. CCC 1377, 1376 For your life Where have I treated holy things carelessly? How can I make an act of reparation for the indifference shown to the Eucharist? Go further John 6:53–56 ↗ Watch a video ↗ The Miracle of Lanciano →

The girl who saw Mary at Lourdes, her body spared from decay for decades. Nevers, France Bernadette’s body, 1925 · Anonymous photograph What happened Bernadette, the visionary of Lourdes, died in 1879 at thirty-five. When her body was exhumed in 1909, thirty years after burial, her skin looked astonishingly natural. When it was decided in 1925 to display the body permanently, her face and hands were covered with a thin wax mask. Today she lies in a glass reliquary in Nevers; beneath the mask is the body that stayed incorrupt for decades. Bernadette was canonized in 1933. At a glance Where the convent chapel of Saint-Gildard, Nevers, France Died 1879, aged thirty-five Exhumed 1909, thirty years after burial Canonized 1933 What it means Bernadette never claimed to be holy because of what she saw. She became a nun, suffered long illness and said she was used “like a broom” and then put back in the corner. Her incorrupt body is not proof of sanctity by itself; her humble life is. What the Church teaches The Church canonizes saints for their heroic virtue, not for an incorrupt body. It honors their relics, and asks them to pray for us as models and intercessors. CCC 828, 1674 For your life Bernadette was content to be forgotten. Where do I need to let go of wanting to be noticed? Which saint could I ask to pray for me this week? Go further 1 Corinthians 15:42–44 ↗ Our Lady of Lourdes → Saints →

A friar bore the wounds of Christ for fifty years, and they closed without a scar. San Giovanni Rotondo, Italy Padre Pio · Anonymous photograph What happened On 20 September 1918, while the Italian Capuchin friar Padre Pio was praying after Mass, wounds like those of Christ appeared on his hands, his feet and his side (the stigmata). They bled for fifty years. When he died on 23 September 1968, his doctor and photographs taken that night showed the wounds had closed without a scar. When his body was exhumed in 2008, the hands and feet were well preserved; a silicone mask was made for his face. Millions of pilgrims visit his shrine in San Giovanni Rotondo every year. At a glance Where San Giovanni Rotondo, Italy The stigmata 20 September 1918 to his death in 1968 Exhumed 2008 Canonized 2002 Why it can’t be explained away The doctors couldn’t explain it. The surgeons Luigi Romanelli and Giorgio Festa wrote that the wounds neither healed nor became infected; an ordinary wound either closes or festers. The atheist professor of pathology Amico Bignami thought the wounds were kept open with iodine tincture. For eight days they were kept under sealed bandages with no medicine at all; they went on bleeding every day. There was no anemia. Padre Pio ate very little, yet lost blood every day for years, and his blood tests always came back normal. They smelled sweet, not foul. Wounds left open for a long time smell bad. Hundreds of people describe a pleasant fragrance coming from Padre Pio’s wounds and blood. Dr Romanelli at first took it for perfume and thought it unfitting for a friar. Dr Festa, who had no sense of smell, described how the people traveling in his car noticed the fragrance, not knowing he had a bloodstained cloth from the wounds in his case. They closed without a scar. A deep wound always leaves a scar when it heals. Padre Pio’s wounds closed after fifty years, just as he died, and left no mark. Healings. In 1949 a dynamite accident at the friary shattered Giovanni Savino’s face and destroyed his right eye entirely. When the bandages came off ten days later his face had healed and his right eye was there; he saw with it for the rest of his life. In 2000 a young boy, Matteo Colella, whose meningitis had caused nine of his organs to fail, recovered against all expectations while his mother prayed to Padre Pio. His doctors and ten consulted experts found the recovery inexplicable; it is the miracle accepted for Padre Pio’s canonization. The skeptics’ objections “He kept the wounds open with acid.” A note from 1919 was found in which Padre Pio asked a woman for carbolic acid “for sterilizing.” Carbolic acid was a common disinfectant at the time, and Padre Pio spoke about it openly when questioned. Acid doesn’t explain wounds that stayed the same for fifty years, smelled sweet and closed without a scar; as Dr Festa noted, acid would also have destroyed any fragrance. “The famous psychologist Agostino Gemelli thought him a fraud.” Gemelli never examined Padre Pio; he spoke with him for a few minutes in a corridor. In his own 1920 report he admitted that he had seen him without carrying out any medical examination. What it means Padre Pio never wanted the wounds and asked God to take away the visible marks. What he spent his days on was the confessional and the Mass. The stigmata drew the crowds; the sacraments are what he gave them. What the Church teaches St. John Paul II canonized Padre Pio in 2002. The Church teaches that Christ invites His disciples to take up their cross and share in His suffering for the salvation of others. CCC 618, 828 For your life What suffering in my life could I offer to God instead of only enduring it? Padre Pio heard confessions for hours every day. When did I last go to confession? Go further Galatians 6:17 ↗ Watch a video ↗ Saint Pio of Pietrelcina →
St. Jean-Marie Vianney (The Curé of Ars)

The parish priest who heard confessions sixteen hours a day, found intact forty-five years after death. Ars, France The body of St John Vianney, Ars · Photo: Herwig Reidlinger · CC BY-SA 3.0 What happened Jean-Marie Vianney, the parish priest of Ars, heard confessions for up to sixteen hours a day, and people flocked to him from all over France. He is now the patron saint of all parish priests. When his body was exhumed in 1904, forty-five years after his death, it was dried out but intact. His incorrupt heart is displayed in a separate chapel, and his body, its face covered with a wax mask, lies in the basilica at Ars. At a glance Where the basilica at Ars, France Died 1859 Exhumed 1904 Canonized 1925 What it means Jean-Marie Vianney almost failed his studies for the priesthood and was sent to a village nobody wanted. He changed it by staying in the confessional. His life says that holiness does not need talent, only a heart given entirely to God. What the Church teaches The Church honors the relics of the saints and holds them up as models. St. John Vianney is the patron saint of parish priests. CCC 828, 1674 For your life Is there a sin I have been afraid to confess? What keeps me away? How can I pray for my parish priest this week? Go further John 20:22–23 ↗ Confession →

Apparitions, relics, bleeding hosts, bodies that didn’t decay. None of this is required belief: the Church calls it “private revelation”, which adds nothing to the faith. But each case below was investigated closely, and the Church judged it worthy of belief. Here they are, in date order, with the most striking scientific findings. Open any miracle to read what happened, the evidence and what the Church teaches.
Four of the most famous apparitions in the world, each approved after a long investigation.
The two objects scientists have studied most over the centuries.
In the Eucharist, bread and wine become Christ’s Body and Blood while looking exactly the same. In these three cases, tradition holds, the change became visible.
Some saints’ bodies have been found far less decayed than they should be, years or even centuries after death. Bodies on display often have a thin wax or silicone mask over the face to protect them.

Servant of the Poor · 1910-1997 Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu was born to an Albanian family in what is now North Macedonia. At eighteen she joined the Sisters of Loreto in Ireland, who soon sent her to India. There she taught geography at a girls’ school in Calcutta and later became its principal. It was a fairly comfortable, orderly life.

In 1946, on a train to Darjeeling, she felt what she later called "a call within a call": God wanted her to leave the school and live among the poorest and most abandoned people on the streets. It meant stepping well outside the life her order had planned for her. After two years of asking for permission, in 1948 she left her school, put on a white sari with a blue border and went out into the streets of Calcutta.

First she opened a simple school for children from the slums. Then she began taking in the dying whom nobody else would care for, and opened a home where they could spend their last days with dignity and love. In 1950, with the Vatican’s approval, she founded the Missionaries of Charity. The order grew astonishingly fast. Today it has hundreds of houses around the world, where thousands of sisters and brothers serve the poorest, the sickest and the most forgotten: lepers, people with AIDS, street children and the elderly. Mother Teresa received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and asked that the money for the traditional banquet be given to the poor instead. Small and wrinkled, she became one of the most recognized faces in the world. Yet her private letters, published after her death, showed that for many years she had lived through an inner "dark night," a deep spiritual dryness in which God seemed far away, which makes her all the more human. She died in 1997, at eighty-seven, and Pope Francis canonized her in 2016. Her feast day is September 5.
Motu Proprio for the approval and publication of the Compendium of the Catechism of the Catholic Church

Motu Proprio To my Venerable Brothers the Cardinals, Patriarchs, Archbishops, Bishops, Priests, Deacons and to all the People of God. Twenty years ago, work began on the Catechism of the Catholic Church that had been requested by the extraordinary Assembly of the Synod of Bishops held on the occasion of the twentieth anniversary of the close of the Second Vatican Council. I am filled with heartfelt thanks to the Lord God for having given the Church this Catechism, promulgated in 1992 by my venerated and beloved Predecessor, Pope John Paul II. The great value and beauty of this gift are confirmed above all by the extensive and positive reception of the Catechism among Bishops, to whom it was primarily addressed as a sure and authentic reference text for teaching Catholic doctrine and, in particular, for formulating local catechisms. But it was also confirmed by its vast favourable reception in all segments of the People of God, who have come to know and appreciate it in more than fifty translations which to date have been published. It is with great joy that I now approve and promulgate the Compendium of that Catechism. The Compendium had been fervently desired by the participants in the International Catechetical Congress of October 2002, which gave voice to a need widely felt in the Church. My beloved Predecessor, recognizing this desire, decided in February 2003 to begin preparation of the text by entrusting the work to a Commission of Cardinals, over which I presided, and which was assisted by various experts. In the course of the work, a draft of the Compendium was submitted to all the Cardinals and the Presidents of Conferences of Bishops, the vast majority of whom evaluated the text favourably. The Compendium, which I now present to the Universal Church, is a faithful and sure synthesis of the Catechism of the Catholic Church. It contains, in concise form, all the essential and fundamental elements of the Church’s faith, thus constituting, as my Predecessor had wished, a kind of vademecum which allows believers and non-believers alike to behold the entire panorama of the Catholic faith. In its structure, contents and language, the Compendium faithfully reflects the Catechism of the Catholic Church and will thus assist in making the Catechism more widely known and more deeply understood. I entrust this Compendium above all to the entire Church and, in particular, to every Christian, in order that it may awaken in the Church of the third millennium renewed zeal for evangelization and education in the faith, which ought to characterize every community in the Church and every Christian believer, regardless of age or nationality. But this Compendium, with its brevity, clarity and comprehensiveness, is directed to every human being, who, in a world of distractions and multifarious messages, desires to know the Way of Life, the Truth, entrusted by God to His Son’s Church. Through the intercession of Mary Most Holy, Mother of Christ and Mother of the Church, may everyone who reads this authoritative text recognize and embrace ever more fully the inexhaustible beauty, uniqueness and significance of the incomparable Gift which God has made to the human race in His only Son, Jesus Christ, the “Way, the Truth, and the Life” (Jn 14:6). Given on 28 June 2005, the vigil of the Solemnity of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, in the first year of my Pontificate. BENEDICTUS PP. XVI

Bearer of Christ’s Wounds · 1887-1968 Francesco Forgione was born to a poor farming family in the Italian village of Pietrelcina. Even as a child, it is said, he was unusually devout and had unusual spiritual experiences. At sixteen he joined the Capuchin Franciscans and took the name Pio. His health was always poor, and while training for the priesthood he often fell ill and had to be sent home.

In 1918, at his friary in San Giovanni Rotondo, while he was praying after Mass, marks like the five wounds of Christ appeared on his hands, his feet and his side. They bled for fifty years and never closed until his death. It is the longest-lasting and most closely examined case of the stigmata in the Church’s history, and the doctors who examined him again and again could find no medical explanation. At first the Vatican was cautious and even restricted for a time his contact with the public and his saying Mass in public, but in the end the restrictions were lifted.

More than any miracle, what Padre Pio left behind were the countless hours he spent hearing confessions. On some days he heard them for more than twelve hours, and people from all over the world waited for weeks for the chance to speak to him. Extraordinary stories grew up around him: that he could read people’s hearts, that he could be in two places at once (bilocation). He himself was always humble about such things. In 1956 he opened a modern hospital, the "Home for the Relief of Suffering," a very practical fruit of his life of prayer. Padre Pio died in 1968, at eighty-one, and it is said that by then the wounds had completely disappeared. More than a hundred thousand people came to his funeral. Pope John Paul II canonized him in 2002, and today San Giovanni Rotondo is one of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world. His feast day is September 23.

All 73 books of the Douay-Rheims Bible, in modernized English. The Douay-Rheims is the classic Catholic Bible in English, translated from Saint Jerome’s Latin Vulgate and revised by Bishop Challoner in the 1750s. The text here keeps its words, with the old spelling and grammar brought up to date. The books carry the names and order of modern Catholic Bibles, and the Psalms their modern numbers, with the Douay-Rheims number shown beside each. Apocryphal comes from the Greek apokryphos , “hidden”. The Church uses the word for old religious writings that some once read alongside Scripture but that she has never received as the inspired Word of God. They are not part of the Bible. The Council of Trent (1546) set out the 73 books of the Bible. The Latin Vulgate still printed three more after them, “lest they perish altogether”, and the first Douay Bible of 1609 kept them in an appendix: the Prayer of Manasseh, the king’s prayer of repentance in captivity; 3 Esdras, a retelling of the return from Babylon (also called 1 Esdras); and 4 Esdras, visions given to Ezra (also called 2 Esdras). They are shown here for study, in a public-domain English translation, modernized.

Old Testament. This book is so called from its treating of the GENERATION, that is, of the creation and the beginning of the world. The Hebrews call it BERESITH, from the Word with which it begins. It contains not only the history of the Creation of the world; but also an account of its progress during the space of 2369 years, that is, until the death of JOSEPH.

Old Testament. The Second Book of Moses is called EXODUS, from the Greek word EXODOS, which signifies going out: because it contains the history of the going out of the children of Israel out of Egypt. The Hebrews, from the words with which it begins, call it VEELLE SEMOTH: These are the names. It contains transactions for 145 years; that is, from the death of Joseph to the erecting of the tabernacle.

Old Testament. This Book is called LEVITICUS, because it treats of the Offices, Ministries, Rites and Ceremonies of the Priests and Levites. The Hebrews call it VAICRA, from the word with which it begins.

Old Testament. This fourth Book of Moses is called NUMBERS, because it begins with the numbering of the people. The Hebrews, from its first words, call it VAIEDABBER. It contains the transactions of the Israelites from the second month of the second year after their going out of Egypt, until the beginning of the eleventh month of the fortieth year; that is, a history almost of thirty-nine years.

Old Testament. This Book is called DEUTERONOMY, which signifies a SECOND LAW, because it repeats and inculcates the ordinances formerly given on mount Sinai, with other precepts not expressed before. The Hebrews, from the first words in the book, call it ELLE HADDEBARIM.

Old Testament. This Book is called JOSUE, because it contains the history of what passed under him, and according to the common opinion was written by him. The Greeks call him Jesus: for Joshua and Jesus in the Hebrew, are the same name, and have the same signification, viz., A SAVIOUR. And it was not without a mystery that he who was to bring the people into the land of promise should have his name changed from OSEE (for so he was called before, Num. 13.17,) to JOSUE or JESUS, to give us to understand, that Moses by his law could only bring the people within sight of the promised inheritance, but that our S

Old Testament. This Book is called JUDGES, because it contains the history of what passed under the government of the judges, who ruled Israel before they had kings. The writer of it, according to the more general opinion, was the prophet Samuel.

Old Testament. This Book is called RUTH, from the name of the person whose history is here recorded: who, being a Gentile, became a convert to the true faith, and marrying Boaz, the great-grandfather of David, was one of those from whom Christ sprung according to the flesh, and an illustrious figure of the Gentile church. It is thought this book was written by the prophet Samuel.

Old Testament. This and the following Book are called by the Hebrews the books of Samuel, because they contain the history of Samuel, and of the two kings, Saul and David, whom he anointed. They are more commonly named by the Fathers, the first and second book of kings. As to the writer of them, it is the common opinion that Samuel composed the first book, as far as the twenty-fifth chapter; and that the prophets Nathan and Gad finished the first, and wrote the second book. See 1 Paralipomenon, alias 1 Chronicles, 29.29.
Old Testament. This Book relates the transactions from the death of Saul until the end of David's reign, being a history for the space of about forty-six years.

Old Testament. This and the following Book are called by the holy fathers the third and fourth book of Kings; but by the Hebrews, the first and second. They contain the history of the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, from the beginning of the reign of Solomon, to the captivity. As to the writer of these books, it seems most probable they were not written by one man; nor at one time; but as there was all along a succession of prophets in Israel, who recorded, by divine inspiration, the most remarkable things that happened in their days, these books seem to have been written by these prophets. See 2 Paralip. alia

Old Testament. These Books are called by the Greek interpreters, Paralipomenon, that is, of things left out, or omitted; because they are a kind of a supplement of such things as were passed over in the books of the Kings. The Hebrews call them Dibre Haijamim, that is, The words of the days, or The Chronicles.--Not that they are the books which are so often quoted in the Kings, under the title of the words of the days of the kings of Israel, and of the kings of Judah: for the books of Paralipomenon were written after the books of Kings: but because in all probability they have been abridged from those ancien
Old Testament. This Book takes its name from the writer: who was a holy priest, and doctor of the law. He is called by the Hebrews, Ezra.

Old Testament. This Book takes its name from the writer, who was cupbearer to Artaxerxes (surnamed Longimanus) king of Persia, and was sent by him with a commission to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. It is also called the second book of Ezra; because it is a continuation of the history, begun by Ezra, of the state of the people of God after their return from captivity.

Old Testament. This Book takes its name from the holy man Tobit, whose wonderful virtues are herein recorded. It contains most excellent documents of great piety, extraordinary patience, and of a perfect resignation to the will of God. His humble prayer was heard, and the angel Raphael was sent to relieve him: he is thankful and praises the Lord, calling on the children of Israel to do the same. Having lived to the age of one hundred and two years, he exhorts his son and grandsons to piety, foretells the destruction of Nineveh and the rebuilding of Jerusalem: he dies happily.

Old Testament. The sacred writer of this Book is generally believed to be the high priest Eliachim (called also Joachim). The transactions herein related, most probably happened in his days, and in the reign of Manasseh, after his repentance and return from captivity. It takes its name from that illustrious woman, by whose virtue and fortitude, and armed with prayer, the children of Israel were preserved from the destruction threatened them by Holofernes and his great army. It finishes with her canticle of thanksgiving to God.

Old Testament. This Book takes its name from queen Esther, whose history is here recorded. The general opinion of almost all commentators on the Holy Scriptures makes Mordecai the writer of it: which also may be collected below from chap. 9 ver. 20.

Old Testament. These books are so called, because they contain the history of the people of God under the command of Judas Maccabeus and his brethren: and he, as some will have it, was surnamed Maccabeus, from carrying in his ensigns, or standards, those words of Exodus 15.11, Who is like to you among the strong, O Lord: in which the initial letters, in the Hebrew, are M. C. B. E. I. It is not known who is the author of these books. But as to their authority, though they are not received by the Jews, says St. Augustine, (lib. 18, De Civ. Dei, c. 36,) they are received by the church: who, in settling her cano

Old Testament. This second book of MACHABEES is not a continuation of the history contained in the first: nor does is come down so low as the first does: but relates many of the same facts more at large, and adds other remarkable particulars, omitted in the first book, relating to the state of the Jews, as well before as under the persecution of ANTIOCHUS. The author, who is not the same with that of the first book, has given (as we learn from chap. 2.20, etc.) a short abstract of what JASON of Cyrene had written in the five volumes, concerning JUDAS and his brethren. He wrote in Greek, and begins with two l

Old Testament. This Book takes its name from the holy man of whom it treats: who, according to the more probable opinion, was of the race of Esau; and the same as Jobab, king of Edom, mentioned Gen. 36.33. It is uncertain who was the writer of it. Some attribute it to Job himself; others to Moses, or some one of the prophets. In the Hebrew it is written in verse, from the beginning of the third chapter to the forty-second chapter.

Old Testament. The psalms are called by the Hebrews TEHILLIM, that is, Hymns of Praise. The author, of a great part of them at least, was king David: but many are of opinion that some of them were made by Asaph, and others whose names are prefixed in the titles.

Old Testament. This Book is so called, because it consists of wise and weighty sentences: regulating the morals of men: and directing them to wisdom and virtue. And these sentences are also called PARABLES, because great truths are often couched in them under certain figures and similitudes.

Old Testament. This Book is called Ecclesiastes, or The Preacher, (in Hebrew, Coheleth,) because in it, Solomon, as an excellent preacher, sets forth the vanity of the things of this world: to withdraw the hearts and affections of men from such empty toys.

Old Testament. This Book is called the Canticle of Canticles, that is to say, the most excellent of all canticles: because it is full of high mysteries, relating to the happy union of Christ and his spouse: which is here begun by love; and is to be eternal in heaven. The spouse of Christ is the church: more especially as to the happiest part of it, viz., perfect souls, every one of which is his beloved, but, above all others, the immaculate and ever blessed virgin mother.

Old Testament. This Book is so called, because it treats of the excellence of WISDOM, the means to obtain it, and the happy fruits it produces. It is written in the person of Solomon, and contains his sentiments. But it is uncertain who was the writer. It abounds with instructions and exhortations to kings and all magistrates to minister justice in the commonwealth, teaching all kinds of virtues under the general names of justice and wisdom. It contains also many prophecies of Christ's coming, passion, resurrection, and other Christian mysteries. The whole may be divided into three parts. In the first six ch

Old Testament. The knowledge of many and great things has been shewn us by the law, and the prophets, and others that have followed them: for which things Israel is to be commended for doctrine and wisdom, because not only they that speak must needs be skilful, but strangers also, both speaking and writing, may by their means become most learned. My grandfather Jesus, after he had much given himself to a diligent reading of the law, and the prophets, and other books, that were delivered to us from our fathers, had a mind also to write something himself, pertaining to doctrine and wisdom; that such as are des

Old Testament. This inspired writer is called by the Holy Spirit, the great prophet, (Ecclesiasticus:48.25,) from the greatness of his prophetic spirit, by which he has foretold so long before, and in so clear a manner, the coming of Christ, the mysteries of our redemption, the calling of the Gentiles, and the glorious establishment, and perpetual flourishing of the church of Christ: insomuch that he may seem to have been rather an evangelist than a prophet. His very name is not without mystery; for Isaiah in Hebrew signifies the salvation of the Lord, or Jesus is the Lord. He was, according to the tradition

Old Testament. Jeremiah was a priest, a native of Anathoth, a priestly city in the tribe of Benjamin: and was sanctified from his mother's womb, to be a prophet of God; which office he began to execute when he was yet a child in age. He was in his whole life, according to the signification of his name, Great before the Lord; and a special figure of Jesus Christ, in the persecutions he underwent for discharging his duty; in his charity for his persecutors; and in the violent death he suffered at their hands: it being an ancient tradition of the Hebrews, that he was stoned to death by the remnant of the Jews w

Old Testament. In these JEREMIAS laments in a most pathetical manner the miseries of his people, and the destruction of JERUSALEM and the temple, in Hebrew verses, beginning with different letters according to the order of the Hebrew alphabet.

Old Testament. BARUCH was a man of noble extraction, and learned in the law, secretary and disciple to the prophet JEREMIAS, and a sharer in his labours and persecutions: which is the reason why the ancient fathers have considered this book as a part of the prophecy of JEREMIAS, and have usually quoted it under his name.

Old Testament. EZECHIEL, whose name signifies the STRENGTH OF God, was of the priestly race; and of the number of captives that were carried away to Babylon with king JOACHIN. He was contemporary with JEREMIAS, and prophesied to the same effect in Babylon, as JEREMIAS did in Jerusalem; and is said to have ended his days in like manner, by martyrdom.

Old Testament. DANIEL, whose name signifies THE JUDGMENT OF God, was of the royal blood of the kings of Judah: and one of those that were first of all carried away into captivity. He was so renowned for wisdom and knowledge, that it became a proverb among the Babylonians, AS WISE AS DANIEL (Ezech. 28.3). And his holiness was so great from his very childhood, that at the time when he was as yet but a young man, he is joined by the SPIRIT of God with NOE and JOB, as three persons most eminent for virtue and sanctity, Ezech. 14. He is not commonly numbered by the Hebrews among THE PROPHETS: because he lived at

Old Testament. OSEE, or Hosea, whose name signifies A saviour, was the first in the order of time among those who are commonly called lesser prophets, because their prophecies are short. He prophesied in the kingdom of Israel, that is, of the ten tribes, about the same time that Isaiah prophesied in the kingdom of Judah.

Old Testament. JOEL, whose name, according to ST. JEROME, signifies THE Lord God: or, as others say, THE COMING DOWN OF God: prophesied about the same time in the kingdom of Judea, as OSEE did in the kingdom of Israel. He foretells under figure the great evils that were coming upon the people for their sins: earnestly exhorts them to repentance: and comforts them with the promise of a TEACHER OF JUSTICE, viz., CHRIST JESUS OUR Lord, and of the coming down of his holy SPIRIT.

Old Testament. AMOS prophesied in Israel about the same time as Hoshea: and was called from following the cattle to denounce God'S judgments to the people of Israel, and the neighbouring nations, for their repeated crimes, in which they continued without repentance.

Old Testament. ABDIAS, whose name is interpreted THE SERVANT OF THE Lord, is believed to have prophesied about the same time as OSEE, JOEL, and AMOS: though some of the Hebrews, who believe him to be the same with ACHAB's steward, make him much more ancient. His prophecy is the shortest of any in number of words, but yields to none, says ST. JEROME, in the sublimity of mysteries. It contains but one chapter.

Old Testament. JONAS prophesied in the reign of JEREBOAM the second: as we learn from 4 Kings 14.25. To whom also he foretold his success in restoring all the borders of Israel. He was of GETH OPHER in the tribe of ZABULON, and consequently of GALILEE: which confutes that assertion of the Pharisees, John 7.52, that no prophet ever rose out of GALILEE. He prophesied and prefigured in his own person the death and resurrection of CHRIST: and was the only one among the prophets that was sent to preach to the Gentiles.

Old Testament. MICHEAS, of Morasti, a little town in the tribe of JUDA, was contemporary with the prophet ISAIAS: whom he resembles both in his spirit and his style. He is different from the prophet MICHEAS mentioned in the third book of Kings, chap. 22. For that MICHEAS lived in the days of king ACHAB, one hundred and fifty years before the time of EZECHIAS, under whom this MICHEAS prophesied.

Old Testament. NAHUM, whose name signifies A COMFORTER, was a native of Elcese, or Elcesai, supposed to be a little town in Galilee. He prophesied, after the ten tribes were carried into captivity, and foretold the utter destruction of Nineveh, by the Babylonians and Medes: which happened in the reign of JOSIAS.

Old Testament. HABACUC was a native of Bezocher, and prophesied in JUDA, some time before the invasion of the CHALDEANS, which he foretold. He lived to see this prophecy fulfilled, and for many years after, according to the general opinion, which supposes him to be the same that was brought by the ANGEL to DANIEL in BABYLON, Dan. 14.

Old Testament. SOPHONIAS, whose name, says St. Jerome, signifies The Watchman of the Lord, or The hidden of the Lord, prophesied in the beginning of the reign of Josiah. He was a native of Sarabatha, and of the tribe of Simeon, according to the more general opinion. He prophesied the punishments of the Jews, for their idolatry and other crimes; also the punishments that were to come on divers nations; the coming of Christ, the conversion of the Gentiles, the blindness of the Jews, and their conversion towards the end of the world.

Old Testament. AGGEUS was one of those that returned from the captivity of Babylon, in the first year of the reign of king Cyrus. He was sent by the Lord, in the second year of the reign of king Darius, the son of Hystaspes, to exhort Zerubbabel the prince of Judah, and Jesus the high priest, to the building of the temple; which they had begun, but left off again through the opposition of the Samaritans. In consequence of this exhortation they proceeded in the building and finished the temple. And the prophet was commissioned by the Lord to assure them that this second temple should be more glorious than the

Old Testament. ZACHARIAS began to prophesy in the same year as Haggai, and upon the same occasion. His prophecy is full of mysterious figures and promises of blessings, partly relating to the synagogue, and partly to the church of Christ.

Old Testament. MALACHIAS, whose name signifies The Angel of the Lord, was contemporary with NEHEMIAS, and by some is believed to have been the same person as ESDRAS. He was the last of the prophets, in the order of time, and flourished about four hundred years before Christ. He foretells the coming of Christ; the reprobation of the Jews and their sacrifices; and the calling of the Gentiles, who shall offer up to God in every place an acceptable sacrifice.

New Testament. Saint Matthew, one of the twelve Apostles, who from being a publican, that is, a taxgatherer, was called by our Saviour to the Apostleship: in that profession his name is Levi. (Luke 5.27, and Mark 2.14.) He was the first of the Evangelists that wrote the Gospel, and that in Hebrew or Syro-Chaldaic which the Jews in Palestine spoke at that time. The original is not now extant; but it was translated in the time of the Apostles into Greek, that version was of equal authority. He wrote about six years after the Lord's Ascension.

New Testament. St. Mark, the disciple and interpreter of St. Peter (says St. Jerome), according to what he heard from Peter himself, wrote at Rome a brief Gospel at the request of the Brethren, about ten years after our lord's Ascension; which when Peter had heard, he approved of it and with his authority published it to the church to be read. Baronius and others say that the original was written in Latin: but the more general opinion is that the Evangelist wrote it in Greek.

New Testament. St. Luke was a native of Antioch, the capital of Syria. He was by profession a physician; and some ancient writers say, that he was very skillful in painting. He was converted by St. Paul and became his disciple and companion in his travels, and fellow-labourer in the ministry of the Gospel. He wrote in Greek, about twenty-four years after our Lord's Ascension.

New Testament. St. John the Apostle and Evangelist was the son of Zebedee and Salome, brother to James the Greater. He was called the Beloved disciple of Christ and stood by at his Crucifixion. He wrote the Gospel after the other Evangelists, about sixty-three years after our Lord's Ascension. Many things that they had omitted were supplied by him. The original was written in Greek; and by the Greeks he is titled: The Divine, St. Jerome relates that, when he was earnestly requested by the brethren to write the Gospel, he answered he would do it, if by ordering a common fast, they would all put up their praye

New Testament. This Book, which, from the first ages, has been called, THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES, is not to be considered as a history of what was done by all the Apostles, who were dispersed into different nations; but only a short view of the first establishment of the Christian Church. A part of the preaching and action of St. Peter are related in the first twelve chapters; and a particular account of St. Paul's apostolical labours in the subsequent chapters. It was written by St. Luke the Evangelist, and the original in Greek. Its history commences from the Ascension of Christ our Lord and ends in the yea

New Testament. St. Paul wrote this epistle at Corinth, when he was preparing to go to Jerusalem with the charitable contributions collected in Achaia and Macedonia for the relief of the Christians in Judea; which was about twenty-four years after Our Lord's Ascension. It was written in Greek; but at the same time translated into Latin, for the benefit of those who did not understand that language.  And though it is not the first of his Epistles in the order of time, yet it is first placed on account of sublimity of the matter contained in it, of the preeminence of the place to which it was sent, and in vener

New Testament. St. Paul, having planted the faithful in Corinth, where he had preached a year and a half and converted a great many, went to Ephesus. After being there three years, he wrote this first Epistle to the Corinthians and sent it by the same persons, Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, who had brought their letter to him. It was written about twenty-four years after our Lord's Ascension and contains several matters appertaining to faith and morals and also to ecclesiastical discipline.

New Testament. In this Epistle St. Paul comforts those who are now reformed by his admonitions to them in the former and absolves the incestuous man on doing penance, whom he had before excommunicated for his crime. Hence he treats of true penance and of the dignity of the ministers of the New Testament. He cautions the faithful against false teachers and the society of infidels. He gives an account of his sufferings and also of the favours and graces which God has bestowed on him. This second Epistle was written in the same year with the first and sent by Titus from some place in Macedonia.

New Testament. The Galatians, soon after St. Paul had preached the Gospel to them, were seduced by some false teachers, who had been Jews and who were for obliging all Christians, even those who had been Gentiles, to observe circumcision and the other ceremonies of the Mosaical law. In this Epistle, he refutes the pernicious doctrine of those teachers and also their calumny against his mission and apostleship. The subject matter of this Epistle is much the same as that to the Romans. It was written at Ephesus, about twenty-three years after our Lord's Ascension.

New Testament. Ephesus was the capital of Lesser Asia, and celebrated for the temple of Diana, to which the most part of the people of the East went frequently to worship. But St. Paul having preached the Gospel there, for two years the first time and afterwards for about a year, converted many. He wrote this Epistle to them when he was a prisoner in Rome; and sent it by Tychicus. He admonishes them to hold firmly the faith which they had received and warns them, and also those of the neighbouring cities, against the sophistry of philosophers and doctrine of false teachers who were come among them. The matte

New Testament. The Philippians were the first among the Macedonians converted to the faith. They had a great veneration for St. Paul and supplied his wants when he was a prisoner in Rome, sending to him by Epaphroditus, by whom he sent this Epistle; in which he recommends charity, unity and humility and warns them against false teachers, whom he calls dogs and enemies of the cross of Christ. He also returns thanks for their benefactions. It was written about twenty-nine years after our Lord's Ascension.

New Testament. Colossa was a city of Phrygia, near Laodicea. It does not appear that St. Paul had preached there himself, but that the Colossians were converted by Epaphras, a disciple of the Apostles. However, as St. Paul was the great Apostle of the Gentiles, he wrote this Epistle to the Colossians when he was in prison, and about the same time that he wrote to the Ephesians and Philippians. The exhortations and doctrine it contains are similar to that which is set forth in his Epistle to the Ephesians.

New Testament. Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia, in which St. Paul, having preached the Gospel, converted some Jews and a great number of the Gentiles: but the unbelieving Jews, envying his success, raised such a commotion against him that he, and his companion, Silvanus were obliged to quit the city. Afterwards he went to Athens, where he heard that the converts in Thessalonica were under a severe persecution, ever since his departure; and lest they should lose their fortitude, he sent Timothy to strengthen and comfort them in their sufferings. In the meantime St. Paul came to Corinth, where he wro

New Testament. In this Epistle St. Paul admonishes the Thessalonians to be constant in the faith of Christ and not to be terrified by the insinuations of false teachers telling them that the day of judgment was near at hand, as there must come many signs and wonders before it. He bids them to hold firm the traditions received from him, whether by word, or by epistle, and shews them how they may be certain of his letters by the manner he writes.

New Testament.
