St. Paul write this Epistle to his BELOVED TIMOTHY, being then bishop of Ephesus, to instruct him in the duties of a bishop, both in respect to himself and to his charge; and that he ought to be well informed of the good morals of those on whom he was to impose hands: Impose not hands lightly upon any man. He tells him also how he should behave towards his clergy. The Epistle was written about 33 years after our Lord's Ascension; but where it was written is uncertain: the more general opinion is, that it was in Macedonia.

New Testament. In this Epistle, the Apostle again instructs and admonishes Timothy in what belonged to his office, as in the former; and also warns him to shun the conversation of those who had erred from the truth, describing at the same time their character, He tells him of his approaching death and desires him to come speedily to him. It appears from this circumstance that he wrote this second Epistle in the time of his last imprisonment at Rome and not long before his martyrdom.

New Testament. St. Paul, having preached the faith in the island of Crete, he ordained his beloved disciple and companion, Titus, bishop, and left him there to finish the work which he had begun. Afterwards the Apostle, on a journey to Nicopolis, a city of Macedonia, wrote this Epistle to Titus, in which he directs him to ordain bishops and priests for the different cities, shewing him the principal qualities necessary for a bishop. He also gives him particular advice for his own conduct to his flock, exhorting him to hold to strictness of discipline, but seasoned with lenity. It was written about thirty-thr

New Testament. Philemon, a noble citizen of Colossa, had a servant named Onesimus, who robbed him and fled to Rome, where he met St. Paul, who was then a prisoner there the first time. The apostle took compassion on him and received him with tenderness and converted him to the faith; for he was a Gentile before.  St. Paul sends him back to his master with this Epistle in his favour: and though he beseeches Philemon to pardon him, yet the Apostle writes with becoming dignity and authority. It contains divers profitable instructions and points out the charity and humanity that masters should have for their ser

New Testament. St. Paul wrote this Epistle to the Christians in Palestine, the most part of whom being Jews before their conversion, they were called Hebrews. He exhorts them to be thoroughly converted and confirmed in the faith of Christ, clearly shewing them the preeminence of Christ's priesthood above the Levitical, and also the excellence of the new law above the old. He commends faith by the example of the ancient fathers: and exhorts them to patience and perseverance and to remain in fraternal charity.  It appears from chap. 13 that this Epistle was written in Italy, and probably at Rome, about twenty-

New Testament. This Epistle is called Catholic or Universal, as formerly were also the two Epistles of St. Peter, the first of St. John and that of St. Jude, because they were not written to any peculiar people or particular person, but to the faithful in general. It was written by the apostle St. James, called the Less, who was also called the brother of our Lord, being his kinsman (for cousins german with the Hebrews were called brothers). He was the first Bishop of Jerusalem. In this Epistle are set forth many precepts appertaining to faith and morals; particularly, that faith without good works will not

New Testament. The first Epistle of St. Peter, though brief, contains much doctrine concerning Faith, Hope, and Charity, with divers instructions to all persons of what state or condition soever.  The Apostle commands submission to rulers and superiors and exhorts all to the practice of a virtuous life in imitation, of Christ. This Epistle is written with such apostolical dignity as to manifest the supreme authority with which its writer, the Prince of the Apostles, had been vested by his Lord and Master, Jesus Christ. He wrote it at Rome, which figuratively he calls Babylon, about fifteen years after our Lo

New Testament. In this Epistle St. Peter says (chap, 3): Behold this second Epistle I write to you: and before (chap. 1,): Being assured that the laying away of this my tabernacle is at hand. This shews, that it was written a very short time before his martyrdom, which was about thirty-five years after our Lord's Ascension. In this Epistle he admonishes the faithful to be mindful of the great gifts they received from God and to join all other virtues with their faith. He warns them against false teachers, by describing their practices and foretelling their punishments. He describes the dissolution of this wo

New Testament. The same vein of divine love and charity towards our neighbour, which runs throughout the Gospel written by the beloved disciple and Evangelist, St. John, is found also in his Epistles. He confirms the two principal mysteries of faith: The mystery of the Trinity and the mystery of the incarnation of Jesus Christ the Son of God. The sublimity and excellence of the evangelical doctrine he declares: And this commandment we have from God, that he, who loves God, love also his brother (chap. 4,21). And again: For this is the charity of God, that we keep his commandments, and: His commandments are n

New Testament. The Apostle commends Electa and her family for their steadfastness in the true faith and exhorts them to persevere, lest they lose the reward of their labours. He exhorts them to love one another. But with heretics to have no society, even not to salute them. Although this Epistle is written to a particular person, yet its instructions may serve as a lesson to others, especially to those who, from their connections, situation, or condition in life, are in danger of perversion.
New Testament. St. John praises Gaius for his walking in truth and for his charity, complains of the bad conduct of Diotrephes and gives a good testimony to Demetrius.

New Testament. St. Jude, who wrote this Epistle, was one of the twelve Apostles and brother to St. James the Less. The time it was written is uncertain: only it may be inferred from verse 17 that few or none of the Apostles were then living, except St. John. He inveighs against the heresies and wicked practices of the Simonians, Nicolaitans, and Gnostics, etc., describing them and their leaders by strong epithets and similes, He exhorts the faithful to contend earnestly for the faith first delivered to them and to beware of heretics.

New Testament. In the first, second, and third chapters of this Book are contained instructions and admonitions which St. John was commanded to write to the seven bishops of the churches in Asia. And in the following chapters, to the end, are contained prophecies of things that are to come to pass in the Church of Christ, particularly towards the end of the world, in the time of Antichrist. It was written in Greek, in the island of Patmos, where St. John was in banishment by order of the cruel emperor Domitian, about sixty-four years after our Lord's Ascension.
Apocryphal: the prayer of repentance of King Manasseh in captivity. In the appendix of the 1609 Douay Bible.
Apocryphal: a retelling of the return from Babylon, also called 1 Esdras. In the appendix of the 1609 Douay Bible.
Apocryphal: visions given to Ezra, also called 2 Esdras. In the appendix of the 1609 Douay Bible.

God’s word only bears fruit in a heart that truly receives it. Matthew 13:1–23 · Mark 4:1–20 · Luke 8:4–15 The story A farmer's seed is eaten by birds, withers on rocky ground and is choked by thorns; the seed that falls on good soil yields thirty, sixty and a hundredfold. Why Jesus told it Jesus is teaching from a boat to a huge crowd on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. Many are drawn to Him, but few will follow Him to the end. Later, alone with the disciples, He explains the parable Himself, one of the few times He does so. The key The sower Christ, and everyone who passes on His word The seed the word of God The path a heart that hears but does not understand, so the evil one snatches the word away Rocky ground enthusiasm without roots, which gives up when trouble comes Thorns the cares of the world and the lure of riches that choke the word Good soil a heart that hears, understands and bears fruit What it means The sower is surprisingly generous: he throws seed everywhere, even where it seems wasted. God offers His word to everyone, with no one written off in advance. The difference lies in the soil. Most of us recognize all four soils in ourselves on different days: distracted, eager then discouraged, crowded with worries. The parable is less a verdict than an invitation to clear the ground. Soil can be tilled; stones can be removed; thorns can be pulled up. A heart that keeps making room for the word will in time bear fruit far beyond its own effort. What the Church teaches The Catechism says the parables are like mirrors: in them we ask whether we are hard soil or good earth. Hearing is not enough; deeds are required. CCC 546 For your life Which of the four soils best describes how I received God’s word this week? What is one “thorn” I could pull up to give the word more room? Read it in the Bible Matthew 13:1–23 ↗ Mark 4:1–20 ↗ Luke 8:4–15 ↗

Good and evil grow together until the harvest; judgment belongs to God. Matthew 13:24–30, 36–43 The story While a man sleeps, an enemy sows weeds among his wheat. He won't let his servants pull them up in case the wheat comes up with them; the sorting can wait for the harvest. Why Jesus told it This follows straight after the Sower in Matthew 13. The first Christians were puzzled: if the Kingdom has come, why is there still so much evil, even among believers? Jesus later explains the parable to His disciples in private (Matthew 13:36–43). The key The man who sows good seed the Son of Man The field the world The good seed the children of the Kingdom The weeds the children of the evil one The enemy the devil The harvest the end of the age, when the angels will gather and sort What it means The weed in question, darnel, looks almost identical to wheat while young. Pulling it up early would tear out good plants with it. The servants are eager to purify the field; the master is patient. This is a warning against the temptation to build a “pure” community by our own hand, deciding who is beyond hope. People change: today’s weed can become tomorrow’s saint, as St Paul and St Augustine show. Evil is real and will be judged, but the sorting is God’s work, done at the right time. Our task in the meantime is to be good wheat. What the Church teaches The Catechism applies this to the Church herself: until the end of time, the weeds of sin are found mixed with the good wheat of the Gospel in all her members. CCC 827 For your life Is there someone I have quietly written off as a “weed”? Where in my own heart do wheat and weeds grow side by side? Read it in the Bible Matthew 13:24–43 ↗

God’s Kingdom starts tiny and grows beyond anything we imagine. Matthew 13:31–32 · Mark 4:30–32 · Luke 13:18–19 The story The mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, grows into a tree where birds build their nests. Why Jesus told it The disciples were a handful of fishermen and tax collectors in a small province of the Roman Empire. Expectations for the Messiah were grand and political. Jesus answers with an image from the kitchen garden. The key The mustard seed the Kingdom in its beginning: Jesus and His little band of disciples The great plant the Church spread through the world The birds that nest in its branches the nations who find shelter in it What it means Twelve men, a crucified leader, an empty tomb: from the outside, Christianity began as almost nothing. Within three centuries it filled the Roman world, and today it reaches every continent. The same pattern holds in a single life. God rarely starts with something impressive. A short prayer, a small act of kindness, a first step back to Mass can be the mustard seed. We are not asked to produce the tree, only to plant the seed and trust God with the growth. What the Church teaches The Catechism calls the “little flock” gathered around Jesus the seed and beginning of the Kingdom, which God makes grow. CCC 764 For your life What small seed of faith has God planted in me that I have overlooked? Do I despise small beginnings, in myself or in others? Read it in the Bible Matthew 13:31–32 ↗ Mark 4:30–32 ↗ Luke 13:18–19 ↗

The Kingdom changes the world quietly, from the inside out. Matthew 13:33 · Luke 13:20–21 The story A woman mixes a little yeast into a large batch of flour, and the whole dough rises. Why Jesus told it Told as a pair with the Mustard Seed. One is a man’s work in the field, the other a woman’s work in the kitchen: the Kingdom touches every part of life. The key The leaven (yeast) the Kingdom, the Gospel, the grace of God Three measures of flour the world, or the whole of a person’s life The woman Christ, or the Church, working the Kingdom into the world What it means Three measures of flour is roughly 40 liters, enough bread for a large crowd. A pinch of yeast hidden in it changes all of it, silently and completely. Christians are not meant to stay apart in a sealed jar. Like yeast, they are mixed into families, offices and neighborhoods, and the change happens there. It is slow and mostly unseen. The same is true inside us: grace does not usually transform us overnight, but works through every corner of our lives until “till it was all leavened.” What the Church teaches The Catechism, explaining the Our Father, says that the newness of the Kingdom should make the earth “rise” like leaven in the dough, through the Spirit of Christ. CCC 2832 For your life Where has God placed me to be “yeast” right now? Which part of my life have I kept sealed off from grace? Read it in the Bible Matthew 13:33 ↗ Luke 13:20–21 ↗

The Kingdom is worth everything, and finding it brings joy. Matthew 13:44 The story A man finds treasure buried in a field and, overjoyed, sells everything he owns to buy the field. Why Jesus told it In a land often crossed by armies, people buried their valuables for safekeeping. Treasures were sometimes found centuries later by a farmhand working someone else’s field. The key The treasure the Kingdom of God, and Christ Himself The field the place where we stumble on it, often in ordinary life Selling everything a whole-hearted response that holds nothing back What it means The key word is joy. The man is not grimly making a sacrifice; he is a man who has just found a fortune and can’t believe his luck. Selling everything is the obvious, happy thing to do. Saints often describe their conversion this way. What looks like giving things up from the outside feels, from the inside, like gaining something far greater. If faith feels only like a list of losses, we may not yet have seen the treasure clearly. What the Church teaches The Catechism says that through His parables Jesus asks for a radical choice: to gain the Kingdom, one must give everything. CCC 546 For your life When did I last feel joy, not just duty, in my faith? What am I holding on to that I value more than the treasure? Read it in the Bible Matthew 13:44 ↗

For the one who searches, Christ is the pearl worth more than all else. Matthew 13:45–46 The story A merchant looking for fine pearls finds one of great value and sells everything to buy it. Why Jesus told it A twin to the Hidden Treasure. In the ancient world pearls were among the most precious things anyone could own, more valuable than gold. The key The merchant the seeker who is looking for truth and goodness Fine pearls the good things of life: wisdom, beauty, love The one great pearl Christ and His Kingdom, which fulfill all the others What it means The man with the treasure stumbled on it; the merchant was searching. Some meet God by surprise, others after a long quest through philosophies and religions. Both are welcome. The merchant already deals in fine pearls. The good things he loved were real, but they pointed beyond themselves. When he finds the one pearl, everything else is reordered around it. Faith does not throw away beauty, learning or love; it finds their source. What the Church teaches The same Catechism passage applies: the Kingdom asks for a radical choice, giving everything to gain it. CCC 546 For your life What “fine pearls” am I seeking, and where do they point? Is Christ the pearl at the center of my life, or one among many? Read it in the Bible Matthew 13:45–46 ↗

The net gathers everyone now; the sorting comes at the end. Matthew 13:47–50 The story A net thrown into the sea gathers fish of every kind; the fishermen keep the good ones and throw the bad away. Why Jesus told it Several of the apostles were fishermen on the Sea of Galilee who used large dragnets. Jesus closes His chapter of Kingdom parables with an image they knew from their own work. The key The net the Kingdom, and the Church in the world Fish of every kind all kinds of people drawn in by the Gospel Sorting on the shore the final judgment, carried out by the angels What it means The net does not choose: it pulls in every kind of fish. The Church’s mission is the same, casting the net wide to everyone without picking who seems worthy. But the story does not end in the water. On the shore there is a sorting, and it is serious. Being in the net, a member of the Church in name, is not the same as being good fish. The parable calls us to take our own conversion seriously while leaving the judgment of others to God. What the Church teaches The Catechism teaches that at the Last Judgment the truth of each person’s relationship with God will be laid bare, and Jesus speaks plainly of the danger of being lost. CCC 1038, 1034 For your life Do I treat belonging to the Church as a guarantee, or as a calling? How would I live today if the net were drawn ashore tonight? Read it in the Bible Matthew 13:47–50 ↗

We sow; God gives the growth, in His own time. Mark 4:26–29 The story A man scatters seed; whether he sleeps or wakes, it sprouts and grows, and he doesn’t know how. Why Jesus told it This short parable is found only in Mark. It sits between the Sower and the Mustard Seed, and it was a comfort to early missionaries who saw little result from their work. The key The man the disciple who spreads the word The seed the word of God Growth while he sleeps God’s hidden work, which we cannot see or control The harvest the full coming of the Kingdom What it means The farmer does his part and then goes to bed. He cannot make the seed grow faster by worrying over it. The earth bears fruit “of itself”. This frees us from two errors: laziness (doing nothing) and anxiety (thinking everything depends on us). Parents praying for children who have left the faith, catechists who see no results, anyone working for good with little to show: the seed is growing, even when nothing seems to happen. What the Church teaches The Catechism describes the Kingdom as present in the word of Christ, compared to a seed sown in a field, growing by its own power until the harvest. CCC 764 For your life Where am I trying to force growth that only God can give? Whose slow growth am I tempted to give up on? Read it in the Bible Mark 4:26–29 ↗

God goes looking for the one who is lost, and rejoices to find Him. Luke 15:3–7 · Matthew 18:12–14 The story A shepherd with a hundred sheep leaves the ninety-nine to search for the one that is lost, and carries it home on his shoulders with joy. Why Jesus told it Tax collectors and sinners were gathering to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes grumbled: “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” Jesus answers with three stories in a row: the lost sheep, the lost coin and the lost son. The key The shepherd God, and Jesus the Good Shepherd The lost sheep a sinner who has wandered away The ninety-nine those who think they have no need of repentance Carrying it home God does the work of bringing us back The celebration the joy of heaven over one who repents What it means Leaving ninety-nine sheep to look for one seems reckless. That is the point: God’s love is not careful accounting. Every single person matters to Him as if they were the only one. Notice that the shepherd does not drive the sheep home or scold it; he lifts it onto his shoulders. The early Christians loved this image and painted it in the catacombs long before they painted the cross. Whoever feels too far gone should know that God is already out looking. What the Church teaches The Catechism notes that Jesus invites sinners to the table of the Kingdom and speaks of the Father’s joy over even one sinner who repents. CCC 545 For your life Have I ever felt like the lost sheep? How did God find me? Who in my life is “lost”, and how can I go after them? Read it in the Bible Luke 15:3–7 ↗ Matthew 18:12–14 ↗

Each person is precious to God, worth searching the whole house for. Luke 15:8–10 The story A woman with ten silver coins loses one, lights a lamp and sweeps the house until she finds it, then celebrates with her neighbors. Why Jesus told it The second of the three “lost” parables of Luke 15, told to the same grumbling listeners. This time the searcher is a woman, which would have surprised Jesus’ audience. The key The woman God, searching with patient care The lost coin a soul that has gone missing The lamp and broom the light and effort God spends to find us The friends and neighbors the angels, who share the joy What it means A silver drachma was about a day’s wage. For a poor household, losing one was a real loss, and it may have been part of a woman’s dowry. The search is thorough: she lights a lamp and sweeps every corner. A sheep wanders off on its own, but a coin is simply lost; it cannot even know it is missing. Some people are far from God not through rebellion but through neglect, wounds or circumstance. God searches for them too, and the joy of finding is shared with all heaven. What the Church teaches With the lost sheep, this parable shows what the Catechism calls Jesus’ invitation to sinners, and heaven’s joy over each one who returns. CCC 545 For your life Do I see myself as precious to God, or as easily replaced? Who around me is lost without even knowing it? Read it in the Bible Luke 15:8–10 ↗

The Father runs to welcome the sinner home, and longs for both His sons. Luke 15:11–32 The story The younger son takes his inheritance, squanders it far away and ends up feeding pigs. When he decides to come home as a hired hand, his father sees him from afar, runs to him, embraces him and throws a feast. The elder son is angry and won't go in, and the father comes out to plead with him too. Why Jesus told it The third and longest story in Luke 15, aimed at the same Pharisees and scribes who resented Jesus eating with sinners. They would have seen themselves, uncomfortably, in the elder son. The key The father God the Father, rich in mercy The younger son the sinner who leaves God and comes back The far country and the pigs the emptiness and degradation of life without God The robe, ring and shoes restored dignity as a son, not a servant The elder son the religious person who obeys but does not share the Father’s heart What it means Asking for his inheritance early was like telling his father, “I wish you were dead.” Yet the father never stops watching the road. When he sees his son, he runs, something a dignified elder of the time would never do, and cuts short the speech the son had rehearsed. The son hoped to come back as a servant; he is restored as a son. The story has two halves. The elder son has never left home, but he is just as far from his father’s heart. He calls himself a slave and his brother “this son of yours”. The father goes out to him too, with the same tenderness. Jesus ends without telling us whether he goes in to the feast. The question is left for each listener: am I willing to rejoice when God forgives someone I think does not deserve it? What the Church teaches The Catechism uses this parable to describe the whole process of conversion and repentance: the fascination of illusory freedom, the misery, the decision to return, the father’s welcome and the festive joy, which only the heart of Christ could reveal so simply and beautifully. CCC 1439 For your life Am I more like the younger son or the elder son right now? Is there a “rehearsed speech” keeping me from going to Confession? Read it in the Bible Luke 15:11–32 ↗

Having been forgiven so much, we must forgive others from the heart. Matthew 18:23–35 The story A king forgives a servant a debt too great ever to repay. That same servant has a fellow servant thrown into prison over a small debt, and the king takes back his pardon. Why Jesus told it Peter has just asked: “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? As many as seven times?” Jesus answers “seventy times seven”, then tells this story to show why. The key The king God Ten thousand talents our debt of sin, impossible to repay The first servant each of us, forgiven by God A hundred denarii the real but small wrongs others do to us The torturers the consequence of a heart that refuses mercy What it means The numbers are deliberately absurd. Ten thousand talents was more than the tax revenue of a whole province, a debt no servant could repay in a hundred lifetimes. A hundred denarii was about three months’ wages: a real debt, but tiny by comparison. The servant’s fault is not that he wanted his money; it is that he forgot what had just been done for him. Forgiveness received but not passed on has not really been received. This is why we pray, “forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us.” Forgiving does not mean pretending the wrong did not happen; it means releasing the debt, as God released ours. What the Church teaches Explaining the Our Father, the Catechism points to this parable: it is in the depths of the heart that everything is bound and loosed, and our openness to God’s mercy depends on our forgiving others. CCC 2843 For your life Whose “hundred denarii” am I still holding on to? Do I remember often enough how much I have been forgiven? Read it in the Bible Matthew 18:23–35 ↗
The Pharisee and the Tax Collector

God hears the humble who ask for mercy, not the proud who list their virtues. Luke 18:9–14 The story In the Temple a Pharisee lists his virtues and thanks God he isn't like others. A tax collector, not daring to look up, beats his breast: "God, be merciful to me, a sinner." Why Jesus told it Luke says Jesus told this “to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous and despised others.” It follows straight after the Persistent Widow, so it is also a lesson on how to pray. The key The Pharisee a person confident in his own goodness The tax collector a sinner who knows he has nothing to offer God The Temple the place of prayer, where both stand before the same God Going home justified being made right with God, as a gift What it means Pharisees were respected for their devotion, and this one really did fast and tithe more than the law required. Tax collectors worked for the Roman occupiers and often cheated their own people. Jesus’ listeners would have expected the verdict to go the other way. The Pharisee’s prayer is really about himself, and about how he compares with others. The tax collector stands at a distance, eyes down, and says a single sentence. He hides nothing and asks for everything. The Church has made his prayer her own: it lives on in the Kyrie at Mass and in the Jesus Prayer, “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.” What the Church teaches The Catechism names this as one of Luke’s three great parables on prayer. It teaches that humility is the foundation of prayer and that petition begins, like the tax collector’s, with asking forgiveness. CCC 2613, 2631, 2559 For your life When I pray, do I compare myself with others? Can I pray the tax collector’s prayer slowly today, meaning every word? Read it in the Bible Luke 18:9–14 ↗

The one who knows how much they are forgiven loves the most. Luke 7:41–43 The story A creditor cancels the debts of two men, one owing five hundred denarii, the other fifty. Jesus asks His host, Simon the Pharisee: which will love him more? Why Jesus told it Jesus is dining at the house of Simon, a Pharisee. A woman known in the town as a sinner comes in, weeps over Jesus’ feet, dries them with her hair and anoints them. Simon thinks to himself that a real prophet would know what sort of woman she is. Jesus answers his thought with this story. The key The creditor God, who forgives freely The debtor of five hundred the sinful woman, aware of how much she has been forgiven The debtor of fifty Simon, who thinks he owes little Cancelling the debts God’s free forgiveness, which neither could earn What it means Five hundred denarii was well over a year’s wages; fifty, about two months. Neither man could pay, and the creditor forgives both. Simon gives the obvious answer: the one forgiven more will love more. Jesus then turns to the woman and contrasts her extravagant love with Simon’s cool hospitality: no water for His feet, no kiss, no oil. The difference is not that Simon is sinless. It is that he does not see his need. The saints often called themselves the greatest of sinners, not out of false modesty, but because the closer they came to God, the more they saw how much they had been forgiven, and the more they loved. What the Church teaches The Catechism describes contemplative prayer as the prayer of the forgiven sinner who welcomes the love by which he is loved and wants to respond by loving even more, pointing to this scene. CCC 2712 For your life Do I think of myself as someone who owes God fifty or five hundred? How does gratitude for forgiveness show in the way I love? Read it in the Bible Luke 7:41–43 ↗

God is patient and gives us time to bear fruit, but the time is not endless. Luke 13:6–9 The story A fig tree that has borne no fruit for three years is about to be cut down; the gardener asks for one more year to dig around it and fertilize it. Why Jesus told it People had just told Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate, and He recalled eighteen people crushed when a tower fell. Were they worse sinners than others? “No,” He says, “but unless you repent you will all likewise perish.” Then He tells this parable. The key The owner of the vineyard God the Father The fig tree God’s people, and each of us Three years without fruit a life that has received much but given little back The vinedresser Christ, who intercedes for us Digging and manure the graces God gives to help us change What it means A fig tree takes up space, water and nutrients. After three barren years, cutting it down is common sense. The vinedresser pleads for one more year and promises to work on it himself. This is the season we live in: the extra year. Christ stands between us and judgment, not only pleading but digging and feeding the roots with grace. The parable is both a comfort and a warning. God’s patience is great, but it is meant to lead us to repentance, not to be presumed upon. The story ends before we learn whether the tree bears fruit. That ending is ours to write. What the Church teaches The Catechism calls conversion first of all a work of the grace of God, who makes our hearts return to Him. CCC 1432 For your life What fruit is God looking for in my life this year? How am I using the “extra year” I have been given? Read it in the Bible Luke 13:6–9 ↗

My neighbor is anyone in need, and love crosses every boundary. Luke 10:25–37 The story A man is robbed, beaten and left half dead by the road. A priest and a Levite pass by on the other side; a Samaritan, from a people the Jews despised, binds his wounds, takes him to an inn and pays for his care. Why Jesus told it A lawyer asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. He answers correctly: love God and love your neighbor. Then, “desiring to justify himself”, he asks: “And who is my neighbor?” This story is Jesus’ reply. The key The traveler every person in need, and humanity wounded by sin The priest and the Levite religion that keeps its distance from suffering The Samaritan the unexpected neighbor, and in the Fathers’ reading, Christ Himself Oil and wine healing care, and for the Fathers, the sacraments The inn the Church, where the wounded are cared for until Christ returns What it means The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops about a kilometer in 27 kilometers through desert, and was notorious for bandits. The priest and Levite may have feared ritual impurity from touching a dead body. Samaritans and Jews despised each other; for Jesus’ audience, “good” and “Samaritan” did not belong together. Notice how Jesus flips the question. The lawyer asked, “Who is my neighbor?”, looking for the limit of his duty. Jesus asks, “Which of these was neighbor to the man?” The question is not who deserves my love, but whether I will become a neighbor to whoever is in front of me. The Church Fathers, such as St Augustine, also saw Christ as the Samaritan who came down to wounded humanity, healed us and paid the cost of our care. What the Church teaches The Catechism teaches that charity asks us to love as Christ loves, even our enemies, and to make ourselves the neighbor of those farthest away. The works of mercy are its concrete form. CCC 1825, 2447 For your life Who have I “passed by on the other side” recently? Is there a group of people I find it hard to see as my neighbor? Read it in the Bible Luke 10:25–37 ↗

Keep praying and never lose heart: God hears His children. Luke 18:1–8 The story A judge who neither fears God nor respects people finally gives a persistent widow her rights, just so she'll stop bothering him. Why Jesus told it Luke tells us the purpose before the story: Jesus told it “that they ought always to pray and not lose heart.” It comes after His teaching on the day the Son of Man will be revealed, and ends with a question: “when the Son of man comes, will he find faith on earth?” The key The unjust judge not a picture of God, but His opposite The widow those who are powerless and depend on God alone Her persistence prayer that keeps going when nothing seems to change Justice at last God’s sure answer, in His time What it means In Jesus’ time a widow had no husband to speak for her in court and often no money to bribe a judge. Her only weapon is to keep coming back. The judge gives in purely to get rid of her. The parable argues from the lesser to the greater. If a corrupt judge gives in to persistence, how much more will a loving Father hear His children who cry to Him day and night? Persistence in prayer does not wear God down; it changes us. It deepens our desire, purifies what we ask for and keeps our faith alive while we wait. St Monica prayed for her son Augustine for some seventeen years. What the Church teaches The Catechism lists this among the three principal parables on prayer in Luke, teaching the patience of faith: we must pray always without losing heart. CCC 2613 For your life What have I stopped praying for because the answer seemed slow? Does my prayer show that I trust God more than the widow trusted the judge? Read it in the Bible Luke 18:1–8 ↗

Ask boldly and keep knocking: God loves to give good things. Luke 11:5–8 The story A man with an unexpected midnight guest knocks on his neighbor's door to borrow bread. The neighbor doesn't want to get up, but gives him what he needs because he keeps knocking. Why Jesus told it The disciples have just asked, “Lord, teach us to pray,” and Jesus has given them the Our Father. This parable follows immediately, and then: “Ask, and it will be given you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.” The key The man knocking each of us at prayer The friend in bed not God, who never sleeps, but a contrast to Him The three loaves what we need, for ourselves and for others The unexpected guest the needs of others that send us to God What it means Hospitality was a sacred duty, and a traveler arriving at midnight could not be turned away hungry. Villages baked bread daily, so everyone knew who might have some left. The whole family sleeps in one room; getting up means waking everyone. The man is not asking for himself but for a guest. Much of our prayer is like this: we go to God because someone else needs bread. Jesus encourages a holy boldness, even a kind of shamelessness, in asking. And Luke ends the passage with the best gift of all: the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him. What the Church teaches The Catechism names this as the first of Luke’s three great parables on prayer, inviting urgent, persistent prayer: “Knock, and it will be opened to you.” CCC 2613 For your life For whom do I need to go and knock today? Do I ask God boldly, or do I hold back as if bothering Him? Read it in the Bible Luke 11:5–8 ↗

Be ready for Christ at every moment; a faithful life can’t be borrowed at the last minute. Matthew 25:1–13 The story Of ten virgins waiting for the bridegroom, five bring extra oil and five don't. When he arrives at midnight, the ones who ran out have gone to buy more, and the door is shut. Why Jesus told it This is the first of three parables in Matthew 25, spoken on the Mount of Olives in the last days before Jesus’ Passion. His disciples have asked about the end of the age and the signs of His coming. The key The bridegroom Christ, who will come again The ten virgins the Church, all those waiting for Him The lamps the faith we profess The oil a living faith: love, good works and grace that can’t be borrowed The delay and the sleep the long wait, and death The closed door the moment when the time for preparing is over What it means At a Jewish wedding, the bridegroom came at night to take his bride to his home, and the bridesmaids lit the way with torches. Delays were common; no one knew exactly when he would arrive. All ten fall asleep, so sleep is not the fault. The difference is the oil. The wise ones refuse to share, which sounds unkind until we see what the oil stands for: the inner life of faith and love that each person must build. Nobody can pray, love or repent on our behalf. The parable is sobering, but its message is hopeful: the bridegroom is coming, and it is a wedding feast. What the Church teaches The Catechism teaches that since we know neither the day nor the hour, we should follow the Lord’s advice and watch constantly, living this present time as a time of waiting and watching. CCC 1036, 672 For your life What “oil” am I storing up in my daily life? If Christ came tonight, what would I wish I had done today? Read it in the Bible Matthew 25:1–13 ↗

A life is not measured by possessions; be rich toward God. Luke 12:16–21 The story A rich man with a bumper harvest decides to build bigger barns and take life easy. God tells him: "Fool! This night your soul is required of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" Why Jesus told it A man in the crowd asks Jesus to make his brother share an inheritance. Jesus refuses to be a judge in the matter, warns, “Take heed, and beware of all covetousness,” and tells this story. The key The rich man anyone who builds life around possessions The bigger barns storing up security for ourselves alone “Soul, take your ease” the illusion that wealth makes us safe “This night” death, which no one can schedule Rich toward God a life spent in love, prayer and generosity What it means The man is not a thief. His harvest was a blessing, and planning is not a sin. What makes him a fool is that he talks only to himself (“my barns, my goods, my soul”) and never once thinks of God or of his neighbor. The question God asks is striking: “The things you have prepared, whose will they be?” Everything we own will one day belong to someone else. What we keep is what we have given away in love. Jesus goes on in the same chapter: “Do not be anxious about your life... seek his kingdom.” What the Church teaches The Catechism, speaking of poverty of heart, says the Lord grieves over the rich because they find their consolation in the abundance of goods. CCC 2544, 2547 For your life What are my “bigger barns”, the things I count on for security? What practical step would make me richer toward God this month? Read it in the Bible Luke 12:16–21 ↗

Stay awake and faithful; the Master who returns will serve us himself. Luke 12:35–40 The story Servants who don't know when their master will return from the wedding wait ready to open the door at once. Finding them awake, the master serves them himself. Why Jesus told it Right after the Rich Fool and the teaching on not being anxious, Jesus turns to readiness. He says to His “little flock”: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning.” The key The master Christ, who will return The wedding the time between His going and his coming The servants His disciples Girded loins and burning lamps being dressed for work and ready at any moment The master serving them the astonishing reward of heaven What it means In Jesus’ day, men wore long robes and tucked them into a belt for work or travel. A servant who was “girded” was ready to move at once. A wedding feast could last for days, so no one knew when the master would come home. The twist is the reward. Normally servants wait on the master. Here the master puts on an apron, seats his servants at table and serves them. Jesus did exactly this at the Last Supper when He washed His disciples’ feet. Watching is not anxious fear; it is the alert love of someone waiting for a friend. What the Church teaches The Catechism describes the time we live in as a time of waiting and watching for Christ’s return, and urges us to watch constantly because we do not know the day or the hour. CCC 672, 1036 For your life What helps me stay spiritually awake, and what makes me drowsy? Do I wait for Christ with fear or with longing? Read it in the Bible Luke 12:35–40 ↗
The Faithful and the Foolish Steward

Authority is a trust to be accounted for, not a privilege to enjoy. Luke 12:42–48 · Matthew 24:45–51 The story A steward put in charge of feeding the other servants is blessed if his master finds him doing his job. If he thinks the master is delayed and starts beating the servants and getting drunk, the master will come when he least expects it. Why Jesus told it Peter asks, “Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?” Jesus answers with this story, aimed especially at those who will lead His Church. The key The master Christ The steward anyone with responsibility for others: parents, pastors, leaders, teachers Feeding the household on time faithful service to those in our care “My master is delayed in coming” the temptation to live as if there will be no reckoning Beating the servants and getting drunk abuse of power and self-indulgence What it means A household steward was usually a trusted slave put in charge of the other slaves. He held real power, but it was borrowed power, and he would answer for how he used it. The danger is not open rebellion but slow corruption: “my master is delayed” becomes a license to bully and indulge. Jesus also introduces degrees of responsibility. Those who knew what was asked and ignored it bear more blame than those who did not know. Every role that puts us over others, from a parent to a pope, is a stewardship. What the Church teaches The Catechism calls the present time one of watching, marked by trial, until Christ returns to judge. Each person will give account of what was entrusted to them. CCC 672, 1038 For your life Who has God placed in my care, and am I “giving them their food at the proper time”? Where am I tempted to think the Master is a long way off? Read it in the Bible Luke 12:42–48 ↗ Matthew 24:45–51 ↗

Hearing Christ’s words is not enough; build your life on doing them. Matthew 7:24–27 · Luke 6:46–49 The story Whoever hears Jesus' words and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on rock; when the storm comes, it stands. Whoever hears and doesn't act built on sand, and the house falls. Why Jesus told it These are the closing words of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), after the Beatitudes, the Our Father and Jesus’ teaching on love of enemies. The crowds, Matthew says, were astonished at His teaching. The key The wise builder the one who hears Christ’s words and does them The foolish builder the one who hears and does nothing The rock Christ and His word, put into practice The sand good intentions without action The rain, floods and winds trials, temptations and finally judgment What it means In Galilee, dry riverbeds (wadis) can look like level building ground in summer. When winter rains come, they turn into rushing torrents in hours. A house built there with no deep foundation simply collapses. Both builders heard exactly the same sermon, and from outside, both houses look fine in good weather. The difference shows only when the storm comes, and it always comes. Faith that is lived day by day, in small acts of obedience, is the foundation that holds. Faith that stays at the level of feelings and opinions does not. What the Church teaches The Catechism teaches that the Law of the Gospel calls for a decisive choice between the two ways and for putting the words of the Lord into practice. CCC 1970 For your life Which of Jesus’ words do I admire but not yet practice? When the last storm came, what held, and what gave way? Read it in the Bible Matthew 7:24–27 ↗ Luke 6:46–49 ↗

Use the gifts God gave you; fear that buries them is the real failure. Matthew 25:14–30 The story A master going on a journey entrusts five, two and one talents to three servants. The first two double the money; the third, afraid, buries it. The master rewards the first two and rebukes the third. Why Jesus told it The second of the three parables in Matthew 25, told shortly before the Passion. It sits between the Ten Virgins (be ready) and the Sheep and the Goats (the judgment), and answers the question: what do we do while we wait? The key The master Christ, who goes away and will return The talents every gift God entrusts to us: abilities, faith, time, opportunities “To each according to his ability” God gives each person what fits them Trading and doubling putting gifts to work for God and others Burying the talent letting fear or laziness waste what we received “Enter into the joy of your master” eternal life, sharing God’s own joy What it means A talent was not an ability but a huge sum of money, about twenty years’ wages for a laborer. Even the servant who received “only” one was trusted with a fortune. Our English word “talent” actually comes from this parable. The first two servants receive the same praise, word for word, though one made more than the other. God does not compare our results; He looks at faithfulness. The third servant’s problem is his picture of the master: “I knew you to be a hard man... so I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent in the ground.” Fear of failure, or a false image of God as harsh, can paralyze us. The only way to lose a gift is to refuse to use it. What the Church teaches The Catechism teaches that our differences in talents belong to God’s plan: those endowed with particular talents are to share their benefits with those who need them. CCC 1936 For your life What gift have I buried out of fear or comparison? How do I imagine God: as a “hard man”, or as a generous Master? Read it in the Bible Matthew 25:14–30 ↗

The Kingdom will surely come; until then, work faithfully with what you were given. Luke 19:11–27 The story A nobleman going to a far country to receive a kingdom gives each of ten servants a mina. On his return he gives cities to those who made it grow, and takes the coin from the one who kept it wrapped in a cloth. Why Jesus told it Jesus is near Jerusalem, just after meeting Zacchaeus. Luke says He told it “because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately.” The crowd expected a triumph; Jesus was heading to the cross. The key The nobleman Christ, who goes to receive His kingdom and will return The far country His Ascension to the Father The ten servants and their minas disciples, each given the same basic gift: the faith The citizens who hated him those who reject Christ’s kingship Authority over cities reward in proportion to faithfulness What it means Jesus’ listeners knew this story from recent history: Archelaus, a son of Herod, had travelled to Rome to receive his kingdom, and a Jewish delegation followed him to protest. A mina was about three or four months’ wages. Unlike the Talents, here every servant starts with the same amount, perhaps pointing to what all believers share: faith, baptism, the Gospel. The results differ, and so do the rewards. The Kingdom is not a sudden spectacle to wait for passively; it is entrusted to us now, and the time between Christ’s going and His return is a time for work. What the Church teaches As with the Talents, the Catechism sees our gifts as given by God to be shared and put at the service of others. CCC 1936 For your life What have I done with the faith I received at baptism? Am I waiting for God to act while neglecting what He has already put in my hands? Read it in the Bible Luke 19:11–27 ↗

Use worldly goods wisely for eternity; no one can serve both God and money. Luke 16:1–13 The story A steward about to be fired reduces the debts of his master's debtors to win friends for later. His master praises his shrewdness, dishonest as the move is. Why Jesus told it Told to the disciples straight after the Prodigal Son, which ends with a son who squandered property. Luke notes that the Pharisees, “who were covetous”, heard all this and mocked Him. The key The rich man the owner of all things, God The steward each of us, managing goods that are not really ours Being dismissed death, when our stewardship ends Reducing the debts using what we have now to help others “Eternal dwellings” heaven, where friendships made through generosity endure What it means This is often called the hardest of all the parables. The master praises a man who is being fired for waste and then cheats him further. Jesus is not praising the dishonesty. He is praising the steward’s clear-eyed realism: knowing his time was short, he acted decisively to secure his future. Jesus’ point is a challenge: worldly people put enormous energy into their earthly future. Do we put as much into our eternal one? Money and possessions are not ours; we are stewards for a while. Used generously, especially for the poor, they become a way to love. Held on to, they become a master. Jesus ends: “You cannot serve God and money.” What the Church teaches The Catechism teaches the universal destination of goods: what we own is entrusted to us to bear fruit for ourselves and for others, especially those in need. CCC 2404 For your life If I knew my stewardship ended next year, what would I do differently with my money? Is money a servant in my life, or a master? Read it in the Bible Luke 16:1–13 ↗

God’s generosity goes beyond our idea of fair: grace is a gift, not a wage. Matthew 20:1–16 The story A landowner hires workers at different hours from morning to evening, and pays them all the same wage, one denarius. When those hired first complain, he reminds them they got what was agreed. Why Jesus told it Peter has just said, “Lo, we have left everything and followed you. What then shall we have?” Jesus promises a great reward, then adds, “many that are first will be last, and the last first,” and tells this story. The key The landowner God The vineyard the Kingdom, and the Church The workers those called into the Kingdom The hours of hiring different moments in history or in a life when people come to God The denarius eternal life, the same gift for all The grumbling first workers those who think their long service earns them more What it means A denarius was the normal day’s wage, just enough to feed a family. Workers not hired by evening would go home with nothing. The landowner keeps going back to the marketplace because he cannot bear to see anyone left idle and empty-handed. The early workers are not cheated; they got exactly what was agreed. What offends them is generosity to others. That is the real test: can we rejoice when God is generous to someone who “started late”, like the good thief on the cross? Eternal life is not a wage we earn by the hour. It is God Himself, and He gives Himself fully to everyone who comes. What the Church teaches The Catechism teaches that, with regard to God, there is no strict right to any merit on our part; any merit we have is itself a gift of His grace. CCC 2007 For your life Do I resent God’s generosity to someone else? Do I think of heaven as a wage I am earning or a gift I am receiving? Read it in the Bible Matthew 20:1–16 ↗

Real obedience shows in what we do, not in what we say. Matthew 21:28–32 The story A father asks his two sons to work in the vineyard. One says "I won't" but later goes; the other says "I will" but doesn't. Which one did his father's will? Why Jesus told it Jesus has just entered Jerusalem and cleansed the Temple. The chief priests and elders challenge His authority. This is the first of three parables He tells them in reply, followed by the Wicked Tenants and the Wedding Feast. The key The father God The first son, who says no but goes sinners such as tax collectors and prostitutes who repented at John the Baptist’s preaching The second son, who says yes but does not go religious leaders who professed obedience but rejected God’s messenger The vineyard the work of God’s Kingdom What it means Both sons are disappointing in a way; the perfect son, who says yes and goes, is missing from the story. Some see him in Jesus Himself. The point is sharp. The leaders said all the right words and kept the outward forms of religion, but when God sent John the Baptist, they did not believe. The tax collectors and prostitutes began with a loud “no” to God, but then repented. A past “no” can be changed into a “yes”; and a lifelong “yes” in words can hide a “no” in deeds. What counts is where we end up going. What the Church teaches The Catechism teaches that one enters the Kingdom not by saying words but by doing the will of the Father in heaven. CCC 2826 For your life Is there an area of my life where I say “yes, Lord” but do not go? Is there a “no” from my past that God is inviting me to turn into a “yes”? Read it in the Bible Matthew 21:28–32 ↗

God sent His own Son; rejecting Him is rejecting God’s final word of love. Matthew 21:33–46 · Mark 12:1–12 · Luke 20:9–19 The story The tenants of a vineyard beat and kill the servants the owner sends to collect his share. At last they kill his son as well, to seize the inheritance. Why Jesus told it Told to the chief priests and elders in the Temple in the last week of Jesus’ life. Matthew notes that they “perceived that he was speaking about them” and wanted to arrest Him, but feared the crowds. The key The householder God The vineyard Israel, God’s people, as in Isaiah 5 The tenants the leaders entrusted with God’s people The servants the prophets, often mistreated and killed The son Jesus Himself Killed outside the vineyard Jesus’ death outside the walls of Jerusalem What it means Jesus’ listeners knew Isaiah’s “song of the vineyard”, where Israel is God’s beloved vine. Absentee landlords were common in Galilee, and tenant revolts happened. The tenants’ reasoning is twisted: if the heir is dead, perhaps the land will become theirs. This is the parable where Jesus speaks most openly about who He is and what is about to happen. He is not one more servant; He is the beloved Son, the Father’s last and greatest gift. And He knows they will kill Him. Yet the rejected stone becomes the cornerstone: the crucifixion is not the end of the story but the foundation of the Church. The warning applies to every age: the vineyard is a trust, and its fruits belong to God. What the Church teaches The Catechism points to Jesus’ distinction between Himself as the Son and the servants God sent before Him as a sign of His unique divine sonship. CCC 443 For your life What “fruits” does God rightly expect from the vineyard entrusted to me? Have I ever pushed God’s messengers away because they disturbed me? Read it in the Bible Matthew 21:33–46 ↗ Mark 12:1–12 ↗ Luke 20:9–19 ↗

Everyone is invited to God’s feast; what matters is saying yes and coming dressed for it. Matthew 22:1–14 · Luke 14:15–24 The story A host prepares a great banquet, but his guests make excuses and don't come. He sends his servants into the streets to bring in the poor, the crippled and the blind, and the hall fills up. Why Jesus told it Matthew places it in the Temple during Jesus’ last week, the third parable answering the chief priests and elders. Luke sets a version at a dinner in a Pharisee’s house, after a guest exclaims, “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God!” The key The king God the Father The wedding feast for His son the Kingdom, the marriage of Christ and His Church, and the Eucharist The invited guests who refuse those who had every reason to come but were too busy The guests from the roads sinners, the poor and the Gentiles The wedding garment a life clothed in grace and conversion What it means The invited guests are not wicked; they have farms and businesses to see to. Their excuses are ordinary, which is what makes them dangerous. Ordinary busyness can crowd out God’s invitation as surely as open rebellion. The doors are thrown open to everyone, good and bad alike, and the hall fills. But Matthew adds a guest without a wedding garment. Hosts may have provided garments for their guests, so his refusal is a refusal of the host’s gift. The invitation is free, but it is an invitation to be changed. The Church has long seen the garment as the white robe of baptism and the life of grace. What the Church teaches The Catechism teaches that everyone is called to enter the Kingdom, that it belongs above all to the poor and lowly, and that Jesus invites sinners to His table while calling them to conversion. CCC 543, 545 For your life What ordinary busyness is my excuse for not coming to the feast? What does my “wedding garment” look like right now? Read it in the Bible Matthew 22:1–14 ↗ Luke 14:15–24 ↗

Ignoring the poor at our gate is a choice with eternal weight. Luke 16:19–31 The story A rich man feasts every day while poor Lazarus lies hungry at his gate. Both die; Lazarus goes to Abraham's side, the rich man to torment. He asks that Lazarus be sent to warn his brothers, but is told that those who won't listen to Moses and the prophets won't be convinced even by someone rising from the dead. Why Jesus told it Told in the same chapter as the Dishonest Steward, after the Pharisees, “who were covetous”, mocked Jesus’ teaching on money. It is the only parable in which a character has a name. The key The rich man those who live in comfort and do not see the poor Purple and fine linen luxury, the clothing of kings Lazarus (“God helps”) the poor and overlooked, known by name to God The gate the daily, ordinary place where the poor are found The great chasm the finality of the choices made in this life Moses and the prophets God’s word, already sufficient to call us to conversion What it means The rich man is never said to be cruel. He did not throw Lazarus out; he simply stepped over him every day. Even in torment he still treats Lazarus as a servant: “send Lazarus”. His sin is the blindness that comfort can produce. The parable also speaks to those who want a sign before they believe. Abraham says that someone rising from the dead would not convince those who will not listen to Scripture. Jesus Himself would rise, and many still did not believe. The warning is for now, while there is time: the poor are at our gate, and the word of God is in our hands. What the Church teaches The Catechism cites this parable on the particular judgment at death. It quotes St John Chrysostom: not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them; the goods we possess are not ours, but theirs. CCC 1021, 2446 For your life Who is the “Lazarus at my gate”, someone I see every day without seeing? Am I waiting for a sign before I take God’s word seriously? Read it in the Bible Luke 16:19–31 ↗

Christ is hidden in the least of His brothers and sisters; what we do to them, we do to Him. Matthew 25:31–46 The story When the Son of Man comes in glory, He will separate the nations as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. To those on His right He gives the Kingdom, because they fed the hungry, welcomed the stranger and visited the sick and imprisoned: "Whatever you did for one of the very least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me." Those who didn't are judged by the same words. Why Jesus told it The last of Jesus’ teachings before the Passion in Matthew. Right after it, He says, “after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of man will be delivered up to be crucified.” The key The Son of Man on His throne Christ, the judge of all at the end of time The sheep and the goats the righteous and the unrighteous The hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked, sick and imprisoned the poor and suffering, in whom Christ is present “You did it to me” Christ’s identification with every person in need The Kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world eternal life, God’s plan for us from the beginning What it means Palestinian shepherds often grazed sheep and goats together in the day and separated them at night, because goats need more warmth. To the eye of a stranger, they could look alike. What is striking is that both groups are surprised. The righteous did not know they were serving Christ; they were simply loving whoever was in front of them. The others did not refuse Christ knowingly; they just did not notice the needy. We are judged on love, practical and concrete. St Teresa of Calcutta summed up the Gospel on five fingers: “You did it to me.” What the Church teaches The Catechism teaches that we cannot be united with God if we fail to meet the serious needs of the poor and the little ones who are His brethren, and that the works of mercy are the concrete form of love. CCC 1033, 2447 For your life Where did I meet Christ in disguise this week? Which work of mercy could I take up concretely this month? Read it in the Bible Matthew 25:31–46 ↗

Jesus often taught with parables: short stories from everyday life with a lesson about God and about us (Matthew 13:10-17). Open any parable to read its background, what it means and what the Church teaches.
God’s Kingdom starts small, grows quietly and is worth everything you have.
God’s mercy has no limit, and He expects us to pass it on.
Two short stories about praying with trust, and not giving up.
Be ready: for Christ’s return, for life’s storms, and for the questions that really matter.
What we do with the gifts, time and money God trusts us with, and why His generosity doesn’t follow our idea of fair.
The invitation is open to everyone, and everyone will one day give an account.

Interactive Rosary, bead by bead: each prayer on screen in turn, with the mystery’s painting and the whole rosary lighting up the bead you’re on. Guided rosary, pray along, rosary beads, the Joyful, Luminous, Sorrowful and Glorious Mysteries.
We collect nothing unless you write to us

This site collects nothing about you unless you write to us. There are no analytics, no tracking, no cookies, no ads, no social media buttons and no accounts. The only outside service is Cloudflare Turnstile, a spam check on the Contact page.

Your browser keeps a few things (in its localStorage) so the site stays the way you left it: your settings: theme, text size, accessibility options, keyboard shortcuts and the sidebar your Bible reading tools: text size, font, spacing, page width, background and which extras are shown the pages you opened, so search can list them as recently viewed your progress: chapters read, where you stopped in each book, highlights, bookmarks and notes, the part of the Catechism you last read and your place in today’s Rosary Bible books you opened, so you can read them offline, and the whole Bible if you save it for offline reading None of this is sent to us. We can’t see it. Clear your browser’s data for this site and it’s gone.
You can save your progress and settings to a file and load it again later. Your browser makes the file and it stays on your device. Nothing is stored on our server.
Search runs in your browser. What you type is not sent anywhere.

“Listen” uses the voices built into your browser and device. Some browsers also offer online voices, such as Microsoft’s in Edge or Google’s in Chrome. If you pick one, your browser sends the Bible text being read to that company to turn it into speech. It sends nothing about you. If you’d rather it didn’t, choose a voice that works offline. “Keep the screen on” only stops your screen from dimming while a chapter is open. Sharing a verse uses your device’s own share menu.
Some links go to other sites, such as BibleGateway, Vatican News or vatican.va. Nothing loads from them until you click, and once you’re there, their privacy policies apply.

Cloudflare hosts the site. Like any web host, it may keep standard server logs for security and performance. We don’t have access to them. See Cloudflare’s Privacy Policy. All fonts come from this site, not from Google Fonts or any other service.

When you send a message from the Contact page, your name (if you give one), your email address and your message reach us by email through Cloudflare. We keep them only in our inbox, and we use them only to reply to you. We don’t share them, add you to a mailing list or market to you. Turnstile checks that you’re not a bot. It runs only on the Contact page and doesn’t track you for advertising. See Cloudflare’s Turnstile privacy statement.

Q1 · What is the plan of God for man?

God, infinitely perfect and blessed in himself, in a plan of sheer goodness freely created man to make him share in his own blessed life. In the fullness of time, God the Father sent his Son as the Redeemer and Savior of mankind, fallen into sin, thus calling all into his Church and, through the work of the Holy Spirit, making them adopted children and heirs of his eternal happiness.
Q2 · Why does man have a desire for God?

God himself, in creating man in his own image, has written upon his heart the desire to see him. Even if this desire is often ignored, God never ceases to draw man to himself because only in God will he find and live the fullness of truth and happiness for which he never stops searching. By nature and by vocation, therefore, man is a religious being, capable of entering into communion with God. This intimate and vital bond with God confers on man his fundamental dignity.
Q3 · How is it possible to know God with only the light of human reason?

Starting from creation, that is from the world and from the human person, through reason alone one can know God with certainty as the origin and end of the universe, as the highest good and as infinite truth and beauty.
Q4 · Is the light of reason alone sufficient to know the mystery of God?

In coming to a knowledge of God by the light of reason alone man experiences many difficulties. Indeed, on his own he is unable to enter into the intimacy of the divine mystery. This is why he stands in need of being enlightened by God’s revelation, not only about those things that exceed his understanding, but also about those religious and moral truths which of themselves are not beyond the grasp of human reason, so that even in the present condition of the human race, they can be known by all with ease, with firm certainty and with no admixture of error.
Q5 · How can we speak about God?

By taking as our starting point the perfections of man and of the other creatures which are a reflection, albeit a limited one, of the infinite perfection of God, we are able to speak about God with all people. We must, however, continually purify our language insofar as it is image-bound and imperfect, realizing that we can never fully express the infinite mystery of God.
Q6 · What does God reveal to man?

God in his goodness and wisdom reveals himself. With deeds and words, he reveals himself and his plan of loving goodness which he decreed from all eternity in Christ. According to this plan, all people by the grace of the Holy Spirit are to share in the divine life as adopted “sons” in the only begotten Son of God.
Q7 · What are the first stages of God’s Revelation?

From the very beginning, God manifested himself to our first parents, Adam and Eve, and invited them to intimate communion with himself. After their fall, he did not cease his revelation to them but promised salvation for all their descendants. After the flood, he made a covenant with Noah, a covenant between himself and all living beings.
Q8 · What are the next stages of God’s Revelation?

God chose Abram, calling him out of his country, making him “the father of a multitude of nations” (Genesis 17:5), and promising to bless in him “all the nations of the earth” (Genesis 12:3). The people descended from Abraham would be the trustee of the divine promise made to the patriarchs. God formed Israel as his chosen people, freeing them from slavery in Egypt, establishing with them the covenant of Mount Sinai, and, through Moses, giving them his law. The prophets proclaimed a radical redemption of the people and a salvation which would include all nations in a new and everlasting covenant. From the people of Israel and from the house of King David, would be born the Messiah, Jesus.
Q9 · What is the full and definitive stage of God’s Revelation?

The full and definitive stage of God’s revelation is accomplished in his Word made flesh, Jesus Christ, the mediator and fullness of Revelation. He, being the only-begotten Son of God made man, is the perfect and definitive Word of the Father. In the sending of the Son and the gift of the Spirit, Revelation is now fully complete, although the faith of the Church must gradually grasp its full significance over the course of centuries.
Q10 · What is the value of private revelations?

While not belonging to the deposit of faith, private revelations may help a person to live the faith as long as they lead us to Christ. The Magisterium of the Church, which has the duty of evaluating such private revelations, cannot accept those which claim to surpass or correct that definitive Revelation which is Christ.
Q11 · Why and in what way is divine revelation transmitted?

God “desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4), that is, of Jesus Christ. For this reason, Christ must be proclaimed to all according to his own command, “Go forth and teach all nations” (Matthew 28:19). And this is brought about by Apostolic Tradition.

Apostolic Tradition is the transmission of the message of Christ, brought about from the very beginnings of Christianity by means of preaching, bearing witness, institutions, worship, and inspired writings. The apostles transmitted all they received from Christ and learned from the Holy Spirit to their successors, the bishops, and through them to all generations until the end of the world.
Q13 · In what ways does Apostolic Tradition occur?

Apostolic Tradition occurs in two ways: through the living transmission of the word of God (also simply called Tradition) and through Sacred Scripture which is the same proclamation of salvation in written form.
Q14 · What is the relationship between Tradition and Sacred Scripture?

Tradition and Sacred Scripture are bound closely together and communicate one with the other. Each of them makes present and fruitful in the Church the mystery of Christ. They flow out of the same divine well-spring and together make up one sacred deposit of faith from which the Church derives her certainty about revelation.
Q15 · To whom is the deposit of faith entrusted?

The Apostles entrusted the deposit of faith to the whole of the Church. Thanks to its supernatural sense of faith the people of God as a whole, assisted by the Holy Spirit and guided by the Magisterium of the Church, never ceases to welcome, to penetrate more deeply and to live more fully from the gift of divine revelation.
Q16 · To whom is given the task of authentically interpreting the deposit of faith?

The task of giving an authentic interpretation of the deposit of faith has been entrusted to the living teaching office of the Church alone, that is, to the successor of Peter, the Bishop of Rome, and to the bishops in communion with him. To this Magisterium, which in the service of the Word of God enjoys the certain charism of truth, belongs also the task of defining dogmas which are formulations of the truths contained in divine Revelation. This authority of the Magisterium also extends to those truths necessarily connected with Revelation.
Q17 · What is the relationship between Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium?

Scripture, Tradition, and the Magisterium are so closely united with each other that one of them cannot stand without the others. Working together, each in its own way, under the action of the one Holy Spirit, they all contribute effectively to the salvation of souls.
Q18 · Why does Sacred Scripture teach the truth?

Because God himself is the author of Sacred Scripture. For this reason it is said to be inspired and to teach without error those truths which are necessary for our salvation. The Holy Spirit inspired the human authors who wrote what he wanted to teach us. The Christian faith, however, is not a “religion of the Book”, but of the Word of God – “not a written and mute word, but incarnate and living” (Saint Bernard of Clairvaux).
Q19 · How is Sacred Scripture to be read?

Sacred Scripture must be read and interpreted with the help of the Holy Spirit and under the guidance of the Magisterium of the Church according to three criteria: 1) it must be read with attention to the content and unity of the whole of Scripture; 2) it must be read within the living Tradition of the Church; 3) it must be read with attention to the analogy of faith, that is, the inner harmony which exists among the truths of the faith themselves.
Q20 · What is the Canon of Scripture?

The Canon of Scripture is the complete list of the sacred writings which the Church has come to recognize through Apostolic Tradition. The Canon consists of 46 books of the Old Testament and 27 of the New.
Q21 · What is the importance of the Old Testament for Christians?

Christians venerate the Old Testament as the true word of God. All of the books of the Old Testament are divinely inspired and retain a permanent value. They bear witness to the divine pedagogy of God’s saving love. They are written, above all, to prepare for the coming of Christ the Savior of the universe.
Q22 · What importance does the New Testament have for Christians?

The New Testament, whose central object is Jesus Christ, conveys to us the ultimate truth of divine Revelation. Within the New Testament the four Gospels of Mathew, Mark, Luke and John are the heart of all the Scriptures because they are the principle witness to the life and teaching of Jesus. As such, they hold a unique place in the Church.
Q23 · What is the unity that exists between the Old and the New Testaments?

Scripture is one insofar as the Word of God is one. God’s plan of salvation is one, and the divine inspiration of both Testaments is one. The Old Testament prepares for the New and the New Testament fulfills the Old; the two shed light on each other.
Q24 · What role does Sacred Scripture play in the life of the Church?

Sacred Scripture gives support and vigor to the life of the Church. For the children of the Church, it is a confirmation of the faith, food for the soul and the fount of the spiritual life. Sacred Scripture is the soul of theology and of pastoral preaching. The Psalmist says that it is “a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). The Church, therefore, exhorts all to read Sacred Scripture frequently because “ignorance of the Scripture s is ignorance of Christ” (Saint Jerome).
Q25 · How does man respond to God who reveals himself?

Sustained by divine grace, we respond to God with the obedience of faith, which means the full surrender of ourselves to God and the acceptance of his truth insofar as it is guaranteed by the One who is Truth itself.
Q26 · Who are the principal witnesses of the obedience of faith in the Sacred Scriptures?

There are many such witnesses, two in particular: One is Abraham who when put to the test “believed in God” (Romans 4:3) and always obeyed his call. For this reason he is called “the Father of all who believe” (Romans 4:11-18). The other is the Virgin Mary who, throughout her entire life, embodied in a perfect way the obedience of faith: “Let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38).
Q27 · What does it mean in practice for a person to believe in God?

It means to adhere to God himself, entrusting oneself to him and giving assent to all the truths which God has revealed because God is Truth. It means to believe in one God in three Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Q28 · What are the characteristics of faith?

Faith is the supernatural virtue which is necessary for salvation. It is a free gift of God and is accessible to all who humbly seek it. The act of faith is a human act, that is, an act of the intellect of a person - prompted by the will moved by God - who freely assents to divine truth. Faith is also certain because it is founded on the Word of God; it works “through charity” (Galatians 5:6); and it continually grows through listening to the Word of God and through prayer. It is, even now, a foretaste of the joys of heaven.
Q29 · Why is there no contradiction between faith and science?
Though faith is above reason, there can never be a contradiction between faith and science because both originate in God. It is God himself who gives to us the light both of reason and of faith.
Q30 · Why is faith a personal act, and at the same time ecclesial?

Faith is a personal act insofar as it is the free response of the human person to God who reveals himself. But at the same time it is an ecclesial act which expresses itself in the proclamation, “We believe”. It is in fact the Church that believes: and thus by the grace of the Holy Spirit precedes, engenders and nourishes the faith of each Christian For this reason the Church is Mother and Teacher.
Q31 · Why are the formulas of faith important?
The formulas of faith are important because they permit one to express, assimilate, celebrate, and share together with others the truths of the faith through a common language.
Q32 · In what way is the faith of the Church one faith alone?

The Church, although made up of persons who have diverse languages, cultures, and rites, nonetheless professes with a united voice the one faith that was received from the one Lord and that was passed on by the one Apostolic Tradition. She confesses one God alone, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and points to one way of salvation. Therefore we believe with one heart and one soul all that is contained in the Word of God, handed down or written, and which is proposed by the Church as divinely revealed.
Q33 · What are the symbols of faith?
