Mystic and Reformer, Doctor of the Church · 1515-1582 Teresa was born in Ávila, in Spain, to a noble family with Jewish roots. As a girl she was outgoing and loved the pleasures of the world, and by her own account she spent a long time torn "between serving God and serving the world." At twenty, without her father’s permission, she entered a Carmelite convent. But convents in those days were busy places, with visitors coming and going, and discipline had become very relaxed.

In her late thirties Teresa went through a deep conversion, and her experiences of union with God in prayer grew more and more intense. She described them in The Interior Castle, where she pictures the soul as a castle with seven sets of rooms. The soul moves step by step from the noise outside toward the center, where God lives in silence. In another book, her Life, she tells her own story and how she learned to pray. Her famous vision of an angel piercing her heart with a golden spear, known as the "transverberation," was later captured by Bernini in one of his best-known sculptures.

Seeing how lax the convents had become, Teresa set out to take her order back to its first spirit of strict poverty and prayer. With a young friar, Saint John of the Cross, she started the reform of the "Discalced" (barefoot) Carmelites. She founded seventeen small, simple convents, crossing the length of Spain by mule to do it. Opponents of the reform put obstacles in her way at every turn, and John of the Cross was even imprisoned for a time, but Teresa never gave up. She was known for her wit and common sense. Once, after falling off her mule into the mud in the rain, she is said to have told God, "If this is how you treat your friends, no wonder you have so few." Teresa died in 1582, while on the road. In 1970 Pope Paul VI made her the first woman Doctor of the Church; Catherine of Siena followed a week later. Her feast day is October 15.

Teacher of the Little Way, Doctor of the Church · 1873-1897 Thérèse Martin was the youngest child of a devout French family. She lost her mother when she was four. She was a sensitive child who cried easily, but at fourteen, one Christmas night, she went through what she called "a complete conversion," and from then on she grew calm and strong. At fifteen, far younger than the usual age for entering, she asked Pope Leo XIII in person to let her join the Carmelites. The Pope told her, "If God wills it, you will enter," and soon afterwards she was given special permission.

Thérèse isn’t remembered for great miracles or dramatic events, but for what she called her "Little Way." Holiness, she believed, doesn’t require heroics. It is enough to do the most ordinary things, like putting up patiently with a difficult sister or getting through a boring job, with great love. She saw herself as a small child throwing herself into God’s arms, and wrote, "I am a very little bird, who only has strength enough to fly to the sun, to Love."
A Book Written in a Convent Cell

Her superiors asked her to write the story of her life. The Story of a Soul, published after her death, soon became known all over the world for its simple, honest and deeply moving voice. Thérèse caught tuberculosis at twenty-three. In her last year and a half she struggled with terrible pain and with deep darkness in her faith, yet she never lost hope. Before she died she said, "I will spend my heaven doing good on earth." She died in 1897, at twenty-four. She was canonized in 1925, only twenty-eight years after her death, one of the fastest canonizations in the Church’s history. In 1997 Pope John Paul II declared her a Doctor of the Church, the youngest of them all. Her feast day is October 1.

The Angelic Doctor · 1225-1274 Thomas was born into a noble Italian family that hoped he would one day become abbot of a famous Benedictine monastery. Instead, the young Thomas wanted to join the Dominicans, a new order of friars who owned nothing and begged for their food in the streets. His family was furious. His brothers kidnapped him and locked him up in a castle, and the story goes that they even sent a woman to his room to tempt him out of his vocation. Thomas chased her out with a burning stick from the fire and marked a cross on the door with it. After a year his family gave up.

He studied in Paris and Cologne under Albert the Great, the leading teacher of the day. Because he was big and quiet, his classmates called him "the dumb ox." Albert is said to have answered them: "We call him the dumb ox, but he will yet bellow so loud his teaching will resound throughout the world." Thomas set out to bring together the philosophy of Aristotle, which Europe was only then rediscovering, and Christian revelation in a single, coherent system. It was one of the boldest projects of his time, because many people saw Aristotle as a threat to the faith.

His greatest work, the Summa Theologiae, covers the whole of Christian teaching, from the existence of God to morality and the sacraments, as a series of questions answered by careful argument. It became the backbone of Catholic theology for centuries. But in 1273, a few months before he died, something happened to him during Mass, and he never wrote again. He told his secretary that compared with what he had seen, everything he had written seemed "like straw." He fell ill on his way to a council the Pope had called him to, and died at a monastery in 1274. He was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1567 and is the patron of Catholic schools and of students of philosophy and theology. His feast day is January 28.

Objective Truth Whoever says “there is no absolute truth” is stating an absolute truth. Tastes differ from person to person; facts don’t. “There is no absolute truth” presents itself as an absolute truth, so it refutes itself. No one is content with a bridge being sound “for me”; we want it to be really sound. No one seriously argues that torturing children could be “right for some cultures”. The question of God is the same: not a matter of taste, but a real question with a real answer. Objection But different societies have held different moral codes. Most of those differences come from disagreeing about facts. Nearly every culture praises courage and justice and despises betrayal. And when we call the end of slavery “progress”, we are measuring it against a real standard of good.
Couldn't the universe just exist on its own?

The Beginning of the Universe The first person to propose the Big Bang was a Catholic priest. Science says the universe had a beginning. Everything that begins has a cause. The first person to propose that the universe began at a single moment was a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist, Georges Lemaître (1931). Today we call it the Big Bang. If time, space and matter began there, their cause must lie outside them: timeless, immaterial and immensely powerful. “Nothing” produces nothing. Even the quantum vacuum is something, with laws of its own. A timeless, immaterial, powerful first cause: that is what people have always meant by God. Objection Then who created God? The argument is that everything that begins to exist has a cause. The universe began; God never began, because He is outside time. An endless chain of causes explains nothing. At some point you reach a being that needs nothing else to exist.
Couldn't life be just a lucky accident?

Fine-Tuning If the universe’s settings were slightly different, there would be no stars, and no us. The basic constants of the universe seem tuned with astonishing precision to allow life. If the strong nuclear force were a few percent different, stars could not burn and the carbon life needs could not form. If the cosmological constant were a little larger, no galaxy could have formed. Even the atheist astronomer Fred Hoyle wrote: “A common sense interpretation of the facts suggests that a superintellect has monkeyed with physics.” Objection Maybe there are countless universes and we’re in a lucky one. No one has ever observed another universe; the multiverse can’t be tested. Believing in infinitely many invisible universes takes more faith than believing in one Creator. And whatever churns out universes would need fine-tuning too, so the problem just moves back a step.
If a good God exists, why is there so much suffering?

The Problem of Evil Our anger at evil shows that goodness is real. This is the hardest question. Christianity does not explain every case of suffering, but it points to Christ, who suffered and died Himself. God gave us real freedom, because love can’t be forced. Most evil is that freedom misused. Without God even the word “evil” loses its meaning: our outrage at evil assumes a real good. The Christian God doesn’t watch suffering from afar: in Christ He went through betrayal, torture and death, and defeated death by rising. Objection An all-powerful God would remove suffering at once. Only by taking away free will, and with it love and forgiveness. The Christian hope is that suffering will end: “He will wipe every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more” (Revelation 21:4).

The Heart's Longing Thirst shows that water exists. No success, no amount of money, no relationship ever fully satisfies us. That is a clue that we were made for something more. Hunger means there is food; thirst means there is water. Our deepest desires point to something real. C. S. Lewis: “If I find in myself a desire which no experience in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that I was made for another world.” Augustine: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Objection That’s just a need for comfort; that’s why people invent religion. Being thirsty doesn’t prove water is imaginary. And Christianity is a strange choice if all you want is comfort: it tells you to love your enemies and give your life away for others.
Did Jesus really live, or is He a legend?

The Historical Jesus Even historians who aren’t believers don’t doubt that Jesus lived. That Jesus lived and was crucified under Pilate is accepted by almost every historian. The Roman historian Tacitus (around AD 116) writes that Christians took their name from Christus, executed by Pontius Pilate; the Jewish historian Josephus also mentions “Jesus, who was called the Christ”. Even the agnostic New Testament scholar Bart Ehrman treats Jesus’ existence as beyond serious dispute. More than 5,800 Greek manuscripts of the New Testament survive; no other ancient work is so well preserved. Objection The Gospels were written long after Jesus, by believers. They were written within a few decades, while eyewitnesses were still alive. The earliest full lives of Alexander the Great come three hundred years after his death. And the Gospels keep details no one would invent: Peter’s denial, and women, whose testimony counted for little then, as the first witnesses of the empty tomb.
Couldn't Jesus just have been a good teacher?

Who Jesus Claimed to Be Jesus was either mad, a liar, or truly God. What Jesus said about Himself rules that option out. He forgave sins, and those present were outraged because they knew only God has that authority (Mark 2:5-7). He said “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30) and called Himself by the name God revealed to Moses, “I am” (John 8:58). A man who talks like that is a lunatic, a liar, or exactly who he says he is. His teaching and His life don’t fit the first two. Objection Maybe later generations put these words in His mouth. Less than thirty years after His death, Paul is already writing about Jesus as the Lord worshipped as God (Philippians 2:6-11). Legends take generations. Here a man is worshipped while the eyewitnesses are still alive, by people fiercely devoted to the one God.
How can anyone believe a man rose from the dead?

The Resurrection Frightened disciples in hiding would not die for something they knew was a lie. Christianity rests on a testable historical claim: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Even most skeptical historians accept that Jesus died on the cross and was buried, that His tomb was found empty, and that His disciples sincerely believed they had seen Him risen. The creed in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 goes back to within a few years of the event and names more than five hundred witnesses. Within weeks, the same disciples who had been hiding in fear were preaching the resurrection openly, in the city where He was killed. James the skeptic and Paul the persecutor joined them. Objection Maybe they hallucinated, or stole the body. Five hundred people don’t share one hallucination, and hallucinations don’t empty tombs. If they had stolen the body, they died for what they knew was a lie. And their enemies could have ended the whole thing by producing the body. They never did.
Isn't believing in Jesus enough? Why a Church?

One Church and Peter Jesus left behind not a book, but a Church. Jesus entrusted His teaching not to scattered individuals but to a visible community with authority. He told Peter, “On this rock I will build my church,” and gave him the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 16:18-19). Without a shared authority, everyone reads the Bible their own way, and the thousands of separate denominations today are the result. Christ prayed that His disciples would “be one” (John 17:21). None of this means looking down on other Christians: by baptism they are our brothers and sisters in Christ, and we have plenty to learn from their faith (CCC 818). Today’s pope is the latest link in a chain of more than 260 that began with Peter and has held for two thousand years. Objection The Church later turned Jesus’ simple message into an institution. It was the other way round. The Church came before the New Testament: Jesus wrote no book, but He chose twelve apostles and gave them authority. Around AD 107, Ignatius of Antioch was already calling it “the Catholic Church”.
Why isn't the Bible alone enough?

Scripture and Tradition The Church decided the Bible’s table of contents. The Church decided which books belong in the Bible. The Book was born inside the Church, not the other way round. The 27-book New Testament list was settled at the councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397). The Bible itself tells us to keep the teaching handed on by word of mouth: “Hold to the traditions which you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by letter” (2 Thessalonians 2:15). Scripture, Tradition and the Church’s teaching office form one whole, coming from one source, Christ. Nowhere does the Bible say “Scripture alone.” Instead it speaks of teaching handed on by word of mouth and entrusted to faithful men (2 Timothy 2:2), and John says that not everything Jesus did was written down (John 21:25). Objection So the Church puts itself above the Bible. The Church is Scripture’s servant, not its master. It guards and explains the Bible but can’t change a word of it. Think of a museum that can tell an original painting from a forgery: it didn’t paint the picture, but it knows it, and it protects it.
Can water, bread and oil really have a spiritual effect?

The Sacraments Jesus said “This is my body,” not “This is a symbol.” God made us body and soul, so He gives His grace through signs we can see and touch. Jesus touched people when He healed, used mud and water, and told His disciples to baptize, to offer the bread “in remembrance of me” and to forgive sins: “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven” (John 20:22-23). The seven sacraments accompany every important moment of life, from birth to death. The first Christians didn’t treat the Eucharist as a symbol: Ignatius of Antioch criticized those who denied it was “the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ”. Jesus said, “My flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed” (John 6:55). Many of His disciples could not accept this and left Him, yet He did not call them back to say He only meant a symbol (John 6:66). At the Last Supper He took the bread and said, “This is my body” (Mark 14:22). Objection Isn’t this a kind of magic? Magic tries to bend supernatural power to your will. In the sacraments nobody controls God; God keeps His own promise. Their power doesn’t depend on how holy the priest is, but on Christ’s word.
How can the Church be holy with so many scandals?

Scandals in the Church Even one of the apostles was a traitor; the Church still stands. The Church is holy because Christ is, not because its members are. Its members are sinners, and it exists to heal them. Abuse and cover-ups are real, grave and shameful. The Church has to confess them and do justice to the victims. One of the Twelve betrayed Jesus and Peter denied Him three times; Christ knew His Church would be made of flawed people. A bad doctor doesn’t disprove medicine. The same Church also formed Teresa of Calcutta, Maximilian Kolbe and millions of holy people. Objection It has survived two thousand years only because it is well organized. No merely human institution has lasted twenty centuries with the same teaching through so many failed leaders, schisms and persecutions. Jesus promised: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18).
Has religion really done humanity any good?

Known by Its Fruit The first hospitals and universities grew out of the Church. Hospitals, universities and the idea of human rights all have roots in the Church. In the fourth century St. Basil of Caesarea founded a large complex for the sick and the poor; many historians count it among the first hospitals. The first great universities (Paris, Oxford, Bologna) grew up under the Church; Mendel, the father of genetics, was a friar, and Lemaître a priest. The idea that every person is made in God’s image and has equal dignity is one of the roots of human rights. Objection But there were the Crusades and the Inquisition. The Church has admitted those sins openly; St. John Paul II asked forgiveness for them in public in 2000. And the standard we judge them by is Christ’s own command to love even our enemies.
Do you get to heaven by being a good person?

Grace and Good Works Salvation can’t be bought, but real faith doesn’t sit idle. No. Salvation isn’t a prize we earn; it is God’s gift. But real faith always shows up in what we do. None of us can reach God’s perfect goodness on our own, so God made the first move. Christianity is the story of God setting out to find us, like the shepherd looking for his lost sheep (Luke 15:4-7). “Faith without works is dead” (James 2:26): good works don’t buy salvation; they answer a love already received. Salvation is not a single moment; it lasts a whole life: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2:12). That is why there is Confession after Baptism. Whoever falls along the way can repent and get up again. Objection So a bad person can repent at the last minute and be saved? Is that fair? Yes. Jesus told the criminal on the cross, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Grace goes beyond fairness, because none of us deserves it. But repentance means a real change of heart, and no one is promised tomorrow.
Do Catholics worship Mary and the saints?

Mary and the Saints If you can ask a friend to pray for you, you can ask one in heaven. No. Worship belongs to God alone. We ask the saints to pray for us, the way you would ask a friend. “The prayer of a righteous man has great power” (James 5:16), and death doesn’t separate people who are one in Christ. Mary is honored as Jesus’ mother and first disciple; she always points to her Son: “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5). The saints prove that the Christian life can actually be lived. Many of them, like Augustine, were great sinners first. Mary said, “Henceforth all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1:48). God tells us to honor our father and mother (Exodus 20:12). Surely He wants His own Son’s mother honored. Objection Why not pray to God directly? We do. The heart of Catholic prayer is the Mass, offered to the Father through Christ. Asking a friend to pray for you doesn’t mean you trust God less, and neither does asking a friend in heaven.
Why are the Church's rules so strict?

Moral Truths The Church’s moral teaching aims at freedom, not control. The Church’s moral teaching isn’t a list of random bans. It is a whole picture of what a human being is, and its goal is freedom. Every human life, from the unborn child to the very old, is sacred. A person’s worth doesn’t depend on how useful they are. Your body isn’t something you own; it is you. That is why sex finds its full meaning in a lifelong promise: marriage. A train isn’t less free because it runs on rails; the rails get it where it’s going. Morality works the same way: it leads to real happiness. The Church doesn’t change its teaching with the times. Until 1930 all the major Christian churches held contraception to be morally wrong. That year the Anglican Church allowed some exceptions, and in time most Protestant churches followed. The Catholic Church kept its teaching. Objection As long as I don’t hurt anyone, what I do is nobody’s business. The Church doesn’t force anyone; it invites. But we can harm ourselves, and what we do touches others in ways we don’t see. And no one who struggles is shut out: Confession exists so we can start again after every fall.
How could a loving God send anyone to hell?

Heaven, Hell and Purgatory The doors of hell are locked from the inside. God forces no one into heaven or hell. Eternity is the answer we freely give in this life, made permanent. Heaven is eternal union with God, the source of all goodness and love. Hell is what happens when someone freely and stubbornly chooses to stay away from God. As C. S. Lewis put it, its doors are locked from the inside. Purgatory is where those who die in God’s friendship, but not yet fully purified, are made ready for heaven. It is a final purification before heaven (2 Maccabees 12:45). Objection Isn’t eternal punishment out of proportion to the sins of a finite life? Hell isn’t revenge. It is a will that rejects God to the very end, and stays that way. God keeps the door open until the last moment and wants no one to be lost (1 Timothy 2:4).
We’re Catholic because we believe it’s true. The case has three steps: there is a God, He showed Himself in Jesus, and Jesus founded the Catholic Church. Start wherever you are.

A universe that had a beginning, laws tuned for life, a conscience that knows right from wrong, a heart that always wants more: a Creator explains all of it better than chance does. If you are an atheist or an agnostic: Answering Atheism Part 2 of 3

If there is a Creator, He may have spoken. Christianity rests on an event that can be checked like any other piece of history: the resurrection of Jesus. If you come from a Muslim background: Answering Islam Part 3 of 3

If Jesus rose, what He said matters. And He didn’t leave a book behind: He left a Church, built on the apostles, that is still here. Four reasons it is the Catholic Church come first, then the hard questions.

In Short The main points of this page. “There is no truth” is itself a claim to truth. Truth is real, so the question of God has a real answer. The universe had a beginning. Whatever begins has a cause, and whatever caused time, space and matter can’t be made of them. Change gravity or the nuclear forces by a few percent and there are no stars and no people. Luck is a weak explanation. You can only call something evil if real good exists. Your anger at injustice points to God, not away from Him. We get hungry because food exists and thirsty because water exists. We also want something no job, money or person can give. Tacitus, a Roman historian with no love for Christians, records that Jesus was executed under Pilate. Jesus forgave sins and said “I and the Father are one.” A good teacher who was only a man doesn’t talk like that. After the crucifixion the apostles hid in fear. Weeks later they were preaching in the same city, and most died for it. People don’t die for a story they made up. Jesus wrote no book. He chose twelve men, put Peter in charge, and promised His Church would last. It has, for 2,000 years. The Church decided which books go in the New Testament, in the 390s. Without the Church there is no Bible. Jesus said “This is my body.” Many followers left over it, and He let them go instead of saying it was only a symbol. Catholics don’t worship Mary or the saints. We ask them to pray for us, the way you’d ask a friend. Judas was one of the Twelve. Sinners in the Church are nothing new, and its teaching has outlasted every one of them. Heaven isn’t earned. It’s a gift, and Confession lets you start again every time you fall. Each step leads to the next: God, then Jesus, then His Church. That is why we’re Catholic.

Where to go from here None of this is a mathematical proof on its own. Reason can bring you close to faith, but the last step is yours to take. If you have questions, you’re not alone: walk into any Catholic church, or write to us. Verbum Domini, Latin for “the Word of the Lord”, is a free guide to the Catholic faith in plain English. It is for the curious, for anyone on the way into the Church, and for Catholics who want to know their faith better. Everything here comes from Scripture, the Catechism and the Church’s own documents, and every page names its sources.

Divine Mercy Caravaggio · The Seven Works of Mercy God’s mercy is not a new idea. It runs through the whole Bible, from the Psalms (“his mercy endures for ever”, Psalm 136:1 ) to the father who runs to meet his prodigal son ( Luke 15:11-32 ). In the 1930s Jesus asked a young Polish nun, Saint Faustina Kowalska, to remind the world of it in a simple way: an image, a short prayer on rosary beads, an hour of the day and a feast. Saint John Paul II gave the feast to the whole Church in the year 2000. The heart of it all fits in five words: Jesus, I trust in you. Pray it today. The Chaplet of Divine Mercy takes about seven minutes on ordinary rosary beads. Many people pray it at three in the afternoon, the hour Jesus died. Pray the Chaplet Every prayer, bead by bead, and the words at a glance. Divine Mercy Sunday The feast after Easter, the novena and the indulgence.

About seven minutes The Chaplet of Divine Mercy Giotto · The Crucifixion Jesus taught this prayer to Saint Faustina in Vilnius in September 1935. You pray it on the beads of an ordinary rosary, offering the Father the sacrifice of His Son on the cross and asking mercy for yourself and for the whole world. 1 Begin Make the Sign of the Cross. You may begin with this prayer, which Saint Faustina wrote in her Diary: “You expired, Jesus, but the source of life gushed forth for souls, and the ocean of mercy opened up for the whole world. O Fount of Life, unfathomable Divine Mercy, envelop the whole world and empty yourself out upon us.” Then, three times: “O Blood and Water, which gushed forth from the Heart of Jesus as a fount of mercy for us, I trust in you!” 2 Our Father, Hail Mary, Creed On the first beads of the rosary, pray one Our Father, one Hail Mary and the Apostles’ Creed. The words are in Common Prayers . 3 On each large bead Before each decade, offer the whole Christ to the Father: “Eternal Father, I offer you the Body and Blood, Soul and Divinity of your dearly beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, in atonement for our sins and those of the whole world.” 4 On the ten small beads On each of the ten beads of the decade: “For the sake of his sorrowful Passion, have mercy on us and on the whole world.” Then: go on to the next large bead and repeat steps 3 and 4, five decades in all. 5 Conclude After the fifth decade, pray three times: “Holy God, Holy Mighty One, Holy Immortal One, have mercy on us and on the whole world.” You may add Saint Faustina’s closing prayer: “Eternal God, in whom mercy is endless and the treasury of compassion inexhaustible, look kindly upon us and increase your mercy in us, that in difficult moments we might not despair nor become despondent, but with great confidence submit ourselves to your holy will, which is Love and Mercy itself.” End with the Sign of the Cross. The words at a glance Start Sign of the Cross; Our Father, Hail Mary, Apostles’ Creed Large bead Eternal Father, I offer you the Body and Blood, Soul and Divinity of your dearly beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, in atonement for our sins and those of the whole world. Small beads (×10) For the sake of his sorrowful Passion, have mercy on us and on the whole world. End (×3) Holy God, Holy Mighty One, Holy Immortal One, have mercy on us and on the whole world. Alone or together. In a group, one person says the first half of each prayer and everyone answers with the second half, from “in atonement” and “have mercy” on. It is often sung, too.

Płock, 22 February 1931 The image One evening in her convent cell, Saint Faustina saw Jesus dressed in white, His right hand raised in blessing and His left hand touching His garment at the breast. From there two great rays shone out, one pale and one red. He asked her to have the image painted, with the words “Jesus, I trust in you” beneath it. The pale ray stands for the Water that makes souls righteous: baptism and the forgiveness of sins. The red ray stands for the Blood that is the life of souls: the Eucharist. Both flowed from the side of Jesus when the soldier’s lance opened His heart on the cross: “and at once there came out blood and water” ( John 19:34 ). The Fathers of the Church saw in them the two great sacraments that give birth to the Church. Jesus, I trust in you. The first painting was made in Vilnius in 1934 by Eugeniusz Kazimirowski, under the eye of Saint Faustina and her confessor, Blessed Michał Sopoćko. The best-known version, by Adolf Hyła, hangs in the Shrine of Divine Mercy at Łagiewniki in Kraków. Catholics do not worship the image. Like any holy picture, it points beyond itself to the one it shows (CCC 2132), and its message is in the words at its foot.

Every day The Hour of Mercy Jesus died at about three in the afternoon ( Mark 15:33-37 ). He asked Saint Faustina to remember that hour every day and to ask for mercy then, above all for sinners. It does not have to be long. If you can, pray the Chaplet or make the Stations of the Cross, or stop by a church and spend a few minutes before the Blessed Sacrament. If you are at work or on the road, a moment is enough: stop, think of Jesus on the cross, and say “Jesus, I trust in you.”

The Second Sunday of Easter Divine Mercy Sunday Jesus asked Saint Faustina for a feast of mercy on the Sunday after Easter. On 30 April 2000, the day he canonized her, Saint John Paul II gave that Sunday the name Divine Mercy Sunday for the whole Church. The day fits. Its Gospel is the evening of the Resurrection, when the risen Jesus breathes the Holy Spirit on the apostles and gives them the power to forgive sins, and then shows Thomas His wounds ( John 20:19-31 ). Easter is where mercy comes from: “God, who is rich in mercy, out of the great love with which he loved us” made us alive with Christ ( Ephesians 2:4-5 ). 1 The novena: Good Friday to Saturday Saint Faustina’s Diary gives a novena of nine days, beginning on Good Friday. Each day brings a different group of people before Jesus, from all mankind and sinners to the souls in purgatory and the lukewarm, and closes with the Chaplet. 2 Confession Go to confession in the days around the feast. Many parishes add extra times in Easter week. 3 Mass and Holy Communion On the Sunday itself, receive Communion in a state of grace. 4 The indulgence A decree of the Apostolic Penitentiary (29 June 2002) grants a plenary indulgence on Divine Mercy Sunday. Besides the usual conditions (confession, Communion, prayer for the Pope’s intentions and a heart free of any attachment to sin), take part in prayers and devotions in honor of Divine Mercy in a church or chapel, or at least pray the Our Father and the Creed before the Blessed Sacrament, adding a prayer to the merciful Lord Jesus such as “Merciful Jesus, I trust in you.” Those who cannot get to church, such as the sick, can still receive it in the ways the decree sets out (CCC 1471).

1905-1938 Saint Faustina Helena Kowalska was born in 1905 in the village of Głogowiec, in central Poland, the third of ten children of a poor farming family. She had less than three years of school. At twenty she joined the Congregation of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy in Warsaw and took the name Sister Maria Faustina of the Most Blessed Sacrament. For thirteen years she worked as a cook, a gardener and a porter in the order’s houses. Few around her guessed that Jesus was speaking to her. At her confessor’s request she wrote down what she heard, in notebooks now published as her Diary, Divine Mercy in My Soul . She died of tuberculosis in Kraków on 5 October 1938, aged thirty-three. The devotion spread quickly during the Second World War. In 1959 the Holy See halted its spread, because of poor translations of the Diary. After a careful study of the original text, begun in Kraków under its archbishop, Karol Wojtyła, the ban was lifted in 1978. The same man, as Pope John Paul II, beatified Faustina in 1993 and canonized her in 2000, the first saint of the new millennium. He died in 2005 on the eve of Divine Mercy Sunday. Her feast is on 5 October.

Good to know What the Church teaches The revelations to Saint Faustina are private revelations. The Church has judged them worthy of belief, but no Catholic is bound to accept them, and they add nothing to the faith. Their role is to help us live the Gospel more fully in our own time (CCC 67). What they point to is the Gospel itself. God’s mercy is greater than any sin, and no one is too far gone to come home. Mercy does not ignore sin. It forgives the sinner who turns back, and the first step is to admit the sin (CCC 1846-1848). Saint John Paul II made the same point in his encyclical Rich in Mercy (1980), and Pope Francis opened a Jubilee Year of Mercy in 2015. Mercy received is also mercy to be passed on. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” ( Matthew 5:7 ). Saint Faustina named three ways: by deed, by word and by prayer. The Church lists them as the corporal and spiritual works of mercy (CCC 2447): feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, welcoming the stranger, visiting the sick and the imprisoned, burying the dead; and instructing, advising, consoling, comforting, forgiving and bearing wrongs patiently. The painting at the top of this page shows the corporal works in one street in Naples.
What Verbum Domini is, what you’ll find here, and how to use it

Verbum Domini (Latin for “the Word of the Lord”) is a free guide to the Catholic faith in plain English. It’s for anyone: the curious, people on their way into the Church, and Catholics who want to know their faith better. Everything is taken from the Bible, the Catechism and the Church’s own documents, and every page says where its sources come from. There are no ads, no accounts, no paywall and no tracking. One person writes and maintains it, and it keeps growing.

The site has five sections, in this order in the menu: Library: the Holy Bible , all 73 books of the Douay-Rheims chapter by chapter, with modern book names, Bishop Challoner’s notes, a short guide to each chapter and a study appendix of apocryphal and Ethiopian books; the whole Catechism (the Compendium, 598 questions and answers); Canon Law in plain words; and a glossary of 877 Catholic terms. Guides: the Order of the Mass step by step, the Roman Missal Guide to how a parish should celebrate it, Confession with an examination of conscience, and how to become Catholic . Prayer: the Rosary with today’s mysteries, prayed bead by bead if you like; Divine Mercy , with the Chaplet, the image “Jesus, I trust in you”, the Hour of Mercy and Divine Mercy Sunday; and the Church’s common prayers in English and Latin. Answers: the Frequently Asked Questions , the parables of Jesus , Why We’re Catholic , and answers for atheists , Muslims and Jewish friends , each argued from reason and their own sources. History: the history of the Rosary , the history of the Church in 62 paintings, a saint for every day of the year, and the miracles the Church has examined.

Home: the logo always takes you to the Welcome page. It picks up where you left off in the Bible, the Catechism and today’s Rosary, lets you load your progress and settings from another device, and answers questions through search. The menu: on a computer, the sidebar lists every page by section; each section folds away with a click on its heading, and [ hides or shows the whole sidebar. On a tablet the bar at the top, and on a phone the bar at the bottom, has Home, Bible, Today and More; More lists every section. Search: press Ctrl + K ( ⌘ + K on a Mac) or the magnifier. It searches every page, section, Catechism question, FAQ answer, glossary term, saint, parable and prayer. Type a Bible reference such as “John 3:16” and it goes straight there. Accents don’t matter: “Avila” finds Ávila. Today: press T or the date at the top. It shows the liturgical season, the day’s Mass readings, the saint of the day and the feasts ahead. The arrows step to other days. References: a Bible reference anywhere on the site opens the passage in a small window over the page, with the words of Christ in red, so you never lose your place. Its link opens the full chapter in our Bible. Long pages have a list of their sections, beside the text on a computer and at the top of the page on a phone; the section you are reading is marked. Pictures open full size when you tap them, with a short description where we have one. Settings: the gear at the top opens accessibility profiles and settings (larger text, contrast, a dyslexia-friendly font and more), the theme and other display options, and Backup. The page stays visible while the panel is open, so you see each change at once; the arrow beside the close button tucks the panel away. Keyboard shortcuts are listed there when your device has a keyboard. Light or dark: the sun and moon button switches the theme. The site follows your device until you choose.

Going to a passage: on the Holy Bible page, type a reference (“Psalm 23”, “Matthew 5:3”) or any words. Words search all 37,000 verses, in any order; put a phrase in “quotes” to find it exactly. You can search the whole Bible or just one part of it. Reading tools: text size, font, line and letter spacing, page width, background, and which extras show (verse numbers, words of Christ in red, notes, pictures). Focus mode hides everything but the text. Tap a verse to copy it, share it, or highlight it in one of several colors. Highlights, bookmarks and notes: the bookmark button keeps a chapter, and the notepad lists everything you have marked, ready to jump back to. Listen: reads the chapter aloud with your device’s voices, verse by verse. Choose the voice and the speed, and skip back or forward a verse. Auto-scroll moves the page down slowly as you read. Touching the screen stops it. Hard words carry a small ring; tap it for the meaning in everyday English. Keys while reading: the arrow keys turn the chapter, F switches focus mode, L starts listening and S starts auto-scroll. New to the Douay-Rheims? On the Holy Bible page, “Why the Douay-Rheims reads differently” explains its Psalm numbers, its wording and its extra verses.

Your progress is kept in your browser: the Bible chapters you have read, where you stopped in each book, your highlights, bookmarks and notes, the section of the Catechism you last read, and your place in today’s Rosary. So are your settings. There’s no account. Backup keeps a copy of all of it. You’ll find it on the Welcome page, under Settings, on the Holy Bible page and in each chapter’s tools; it is the same everywhere. Save to a file: download your progress and settings as a small file. Nothing is sent anywhere. Restore from a file: open that file later, on this device or another, and you pick up where you left off.

The Bible works without a connection. Each book you open is kept on your device the first time it loads, so the next time it opens straight from your device, even on a plane or in a church with no signal. The other pages you visit are kept too, and the last copy is shown when you’re offline. To have every book ready before you need it, open Backup on the Holy Bible page and press Save the whole Bible offline . It downloads all 73 books with their notes (about 7 MB) and shows its progress as it goes. Once saved, the same button reads Update the offline copy , in case the text has been corrected since. The offline copy lives in your browser’s storage for this site. Clearing your browser data removes it, and the books simply download again the next time you open them. Offline reading needs a browser that supports it (all current ones do) and is not available in private windows on some browsers.

The site collects nothing about you unless you write to us. Your settings and reading stay in your browser, and searching happens on your device. The details are in the Privacy Policy ; for screen readers, the keyboard and other help with reading, see Accessibility .
Found a mistake, or something that doesn’t work? We read every message: write to us through the Contact page.

Dear Jesus, in the Sacrament of the Altar, be forever thanked and praised. Love, worthy of all heavenly and earthly love! Who, out of infinite love for me, an ungrateful sinner, assumed our human nature, shed Your Most Precious Blood in the cruel scourging, and expired on a shameful cross for our eternal welfare! Now, illumined with lively faith, with the outpouring of my whole soul and the fervor
Close by asking for protection from any retaliation and by commending body and soul to the care of Mary and the angels.

Lord Jesus Christ, in your love and mercy, pour Your Precious Blood over me so that no demon or disembodied spirit may retaliate against me. Mary, surround me with your mantle, blocking any retaliating spirits from having any authority over me. St. Michael, surround me with your shield, so that no evil spirit may take revenge on me. Queen of Heaven and St. Michael, send down the legions of angels

Lord Jesus Christ, I ask You that from now and until I fall asleep, while I sleep and during my dreams, if any evil spirit tries to affect me, that You would punish him by making him focus on the thing that causes the most pain during the entire time he tries to affect me and for ten minutes more. I also ask You to not allow him to retaliate. Amen. (The above prayer may be modified for any form of
Commission of the Care of Soul and Body

May be prayed at any time, but especially before sleeping. For yourself For another person For several people Into your hands, Mary, I commend my body and my soul. I ask you to provide for them and to protect them. I ask you to protect them from the evil one. I ask you to enlighten my mind, strengthen my will, and refrain my appetites by grace. Our Lady and St. Michael, call down from Heaven the l
In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Latin text: Signum Crucis In nómine Patris et Fílii et Spíritus Sancti. Amen.

Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us, and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Latin text: Pater Noster Pater noster, qui es in cælis: sanctificétur Nomen Tuum: advéniat Regnum Tuum: fiat volúntas Tua, sicut in cælo, et in terra. Panem nostrum cotidiánum da nobis hódie, et dimítte nobis débita nostra, sicut et nos dimíttimus debitóribus nostris. et ne nos indúcas in tentatiónem; sed líbera nos a Malo.

Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. Blessed art thou among women and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus. Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen. Latin text: Ave, Maria Ave, María, grátia plena, Dóminus tecum. Benedícta tu in muliéribus, et benedíctus fructus ventris tui, Iesus. Sancta María, Mater Dei, ora pro nobis peccatóribus, nunc et in hora mortis nostræ. Amen.

Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning is now, and ever shall be world without end. Amen. Latin text: Gloria Patri Glória Patri et Fílio et Spirítui Sancto. Sicut erat in princípio, et nunc et semper et in sǽcula sæculórum. Amen.

O my Jesus, forgive us our sins, save us from the fires of hell, lead all souls to heaven, especially those in most need of thy mercy. Latin text: Oratio Fatimensis Dómine Iesu, dimítte nobis débita nostra, salva nos ab igne inferióri, perduc in cælum omnes ánimas, præsértim eas, quæ misericórdiæ tuæ máxime índigent.

Angel of God, my guardian dear, to whom God’s love commits me here, ever this day be at my side, to light and guard, to rule and guide. Amen. Latin text: Angele Dei Ángele Dei, qui custos es mei, me, tibi commíssum pietáte supérna, illúmina, custódi, rege et gubérna. Amen.

Saint Michael the Archangel, defend us in battle. Be our protection against the wickedness and snares of the devil. May God rebuke him, we humbly pray; and do thou, O Prince of the heavenly host, by the power of God, cast into hell Satan and all the evil spirits who prowl about the world seeking the ruin of souls. Amen. Latin text: Oratio ad Sanctum Michaëlem Sancte Míchael Archángele, defénde nos in prǽlio; contra nequítiam et insídias diáboli esto præsídium. Ímperet illi Deus, súpplices deprecámur: tuque, Princeps milítiæ cæléstis, Sátanam aliósque spíritus malígnos, qui ad perditiónem animárum pervagántur in mundo, divína virtúte in inférnum detrúde. Amen.

I believe in God the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth. And in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord, Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried. He descended into hell; the third day He rose again from the dead; He ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty, from thence He shall come to judge the living and the dead. I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy Catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body and life everlasting. Amen. Latin text: Symbolum Apostolicum Credo in Deum Patrem omnipoténtem, Creatorem cæli et terræ, et in Iesum Christum, Filium Eius unicum, Dominum nostrum, qui concéptus est de Spíritu Sancto, natus ex Maria Virgine, passus sub Póntio Piláto, crucifixus, mórtuus, et sepúltus, descéndit ad ínferos, tértia die resurréxit a mórtuis, ascéndit ad cælos, sedet ad déxteram Dei Patris omnipoténtis, inde ventúrus est iudicáre vivos et mórtuos. Et in Spíritum Sanctum, sanctam Ecclésiam cathólicam, sanctórum communiónem, remissiónem peccatórum, carnis resurrectiónem, vitam ætérnam. Amen.

I believe in one God, the Father, the Almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all that is, seen and unseen. I believe one Lord, Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, eternally begotten of the Father, God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, one in Being with the Father. Through Him all things were made. For us men and for our salvation, He came down from heaven: by the power of the Holy Spirit He was born of the Virgin Mary, and became Man. For our sake He was crucified under Pontius Pilate; He suffered, died, and was buried. On the third day He rose again in fulfillment of the Scriptures; He ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of the Father. He will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead, and His kingdom will have no end. I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the Giver of life, Who proceeds from the Father and the Son. With the Father and the Son He is worshiped and glorified. He has spoken through the prophets. I believe in one, holy, catholic, and apostolic Church. I acknowledge one Baptism for the forgiveness of sins. I look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come. Amen. Latin text: Symbolum Nicænum Costantinopolitanum Credo in unum Deum, Patrem omnipoténtem, Factorem cæli et terræ, visibílium ómnium et invisibílium. Et in unum Dóminum Iesum Christum, Filium Dei unigénitum et ex Patre natum ante ómnia sǽcula: Deum de Deo, Lumen de Lúmine, Deum verum de Deo vero, génitum, non factum, consubstantiálem Patri: per quem ómnia facta sunt; qui propter nos hómines et propter nostram salútem, descéndit de cælis, et incarnátus est de Spíritu Sancto ex Maria Vírgine et homo factus est, crucifíxus étiam pro nobis sub Póntio Piláto, passus et sepúltus est, et resurréxit tértia die secúndum Scriptúras, et ascéndit in cælum, sedet ad déxteram Patris, et íterum ventúrus est cum glória, iudicáre vivos et mórtuos, cuius regni non erit finis. Credo in Spíritum Sanctum, Dominum et vivificántem, qui ex Patre Filióque procédit, qui cum Patre et Fílio simul adorátur et conglorificátur, qui locútus est per prophétas. Et unam sanctam cathólicam et apostólicam Ecclésiam. Confíteor unum Baptísma in remissiónem peccatórum. Et exspécto resurrectiónem mortuórum, et vitam ventúri sæculi. Amen.
Acts of Faith, Hope, Love and Contrition
Acts of Faith, Hope, Love and Contrition

O my God, I firmly believe that you are one God in three divine Persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I believe that your divine Son became man and died for our sins and that he will come to judge the living and the dead. I believe these and all the truths which the Holy Catholic Church teaches because you have revealed them who are eternal truth and wisdom, who can neither deceive nor be deceived. In this faith I intend to live and die. Amen. Latin text: Actus fidei Dómine Deus, firma fide credo et confíteor ómnia et síngula quæ sancta Ecclésia Cathólica propónit, quia tu, Deus, ea ómnia revelásti, qui es ætérna véritas et sapiéntia quæ nec fállere nec falli potest. In hac fide vívere et mori státuo. Amen.

O Lord God, I hope by your grace for the pardon of all my sins and after life here to gain eternal happiness because you have promised it who are infinitely powerful, faithful, kind, and merciful. In this hope I intend to live and die. Amen. Latin text: Actus spei Dómine Deus, spero per grátiam tuam remissiónem ómnium peccatórum, et post hanc vitam ætérnam felicitátem me esse consecutúrum: quia tu promisísti, qui es infiníte potens, fidélis, benígnus, et miséricors. In hac spe vívere et mori státuo. Amen.

O Lord God, I love you above all things and I love my neighbor for your sake because you are the highest, infinite and perfect good, worthy of all my love. In this love I intend to live and die. Amen. Latin text: Actus caritatis Dómine Deus, amo te super ómnia et próximum meum propter te, quia tu es summum, infinítum, et perfectíssimum bonum, omni dilectióne dignum. In hac caritáte vívere et mori státuo. Amen.

O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended Thee, and I detest all my sins because of thy just punishments, but most of all because they offend Thee, my God, who art all good and deserving of all my love. I firmly resolve with the help of Thy grace to sin no more and to avoid the near occasion of sin. Amen. Latin text: Actus contritionis Deus meus, ex toto corde pænitet me ómnium meórum peccatórum, éaque detéstor, quia peccándo, non solum pœnas a te iuste statútas proméritus sum, sed præsértim quia offéndi te, summum bonum, ac dignum qui super ómnia diligáris. Ídeo fírmiter propóno, adiuvánte grátia tua, de cétero me non peccatúrum peccandíque occasiónes próximas fugitúrum. Amen.

V. The Angel of the Lord declared unto Mary. R. And she conceived of the Holy Spirit. Hail, Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee… V. Behold the handmaid of the Lord. R. Be it done unto me according to thy word. Hail Mary… V. And the Word was made flesh. R. And dwelt among us. Hail Mary… V. Pray for us, O holy Mother of God. R. That we may be made worthy of the promises of Christ. Let us pray: Pour forth, we beseech thee, O Lord, thy grace into our hearts; that we, to whom the Incarnation of Christ, thy Son, was made known by the message of an angel, may by his Passion and Cross be brought to the glory of his Resurrection. Through the same Christ, our Lord. Amen. Glory be to the Father… Latin text: Angelus Domini V. Ángelus Dómini nuntiávit Maríæ. R. Et concépit de Spíritu Sancto. Ave, María… V. Ecce ancílla Dómini. R. Fiat mihi secúndum verbum tuum. Ave, María… V. Et Verbum caro factum est. R. Et habitávit in nobis. Ave, María… V. Ora pro nobis, sancta Dei génetrix. R. Ut digni efficiámur promissiónibus Christi. Orémus. Grátiam tuam, quæsumus, Dómine, méntibus nostris infúnde; ut qui, Ángelo nuntiánte, Christi Fílii tui incarnatiónem cognóvimus, per passiónem eius et crucem, ad resurrectiónis glóriam perducámur. Per eúndem Christum Dóminum nostrum. Amen. Glória Patri…

Queen of heaven, rejoice, alleluia. The Son whom you merited to bear, alleluia, has risen as he said, alleluia. Rejoice and be glad, O Virgin Mary, alleluia! For the Lord has truly risen, alleluia. Let us pray: O God, who through the resurrection of your Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, did vouchsafe to give joy to the world; grant, we beseech you, that through his Mother, the Virgin Mary, we may obtain the joys of everlasting life. Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen. Latin text: Regina Cæli Regína cæli lætáre, allelúia. Quia quem meruísti portáre, allelúia. Resurréxit, sicut dixit, allelúia. Ora pro nobis Deum, allelúia. V. Gaude et lætáre, Virgo María, allelúia. R. Quia surréxit Dóminus vere, allelúia. Orémus. Deus, qui per resurrectiónem Fílii tui Dómini nostri Iesu Christi mundum lætificáre dignátus es, præsta, quæsumus, ut per eius Genetrícem Vírginem Maríam perpétuæ capiámus gáudia vitæ. Per Christum Dóminum nostrum. Amen.

Hail, Holy Queen, Mother of Mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope. To you do we cry, poor banished children of Eve. To you do we send up our sighs, mourning and weeping in this valley of tears. Turn then, most gracious advocate, your eyes of mercy toward us, and after this exile show unto us the blessed fruit of thy womb, Jesus. O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary. Latin text: Salve, Regina Salve, Regína, Mater misericórdiæ, vita, dulcédo et spes nostra, salve. Ad te clamámus, éxsules fílii Evæ. Ad te suspirámus geméntes et flentes in hac lacrimárum valle. Eia ergo, advocáta nostra, illos tuos misericórdes óculos ad nos convérte. Et Iesum benedíctum fructum ventris tui, nobis, post hoc exsílium, osténde. O clemens, o pia, o dulcis Virgo María!

Remember, O most gracious Virgin Mary, that never was it known that anyone who fled to thy protection, implored thy help, or sought thy intercession, was left unaided. Inspired by this confidence I fly unto thee, O Virgin of virgins, my Mother. To thee do I come, before thee I stand, sinful and sorrowful. O Mother of the Word Incarnate, despise not my petitions, but in thy mercy hear and answer me. Amen. Latin text: Memorare Memoráre, o piíssima Virgo María, non esse audítum a sæculo, quemquam ad tua curréntem præsídia, tua implorántem auxília, tua peténtem suffrágia, esse derelíctum. Ego tali animátus confidéntia, ad te, Virgo Vírginum, Mater, curro, ad te vénio, coram te gemens peccátor assísto. Noli, Mater Verbi, verba mea despícere; sed áudi propítia et exáudi. Amen.

We fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God. Despise not our petitions in our necessities, but deliver us always from all dangers O glorious and blessed Virgin. Latin text: Sub tuum præsidium Sub tuum præsídium confúgimus, sancta Dei Génetrix; nostras deprecatiónes ne despícias in necessitátibus; sed a perículis cunctis líbera nos semper, Virgo gloriósa et benedícta.

My soul proclaims the greatness of the Lord, my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, for he has looked with favor on his lowly servant. From this day all generations will call me blessed: the Almighty has done great things for me, and holy is his Name. He has mercy on those who fear him in every generation. He has shown the strength of his arm, he has scattered the proud in their conceit. He has cast down the mighty from their thrones, and has lifted up the lowly. He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. He has come to the help of his servant Israel for he has remembered his promise of mercy, the promise he made to our fathers, to Abraham and his children forever. Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning, is now, and will be forever. Amen. Latin text: Magnificat Magníficat ánima mea Dóminum, et exsultávit spíritus meus in Deo salvatóre meo, quia respéxit humilitátem ancíllæ suæ. Ecce enim ex hoc beátam me dicent omnes generatiónes, quia fecit mihi magna, qui potens est, et sanctum nomen eius, et misericórdia eius in progénies et progénies timéntibus eum. Fecit poténtiam in bráchio suo, dispérsit supérbos mente cordis sui; depósuit poténtes de sede et exaltávit húmiles. Esuriéntes implévit bonis et dívites dimísit inánes. Suscépit Ísrael púerum suum, recordátus misericórdiæ, sicut locútus est ad patres nostros, Ábraham et sémini eius in sæcula. Glória Patri et Fílio et Spirítui Sancto. Sicut erat in princípio, et nunc et semper, et in sæcula sæculórum. Amen.

Come, Holy Spirit, Creator come, From your bright heavenly throne! Come, take possession of our souls, And make them all your own. You who are called the Paraclete, Best gift of God above, The living spring, the living fire, Sweet unction, and true love! You who are sevenfold in your grace, Finger of God’s right hand, His promise, teaching little ones To speak and understand! O guide our minds with your blessed light, With love our hearts inflame, And with your strength which never decays Confirm our mortal frame. Far from us drive our hellish foe True peace unto us bring, And through all perils guide us safe Beneath your sacred wing. Through you may we the Father know, Through you the eternal Son And you the Spirit of them both Thrice-blessed three in one. All glory to the Father be, And to the risen Son; The same to you, O Paraclete, While endless ages run. Amen. Latin text: Veni, Creator Spiritus Veni, creátor Spíritus, mentes tuórum vísita, imple supérna grátia, quæ tu creásti péctora. Qui díceris Paráclitus, altíssimi donum Dei, fons vivus, ignis, cáritas, et spiritális únctio. Tu septifórmis múnere, dígitus patérnæ déxteræ, tu rite promíssum Patris, sermóne ditans gúttura. Accénde lumen sénsibus, infúnde amórem córdibus, infírma nostri córporis virtúte firmans pérpeti. Hostem repéllas lóngius pacémque dones prótinus; ductóre sic te prævio vitémus omne nóxium. Per Te sciámus da Patrem noscámus atque Fílium, teque utriúsque Spíritum credámus omni témpore. Deo Patri sit glória, et Fílio, qui a mórtuis surréxit, ac Paráclito, in sæculórum sæcula. Amen.

Come, Holy Spirit, come! And from your celestial home Shed a ray of light divine! Come, Father of the poor! Come, source of all our store! Come, within our bosoms shine. You, of comforters the best; You, the soul’s most welcome guest; Sweet refreshment here below; In our labor, rest most sweet; Grateful coolness in the heat; Solace in the midst of woe. O most blessed Light divine, Shine within these hearts of yours, And our inmost being fill! Where you are not, we have naught, Nothing good in deed or thought, Nothing free from taint of ill. Heal our wounds, our strength renew; On our dryness pour your dew; Wash the stains of guilt away: Bend the stubborn heart and will; Melt the frozen, warm the chill; Guide the steps that go astray. On the faithful, who adore And confess you, evermore In your sevenfold gift descend: Give them virtue’s sure reward; Give them your salvation, Lord; Give them joys that never end. Latin text: Veni, Sancte Spiritus Veni, Sancte Spíritus, et emítte cælitus lucis tuæ rádium. Veni, pater páuperum, veni, dator múnerum, veni, lumen córdium. Consolátor óptime, dulcis hospes ánimæ, dulce refrigérium. In labóre réquies, in æstu tempéries, in fletu solácium. O lux beatíssima, reple cordis íntima tuórum fidélium. Sine tuo númine, nihil est in hómine nihil est innóxium. Lava quod est sórdidum, riga quod est áridum, sana quod est sáucium. Flecte quod est rígidum, fove quod est frígidum, rege quod est dévium. Da tuis fidélibus, in te confidéntibus, sacrum septenárium. Da virtútis méritum, da salútis éxitum, da perénne gáudium. Amen.

Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel; he has come to his people and set them free. He has raised up for us a mighty savior, born of the house of his servant David. Through his holy prophets he promised of old that he would save us from our enemies, from the hands of all who hate us. He promised to show mercy to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant. This was the oath he swore to our father Abraham: to set us free from the hands of our enemies, free to worship him without fear, holy and righteous in his sight all the days of our life. You, my child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his way, to give his people knowledge of salvation by the forgiveness of their sins. In the tender compassion of our God the dawn from on high shall break upon us, to shine on those who dwell in darkness and the shadow of death, and to guide our feet into the way of peace. Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning, is now, and will be forever. Amen. Latin text: Benedictus Benedíctus Dóminus, Deus Ísrael, quia visitávit et fecit redemptiónem plebi suæ, et eréxit cornu salútis nobis in domo David púeri sui, sicut locútus est per os sanctórum, qui a sæculo sunt, prophetárum eius, salútem ex inimícis nostris et de manu ómnium, qui odérunt nos; ad faciéndam misericórdiam cum pátribus nostris et memorári testaménti sui sancti, iusiurándum, quod iurávit ad Ábraham patrem nostrum, datúrum se nobis, ut sine timóre, de manu inimicórum liberáti, serviámus illi in sanctitáte et iustítia coram ipso ómnibus diébus nostris. Et tu, puer, prophéta Altíssimi vocáberis: præíbis enim ante fáciem Dómini paráre vias eius, ad dandam sciéntiam salútis plebi eius in remissiónem peccatórum eórum, per víscera misericórdiæ Dei nostri, in quibus visitábit nos óriens ex alto, illumináre his, qui in ténebris et in umbra mortis sedent, ad dirigéndos pedes nostros in viam pacis. Glória Patri et Fílio et Spirítui Sancto. Sicut erat in princípio, et nunc et semper, et in sæcula sæculórum. Amen.

You are God: we praise you; You are God: we acclaim you; You are the eternal Father: All creation worships you. To you all angels, all the powers of heaven, Cherubim and Seraphim, sing in endless praise: Holy, holy, holy, Lord, God of power and might, Heaven and earth are full of your glory. The glorious company of apostles praise you. The noble fellowship of prophets praise you. The white-robed army of martyrs praise you. Throughout the world the holy Church acclaims you: Father, of majesty unbounded, Your true and only Son, worthy of all worship, And the Holy Spirit, advocate and guide. You, Christ, are the king of glory, The eternal Son of the Father. When you became man to set us free You did not spurn the Virgin’s womb. You overcame the sting of death, And opened the kingdom of heaven to all believers. You are seated at God’s right hand in glory. We believe that you will come, and be our judge. Come then, Lord, and help your people, Bought with the price of your own blood, And bring us with your saints To glory everlasting. Save your people, Lord, and bless your inheritance. Govern and uphold them now and always. Day by day we bless you. We praise your name forever. Keep us today, Lord, from all sin. Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy. Lord, show us your love and mercy; For we put our trust in you. In you, Lord, is our hope: And we shall never hope in vain. Latin text: Te Deum Te Deum laudámus: te Dóminum confitémur. Te ætérnum Patrem, omnis terra venerátur. Tibi omnes ángeli, tibi cæli et univérsæ potestátes: tibi chérubim et séraphim incessábili voce proclámant: Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus, Dóminus Deus Sábaoth. Pleni sunt cæli et terra maiestátis glóriæ tuæ. Te gloriósus apostolórum chorus, te prophetárum laudábilis númerus, te mártyrum candidátus laudat exércitus. Te per orbem terrárum sancta confitétur Ecclésia, Patrem imménsæ maiestátis; venerándum tuum verum et únicum Fílium; Sanctum quoque Paráclitum Spíritum. Tu rex glóriæ, Christe. Tu Patris sempitérnus es Fílius. Tu, ad liberándum susceptúrus hóminem, non horruísti Vírginis úterum. Tu, devícto mortis acúleo, aperuísti credéntibus regna cælórum. Tu ad déxteram Dei sedes, in glória Patris. Iudex créderis esse ventúrus. Te ergo quæsumus, tuis fámulis súbveni, quos pretióso sánguine redemísti. Ætérna fac cum sanctis tuis in glória numerári. Salvum fac pópulum tuum, Dómine, et bénedic hereditáti tuæ. Et rege eos, et extólle illos usque in ætérnum. Per síngulos dies benedícimus te; et laudámus nomen tuum in sæculum, et in sæculum sæculi. Dignáre, Dómine, die isto sine peccáto nos custodíre. Miserére nostri, Dómine, miserére nostri. Fiat misericórdia tua, Dómine, super nos, quemádmodum sperávimus in te. In te, Dómine, sperávi: non confúndar in ætérnum.

Soul of Christ, be my sanctification. Body of Christ, be my salvation. Blood of Christ, fill all my veins. Water of Christ’s side, wash out my stains. Passion of Christ, my comfort be. O good Jesus, listen to me. In Thy wounds I fain would hide, N’er to be parted from Thy side, Guard me, should the foe assail me. Call me when my life shall fail me. Bid me come to Thee above, With Thy saints to sing Thy love, World without end. Amen. Latin text: Anima Christi Ánima Christi, sanctífica me. Corpus Christi, salva me. Sanguis Christi, inébria me. Aqua láteris Christi, lava me. Pássio Christi, confórta me. O bone Iesu, exáudi me. Intra tua vúlnera abscónde me. Ne permíttas me separári a te. Ab hoste malígno defénde me. In hora mortis meæ voca me. Et iube me veníre ad te, ut cum Sanctis tuis laudem te in sæcula sæculórum. Amen.

Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen. Latin text: Benedictio mensæ Bénedic, Dómine, nos et hæc tua dona, quæ de tua largitáte sumus sumptúri. Per Christum Dóminum nostrum. Amen.

We give thee thanks, almighty God, for all thy benefits, who livest and reignest for ever and ever. Amen. Latin text: Gratiarum actio post mensam Ágimus tibi grátias, omnípotens Deus, pro univérsis benefíciis tuis, qui vivis et regnas in sǽcula sæculórum. Amen.

Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them. May they rest in peace. Amen. Latin text: Requiem Æternam Réquiem ætérnam dona eis, Dómine, et lux perpétua lúceat eis. Requiéscant in pace. Amen.

God of the spirits and of all flesh, who have trampled death and annihilated the devil and given life to your world, may you yourself, O Lord, grant to the soul of your deceased servant N. rest in a place of light, a verdant place, a place of freshness, from where suffering, pain and cries are far removed. Do You, O good and compassionate God forgive every fault committed by him in word, work or thought because there is no man who lives and does not sin. You alone are without sin and your justice is justice throughout the ages and your word is truth. Since you, O Christ our God, are the resurrection, the life and the repose of your deceased servant N., we give you glory together with your un-begotten Father and your most holy, good and life-creating Spirit, now and always and forever and ever.

O King of peace, give us your peace and pardon our sins. Dismiss the enemies of the Church and protect her so that she never fail. Emmanuel our God is in our midst in the glory of the Father and of the Holy Spirit. May he bless us and purify our hearts and cure the sicknesses of our soul and body. We adore you, O Christ, with your good Father and the Holy Spirit because you have come and you have saved us.

Remain in peace, O Altar of God. May the offering that I have taken from you be for the remission of my debts and the pardon of my sins and may it obtain for me that I may stand before the tribunal of Christ without condemnation and without confusion. I do not know if I will have the opportunity to return and offer another sacrifice upon you. Protect me, O Lord, and preserve your holy Church as the way to truth and salvation. Amen.

Jesus gave Peter the keys of the kingdom and told him to feed his sheep. Every Bishop of Rome since has inherited that task. Here are all of them, in order: search by name, browse by era, or open any pope to read his life, what he did for the Church, and the documents he published, with links to the official texts on the Vatican’s website.

1. 33-64. Born Simon, son of John (Jonah) in Bethsaida, Galilee. The fisherman Jesus called the Rock, chief of the Apostles and first Bishop of Rome. Christ chose a fisherman to be the Rock: Peter’s faith, his failures and his return to the Lord are the foundation every pope since has stood on. Simon was a fisherman from Bethsaida who worked the Sea of Galilee with his brother Andrew. Jesus called him to follow, gave him the name Cephas, “Rock” (Peter), and said: “Upon this rock I will build my Church... I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:18-19). He was the first to confess Jesus as the Christ, and the one who denied Him three times on the night of the Passion. After the Resurrection the Lord asked him three times “Do you love me?” and charged him: “Feed my sheep” (John 21). After Pentecost Peter led the Church in Jerusalem, preached the first Christian sermon, received the first Gentile convert, Cornelius, and spoke decisively at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15). Ancient witnesses, among them Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch and Irenaeus, agree that he came to Rome, led the Church there and was martyred under Nero, crucified, by tradition upside down at his own request. Excavations under St. Peter’s Basilica found the shrine built over his grave on the Vatican Hill. Two letters of the New Testament bear his name. His reign is traditionally counted from about 30-33 to 64 or 67. Received the keys of the kingdom and the charge to feed Christ’s flock Led the Apostles and the first Church in Jerusalem Opened the Church to the Gentiles (Acts 10) Martyred in Rome under Nero; buried on the Vatican Hill Called from his nets on the Sea of Galilee with his brother Andrew Confesses Jesus as the Christ at Caesarea Philippi and receives the keys of the kingdom Witnesses the Transfiguration; denies the Lord three times on the night of the Passion The risen Christ appears to him and three times charges him: “Feed my sheep” Preaches at Pentecost; about three thousand are baptized Receives the centurion Cornelius, the first Gentile convert, into the Church Imprisoned by Herod Agrippa and freed by an angel Speaks decisively at the Council of Jerusalem Martyred in Rome under Nero and buried on the Vatican Hill Pius XII announces that excavations have found Peter’s tomb under St. Peter’s Paul VI announces that bones found there have been identified as Peter’s You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. He was married: the Gospels tell how Jesus healed his mother-in-law (Mark 1:30-31). No pope has ever taken the name Peter II. Around the inside of the dome of St. Peter’s, in giant letters, runs the Latin of Matthew 16:18: “You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church.” He is the only pope named in the Bible.

2. 67-76. in Tuscia (Tuscany), by tradition. The first successor of Peter, probably the Linus greeted by St. Paul.  Irenaeus of Lyons, writing around 180, names Linus as the first bishop of Rome after the Apostles and identifies him with the Linus St. Paul mentions in 2 Timothy 4:21. Almost nothing else is known for certain. The Liber Pontificalis, a much later collection of papal lives, says he came from Tuscany and ruled that women should cover their heads in church, but this cannot be checked. He is honored as a martyr and is named in the Roman Canon of the Mass. First successor of St. Peter in the list of Irenaeus Named in the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I)

3. 76-88. Born Anacletus (Cletus) in Rome, by tradition. Third Bishop of Rome, also called Cletus, named in the Roman Canon.  Anacletus, also called Cletus, follows Linus in every ancient list. Later writers sometimes split him into two popes, but the Church has long recognized one man. Tradition says he ordained priests for the growing Roman community and was buried near St. Peter. He is commemorated as Cletus in the Roman Canon of the Mass. Named in the Roman Canon as Cletus

4. 88-97. Born Clement in Rome. Author of the earliest Christian writing outside the New Testament, the Letter to the Corinthians. His letter to Corinth is the first we have from a Bishop of Rome: within living memory of the Apostles, it shows the Church of Rome caring for another Church and calling it back to peace. Clement is the first Bishop of Rome whose own words survive. Around 96 he wrote to the Church in Corinth, which had deposed its presbyters, urging peace, order and obedience to lawful leaders. The letter was so respected that it was read in some churches alongside Scripture. It also gives early testimony to the martyrdoms of Peter and Paul in Rome. A later tradition says he was exiled to the Crimea and martyred there; St. Cyril, the apostle of the Slavs, brought relics believed to be his back to Rome, where they rest in the Basilica of San Clemente. Wrote the First Letter of Clement to the Corinthians (c. 96) Witness to the Roman martyrdom of Peter and Paul Named in the Roman Canon Becomes Bishop of Rome, third in line after Peter, following Linus and Anacletus Writes to the Church in Corinth, which had removed its presbyters, urging peace and order Dies; a later tradition says in exile in the Crimea, as a martyr Bishop Dionysius of Corinth writes that Clement’s letter is still read aloud in church there Sts. Cyril and Methodius bring relics believed to be his to Rome Excavations under San Clemente in Rome uncover the 4th-century church where he was honored Let us fix our eyes on the blood of Christ and understand how precious it is to his Father, because, poured out for our salvation, it brought the grace of repentance to the whole world. Peter, through unjust envy, endured not one or two but many labors, and having borne his witness went to the place of glory that was his due. He is named in the Roman Canon, the First Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass, after Linus and Cletus. Some early Christians counted his letter as part of Scripture: it is copied at the end of the Codex Alexandrinus, one of the oldest Bibles. Under the Basilica of San Clemente you can walk down through a 4th-century church to a 1st-century Roman house. Tradition says he was drowned with an anchor tied to him, so artists show him with an anchor.

5. 97-105. in Bethlehem, by tradition (of Greek Jewish family). Fourth successor of Peter, honored as a martyr.  Evaristus appears in all the early lists of Roman bishops, but little is known of his life. The Liber Pontificalis says he was the son of a Greek-speaking Jew from Bethlehem and divided Rome’s titular churches among the priests, which is probably a later author’s guess at the origins of the parish system.

6. 105-115. Born Alexander in Rome, by tradition. Early Bishop of Rome to whom tradition credits the blessing of holy water.  Irenaeus lists Alexander as the fifth successor of Peter. Later tradition credits him with adding the words of the Institution narrative to the Mass and with blessing water mixed with salt for homes, customs that probably grew up over time rather than by one decree. He is venerated as a martyr, though he is no longer confused with a different Roman martyr Alexander buried on the Via Nomentana.

7. 115-125. Born Xystus in Rome, by tradition. Sixth successor of Peter, honored as a martyr.  Sixtus (in Greek, Xystus) is named in the earliest lists of popes. Later tradition said he ordered that the sacred vessels be handled only by clergy and that the Sanctus be sung at Mass. Nothing further is known with certainty.

8. 125-136. in Greece, by tradition. The one early pope whose martyrdom is attested by Irenaeus.  Telesphorus is the only second-century Bishop of Rome whose martyrdom is recorded by Irenaeus, who says he “bore witness gloriously.” Later tradition, which cannot be confirmed, credits him with a Christmas midnight Mass and with a seven-week Lenten fast. Irenaeus also notes that he kept peace with Christians who celebrated Easter on a different date. Martyrdom recorded by St. Irenaeus

9. 136-140. in Athens, by tradition. Pope when the Gnostic teachers Valentinus and Cerdo came to Rome.  According to Irenaeus, the Gnostic teachers Valentinus and Cerdo arrived in Rome during Hyginus’ time, opening a long struggle over true and false teaching. Later tradition says he was a philosopher from Athens and that he organized the ranks of the clergy and introduced godparents at Baptism.

10. 140-155. Born Pius in Aquileia, by tradition. Brother of the author of the Shepherd of Hermas; faced the heretic Marcion.  The Muratorian Fragment, an early list of Scripture, says that the Shepherd of Hermas was written by Hermas, brother of Pius, while Pius was bishop in Rome. During his time the shipowner Marcion, who rejected the Old Testament and the God of Israel, was expelled from the Roman Church (around 144). St. Justin Martyr was teaching in Rome in these years. Marcion was excommunicated by the Roman Church in his time (c. 144)

11. 155-166. in Emesa, Syria, by tradition. Received St. Polycarp in Rome and kept peace despite their different Easter dates.  Anicetus welcomed the aged bishop Polycarp of Smyrna, a disciple of the Apostle John, around 155. They could not agree on the date of Easter (the churches of Asia kept it on the 14th of Nisan), but Irenaeus records that they parted in peace and that Anicetus let Polycarp celebrate the Eucharist in his place. During his time the historian Hegesippus visited Rome to collect the succession of its bishops. Received St. Polycarp of Smyrna (c. 155) Kept communion despite the Easter dispute

12. 166-175. in Fondi, Campania, by tradition. Known for the generous charity of the Roman Church toward other churches.  A letter of Bishop Dionysius of Corinth, quoted by Eusebius, praises Soter and the Roman Church for sending help to poor Christians and those condemned to the mines, and says that a letter from Soter was read aloud in Corinth. Some historians think the yearly celebration of Easter on a Sunday became fixed in Rome in his time. Praised for the Roman Church’s charity to other churches

13. 175-189. in Nicopolis, Epirus (Greece), by tradition. Pope when the Montanist movement and the martyrs of Lyon reached Rome.  Eleutherius had been a deacon under Anicetus. Irenaeus came to Rome during his reign carrying a letter from the martyrs of Lyon about the Montanist movement in Asia Minor. A later legend says a British king named Lucius asked him for missionaries; most historians doubt it.

14. 189-199. Born Victor in Roman Africa. The first Latin-speaking pope from Africa; insisted on Easter on Sunday.
