Proclaimed the First Crusade at Clermont (1095) Organized the Roman Curia Odo of Lagery is born in Champagne Becomes a monk at Cluny, and later its prior Made Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia by Gregory VII Elected at Terracina, since Rome is held by the antipope At the Council of Piacenza, envoys of the Byzantine emperor ask for help Consecrates the high altar of the great new abbey church of Cluny At Clermont calls the knights of the West to help the East and free Jerusalem Council of Bari, where St. Anselm defends the Filioque The crusaders take Jerusalem Dies before the news reaches him Beatified by Leo XIII The cry “Deus vult!”, “God wills it!”, rose from the crowd at Clermont. He died two weeks after Jerusalem fell, without hearing the news. He was a monk of Cluny, whose new abbey church was the largest in Christendom. The word “Curia” for the pope’s government comes from his reorganization of it.

160. 1099-1118. Born Raniero of Bleda in Bleda, Romagna. Approved the Knights Hospitaller; captured by Henry V in the investiture struggle.  Raniero, a monk, continued the investiture struggle. In 1111 Emperor Henry V seized him and forced him to grant the right of investiture, a concession a later synod revoked. He settled the conflict in England and France by compromise, and in 1113 recognized the Order of St. John (the Knights Hospitaller). Recognized the Knights Hospitaller (1113)

161. 1118-1119. Born Giovanni Caetani in Gaeta. Attacked at his election by the Frangipani; died in exile at Cluny.  John of Gaeta, long papal chancellor, was attacked and beaten by the Frangipani family during his election. Henry V set up an antipope and Gelasius fled to France, where he died at Cluny a year later.

162. 1119-1124. Born Guy of Burgundy in Quingey, Burgundy. Ended the investiture struggle with the Concordat of Worms and held the First Lateran Council.  Guy, Archbishop of Vienne and a relative of kings, ended the Investiture Controversy with the Concordat of Worms (1122): the emperor gave up investing bishops with ring and staff, while being present at elections and investing them with their lands. The First Lateran Council (1123), the first ecumenical council held in the West, confirmed the settlement. He also issued Sicut Judaeis, protecting Jews from forced baptism and violence. Concordat of Worms (1122) First Lateran Council (1123) Sicut Judaeis, protecting the Jews

163. 1124-1130. Born Lamberto Scannabecchi in Fiagnano, near Imola. Approved the Premonstratensians and, through the Council of Troyes, the Knights Templar.  Lambert, the cardinal who negotiated Worms, was installed amid a fight between the Frangipani and the Pierleoni families. He approved the Premonstratensian canons of St. Norbert (1126), and the Council of Troyes (1129), under his legate, approved the rule of the Knights Templar drawn up with St. Bernard. Approved St. Norbert’s Premonstratensians (1126) Knights Templar recognized at Troyes (1129)

164. 1130-1143. Born Gregorio Papareschi in Rome. Overcame the schism of Anacletus II with St. Bernard’s help; held the Second Lateran Council.  A minority of cardinals elected Gregory hastily, and the majority chose Anacletus II, who held Rome for eight years. St. Bernard of Clairvaux won Europe’s kings to Innocent’s side. After Anacletus died, the Second Lateran Council (1139) ended the schism and condemned simony and clerical marriage. He rebuilt Santa Maria in Trastevere, where he is buried, and condemned Peter Abelard (1140). Second Lateran Council (1139) Rebuilt Santa Maria in Trastevere

165. 1143-1144. Born Guido of Città di Castello in Città di Castello. A learned pupil of Abelard who lifted the interdict on France.  Guido, said to have studied under Abelard, lifted the interdict that Innocent II had placed on France. He reigned only about six months.

166. 1144-1145. Born Gherardo Caccianemici in Bologna. Died of wounds received while leading an attack on the rebel Roman Senate.  Lucius faced the Commune of Rome, which had set up a senate and rejected papal rule. He led an armed attack on the Capitol and, according to a later chronicle, was struck by stones and died of his injuries.

167. 1145-1153. Born Bernardo Pignatelli (of Pisa) in Pisa area. The first Cistercian pope, a disciple of St. Bernard; launched the Second Crusade.  Bernard of Pisa, a Cistercian monk and abbot of Tre Fontane, was a surprise choice. St. Bernard wrote him On Consideration, advice for a pope. He spent much of his reign away from the rebellious city of Rome, launched the Second Crusade (1145) after the fall of Edessa, and recognized the writings of St. Hildegard of Bingen. He was beatified in 1872. First Cistercian pope Called the Second Crusade (1145) Encouraged St. Hildegard of Bingen

168. 1153-1154. Born Corrado della Suburra in Rome. An elderly Roman who made peace in the city.  Conrad, already about eighty, was a peacemaker. He settled disputes with Frederick Barbarossa over the see of Magdeburg and with England over the see of York, and gave privileges to the Knights Hospitaller.

169. 1154-1159. Born Nicholas Breakspear in Abbots Langley, England. The only English pope.  Nicholas Breakspear left England poor, became abbot of St. Rufus near Avignon, and as legate reorganized the Church in Scandinavia. As pope he placed Rome under interdict to expel Arnold of Brescia, crowned Frederick Barbarossa (1155) and then clashed with him over whether the empire was a papal “benefice.” The bull Laudabiliter, said to grant Ireland to Henry II, is attributed to him, though its authenticity is debated. The only English pope Crowned Frederick Barbarossa (1155)

170. 1159-1181. Born Rolando of Siena in Siena. Canon lawyer who outlasted Barbarossa’s antipopes and held the Third Lateran Council. A great canon lawyer, he kept the Church free through eighteen years of schism and gave it the rule by which every pope is still elected. Roland, a canon lawyer from Bologna, faced eighteen years of schism with antipopes supported by Frederick Barbarossa. Allied with the Lombard League, whose victory at Legnano (1176) defeated the Emperor, he made peace with Frederick at Venice in 1177. He imposed penance on Henry II for the murder of St. Thomas Becket and canonized Becket (1173). The Third Lateran Council (1179) required a two-thirds majority of cardinals to elect a pope, a rule still in force. He reserved canonizations to the Holy See. Third Lateran Council (1179): two-thirds rule for papal elections Canonized St. Thomas Becket (1173) Peace of Venice with Barbarossa (1177) Roland is born at Siena Made a cardinal by Eugene III Chancellor of the Roman Church As legate at Besançon, stands up to Emperor Frederick Barbarossa Elected; a minority, backed by the emperor, sets up an antipope Takes refuge in France, until 1165 St. Thomas Becket is murdered in Canterbury Cathedral King Henry II does penance for Becket’s death at Avranches Canonizes Thomas Becket The Lombard League defeats Frederick at Legnano Peace of Venice: Frederick kneels before him at St. Mark’s Third Lateran Council: a pope must be elected by two-thirds of the cardinals Dies at Civita Castellana The two-thirds rule he set in 1179 is still how popes are elected. He canonized St. Bernard of Clairvaux in 1174, the year after Becket. In 1179 he recognized Afonso I as the first King of Portugal. He began reserving canonizations to the pope, the practice the Church follows today.

171. 1181-1185. Born Ubaldo Allucingoli in Lucca. Issued Ad abolendam against heresy, a step toward the medieval Inquisition.  Ubald, an elderly Cistercian, spent most of his reign outside Rome. With Barbarossa at Verona in 1184 he issued the decree Ad abolendam, which required bishops to seek out heretics such as the Cathars and Waldensians and hand the obstinate to secular rulers. Decree Ad abolendam (1184)

172. 1185-1187. Born Uberto Crivelli in Milan. Clashed with Barbarossa and died, by tradition, on hearing of the defeat at Hattin.  Archbishop of Milan, Hubert was elected at Verona and never entered Rome. He quarreled with the Emperor over church property and the see of Trier. Tradition says he died of grief after the news of the Christian defeat at Hattin (July 1187), though Jerusalem itself fell just after his death.

173. 1187-1187. Born Alberto di Morra in Benevento. Called the Third Crusade with the bull Audita tremendi during a two-month reign.  Albert, a canonist and chancellor, issued Audita tremendi soon after the fall of Jerusalem, calling Christians to repentance and to the Third Crusade. He made peace with Barbarossa and died at Pisa after fifty-seven days. Bull Audita tremendi calling the Third Crusade (1187)

174. 1187-1191. Born Paolo Scolari in Rome. Made peace with the Roman Commune and returned the papacy to Rome.  Paul, a Roman, ended the long quarrel with the Commune of Rome by a treaty in 1188, allowing the popes to live in the city again. He organized support for the Third Crusade and recognized the Scottish Church as directly subject to Rome.

175. 1191-1198. Born Giacinto Bobone in Rome. Ordained priest the day before his consecration, at about 85; crowned Henry VI.  Hyacinth, a cardinal deacon for over forty years and once a defender of Abelard, was ordained priest only after his election, at about 85. He crowned Henry VI, approved the Teutonic Knights (1196) and excommunicated Duke Leopold of Austria for imprisoning King Richard the Lionheart. Approved the Teutonic Order (1196)

176. 1198-1216. Born Lotario dei Conti di Segni in Gavignano, Lazio. The most powerful medieval pope; approved St. Francis and held the Fourth Lateran Council. He brought the medieval papacy to its height and, at the Fourth Lateran Council, gave the Church rules of faith and practice that still guide Catholics today. Lothar was elected at 37 and governed with energy across Christendom. He placed England under interdict until King John accepted Stephen Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury, and he arbitrated disputes among kings. He approved the first rule of St. Francis of Assisi (1209 or 1210) and encouraged St. Dominic. The Fourth Crusade he called turned against Constantinople (1204), which he condemned. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) defined transubstantiation, required yearly confession and Easter Communion, and reformed clergy. He also launched the Albigensian Crusade against the Cathars. Fourth Lateran Council (1215): yearly confession, Easter Communion, transubstantiation Approved St. Francis’ way of life (1209/1210) Called the Fourth Crusade and the Albigensian Crusade Lotario dei Conti di Segni is born at Gavignano, near Anagni Studies theology in Paris and law in Bologna Made a cardinal by his uncle, Clement III Elected at 37, on the day Celestine III died The Fourth Crusade, which he called, sacks Christian Constantinople; he condemns it Places England under interdict over the choice of the Archbishop of Canterbury Approves the way of life of St. Francis of Assisi and his first brothers King John of England submits and accepts Stephen Langton Annuls Magna Carta; in November opens the Fourth Lateran Council, with over 400 bishops Dies at Perugia Leo XIII moves his remains to the Lateran Basilica Every Christian of either sex, after reaching the age of discernment, should faithfully confess all his sins at least once a year to his own priest. Just as the founder of the universe established two great lights in the firmament of heaven, the greater to rule the day and the lesser to rule the night, so he set two great dignities in the firmament of the universal Church. He dreamed, the story goes, that the Lateran Basilica was falling and a small poor man held it up. Soon after, Francis of Assisi came to see him. Giotto painted the dream at Assisi. The Easter duty, to confess once a year and receive Communion at Easter, comes from his council. The night he died, thieves stripped his body of its rich vestments; a visiting bishop, Jacques de Vitry, found it almost naked in the church. He wrote a book, On the Misery of the Human Condition, before he became pope.

177. 1216-1227. Born Cencio Savelli in Rome. Approved the Dominicans (1216), the Franciscan Rule (1223) and the Carmelite rule.  Cencio, a gentle and learned administrator, compiled papal decrees and the Liber censuum, a record of Church revenues. He confirmed the Order of Preachers of St. Dominic in 1216 and the Rule of St. Francis in 1223 (the Regula bullata, still in use), and approved the rule of the Carmelites (1226). He crowned Frederick II emperor and urged the Fifth Crusade. Approved the Dominican Order (1216) Approved the Franciscan Rule (1223)

178. 1227-1241. Born Ugolino dei Conti di Segni in Anagni. Friend of St. Francis; canonized him, issued the Decretals and created the papal Inquisition.  Hugolino, nephew of Innocent III, was protector of the Franciscans and a friend of St. Francis and St. Clare. He canonized Francis (1228), Anthony of Padua (1232), Dominic (1234) and Elizabeth of Hungary (1235). He commissioned St. Raymond of Penyafort to compile the Decretals (1234), the core of Church law until 1917. He entrusted the hunt for heresy to Dominican and Franciscan inquisitors (1231), and fought long with Emperor Frederick II, whom he excommunicated twice. Canonized Sts. Francis, Anthony, Dominic and Elizabeth Decretals of Gregory IX (1234), basis of canon law until 1917 Papal Inquisition (1231)

179. 1241-1241. Born Goffredo da Castiglione in Milan. Elected in the first “conclave,” locked in by a Roman senator; died seventeen days later.  With Frederick II holding two cardinals prisoner, the ten remaining cardinals were locked in a ruinous palace in Rome by the senator Matteo Orsini, in heat and filth, until they chose an elderly Milanese, Godfrey. He died after seventeen days, before his coronation. The papacy then stood vacant for over eighteen months.

180. 1243-1254. Born Sinibaldo Fieschi in Genoa. Great canon lawyer; deposed Frederick II at the First Council of Lyon.  Sinibaldo, among the leading jurists of his age, fled to Lyon, where the First Council of Lyon (1245) declared Frederick II deposed. He sent Franciscan envoys, including John of Plano Carpini, to the Mongol Great Khan, gave cardinals their red hat, and sadly in 1252 authorized the use of torture by inquisitors in the bull Ad extirpanda. First Council of Lyon (1245) Sent envoys to the Mongols

181. 1254-1261. Born Rinaldo dei Conti di Segni in Jenne, Lazio. Canonized St. Clare and defended the mendicant friars at Paris.  Rinaldo, nephew of Gregory IX, canonized St. Clare of Assisi (1255), united several hermit groups into the Order of St. Augustine (the Grand Union, 1256), and defended the friars, including Sts. Thomas Aquinas and Bonaventure, against attacks at the University of Paris. Canonized St. Clare (1255) Grand Union of the Augustinian friars (1256)

182. 1261-1264. Born Jacques Pantaléon in Troyes, France. A shoemaker’s son who made Corpus Christi a feast for the whole Church.  Jacques, son of a cobbler from Troyes, had been Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem. Moved by the visions of St. Juliana of Liège and the reports of the miracle of Bolsena, he extended the feast of Corpus Christi to the whole Church with the bull Transiturus (1264); St. Thomas Aquinas composed its texts. He invited Charles of Anjou to take the Kingdom of Sicily from the Hohenstaufen. Instituted the feast of Corpus Christi (1264)

183. 1265-1268. Born Guy Foucois in Saint-Gilles, France. A widower and former lawyer to the King of France; patron of Roger Bacon.  Guy, a married lawyer in the service of St. Louis IX, became a priest after his wife died and rose to cardinal. As pope he crowned Charles of Anjou King of Sicily and asked the Franciscan Roger Bacon to send him his scientific works, the Opus Maius. His death began the longest vacancy in papal history, almost three years. Patron of Roger Bacon’s Opus Maius

184. 1271-1276. Born Teobaldo Visconti in Piacenza. Elected after nearly three years; created the conclave rules at the Second Council of Lyon.  The vacancy lasted until the people of Viterbo locked in the cardinals, reduced their food and took off the roof of the palace. They chose Theobald, not a cardinal and then on crusade in Acre. At the Second Council of Lyon (1274), attended by St. Bonaventure (St. Thomas Aquinas died on the way), he achieved a brief reunion with the Greeks and issued Ubi periculum, creating the conclave: cardinals locked in, with food reduced if they delayed. He was beatified in 1713. Second Council of Lyon (1274): brief reunion with the Greeks Created the conclave (Ubi periculum)

185. 1276-1276. Born Pierre de Tarentaise in Tarentaise, Savoy. The first Dominican pope, a theologian and colleague of St. Thomas.  Peter, a Dominican master at Paris, wrote a commentary on Peter Lombard’s Sentences and worked with St. Thomas on the order’s plan of studies. He preached at the funeral of St. Bonaventure. As pope for five months he tried to make peace among Italian cities. He was beatified in 1898. First Dominican pope

186. 1276-1276. Born Ottobuono Fieschi in Genoa. Died before being ordained priest, after suspending the strict conclave rules.  Ottobuono, nephew of Innocent IV, had been legate in England and helped make peace between Henry III and his barons. Elected as a deacon, he suspended Gregory X’s conclave rules and died five weeks later, before being ordained priest or crowned.

187. 1276-1277. Born Pedro Julião (Peter of Spain) in Lisbon. The only Portuguese pope, a physician and author of a famous logic textbook.  Peter of Spain is usually identified with the author of the Summulae logicales, the standard logic textbook of the late Middle Ages, and of the Thesaurus pauperum, a medical handbook. As pope he ordered an inquiry at Paris that led to Bishop Tempier’s condemnation of 219 propositions (1277). He died when the ceiling of a room he had added to the palace at Viterbo collapsed. He took the number XXI because of earlier confusion in the count of the Johns; there was no John XX. Only Portuguese pope Author of the Summulae logicales

188. 1277-1280. Born Giovanni Gaetano Orsini in Rome. First pope to live at the Vatican; Dante placed him among the simoniacs.  John, of the powerful Orsini family, made the Vatican the main papal residence and enlarged it. He issued Exiit qui seminat (1279), defining Franciscan poverty. He enriched his relatives so openly that Dante placed him head down among the simoniacs in the Inferno. Made the Vatican the main papal residence Exiit qui seminat on Franciscan poverty (1279)

189. 1281-1285. Born Simon de Brion in Brie, France. A French pope who backed Charles of Anjou and broke the union with the Greeks.  Simon, a former chancellor of France, was elected under Charles of Anjou’s pressure. He excommunicated Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos, which wrecked the union of Lyon, and supported Charles after the Sicilian Vespers (1282). He is called Martin IV because two popes named Marinus were mistakenly counted as Martins.

190. 1285-1287. Born Giacomo Savelli in Rome. Elderly Roman, crippled by gout, who encouraged the study of oriental languages.  James, a grand-nephew of Honorius III, was so crippled by gout that he said Mass seated. He supported the Franciscan and Dominican missions and planned schools of Arabic and other languages at Paris for missionaries.

191. 1288-1292. Born Girolamo Masci in Lisciano, near Ascoli. The first Franciscan pope; sent the first missionaries to China.  Jerome had been Minister General of the Franciscans. He sent John of Montecorvino to China (1289), where he became the first Archbishop of Peking, adorned Santa Maria Maggiore and the Lateran with mosaics, and founded the University of Montpellier. Acre, the last crusader stronghold, fell in 1291. First Franciscan pope Sent John of Montecorvino to China (1289)

192. 1294-1294. Born Pietro Angelerio (Pietro da Morrone) in Molise. The hermit pope who resigned after five months; a saint. A holy hermit called from his mountain to the papacy, he had the humility to lay it down, and left the Church a lasting gift of pardon. After a vacancy of over two years, the cardinals chose Peter of Morrone, an 84-year-old hermit and founder of the Celestine monks, after he wrote warning them of God’s judgment. Out of his depth and manipulated by Charles II of Naples, he issued a decree confirming a pope’s right to resign and then did so on 13 December 1294. His successor kept him confined at Fumone, where he died in 1296. He was canonized in 1313. He also established the Perdono of L’Aquila, a plenary indulgence still celebrated. Resigned the papacy (1294), after confirming a pope may do so Founded the Celestine monks; established the Perdono of L’Aquila Pietro Angelerio is born in Molise, the eleventh of twelve children Lives as a hermit on Mount Morrone, near Sulmona Gathers the hermits later called the Celestines Pope Nicholas IV dies; the see stays vacant for over two years Elected as an aged hermit, after writing to warn the cardinals of God’s judgment Crowned at L’Aquila; grants the Perdono, the pardon of Collemaggio Resigns the papacy Dies at Fumone Canonized by Clement V After the L’Aquila earthquake, Benedict XVI prays at his tomb and leaves his own pallium on it Benedict XVI left his pallium on Celestine’s tomb in 2009, four years before he resigned himself. He rode into L’Aquila for his coronation on a donkey. The Perdono he granted is still celebrated every August at Collemaggio, and is listed by UNESCO as intangible heritage. The rule he issued, that a pope may freely resign, was kept by his successor and remains in Church law.

193. 1294-1303. Born Benedetto Caetani in Anagni. Proclaimed the first Jubilee (1300) and issued Unam Sanctam; humiliated at Anagni. He began the Holy Years that still bring millions of pilgrims to Rome, and gave the Church a major book of law and the University of Rome. Benedict, a brilliant canon lawyer, proclaimed the first Holy Year in 1300, drawing huge crowds of pilgrims to Rome. He published the Liber Sextus of canon law and founded the University of Rome (La Sapienza, 1303). He clashed with King Philip IV of France over taxing the clergy, issuing the bull Unam Sanctam (1302), which asserts that submission to the Roman Pontiff is necessary for salvation. Philip’s agents seized him at Anagni in September 1303; he was freed by the townspeople but died weeks later. First Jubilee Year (1300) Bull Unam Sanctam (1302) Founded the University of Rome (1303) Benedetto Caetani is born at Anagni Created a cardinal Pope Celestine V resigns Elected at Naples Clericis laicos forbids rulers to tax the clergy without the pope’s consent Canonizes King Louis IX of France Publishes the Liber Sextus of canon law Proclaims the first Holy Year Unam Sanctam Founds the University of Rome Seized at Anagni by agents of King Philip IV Dies in Rome We declare, say, define and pronounce that it is altogether necessary for salvation for every human creature to be subject to the Roman Pontiff. The Holy Year he began in 1300 continues: the Church kept its most recent Jubilee in 2025. A fresco of him proclaiming the first Jubilee, attributed to Giotto, survives in the Lateran Basilica. He canonized St. Louis IX, the grandfather of the king who later had him seized. The university he founded is today La Sapienza, one of the largest in Europe.

194. 1303-1304. Born Niccolò Boccasini in Treviso. Dominican Master who stood by Boniface VIII at Anagni; a peacemaker.  Nicholas, son of a notary and Master General of the Dominicans, was one of two cardinals who stayed with Boniface VIII at Anagni. As pope he lifted some of Boniface’s penalties on France while excommunicating those who had assaulted Boniface. He died after eight months, possibly poisoned. He was beatified in 1736.

195. 1305-1314. Born Bertrand de Got in Villandraut, Gascony (France). The first Avignon pope; suppressed the Knights Templar at the Council of Vienne.  Bertrand, Archbishop of Bordeaux, was crowned in Lyon and never went to Rome; from 1309 he lived at Avignon, beginning about seventy years of papal residence there. Under pressure from Philip IV he allowed the trial of the Knights Templar and suppressed the order at the Council of Vienne (1311-1312) without condemning it. He founded universities and appointed many relatives as cardinals. Began the Avignon papacy (1309) Council of Vienne (1311-1312); suppression of the Templars

196. 1316-1334. Born Jacques Duèze in Cahors, France. Organized the papal administration at Avignon; clashed with the Franciscan Spirituals.  Elected at 72 after a two-year vacancy, Jacques ruled for eighteen years with great energy. He centralized church finances and appointments, canonized St. Thomas Aquinas (1323), and condemned the Franciscan Spirituals’ teaching that Christ and the Apostles owned nothing. Late in life he preached that the souls of the just would not see God until the Last Judgment; he withdrew this opinion on his deathbed, and his successor defined the opposite. Canonized St. Thomas Aquinas (1323) Organized the Curia at Avignon

197. 1334-1342. Born Jacques Fournier in Saverdun, France. A Cistercian reformer who defined the beatific vision and began the Palace of the Popes.  A Cistercian theologian, Jacques had led a careful inquisition in the Pyrenees whose records survive. His constitution Benedictus Deus (1336) defined that the souls of the just see God face to face before the final resurrection. He reformed the religious orders and began building the Palace of the Popes in Avignon. Constitution Benedictus Deus on the beatific vision (1336) Began the Palace of the Popes in Avignon

198. 1342-1352. Born Pierre Roger in Maumont, Limousin (France). A generous, splendid pope who protected the Jews during the Black Death.  Peter, a Benedictine and brilliant preacher, bought Avignon from Queen Joanna of Naples in 1348 and lived in lavish style. When the Black Death struck, he stayed at his post, provided for burials and care of the sick, and issued bulls (1348) condemning those who blamed the Jews for the plague and forbidding violence against them. He set Jubilees every fifty years and taught the doctrine of the Church’s treasury of merits (Unigenitus, 1343). Protected the Jews during the Black Death (1348) Purchased Avignon for the papacy

199. 1352-1362. Born Étienne Aubert in Les Monts, Limousin (France). A reforming lawyer who sent Cardinal Albornoz to recover the Papal States.  Stephen cut back the luxury of the Avignon court and sent Cardinal Gil Álvarez de Albornoz to Italy, who reconquered the Papal States and issued their constitutions (1357). He helped negotiate the Treaty of Brétigny between England and France (1360). Recovered the Papal States through Cardinal Albornoz

200. 1362-1370. Born Guillaume de Grimoard in Grizac, Languedoc (France). A Benedictine abbot who briefly brought the papacy back to Rome.  William, abbot of Saint-Victor in Marseille, kept living as a monk. He returned to Rome in 1367, the first pope there in sixty years, and received the Byzantine emperor John V Palaiologos, who professed the Catholic faith. Unrest in Italy and the French cardinals drew him back to Avignon in 1370, against the warnings of St. Bridget of Sweden, and he died soon after. He founded universities and colleges. He was beatified in 1870. Returned to Rome (1367-1370)

201. 1370-1378. Born Pierre Roger de Beaufort in Maumont, Limousin (France). Returned the papacy to Rome in 1377, urged by St. Catherine of Siena. Moved by the prayers and pleading of St. Catherine of Siena, he brought the papacy home to Rome after nearly seventy years in Avignon. Nephew of Clement VI, Peter was made a cardinal at about 18 and became a fine canonist. Urged by St. Catherine of Siena, who came to Avignon, he returned the papal court to Rome, entering on 17 January 1377. He condemned propositions of John Wycliffe (1377). He was the last French pope. Returned the papacy to Rome (1377) Last French pope Pierre Roger de Beaufort is born at Maumont, in the Limousin Made a cardinal by his uncle, Clement VI, at about 18 Elected at Avignon Ordained a priest, days after his election St. Catherine of Siena comes to Avignon and urges his return to Rome Leaves Avignon Enters Rome Condemns propositions of John Wycliffe Dies in Rome; the disputed election that follows begins the Great Western Schism He was the last French pope. He was the last pope to live in Avignon; since him, popes have lived in Rome. His tomb in Santa Francesca Romana, in the Roman Forum, shows his return to Rome in marble. St. Catherine of Siena wrote him letters calling him her “sweet babbo”, her dear father.

202. 1378-1389. Born Bartolomeo Prignano in Naples. His harsh rule led French cardinals to elect a rival, starting the Great Western Schism.  Bartholomew, a capable official, was elected while a Roman crowd demanded an Italian. His violent temper alienated the cardinals; within months most of them declared his election invalid and chose Clement VII, who went to Avignon. Europe split between the two obediences. Urban later had five cardinals suspected of conspiracy tortured and killed. The Church recognizes him as the lawful pope. Beginning of the Western Schism (1378)

203. 1389-1404. Born Pietro Tomacelli in Naples. Roman pope of the Schism who held the Jubilees of 1390 and 1400.  Peter, elected young, restored papal control over Rome and the Papal States, fortified Castel Sant’Angelo and celebrated Jubilees in 1390 and 1400. He raised money by selling offices and indulgences, which damaged his name. He refused proposals for both popes to resign.

204. 1404-1406. Born Cosimo de’ Migliorati in Sulmona. Restored the University of Rome during the Schism.  Cosimo, a learned lawyer, promised to work to end the Schism but did little. He reorganized the University of Rome, adding the study of Greek. Riots forced him to flee Rome for a time.

205. 1406-1415. Born Angelo Correr in Venice. Resigned at the Council of Constance so the Western Schism could end.  Angelo, about eighty, was elected on condition that he would resign if his rival did. The two never met, and in 1409 the Council of Pisa deposed both and elected a third, making three claimants. In 1415 Gregory formally convoked the Council of Constance and then resigned, opening the way to a single election. He was the last pope to resign until Benedict XVI in 2013. Convoked and resigned before the Council of Constance (1415) Last pope to resign until 2013

206. 1417-1431. Born Oddone Colonna in Genazzano, Lazio. Elected at Constance, ending the Western Schism; rebuilt a ruined Rome. Elected by a whole council to end the Great Western Schism, he gave the Church one pope again and began to rebuild Rome. Oddo, of the Roman Colonna family, was elected on St. Martin’s Day 1417 by the cardinals and representatives of the nations at the Council of Constance, ending the Schism. He returned to a ruined Rome in 1420 and began restoring its churches, streets and government. He resisted the idea that councils stood above the pope and opposed the Hussites. End of the Western Schism (1417) Restored Rome after the Schism Oddo Colonna is born at Genazzano Made a cardinal by Innocent VII The Council of Constance opens, with three men claiming to be pope Gregory XII resigns and the council deposes the Pisan claimant The council deposes the Avignon claimant Elected on St. Martin’s Day by the cardinals with delegates of the nations Closes the Council of Constance Enters a ruined Rome and begins to restore it Dies in Rome He took the name Martin because he was elected on St. Martin’s Day. The conclave that chose him was the only one in which 30 delegates of the nations voted beside the cardinals. He is buried before the main altar of the Lateran Basilica, and visitors still toss coins onto his bronze tomb. He was the first pope from the great Roman Colonna family.

207. 1431-1447. Born Gabriele Condulmer in Venice. Presided over the Council of Florence, which reunited the Greek and Latin Churches for a time.  Gabriel, a Venetian nephew of Gregory XII, spent years in conflict with the Council of Basel, which claimed authority over the pope and finally elected an antipope. Eugene moved the council to Ferrara and then Florence (1438-1445), where the Byzantine emperor and Greek bishops agreed to reunion with Rome in Laetentur caeli (1439). Unions with the Armenians, Copts and others followed. The union with the Greeks did not last after the fall of Constantinople, but the council’s decrees on the sacraments and on papal primacy remained important. Council of Florence: reunion with the Greeks (Laetentur caeli, 1439) Decree for the Armenians on the seven sacraments (1439)

208. 1447-1455. Born Tommaso Parentucelli in Sarzana, Liguria. The first Renaissance pope; founded the Vatican Library.  Thomas, a scholar and book collector, ended the Basel schism when the antipope Felix V resigned (1449), and celebrated the Jubilee of 1450. He gathered Greek and Latin manuscripts, many saved from the East, and founded the Vatican Library. He planned the rebuilding of St. Peter’s and the Vatican. Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453 during his reign. Founded the Vatican Library Ended the schism of Basel (1449)

209. 1455-1458. Born Alfonso de Borja in Xàtiva, Valencia (Spain). The first Borgia pope; reopened Joan of Arc’s case, which declared her innocent.  Alfonso, a Spanish canon lawyer, worked to raise a crusade against the Ottomans; the victory at Belgrade (1456) led him to order the noon bells and extend the feast of the Transfiguration. He authorized the retrial that declared Joan of Arc innocent (1456). He made his nephew Rodrigo, later Alexander VI, a cardinal. Annulment of Joan of Arc’s condemnation (1456) Feast of the Transfiguration extended to the whole Church (1457)

210. 1458-1464. Born Enea Silvio Piccolomini in Corsignano (Pienza), near Siena. Humanist writer who became pope, rebuilt his birthplace as Pienza, and died organizing a crusade.  Aeneas Silvius was a famous humanist, poet and diplomat who had supported the Council of Basel before changing sides and becoming a priest. As pope he condemned appeals from the pope to a future council (Execrabilis, 1460). He rebuilt his native village as the model town of Pienza and wrote his Commentaries, the only autobiography by a pope in office. He died at Ancona waiting for a crusading fleet that never came. Bull Execrabilis (1460) Wrote his Commentaries; built Pienza

211. 1464-1471. Born Pietro Barbo in Venice. Built the Palazzo Venezia; quarreled with the humanists of the Roman Academy.  Peter, nephew of Eugene IV, built the Palazzo San Marco (now Palazzo Venezia). He suppressed the Roman Academy of humanists on suspicion of paganism and plotting. He set the Jubilee interval at 25 years, introduced carnival races on the Via del Corso, and first had cardinals wear red caps. Set Jubilees every 25 years

212. 1471-1484. Born Francesco della Rovere in Celle Ligure, near Savona. Franciscan theologian who built the Sistine Chapel and opened the Vatican Library to scholars.  Francis, Minister General of the Franciscans and a respected theologian, built the Sistine Chapel, named after him, and Ponte Sisto; he opened the Vatican Library to scholars and founded the Capitoline Museums. He approved the feast of the Immaculate Conception. He also practiced lavish nepotism, was involved in the Pazzi conspiracy against the Medici (1478), and authorized the Spanish Inquisition (1478), whose abuses he later protested. Built the Sistine Chapel Founded the Capitoline Museums Authorized the Spanish Inquisition (1478)

213. 1484-1492. Born Giovanni Battista Cybo in Genoa. Openly favored his children; his bull of 1484 encouraged the witch hunts.  John Baptist, father of children born before his ordination, married his son into the Medici family. His bull Summis desiderantes (1484) gave authority to two inquisitors in Germany, one of whom wrote the notorious Malleus maleficarum. He kept the Ottoman prince Cem as a hostage in return for payments from the Sultan.

214. 1492-1503. Born Rodrigo de Borja in Xàtiva, Valencia (Spain). Rodrigo Borgia: able administrator, notorious for his mistresses and his children.  Rodrigo, nephew of Callixtus III, served as vice-chancellor for 35 years. His election was secured with promises and gifts. He openly advanced his children, including Cesare and Lucrezia Borgia. He issued Inter caetera (1493) dividing new lands between Spain and Portugal, celebrated the Jubilee of 1500 and had Girolamo Savonarola, his fierce critic, excommunicated; Florence executed the friar in 1498. Inter caetera on the new lands (1493)

215. 1503-1503. Born Francesco Todeschini Piccolomini in Siena. Nephew of Pius II, a reformer who died 26 days after his election.  Francis was respected for his upright life and learning, and built the Piccolomini Library in Siena Cathedral. Old and ill, he was ordained priest and bishop after his election and died within a month.

216. 1503-1513. Born Giuliano della Rovere in Albisola, near Savona. The “warrior pope” who began the new St. Peter’s and commissioned Michelangelo and Raphael.  Julian, nephew of Sixtus IV, led armies in person to recover the Papal States and drive the French from Italy. He laid the foundation stone of the new St. Peter’s Basilica (1506) designed by Bramante, commissioned Michelangelo to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508-1512) and Raphael to fresco the Vatican rooms, and founded the Swiss Guard (1506). He called the Fifth Lateran Council (1512). Laid the foundation of the new St. Peter’s (1506) Commissioned the Sistine Chapel ceiling and the Raphael Rooms Founded the Swiss Guard (1506)

217. 1513-1521. Born Giovanni de’ Medici in Florence. Son of Lorenzo the Magnificent; excommunicated Martin Luther.  John, made a cardinal at 13, was a cultivated patron of art and learning. He closed the Fifth Lateran Council (1517), made the Concordat of Bologna with France (1516), and preached an indulgence to fund St. Peter’s, against which Luther posted his 95 Theses in 1517. He condemned Luther’s errors in Exsurge Domine (1520) and excommunicated him (1521). He gave Henry VIII the title “Defender of the Faith.” Excommunicated Martin Luther (1521) Concluded the Fifth Lateran Council (1517)

218. 1522-1523. Born Adriaan Florensz Boeyens in Utrecht (Netherlands). The last non-Italian pope until John Paul II; admitted the Church’s guilt in the crisis.  Adrian, a theologian from Louvain and tutor of Emperor Charles V, kept his own name as pope. Austere and reforming, he instructed his legate at the Diet of Nuremberg (1522) to confess that the evils of the Church had begun “in the Roman Curia.” He died before his reforms could take hold, and was the last non-Italian pope until 1978. Admitted the Curia’s guilt in the Church’s crisis (1522) Last non-Italian pope until 1978

219. 1523-1534. Born Giulio de’ Medici in Florence. Pope during the Sack of Rome (1527) and Henry VIII’s break with Rome.  Julius, cousin of Leo X, was caught between France and Charles V. In 1527 Imperial troops sacked Rome while he took refuge in Castel Sant’Angelo; the Swiss Guard died defending him. He refused to annul Henry VIII’s marriage to Catherine of Aragon, and England broke with Rome. He commissioned Michelangelo’s Last Judgment and approved the Capuchins (1528). Sack of Rome (1527) Refused Henry VIII’s annulment; English schism Approved the Capuchin Franciscans (1528)

220. 1534-1549. Born Alessandro Farnese in Canino, Lazio. Opened the Council of Trent and approved the Jesuits. He opened the Catholic Reform: he approved the Jesuits, called the Council of Trent and defended the dignity of the native peoples of the Americas. Alexander, a Renaissance prince with children born before his ordination, became the first pope of the Catholic Reform. He named reforming cardinals such as Contarini, Pole and Carafa, approved the Society of Jesus (1540), set up the Roman Inquisition (1542) and opened the Council of Trent (1545). In Sublimis Deus (1537) he declared that the peoples of the Americas are true human beings who must not be enslaved. He commissioned Michelangelo to complete St. Peter’s. Opened the Council of Trent (1545) Approved the Society of Jesus (1540) Sublimis Deus on the dignity of the American peoples (1537) Alessandro Farnese is born at Canino Made a cardinal by Alexander VI Ordained a priest Elected pope Michelangelo begins the Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel Sublimis Deus defends the freedom of the peoples of the Americas; a commission reports on Church reform Approves the Society of Jesus The Last Judgment is unveiled Founds the Roman Inquisition Opens the Council of Trent Makes Michelangelo the architect of St. Peter’s Dies in Rome The Indians and all other peoples who may later be discovered by Christians are by no means to be deprived of their liberty or of their property, even though they are outside the faith of Jesus Christ. He was born on 29 February. Titian painted him several times; his portrait with his grandsons hangs in Naples. His tomb by Guglielmo della Porta stands beside the Chair of St. Peter in the apse of the basilica. St. Ignatius of Loyola and his first companions offered themselves to him, and he approved their order.

221. 1550-1555. Born Giovanni Maria Ciocchi del Monte in Rome. Reopened the Council of Trent; built the Villa Giulia.  John Mary, a former president of Trent, reopened the council (1551-1552) and confirmed the Jesuits again. Mary Tudor restored Catholicism in England in his time. He built the Villa Giulia and named Palestrina choirmaster of the Julian Chapel. His favor to a young adopted relative was a scandal.

222. 1555-1555. Born Marcello Cervini in Montefano, Marche. Reformer who reigned 22 days; Palestrina’s Missa Papae Marcelli honors him.  Marcellus, a learned reformer and former president of Trent, kept his own name and began cutting the court’s expenses. He died after three weeks. Palestrina’s famous Mass for Pope Marcellus was dedicated to his memory.

223. 1555-1559. Born Gian Pietro Carafa in Capriglia Irpina, Campania. Severe reformer; co-founder of the Theatines, he created the Roman ghetto and the Index.  John Peter co-founded the Theatine order with St. Cajetan. As pope, at 79, he fought corruption fiercely but harshly. He confined the Jews of Rome to a ghetto (Cum nimis absurdum, 1555), issued the first Roman Index of Forbidden Books (1559), and fought a disastrous war with Spain. The Romans rioted at his death. Co-founded the Theatines First Roman Index of Forbidden Books (1559)

224. 1559-1565. Born Giovanni Angelo Medici in Milan. Closed the Council of Trent with the help of his nephew St. Charles Borromeo.  John Angelo (not of the Florentine Medici) reconvened the Council of Trent in 1562, guided by his nephew St. Charles Borromeo, and closed it in 1563. He confirmed its decrees, issued the Profession of Faith of Trent (1564) and a new Index. He commissioned Michelangelo to turn the Baths of Diocletian into Santa Maria degli Angeli. Concluded and confirmed the Council of Trent (1563-1564) Tridentine Profession of Faith (1564)

225. 1566-1572. Born Antonio (Michele) Ghislieri in Bosco Marengo, Piedmont. Dominican saint who carried out Trent: the Catechism, Breviary and Missal; the victory of Lepanto. He turned the decisions of the Council of Trent into daily life: the catechism, breviary and Missal he gave the Church shaped Catholic worship for four hundred years. Michael Ghislieri, a shepherd boy who became a Dominican friar and Grand Inquisitor, lived as a friar while pope. He put the Council of Trent into effect: the Roman Catechism (1566), the Breviary (1568) and the Roman Missal (Quo primum, 1570), which remained in use until 1970. He named St. Thomas Aquinas a Doctor of the Church. He formed the Holy League that defeated the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto (7 October 1571), asked Christians to pray the Rosary for victory, and established the feast of Our Lady of Victory, now Our Lady of the Rosary. He excommunicated Elizabeth I of England (1570). Canonized in 1712. Roman Catechism (1566), Breviary (1568) and Missal (1570) Holy League and the victory of Lepanto (1571); feast of the Rosary Declared St. Thomas Aquinas a Doctor of the Church (1567) Antonio Ghislieri is born at Bosco, in Piedmont, to a poor family; he tends sheep as a boy Joins the Dominicans at 14, taking the name Michele Ordained a priest Bishop of Sutri and Nepi Created a cardinal Elected pope Publishes the Roman Catechism of the Council of Trent Declares St. Thomas Aquinas a Doctor of the Church Publishes the reformed Roman Breviary Publishes the Roman Missal with the bull Quo primum The Holy League he formed wins at Lepanto; he gives thanks with a new feast of Our Lady Dies in Rome Canonized by Clement XI We grant and concede in perpetuity that, for the singing or reading of Mass in any church whatsoever, this Missal may be followed absolutely. He kept wearing his white Dominican habit as pope; tradition says this is why popes wear white. He walked barefoot in Rome’s processions and kept a friar’s fasts throughout his reign. Tradition says that on the day of Lepanto he broke off a meeting, went to the window and told those present that the Christian fleet had won, long before any messenger arrived. His body rests in a glass and silver tomb in St. Mary Major, where pilgrims can see it. The feast he founded for Lepanto became the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary, kept on 7 October.

226. 1572-1585. Born Ugo Boncompagni in Bologna. Gave the world the Gregorian calendar (1582) and founded the Gregorian University. His calendar still orders the year for most of the world, and the colleges he founded trained priests for the whole Church. Hugh, a law professor and former member of the Council of Trent, became a reformer after ordination. He introduced the Gregorian calendar in 1582, dropping ten days to bring Easter back in line with the seasons. He founded the Roman College (now the Gregorian University) and many national colleges for training priests, including the German and English Colleges, and expanded the network of nuncios. He also ordered a Te Deum after the St. Bartholomew’s Day Massacre (1572), a lasting stain on his memory. Gregorian calendar (1582) Founded the Gregorian University and the national colleges in Rome Ugo Boncompagni is born at Bologna Teaches law at the University of Bologna Serves as an expert in canon law at the Council of Trent Created a cardinal Elected pope Refounds the German College in Rome Founds the English College in Rome Inter gravissimas announces the new calendar Thursday 4 October is followed by Friday 15 October Builds a new home for the Roman College, later named the Gregorian University after him Dies in Rome The Gregorian calendar is named after him; Gregorian chant is named after Gregory I. Turkey adopted his calendar in 1926; Britain and its colonies had waited until 1752. The Tower of the Winds in the Vatican was built in his time for the astronomers working on the calendar. The dragon of his coat of arms can be spotted on buildings all over Rome.

227. 1585-1590. Born Felice Peretti in Grottammare, Marche. Franciscan swineherd’s son who rebuilt Rome and organized the Curia into congregations. In five tireless years he restored order and water to Rome, finished the dome of St. Peter’s and gave the Curia the shape it kept for centuries. Felix, born poor, became a Franciscan preacher. In five years he cleared the Papal States of bandits, laid out the straight streets that join Rome’s great basilicas, raised the Egyptian obelisks, including the one in St. Peter’s Square, completed the dome of St. Peter’s and built the Acqua Felice aqueduct. He fixed the College of Cardinals at seventy and organized the Curia into fifteen congregations (1588). Reorganized the Curia into congregations (1588) Completed the dome of St. Peter’s; raised the Vatican obelisk Felice Peretti is born at Grottammare to a poor family Enters the Franciscan friars at Montalto Ordained a priest; becomes a famous preacher Bishop of Sant’Agata dei Goti Created a cardinal by Pius V Elected pope The obelisk is raised in St. Peter’s Square Fixes the College of Cardinals at seventy The Acqua Felice aqueduct brings water back to the hills of Rome Organizes the Curia into fifteen congregations The dome of St. Peter’s is completed Dies in Rome As a boy he looked after pigs, and he never forgot his poor beginnings. Raising the obelisk in St. Peter’s Square took about 900 men and many horses, working in silence to hear the commands. Legend says he came to the conclave leaning on a stick like a frail old man, and threw it away once elected. He built the great hall of the Vatican Library that is still in use.

228. 1590-1590. Born Giovanni Battista Castagna in Rome. The shortest reign in papal history: thirteen days.  John Baptist, a respected diplomat, died of malaria before his coronation. In his few days he banned tobacco use in and near churches, the first known smoking ban, and left his fortune to provide dowries for poor girls. Shortest pontificate in history (13 days)

229. 1590-1591. Born Niccolò Sfondrati in Somma Lombardo, near Milan. Supported the Catholic League in France against the Protestant Henry of Navarre.  Nicholas, a friend of St. Charles Borromeo and St. Philip Neri, sent money and troops to the Catholic League in France and renewed the excommunication of Henry of Navarre. He ordered that cardinals be given the red biretta and forbade betting on papal elections.

230. 1591-1591. Born Giovanni Antonio Facchinetti in Bologna. A reforming lawyer who reigned two months.  John Anthony, a canonist who had attended Trent, reorganized the Secretariat of State into sections before dying two months after his election.

231. 1592-1605. Born Ippolito Aldobrandini in Fano, Marche. Reconciled Henry IV of France and published the Clementine Vulgate.  Hippolytus, a friend and penitent of St. Philip Neri, absolved Henry IV of France after his conversion (1595), ending the French wars of religion. He issued the Sixto-Clementine Vulgate (1592), the official Latin Bible until 1979, and revised liturgical books. The Union of Brest (1595-1596) brought the Ruthenian Church into communion with Rome. Giordano Bruno was burned in Rome during his reign (1600). Sixto-Clementine Vulgate (1592) Union of Brest with the Ruthenian Church (1595)

232. 1605-1605. Born Alessandro Ottaviano de’ Medici in Florence. A Medici reformer, disciple of St. Philip Neri, who died after 27 days.  Alexander, a disciple of St. Philip Neri, caught a chill during the ceremony of taking possession of the Lateran and died less than a month after his election.

233. 1605-1621. Born Camillo Borghese in Rome. Completed St. Peter’s façade and nave; warned Galileo in 1616.  Camillo, a jurist, put Venice under interdict in a dispute over church immunities (1606). He finished the nave and façade of St. Peter’s, which bears his name, and the Pauline Chapel in Santa Maria Maggiore. During his reign the Holy Office warned Galileo not to hold Copernicanism as fact (1616). He issued the Roman Ritual (1614) and canonized St. Charles Borromeo. Completed the façade of St. Peter’s (1612) Published the Roman Ritual (1614)

234. 1621-1623. Born Alessandro Ludovisi in Bologna. Founded Propaganda Fide and canonized Ignatius, Francis Xavier, Teresa and Philip Neri.  Alexander, a former Jesuit student, created the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith (Propaganda Fide, 1622) to direct missions worldwide. On 12 March 1622 he canonized Sts. Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila, Philip Neri and Isidore the Farmer. His bull Aeterni Patris (1621) required secret written ballots in conclaves. Founded Propaganda Fide (1622) Canonized Ignatius, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila and Philip Neri (1622)

235. 1623-1644. Born Maffeo Barberini in Florence. Consecrated the new St. Peter’s; patron of Bernini; the pope of Galileo’s trial.  Maffeo, a poet and patron of the arts, consecrated the new St. Peter’s (1626) and commissioned Bernini’s bronze baldacchino. He reformed the procedures for beatification and canonization. Once friendly to Galileo, he felt mocked by the Dialogue (1632), and the Holy Office condemned Galileo in 1633. His nephews enriched themselves, and the Romans joked that “what the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.” Consecrated the new St. Peter’s (1626) Galileo’s trial (1633) Rules on beatification and canonization (1625, 1634)

236. 1644-1655. Born Giovanni Battista Pamphili in Rome. Condemned Jansenism; built Piazza Navona’s church and fountains.  John Baptist, a lawyer, protested the Peace of Westphalia (1648) for its treatment of the Church. His bull Cum occasione (1653) condemned five Jansenist propositions. He built Sant’Agnese in Agone and Bernini’s Fountain of the Four Rivers in Piazza Navona. Velázquez painted his famous portrait. His sister-in-law Olimpia Maidalchini exercised great influence over him. Condemned Jansenism (Cum occasione, 1653)

237. 1655-1667. Born Fabio Chigi in Siena. Commissioned Bernini’s colonnade of St. Peter’s Square.  Fabio, a former nuncio at the Westphalia negotiations, commissioned Bernini’s colonnade around St. Peter’s Square and the Cathedra Petri in the apse. He received Queen Christina of Sweden after her conversion (1655) and supported the teaching of the Immaculate Conception (Sollicitudo omnium Ecclesiarum, 1661). Bernini’s colonnade and Chair of Peter Bull on the Immaculate Conception (1661)

238. 1667-1669. Born Giulio Rospigliosi in Pistoia. Playwright pope who negotiated the Clementine Peace with the Jansenists.  Julius wrote libretti for operas, including the first comic opera. He negotiated a truce in the Jansenist dispute (the Clementine Peace, 1669) and gave large sums to defend Crete against the Ottomans. He commissioned Bernini’s angels on Ponte Sant’Angelo. Clementine Peace (1669)

239. 1670-1676. Born Emilio Altieri in Rome. Elected at 79; canonized St. Rose of Lima, the first saint of the Americas.  Emilio was nearly eighty and left much to his adopted relative, Cardinal Paluzzi Altieri. He canonized St. Rose of Lima (1671), the first saint born in the Americas, and Francis Borgia, celebrated the Jubilee of 1675 and supported King Jan Sobieski of Poland against the Turks. Canonized St. Rose of Lima (1671)

240. 1676-1689. Born Benedetto Odescalchi in Como. Holy reformer who united Europe to save Vienna from the Turks in 1683. A humble and frugal pope, he reformed the papal court, encouraged frequent Communion and spent the Holy See’s own funds to defend Christian Europe. Benedict lived simply, cut the costs of the papal court, fought nepotism and encouraged frequent Communion. He built the alliance that relieved the siege of Vienna in 1683, a victory celebrated with the feast of the Holy Name of Mary, and the Holy League that freed Hungary. He resisted Louis XIV’s claims over the French Church (Gallicanism) and criticized his persecution of Protestants. He was beatified in 1956. Relief of Vienna (1683) through his Holy League Fought nepotism and Gallicanism Benedetto Odescalchi is born at Como Created a cardinal by Innocent X Bishop of Novara Elected pope Encourages frequent Communion Rejects the Gallican Articles of the French clergy The relief of Vienna, by an army he helped to unite Extends the feast of the Holy Name of Mary to the whole Church Forms the Holy League with the Emperor, Poland and Venice Dies in Rome Beatified by Pius XII He cut the costs of the papal court and refused to enrich his own family. After the relief of Vienna, King John III Sobieski wrote to him: “We came, we saw, God conquered.” The feast of the Holy Name of Mary on 12 September recalls the day of Vienna. His body rests in St. Peter’s Basilica, where pilgrims can see it.

241. 1689-1691. Born Pietro Vito Ottoboni in Venice. Condemned Gallicanism and enriched the Vatican Library.  Peter, an elderly canonist, returned to nepotism. He condemned the Four Gallican Articles of 1682 and Jansenist propositions, and bought the library of Queen Christina of Sweden for the Vatican.

242. 1691-1700. Born Antonio Pignatelli in Spinazzola, Apulia. Abolished papal nepotism with the bull Romanum decet Pontificem (1692).  Anthony, a Neapolitan noble, declared “the poor are my nephews” and in 1692 forbade popes to give estates, offices or income to relatives, ending the office of cardinal-nephew. He opened a hospice for the poor at the Lateran, reconciled with Louis XIV, and condemned propositions of Fénelon’s quietism (1699). Abolished papal nepotism (1692)

243. 1700-1721. Born Giovanni Francesco Albani in Urbino. Condemned Jansenism (Unigenitus) and the Chinese Rites; extended the Immaculate Conception feast.  John Francis, a scholar who accepted only after days of hesitation, issued Unigenitus (1713) condemning 101 propositions of the Jansenist Quesnel, and banned the Chinese Rites (1715). He made the feast of the Immaculate Conception a holy day for the whole Church (1708) and was caught in the War of the Spanish Succession. Bull Unigenitus against Jansenism (1713) Immaculate Conception a universal feast of obligation (1708)

244. 1721-1724. Born Michelangelo dei Conti in Poli, Lazio. Last pope from the Conti family; forbade the Jesuits to receive novices in China.  Michelangelo, a former nuncio, upheld Unigenitus and restricted the Jesuits for not observing the ban on the Chinese Rites. He supported the exiled Stuart claimant James III.

245. 1724-1730. Born Pietro Francesco (Vincenzo Maria) Orsini in Gravina in Puglia. A Dominican who lived as a friar and pastor; poorly served by his ministers.  Peter Francis gave up his inheritance to become a Dominican and was a devoted pastor as Archbishop of Benevento. As pope he kept up his religious life, visited the sick and ordered Roman clergy to wear clerical dress. He left government to Cardinal Niccolò Coscia, who abused his trust. The Spanish Steps were completed in his time. His cause of beatification is open.

246. 1730-1740. Born Lorenzo Corsini in Florence. Blind for much of his reign; built the Trevi Fountain and condemned Freemasonry.  Lawrence went blind early in his reign but governed from his bed. He condemned Freemasonry (In eminenti, 1738), the first papal ban, began the Trevi Fountain and the Lateran façade, and opened the Capitoline Museum to the public (1734), among the first public museums in Europe. First papal condemnation of Freemasonry (1738) Commissioned the Trevi Fountain and the Lateran façade

247. 1740-1758. Born Prospero Lorenzo Lambertini in Bologna. Brilliant scholar and canonist, admired even by Voltaire; issued the first modern encyclicals.  Prosper was elected after a six-month conclave, reportedly after joking: “If you want a saint, elect Gotti; a statesman, Aldobrandini; an honest man, me.” His great work on canonization, De servorum Dei beatificatione, is still used. He wrote what is considered the first modern encyclical (Ubi primum, 1740), condemned usury in Vix pervenit (1745), settled the Chinese and Malabar Rites, supported science and the University of Bologna, and was praised by Protestants and by Voltaire. First modern encyclical (Ubi primum, 1740) Encyclical on usury Vix pervenit (1745) Classic work on beatification and canonization

248. 1758-1769. Born Carlo della Torre di Rezzonico in Venice. Defended the Jesuits as Catholic kingdoms expelled them.  Charles, a pious and gentle pope, defended the Society of Jesus with the bull Apostolicum pascendi (1765) when Portugal, France, Spain and Naples expelled it. He approved a Mass and Office of the Sacred Heart for Poland and Rome (1765). He had fig leaves added to classical nude statues in the Vatican. Defended the Jesuits (Apostolicum pascendi, 1765) Approved the liturgical feast of the Sacred Heart for some places (1765)

249. 1769-1774. Born Giovanni Vincenzo Antonio (Lorenzo) Ganganelli in Santarcangelo di Romagna. A Franciscan who suppressed the Jesuits under pressure from the Catholic kings.  Lawrence Ganganelli, a Conventual Franciscan theologian, was elected amid the Bourbon kings’ demand to abolish the Jesuits. In 1773, with the brief Dominus ac Redemptor, he suppressed the Society of Jesus worldwide. It survived in Russia and Prussia, where the rulers would not publish the brief. He founded the Pio-Clementine Museum in the Vatican. Suppressed the Society of Jesus (1773) Founded the Pio-Clementine Museum

250. 1775-1799. Born Giovanni Angelo Braschi in Cesena. Faced the French Revolution and died a prisoner of the French at Valence.  John Angel drained the Pontine Marshes and enlarged the Vatican Museums. He traveled to Vienna (1782) to argue against Emperor Joseph II’s control of the Church, without success. He condemned the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (1791) and the Jansenist Synod of Pistoia (Auctorem fidei, 1794). In 1798 French troops occupied Rome, declared a republic and carried the 81-year-old pope off to France, where he died at Valence. His reign of 24 and a half years was then the longest since St. Peter. Condemned the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (1791) Bull Auctorem fidei (1794) Died a prisoner in France (1799)

251. 1800-1823. Born Barnaba Niccolò Maria Luigi (Gregorio) Chiaramonti in Cesena. Signed the Concordat with Napoleon, endured years of captivity, and restored the Jesuits.  Gregory Chiaramonti, a Benedictine, was elected in Venice in 1800 while Rome was occupied. He signed the Concordat of 1801 with Napoleon, restoring the Church in France, and attended Napoleon’s coronation (1804). When he refused to join the blockade against England, the French annexed the Papal States (1809) and held him prisoner at Savona and Fontainebleau for five years. He returned to Rome in 1814, restored the Society of Jesus (Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum) and, after Napoleon’s fall, sheltered members of Napoleon’s family. His cause of beatification is open. Concordat with Napoleon (1801) Prisoner of Napoleon (1809-1814) Restored the Society of Jesus (1814)

252. 1823-1829. Born Annibale Sermattei della Genga in Genga, Marche. Strict ruler of the Papal States who held the Jubilee of 1825 and rebuilt St. Paul’s.  Annibale, a diplomat, governed the Papal States severely, policing morals and limiting the freedom of the Jews in the ghetto. He held the Jubilee of 1825, the first in fifty years, began rebuilding the Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls after the fire of 1823, and returned the Roman College to the Jesuits. He condemned secret societies and Bible societies. Jubilee of 1825 Began rebuilding St. Paul Outside the Walls

253. 1829-1830. Born Francesco Saverio Castiglioni in Cingoli, Marche. A gentle canonist who saw Catholic Emancipation in Britain.  Francis Xavier, a learned canonist, reigned twenty months. He condemned indifferentism and secret societies in Traditi humilitati (1829), welcomed Catholic Emancipation in Britain (1829), and in a careful brief (1830) allowed mixed marriages in Prussia only if the Catholic party’s faith was protected. Encyclical Traditi humilitati (1829)

254. 1831-1846. Born Bartolomeo Alberto (Mauro) Cappellari in Belluno. A Camaldolese monk who expanded the missions and condemned the slave trade.  Maurus Cappellari, a Camaldolese monk and Prefect of Propaganda Fide, was the last pope not already a bishop when elected. He faced revolution in the Papal States and resisted liberal ideas, condemning the views of Lamennais in Mirari vos (1832). He gave a strong push to the missions, creating many dioceses and vicariates, and condemned the slave trade in In supremo apostolatus (1839). He founded the Etruscan and Egyptian museums in the Vatican. His opposition to railways, which he called “chemins d’enfer,” is often quoted. Condemned the slave trade (In supremo apostolatus, 1839) Great expansion of the missions Encyclical Mirari vos (1832)

255. 1846-1878. Born Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti in Senigallia, Marche. The longest documented reign; defined the Immaculate Conception and held the First Vatican Council. In the longest certain reign in history he saw the end of the Papal States and gave the Church two lasting gifts: the dogma of the Immaculate Conception and the First Vatican Council. Pio Nono began as a reformer welcomed by liberals, but the revolution of 1848, the murder of his minister Pellegrino Rossi and his flight to Gaeta changed him. He defined the dogma of the Immaculate Conception (Ineffabilis Deus, 1854) and issued the Syllabus of Errors with Quanta cura (1864). He restored the Catholic hierarchy in England (1850) and the Netherlands (1853). The First Vatican Council (1869-1870) defined papal primacy and infallibility (Pastor Aeternus) and taught on faith and reason (Dei Filius). Italian troops took Rome on 20 September 1870, ending the Papal States, and Pius lived as a “prisoner in the Vatican.” His reign of 31 years and 7 months is the longest documented in history. He was beatified in 2000. Dogma of the Immaculate Conception (1854) First Vatican Council: papal infallibility and Dei Filius (1870) Loss of the Papal States (1870) Restored the hierarchy in England and the Netherlands Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti is born at Senigallia Ordained a priest after recovering from epilepsy Travels to Chile with a papal mission, until 1825 Archbishop of Spoleto Created a cardinal Elected pope, and welcomed as a reformer After the murder of his minister Pellegrino Rossi, flees Rome in disguise to Gaeta Returns to Rome Defines the dogma of the Immaculate Conception Quanta cura and the Syllabus of Errors Opens the First Vatican Council The Council defines papal infallibility (Pastor aeternus) Italian troops take Rome; he calls himself a prisoner in the Vatican Dies after a reign of 31 years Beatified by John Paul II, on the same day as John XXIII The most Blessed Virgin Mary, in the first instance of her conception, by a singular grace and privilege granted by Almighty God, in view of the merits of Jesus Christ, the Savior of the human race, was preserved free from all stain of original sin. He was the first future pope to set foot in the Americas, on a papal mission to Chile in the 1820s. His reign of 31 years and 7 months is the longest of any pope whose dates are certain. Four years after he defined the Immaculate Conception, the Lady who appeared at Lourdes told St. Bernadette: “I am the Immaculate Conception.” Epilepsy almost kept him from the priesthood; he was ordained only after it eased. He was beatified on the same day as John XXIII, the pope who opened the next Vatican Council.

256. 1878-1903. Born Vincenzo Gioacchino Pecci in Carpineto Romano, Lazio. Founder of modern Catholic social teaching with Rerum Novarum; revived the study of St. Thomas. He brought the Church into the industrial age: Rerum Novarum gave workers a voice and began the social teaching every pope since has built on. Elected at 67 and expected to be a short “caretaker,” Leo reigned 25 years and wrote 86 encyclicals. Aeterni Patris (1879) restored the philosophy of St. Thomas Aquinas to Catholic schools. Rerum Novarum (1891) defended the rights of workers to a just wage and to form unions, and the right of private property, against both unbridled capitalism and socialism, founding modern Catholic social teaching. He opened the Vatican Secret Archives to scholars (1881), encouraged biblical studies (Providentissimus Deus, 1893), promoted the Rosary in twelve encyclicals, wrote the Prayer to St. Michael, and consecrated the world to the Sacred Heart (1899). He declared Anglican orders invalid (Apostolicae curae, 1896). He was the first pope filmed and recorded. Rerum Novarum (1891), founding modern Catholic social teaching Aeterni Patris (1879), revival of Thomism Opened the Vatican Archives to scholars (1881) Consecrated the world to the Sacred Heart (1899) Vincenzo Pecci is born at Carpineto Romano Ordained a priest Governs Benevento for the Papal States and clears it of bandits Nuncio to Belgium, and an archbishop Bishop of Perugia, which he leads for 32 years Created a cardinal Elected pope at 67 Aeterni Patris revives the study of St. Thomas Aquinas; he makes John Henry Newman a cardinal Opens the Vatican Archives to scholars Orders prayers after Low Mass, among them the Prayer to St. Michael Rerum Novarum, on capital and labor Filmed in the Vatican Gardens, the first pope on film Consecrates the human race to the Sacred Heart Dies at 93 Each needs the other: capital cannot do without labor, nor labor without capital. Wages ought not to be insufficient to support a frugal and well-behaved wage-earner. He blessed the camera that filmed him in 1896, at 86. He is one of the earliest-born people ever caught on film. You can still hear his voice: he was recorded praying the Ave Maria aloud in 1903, the year he died. Of all popes whose birth dates are certain, he is the oldest ever to reign: he died in office at 93. He wrote Latin poetry all his life, and published it. His reign of 25 years is the third longest that can be dated with certainty, after Pius IX and John Paul II.

257. 1903-1914. Born Giuseppe Melchiorre Sarto in Riese, Veneto. The parish-priest pope: frequent Communion, children’s First Communion, and the fight against Modernism. A parish priest at heart, he opened the Eucharist to children and to daily communicants, and taught that holiness is for every Catholic. Joseph Sarto, a postman’s son, was a parish priest, seminary director, Bishop of Mantua and Patriarch of Venice. His motto was “to restore all things in Christ.” He encouraged frequent, even daily, Communion (1905) and lowered the age of First Communion to the age of reason (Quam singulari, 1910). He reformed church music, restoring Gregorian chant (Tra le sollecitudini, 1903), reformed the Breviary, and began the codification of canon law. He condemned Modernism in Lamentabili and Pascendi (1907) and required the anti-modernist oath (1910). He opposed the French law separating Church and State (1905). He died at the start of the First World War, grieving over it. He was canonized in 1954, the first pope canonized since Pius V. Frequent Communion and First Communion at the age of reason Restored Gregorian chant (1903) Pascendi against Modernism (1907) Began the 1917 Code of Canon Law Giuseppe Sarto is born at Riese, near Treviso, the son of a postman Ordained a priest; years as a curate and parish priest follow Bishop of Mantua Cardinal and Patriarch of Venice Elected after Austria vetoes the leading candidate Tra le sollecitudini restores Gregorian chant Abolishes the veto of Catholic rulers in papal elections; begins the Code of Canon Law Encourages frequent and daily Communion Pascendi against Modernism Quam singulari: First Communion at the age of reason Dies weeks after the First World War begins Canonized by Pius XII The faithful acquire this spirit from its foremost and indispensable font, which is the active participation in the holy mysteries and in the public and solemn prayer of the Church. I was born poor, I have lived poor, and I wish to die poor. He was the first pope to be canonized since Pius V, who died in 1572. His election came after the Emperor of Austria vetoed another cardinal. As pope he abolished that veto for good. Children make their First Communion at about seven because of him; before, many waited until twelve or fourteen. His motto was “To restore all things in Christ” (Ephesians 1:10).

258. 1914-1922. Born Giacomo Paolo Battista della Chiesa in Genoa (Pegli). The peace pope of the First World War; promulgated the 1917 Code of Canon Law. The pope of the First World War, he pleaded tirelessly for peace and gave all he had to care for its victims, of every nation and faith. Giacomo della Chiesa, a diplomat and Archbishop of Bologna, was elected a month after the war began. He called it “the suicide of civilized Europe,” kept the Holy See neutral, and in August 1917 sent a peace note to the warring nations proposing disarmament, arbitration and the restoration of occupied lands; it was ignored. He set up an office that helped prisoners of war and their families and spent the Vatican’s funds on relief, leaving it nearly bankrupt. He promulgated the first Code of Canon Law (1917). Maximum illud (1919) called for native clergy in mission lands. A statue raised by grateful Turks in Istanbul honors him as “benefactor of the peoples.” Peace note to the warring powers (1917) Promulgated the 1917 Code of Canon Law Maximum illud on the missions (1919) Giacomo della Chiesa is born at Pegli, near Genoa Ordained a priest Secretary to the nuncio in Madrid Substitute of the Secretariat of State Archbishop of Bologna Created a cardinal Elected pope, a month after the war begins Promulgates the first Code of Canon Law Sends his peace note to the warring nations Maximum illud calls for local clergy in mission lands Canonizes St. Joan of Arc A statue of him is raised in Istanbul Dies of pneumonia The struggle which, every day more, appears a useless slaughter. The suicide of civilized Europe. In Istanbul, in the courtyard of the Cathedral of the Holy Spirit, stands a statue raised in his honor in 1921, praising him as a benefactor of the peoples without distinction of nationality or religion. He was so slight that, the story goes, even the smallest of the white cassocks prepared for the new pope was too big for him. Benedict XVI chose his name partly in his honor, as a pope of peace. He spent the Vatican’s funds so freely on war relief that, at his death, the Holy See had to borrow to pay for the conclave.

259. 1922-1939. Born Ambrogio Damiano Achille Ratti in Desio, Lombardy. Signed the Lateran Treaty creating Vatican City; condemned Nazism and Communism. A scholar and mountaineer, he proclaimed Christ the King, founded Vatican City and spoke out against both Nazism and Communism. Achille Ratti, a scholar, librarian of the Ambrosian and Vatican libraries, and mountaineer, had been nuncio in Poland. He instituted the feast of Christ the King (Quas primas, 1925), promoted Catholic Action, and wrote on Christian marriage (Casti connubii, 1930) and the social order (Quadragesimo anno, 1931). The Lateran Treaty with Italy (1929) settled the “Roman Question” and created the independent State of Vatican City. In 1937 he condemned Nazism in Mit brennender Sorge, smuggled into Germany and read from every pulpit, and atheistic Communism in Divini Redemptoris. He founded Vatican Radio with Marconi (1931). He said in 1938, “Spiritually, we are all Semites.” Lateran Treaty and Vatican City State (1929) Mit brennender Sorge against Nazism (1937) Feast of Christ the King (1925); Quadragesimo anno (1931) Founded Vatican Radio (1931) Achille Ratti is born at Desio, near Milan Ordained a priest Joins the Ambrosian Library in Milan, later becoming its prefect Moves to the Vatican Library, which he leads from 1914 Nuncio in Poland; he stays in Warsaw as the Red Army approaches in 1920 Archbishop of Milan and cardinal Elected; gives his first blessing from the outer balcony of St. Peter’s, for the first time since 1870 Quas primas institutes the feast of Christ the King The Lateran Treaty creates Vatican City Quadragesimo anno; opens Vatican Radio with Marconi Mit brennender Sorge against Nazism and Divini Redemptoris against Communism Dies in the Vatican Spiritually, we are all Semites. It is an injustice and at the same time a grave evil and disturbance of right order to assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate organizations can do. He was a serious mountaineer who climbed Monte Rosa, the Matterhorn and Mont Blanc; as pope he named St. Bernard of Menthon patron of mountaineers. He was the first pope to speak on the radio, in 1931. He canonized St. Thérèse of Lisieux, St. Bernadette, St. John Bosco, St. Thomas More and St. John Fisher. Vatican City, the state he founded, is the smallest independent country in the world.

260. 1939-1958. Born Eugenio Maria Giuseppe Giovanni Pacelli in Rome. Led the Church through the Second World War and defined the Assumption of Mary. He led the Church through the Second World War and its aftermath, defined the Assumption of Mary, and opened the way for modern Bible study and liturgical renewal. Eugenio Pacelli, a Roman diplomat, had been nuncio in Germany and Secretary of State. Elected on his 63rd birthday months before the war, he tried to prevent it and then worked for refugees and prisoners. His Christmas message of 1942 spoke of hundreds of thousands killed “because of their nationality or race.” Church institutions in Rome, including the Vatican and Castel Gandolfo, sheltered thousands of Jews during the German occupation. His public restraint during the Holocaust has been debated ever since; the Vatican archives for his reign were opened in 2020. His encyclicals renewed teaching on the Church as the Mystical Body (Mystici Corporis, 1943), opened Catholic biblical scholarship (Divino afflante Spiritu, 1943) and the liturgy (Mediator Dei, 1947). He defined the dogma of the Assumption (Munificentissimus Deus, 1950) and restored the Easter Vigil (1951-1955). He was declared Venerable in 2009. Dogma of the Assumption (1950) Divino afflante Spiritu on biblical studies (1943) Mystici Corporis and Mediator Dei Restored the Easter Vigil and reformed Holy Week Eugenio Pacelli is born in Rome Ordained a priest Ordained a bishop and sent as nuncio to Bavaria Nuncio to Germany Cardinal Secretary of State to Pius XI Elected pope on his 63rd birthday, months before the war His Christmas message speaks of those marked for death for their nationality or race Divino afflante Spiritu on the Bible, and Mystici Corporis on the Church Nazi roundup of Rome’s Jews; thousands hide in convents, monasteries and Church buildings Mediator Dei on the liturgy Defines the dogma of the Assumption Reforms the rites of Holy Week, having restored the Easter Vigil Dies at Castel Gandolfo Declared Venerable by Benedict XVI This vow humanity owes to the hundreds of thousands who, without any fault on their part, sometimes only because of their nationality or race, are marked down for death or gradual extinction. The Immaculate Mother of God, the ever Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory. He was ordained a bishop on 13 May 1917, the very day of the first appearance of Our Lady at Fatima. A note in his own hand says that in 1950, walking in the Vatican Gardens, he saw the sun spin as at Fatima, days before he defined the Assumption. He was elected on his birthday. His full Vatican archives were opened to scholars in March 2020.

261. 1958-1963. Born Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli in Sotto il Monte, Bergamo. “Good Pope John,” who called the Second Vatican Council. Elected as a caretaker at almost 77, he opened the windows of the Church: in under five years he called the Second Vatican Council and spoke to the whole world about peace. Angelo Roncalli, the fourth of thirteen children of sharecroppers, served as a military chaplain in the First World War and spent twenty years as a papal diplomat in Bulgaria, Turkey and Greece, where he helped save Jews during the Second World War, and then in France. Patriarch of Venice at 71, he was elected at nearly 77 as a supposed caretaker. Three months later he announced an ecumenical council, which opened on 11 October 1962.
