He wrote Mater et Magistra (1961) on social justice and Pacem in Terris (1963), addressed “to all men of good will,” on human rights and peace, after helping to calm the Cuban Missile Crisis. His warmth, visits to prisons and hospitals and “moonlight speech” made him beloved. He died of cancer between the Council’s first and second sessions. He was canonized in 2014. Convened the Second Vatican Council (1962) Pacem in Terris (1963) and Mater et Magistra (1961) Began the revision of the Code of Canon Law Angelo Roncalli is born at Sotto il Monte, near Bergamo Ordained a priest in Rome Called up in the First World War: medical orderly, then chaplain Sent to Bulgaria as the pope’s envoy, and made an archbishop Apostolic delegate to Turkey and Greece, living in Istanbul Reads the Gospel in Turkish at Christmas Mass in Istanbul Nuncio to France Cardinal and Patriarch of Venice Elected pope, a month before he turns 77 Announces an ecumenical council at St. Paul Outside the Walls Mater et Magistra, on social justice Opens the Second Vatican Council; that night, the “moonlight speech” Pacem in Terris, addressed to all people of good will Dies of cancer Beatified by John Paul II Canonized with John Paul II by Pope Francis When you go home, you will find your children. Give them a hug and say: this is a hug from the Pope. We feel we must disagree with those prophets of gloom, who are always forecasting disaster. In Istanbul he learned Turkish, had prayers said in Turkish in the churches and read the Gospel in Turkish at Christmas 1935, decades before Mass in the local language became the norm. On his first Christmas as pope he visited sick children, and the next day Rome’s Regina Coeli prison: “You could not come to me, so I came to you.” In October 1962 he took the train to Loreto and Assisi, the first time a pope had travelled outside Rome since 1870. His feast day is 11 October, the day the Council opened, not the day he died. By taking the number XXIII he settled an old question: the “John XXIII” of the Great Schism (1410-1415) was an antipope.

262. 1963-1978. Born Giovanni Battista Enrico Antonio Maria Montini in Concesio, Brescia. Guided the Second Vatican Council to its end and wrote Humanae Vitae; the first pope to travel by plane. He brought the Second Vatican Council to completion and carried out its reforms, and was the first pope to travel the world as a pilgrim. Giovanni Battista Montini worked for thirty years in the Secretariat of State and was Archbishop of Milan. As pope he reopened and concluded the Second Vatican Council (1965), promulgating its sixteen documents, and then carried out its reforms, including the new Roman Missal (1969). He embraced Patriarch Athenagoras in Jerusalem (1964), and together they lifted the excommunications of 1054. He was the first pope to fly and visited six continents, speaking at the United Nations in 1965 (“No more war, war never again!”). He wrote Ecclesiam Suam (1964), Populorum Progressio (1967) on development, and Humanae Vitae (1968), reaffirming the Church’s teaching on contraception amid fierce opposition. Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975) remains a charter for evangelization. He created the Synod of Bishops and internationalized the Curia. He was canonized in 2018. Concluded and implemented the Second Vatican Council Lifted the 1054 excommunications with Patriarch Athenagoras (1965) Humanae Vitae (1968) and Populorum Progressio (1967) First pope to travel by air; addressed the United Nations (1965) Giovanni Battista Montini is born at Concesio, near Brescia Ordained a priest Begins thirty years in the Vatican Secretariat of State Archbishop of Milan The first cardinal created by John XXIII Elected pope; reopens the Council Pilgrimage to the Holy Land; embraces Patriarch Athenagoras in Jerusalem Lays his papal tiara on the altar of St. Peter’s, to be sold for the poor Addresses the United Nations in New York Lifts the excommunications of 1054 with Athenagoras Closes the Second Vatican Council Visits Turkey: Istanbul, Ephesus and Izmir, the first pope to do so Humanae Vitae Promulgates the new Roman Missal Survives a knife attack at Manila airport Dies at Castel Gandolfo, on the feast of the Transfiguration Canonized by Pope Francis No more war, war never again! Modern man listens more willingly to witnesses than to teachers, and if he does listen to teachers, it is because they are witnesses. He was the first pope to visit Turkey (1967), praying at the House of the Virgin Mary near Ephesus. He gave away the papal tiara; it is now in the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception in Washington. He was the first pope to fly in an airplane and the first to visit five continents. He was canonized on the same day as St. Oscar Romero.

263. 1978-1978. Born Albino Luciani in Forno di Canale (Canale d’Agordo), Belluno. “The smiling pope,” who reigned 33 days.  Albino Luciani, son of a migrant worker who was a socialist, was a teacher of seminarians, Bishop of Vittorio Veneto and Patriarch of Venice, where he wrote Illustrissimi, witty letters to famous figures from Dickens to Pinocchio. He was the first pope to take a double name, honoring his two predecessors, and refused a coronation, beginning his ministry with a simple Mass. In his few general audiences he spoke of humility, faith, hope and charity with stories and humor. He died suddenly of a heart attack on the night of 28 September 1978. He was beatified in 2022. First pope with a double name; no coronation Beatified in 2022

264. 1978-2005. Born Karol Józef Wojtyła in Wadowice, Poland. The first Polish pope: philosopher, pilgrim to 129 countries, and witness against Communism. He carried the Gospel to every continent, helped bring down Communism without violence, and gave the Church the Catechism and a new hope in God’s mercy. Karol Wojtyła lost his mother, brother and father by the age of 20. Under Nazi occupation he worked in a quarry and chemical plant, acted in an underground theater and studied for the priesthood in secret. A philosopher and poet, he became Archbishop of Kraków. Elected at 58, the first non-Italian since 1523, he told the world “Be not afraid!” His first visit to Poland (1979) helped give rise to the Solidarity movement and the peaceful fall of Communism in 1989. He survived an assassination attempt in St. Peter’s Square on 13 May 1981 and forgave his attacker in his prison cell. He made 104 foreign journeys to 129 countries, began World Youth Day, and canonized 482 saints. His 14 encyclicals include Redemptor Hominis, Laborem Exercens, Veritatis Splendor, Evangelium Vitae and Fides et Ratio; his Wednesday talks became the Theology of the Body. He promulgated the 1983 Code of Canon Law and the Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992), prayed at the Western Wall and asked forgiveness for the sins of Christians in the Jubilee of 2000, and added the Luminous Mysteries to the Rosary (2002). He endured Parkinson’s disease in public and died on the vigil of Divine Mercy Sunday 2005, a feast he had established. Crowds cried “Santo subito!” He was canonized in 2014. Helped bring the peaceful end of Communism in Europe Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992) and Code of Canon Law (1983) 104 pastoral journeys; founded World Youth Day Encyclicals including Veritatis Splendor, Evangelium Vitae and Fides et Ratio Theology of the Body; Luminous Mysteries; Divine Mercy Sunday Karol Wojtyła is born at Wadowice, Poland His father dies; he is left alone at 20, working in a quarry under Nazi occupation Begins studying for the priesthood in a secret seminary Ordained a priest Auxiliary Bishop of Kraków, at 38 Archbishop of Kraków; a voice at the Second Vatican Council Elected, the first non-Italian pope since Adrian VI in 1522 Returns to Poland; the next year the Solidarity movement is born. In November he visits Turkey Shot in St. Peter’s Square by Mehmet Ali Ağca Visits Ağca in prison and forgives him Institutes World Youth Day Communism falls across Eastern Europe Catechism of the Catholic Church The Great Jubilee; prays at the Western Wall in Jerusalem; institutes Divine Mercy Sunday Dies on the eve of Divine Mercy Sunday Canonized with John XXIII by Pope Francis Do not be afraid! Open wide the doors for Christ! Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth. Before he was a priest he was an actor and playwright in an underground theater in occupied Kraków. He was shot on 13 May 1981, the feast of Our Lady of Fatima, and said that a mother’s hand guided the bullet. The bullet is now set in the crown of her statue at Fatima. He canonized more saints than any pope before him. He made 104 journeys abroad, including a visit to Turkey in 1979. He kept skiing and hiking in the mountains well into his years as pope.

265. 2005-2013. Born Joseph Aloisius Ratzinger in Marktl am Inn, Bavaria (Germany). Theologian pope who taught that “God is love,” and the first pope to resign in nearly 600 years. A great theologian who became a gentle pastor, he taught that faith begins with meeting a Person, Jesus Christ, and showed humility by laying down the papacy. Joseph Ratzinger, son of a Bavarian policeman, was drafted into the German anti-aircraft auxiliary as a teenager and deserted at the end of the war. He became one of the leading theologians of his generation, an adviser at the Second Vatican Council, Archbishop of Munich, and for 24 years Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under John Paul II, overseeing the Catechism. Elected at 78, he called himself “a simple, humble laborer in the vineyard of the Lord.” His encyclicals Deus Caritas Est (2005), Spe Salvi (2007) and Caritas in Veritate (2009) treated love, hope and charity in truth; his three-volume Jesus of Nazareth was written as a personal work. He freed wider use of the 1962 Missal (Summorum Pontificum, 2007), created ordinariates for former Anglicans (Anglicanorum Coetibus, 2009), beatified John Henry Newman, met victims of abuse and strengthened the Church’s procedures against it, and spoke on faith and reason at Regensburg (2006). On 11 February 2013 he announced his resignation, citing failing strength, and lived as Pope Emeritus in the Vatican until his death on 31 December 2022. Deus Caritas Est, Spe Salvi and Caritas in Veritate Summorum Pontificum (2007) and Anglicanorum Coetibus (2009) Jesus of Nazareth trilogy Resigned the papacy (2013), the first since 1415 Joseph Ratzinger is born at Marktl am Inn, Bavaria, on Holy Saturday Ordained a priest with his brother Georg Theological adviser at the Second Vatican Council Introduction to Christianity, his most widely read book Archbishop of Munich and Freising, and a cardinal Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, for 24 years Oversees the new Catechism of the Catholic Church Elected pope at 78 First encyclical, Deus Caritas Est Visits Turkey; in Istanbul he prays in silence in the Blue Mosque Summorum Pontificum, and the first volume of Jesus of Nazareth Announces his resignation, in Latin Resignation takes effect; he becomes Pope Emeritus Dies in the Vatican, at 95 Being Christian is not the result of an ethical choice or a lofty idea, but the encounter with an event, a person, which gives life a new horizon and a decisive direction. The world is redeemed by the patience of God. It is destroyed by the impatience of man. He was the first pope to resign since Gregory XII in 1415. On the evening he announced his resignation, lightning struck the dome of St. Peter’s. He played Mozart on the piano and loved cats. He sent the first papal tweet, in December 2012. He was baptized on the day he was born, Holy Saturday, with the newly blessed Easter water.

266. 2013-2025. Born Jorge Mario Bergoglio in Buenos Aires, Argentina. The first pope from the Americas and the first Jesuit pope, who called the Church to mercy and to the peripheries. The first pope from the Americas, he called the whole Church to go out to the poor and the forgotten, and to show the world the mercy of God. Jorge Mario Bergoglio, son of Italian immigrants, worked as a chemical technician before joining the Jesuits. He was Jesuit provincial of Argentina during the dictatorship and later Archbishop of Buenos Aires, known for riding the bus and visiting the slums. The first pope to take the name Francis, after St. Francis of Assisi, he lived in the Casa Santa Marta guesthouse rather than the papal apartment. Evangelii Gaudium (2013) set out his program of a missionary Church; Laudato si’ (2015) addressed care for our common home; Amoris Laetitia (2016) followed two synods on the family; Fratelli Tutti (2020) addressed fraternity and social friendship; Dilexit Nos (2024) the Sacred Heart. He proclaimed an extraordinary Jubilee of Mercy (2015-2016), reformed the Curia (Praedicate Evangelium, 2022) and Vatican finances, strengthened laws against abuse (Vos Estis Lux Mundi, 2019), signed the Document on Human Fraternity with the Grand Imam of al-Azhar (2019), and held a long Synod on synodality (2021-2024). He prayed alone in an empty St. Peter’s Square during the pandemic (27 March 2020). He opened the Jubilee of 2025, blessed the crowds on Easter Sunday, and died the next morning. At his request he was buried in Santa Maria Maggiore, the first pope buried outside the Vatican in over a century. Mercy is the very foundation of the Church’s life. He chose his name when a cardinal next to him at the conclave said: “Don’t forget the poor.” He thought at once of St. Francis of Assisi. As a young man he worked as a chemical technician and, by his own account, as a nightclub bouncer. He was the first pope from outside Europe since Gregory III, a Syrian, in the 8th century. He was a lifelong fan, and card-carrying member, of the San Lorenzo football club of Buenos Aires. He chose to be buried in St. Mary Major, not St. Peter’s: the first pope buried outside the Vatican since Leo XIII.

267. 2025 to today. Born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago, Illinois, United States. The first pope from the United States, an Augustinian missionary to Peru. The first pope from the United States, a missionary and an Augustinian, he took the name Leo to carry the Church’s social teaching into the age of artificial intelligence. Robert Prevost grew up in Dolton, near Chicago, studied mathematics at Villanova University and joined the Order of St. Augustine in 1977. After studying canon law in Rome he spent much of his life in Peru as a missionary, teacher, judicial vicar and seminary formator, then led the Augustinians worldwide as Prior General for twelve years (2001-2013). He returned to Peru as Bishop of Chiclayo and became a Peruvian citizen. Francis named him Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops in 2023. Elected on 8 May 2025 on the fourth ballot, he greeted the world with “Peace be with all of you” and chose the name Leo in honor of Leo XIII and his social teaching, in view of a new industrial revolution brought by artificial intelligence. His motto, In Illo uno unum (“In the One, we are one”), comes from St. Augustine. He brought the Jubilee of 2025 to its close, issued the apostolic exhortation Dilexi Te on love for the poor (2025) and an apostolic letter for the 1700th anniversary of the Council of Nicaea, which he marked with a visit to Turkey. His first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas (2026), applies the Church’s social teaching to safeguarding the human person in the age of artificial intelligence.
